question_text: Which of the following is the most potent naturally occurring estrogen?
explanation:
Explanation:

Estradiol (E2) is the most potent and biologically active natural estrogen in the human body. It is the primary estrogen secreted by the ovaries during the reproductive years and plays a vital role in:

  • Regulation of the menstrual cycle
  • Development and maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics in females

Estradiol shows the highest binding affinity for estrogen receptors, making it the most potent among all estrogens. It is approximately 12 times more potent than estrone and 80 times more potent than estriol.

Explanation for other options:

Estriol (Option B): A weaker estrogen mainly produced during pregnancy from placental metabolism of estradiol and estrone.

Conjugated estrogen (Option C): A synthetic mixture of estrogens used in hormone replacement therapy; not naturally occurring in the body.

Estrone (Option D): A less potent form of estrogen predominantly found after menopause, derived from peripheral conversion of androstenedione.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3636985/

question_text: A case of 35-week pregnancy with hydramnios and marked respiratory distress is best treated by:
explanation:
The patient in the question has marked respiratory distress (i.e. it is a severe polyhydramnios and requires treatment) and gestational age is 35 weeks (i.e., fetal maturity is not yet achieved).

So our aim should be to relieve the distress of patients in hope of continuing the pregnancy till at least 37 weeks.

This can be achieved by:

  • Amniocentesis or
  • Use of Indomethacin

Amniocentesis:

  • The main aim of amniocentesis is to relieve maternal distress with the added advantage that lung maturity of fetus can be predicted by Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio in the expressed fluid.
  • Slow decompression is done at the rate of 500 ml/hr.
  • Maximum fluid removed is 1.5 – 2 litres.

Use of Indomethacin -Indomethacin should not be used for more than 32 weeks because it leads to premature closure of ductus arteriosus.

Amniotomy: The main disadvantage of amniotomy is the possibility of cord prolapse and placental abruption. Slow removal fluid by amniocentesis helps to obviate these dangers.

— Williams Obs. 22/e, p 530, 23/e, p 495



Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 214; Williams Obs. 22/e, p 529, 530, 23/e, p 494, 495

question_text: Mrs Rekha having her child of 2 years presents with pruritus vulvae & amenorrhea. She gives h/o severe blood loss & failure of lactation during pregnancy. She is lethargic and has cold intolerance, she has multiple skin infections and anemia. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of Sheehan syndrome.

Sheehan syndrome occurs when the anterior pituitary gland is damaged due to significant blood loss.

The symptoms of Sheehan syndrome occur as a result of the low hormone levels. These may include an inability to produce breast milk, irregular or absent periods, hot flashes and a decreased sex drive. Other symptoms may include fatigue, headaches, low blood pressure and hair loss.

Excessive blood loss during or after delivery of a baby may affect the function of the pituitary gland, leading to a form of maternal hypopituitarism known as Sheehan syndrome (SS). Such extensive bleeding may reduce the blood flow to the pituitary gland causing the pituitary cells to be damaged or die(necrosis).

Management is by hormone replacement: Start with glucocorticoids, then FSH,LH,TSH etc

Option B: Asherman syndrome should be having a history of D&C of the uterus followed by amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea, but the hormonal levels will be absolutely fine with no symptoms either.
Option C: Prolactinoma presents with galactorrhea and amenorrhea and no other symptoms.It doesn't fit with the symptom given.

question_text: In normal pregnancy character of vagina is:
explanation:
Changes in vagina during pregnancy:

  • Increased vascularity and hyperemia (causes - violet colour characteristic of Chadwick sign).
  • Vaginal pH: decreases i.e. becomes acidic and varies from 3.5 to 6.
  • Increase in the number of lactobacillus acidophilus (which act on glycogen and cause increased production of lactic acid therefore, pH becomes more acidic).
  • As pH of vagina becomes acidic - it inhibits the growth of pathogenic bacteria.

Histopathology:

  • Early in pregnancy, the vaginal epithelial cells are similar to those seen in the luteal phase.
  • As pregnancy advances:
    • Small intermediate cells known as Navicular cells are seen in abundance in small clusters.
    • Vesicular nuclei without cytoplasm or so called Naked nuclei, are also seen along with abundant Lactobacillus.

Reference: Williams Obs. 23/e, p 111

question_text: Manning score includes/Biophysical score includes:
explanation:
These 5 variables together are called as Biophysical Profile (BPP)/Biophysical score

  • Fetal Tone
  • Fetal Breathing Movements (seen in 30 minutes)
  • Fetal gross body Movements (seen in 30 minutes)
  • Amniotic Fluid Volume
  • Non stress test

Fetal Biophysical Profile (BPP)

  • Principle-Biophysical profile is a screening test for uteroplacental insufficiency. The fetal biophysical activities are initiated, modulated and regulated by the fetal nervous system. The fetal CNS is very much sensitive to diminished oxygenation/ Hypoxia, Metabolic acidosis, CNS depression, Changes in fetal biophysical activity.
  • Indication of BPP scoring -Nonreactive NST'high risk pregnancy.
  • The variables are observed for at least 30 minutes and assigned a score of 2 each to normal variables and a score of 0 to abnormal variables.
  • Thus the highest score possible for a normal fetus is 10.
  • A score of 8 to 10 is normal, 6 is equivocal and 5 or less is abnormal.

Predictive value of All variables is not same :

  • Most important variables are NST and Amniotic fluid volume.
  • Intermediary important: Fetal breathing movement.
  • Least important: Fetal tone and fetal body movement.

Reference: Williams 23/e, p 339, 340; Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 109

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true about round ligament of uterus
option_a: It is a remnant of gubernaculum of testes
option_b: It undergoes hypertrophy in pregnancy increasing in both length and diameter
option_c: After passing inguinal canal it terminates in lower portion of labia minora
option_d: A special artery to the round ligament is called Sampson artery
explanation:
• Round ligaments are remnants of gubernaculum (round ligament +ovarian ligament), Each round ligament extends laterally and down into the inguinal canal, through which it passes, to terminate in the upper portion of the ipsilateral labium majus. The artery to the round ligament (SAMPSON ARTERY) is a small branch of the uterine artery and runs within the ligament.
  • In nonpregnant women, the round ligament varies from 3 to 5 mm in diameter and 10 to 12 cm length. During pregnancy, these ligaments hypertrophy and increase appreciably in both length and diameter.

Reference: williams obstetrics 26th edition chapter 2

question_text: In a normal sperm analysis, what should be the least % of morphologically normal sperm?
explanation:
Semen Analysis (WHO-2010)

Abnormal sperm morphology is termed teratospermia or teratozoospermia.

Kruger and colleagues (1988) developed a detailed characterization of normal sperm morphology, which showed improved correlation with fertilization rates during IVF cycles. Their criteria require careful analysis of the shape and size of the sperm head, the relative size of the acrosome in proportion to the head, and characteristics of the tail, including length, coiling, or presence of two tails. Significantly decreased fertilization rates are seen when normal morphology of the sample falls below 4 percent.

question_text: Normal vaginal pH is
explanation:
Vagina has local inhabitant bacteria called as Doderlein’s bacillus (lactobacilli) which breaks down the glycogen present in vaginal epithelium into lactic acid resulting in acidic pH (Avg, 4.5; Range, 4–5.5) of vagina.

The acidic pH of vagina acts as a barrier for external organisms.

Physiological Discharge

  • Clear, white, and flocculent odorless discharge
  • Smear contains epithelial cells, lactobacilli
  • pH ranges from 3.5 – 4.5
  • Increases with increased estrogen state: pregnancy, OCP, mid-cycle, PCOS, or premenarchal
  • If increased in perimenopausal women, investigate for other effects of excess estrogen (e.g. endometrial cancer).

Reference: J B Sharma, Textbook of Gynecology 1st edition p327

question_text: A 26-year-old unmarried woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles, despite previously having regular periods, and her pelvic examination is normal. What should be the next appropriate step?
option_b: Reassure her that it's normal to have delayed periods
explanation:
Explanation:

When a woman presents with new-onset menstrual irregularities after a history of regular cycles, the first step is to rule out pregnancy, even if she is unmarried.

  • Beta hCG test detects pregnancy early, either in blood or urine, and is highly sensitive, capable of detecting pregnancy as early as 8-9 days after fertilisation.
  • This ensures that irregular cycles are not caused by pregnancy before proceeding with further investigations.

hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)

Explanation for other options:

(Option A) Transvaginal ultrasound: Useful for structural evaluation of the uterus and ovaries, but not first-line if pregnancy is possible.

(Option B) Reassurance: Occasional irregularity may occur, but since the patient had previously regular cycles, pregnancy must be ruled out first.

(Option D) Serum FSH and LH: Important for evaluating ovarian or pituitary causes (e.g., PCOS), but only after pregnancy is excluded.

question_text: Which of the following is a recommendation of WHO in the management of the second stage of labor?
option_a: Manual perineal support and maintain the head in deflexion and deliver
option_d: Delivery should be conducted in the lithotomy position
explanation:
Warm compress to the perineum is recommended in the management of second stage of labour

Option A: Head should be maintained in flexion with controlled delivery of head.

Option D: Delivery can be conducted in any position

WHO latest guidelines

  • Delivery facilities must offer every woman privacy and allow her to be accompanied by her choice of a supportive person(husband, friend, mother, relative, TBA); all women must be treated with respect.
  • Psychosocial support, education, communication, choice of position, and pharmacological methods appropriately used during the first stage are all useful in relieving pain and distress in the second stage of labor.
  • There should be at least 2 people assisting at every birth, whether it is another health professional, family member, TBA, or village health worker. Arrangements for having another person besides the primary skilled attendant should be planned during the pregnancy.
  • Monitoring of the fetal heart beat must be continued during the second stage to allow early detection of bradycardia.
  • Routine episiotomy is harmful and should not be practiced.(Option C ruled out)
  • Women should not be forced or encouraged to push until they feel an urge to push.
  • Health facilities and skilled attendants should be provided with handheld battery powered or hand-cranked Dopplers for fetal heart auscultation after every contraction. These should be added to lists of essential commodities.
  • Local anesthetic should always be given for any episiotomy, episiotomy/laceration repair or forceps delivery.
  • Provision of critical skills for second stage management needs to be supported by policies as well as training, simulations(drills) and linkage with a functioning referral system.
  • Lack of access to instrumental delivery is a major deficit in obstetric care in many facilities; skills necessary for safe instrumental delivery must be emphasized in preservice and in-service education for all skilled attendants.

question_text: Postdate pregnancy is defined as:
option_a: Pregnancy continuing beyond expected date of delivery
option_b: Pregnancy continuing beyond 2 weeks of expected date of delivery
explanation:
Pregnancy continuing beyond 2 weeks of the expected date of delivery (> 294 days) is called postmaturity or post-term pregnancy.

question_text: A 36week pregnant lady with Mitral Valve Replacement was on warfarin. Her INR value is 3. Next step in the management is?
option_c: Stop warfarin and start aspirin & heparin
explanation:
Following are the guidelines for anticoagulation in pregnancy:

  • 1st 12 weeks: LMWH
  • >12 weeks - 36 weeks: Warfarin
  • >36 weeks till term: LMWH
  • LMWH to be discontinued just before delivery and restarted 6 hrs after vaginal delivery and 24 hrs after LSCS.

question_text: On Doppler the most ominous sign indicating fetal compromise is:
explanation:
Umbilical artery DOPPLER :

  • Blood flow across the umbilical arteries provides a comprehensive overview of the - fetal blood supply and helps in detecting fetal circulatory compromise
  • As gestation increases, there is gradual fall in all the resistance indices so the amount of forward diastolic flow increases (Remember: Diastolic flow is inversely related to peripheral resistance). Normally, systolic/diastolic rates decrease as the period of gestation increases.
  • If S/D ratio more than 3 beyond 28 wks is a marker of UPI / IUGR .

In IUGR, there are three abnormal flow patterns; reduced EDF, absent EDF and finally reversal of flow.

Absent end diastolic flow (AEDF):

  • It is an indication of termination of pregnancy, if pregnancy > 34 weeks by cesarean section.

Reversed end diastolic flow (REDF).

  • It is an indication of termination of pregnancy after 32 weeks gestation age. Patient has to be closely monitored and observed for changes in ductus venosus flow. Umbilical artery velocimetry provides a useful adjunct in management of high risk pregnancy. They are however not recommended for screening low risk pregnancies

Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)

  • Doppler measurement of middle cerebral artery velocimetry has been studied and employed clinically for detection of fetal anemia.
  • With fetal anemia, the peak systolic velocity is increased (≥ 1.5 MOM) due to increased cardiac output and decreased blood viscosity. This has permitted the rhesus group alloimmunization.
  • MCA Doppler has also been studied as an adjunct to the evaluation of fetal-growth restriction. It is believed that there is a progression of Doppler findings in severly affected fetuses such that increased impedance of flow in the umbilical artery may be detected first. This is followed by redistribution of flow to the brain, with decreasing resistance that has been termed brain sparing, and eventually by abnormalities in venous flow.

Reference: Williams 23/e, p 645

question_text: A woman has been taking Tamoxifen after mastectomy for breast cancer. How long should the couple wait before planning pregnancy afyter stopping Tamoxifen?
explanation:
To avoid the risk of fetal malformation, pregnancy is contraindicated during tamoxifen treatment and up to 3 months after its interruption.

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator(SERM).

Adverse effects of Tamoxifen:

  • Teratogenicity
  • DES like syndrome

Women having treatment for breast cancer (including the hormone treatment tamoxifen) are recommended to use non-hormonal methods of contraception, such as condoms, Femidoms or a diaphragm. It may also be possible to use a coil (IUD or intrauterine device).

question_text: True statement regarding cholestasis in pregnancy:
option_c: Mild jaundice occurs in majority of patients
option_d: Serum alkaline phosphatase is most sensitive indicaton
explanation:
The correct answer is (A): Recurs in subsequent pregnancy.

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is known to recur in subsequent pregnancies. The other statements are not accurate: SGOT/SGPT levels are often elevated but not severely; mild jaundice occurs in many cases but not the majority; and while alkaline phosphatase levels can be elevated, they are not necessarily the most sensitive indicator for diagnosing ICP compared to other liver function tests.

In idiopathic cholestatic jaundice (intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy), serum bilirubin levels are often elevated, but they can sometimes remain below 5 mg/dl.

It is characterized by accumulation of bile acids in the liver with subsequent accumulation in the plasma causing pruritus and jaundice due to estrogen excess.

Clinical features

  • Manifestations appear in the last trimester (beyond 30 weeks) and only occasionally in the late 2nd trimester.
  • The cardinal clinical finding/1st symptom to appear is severe generalized pruritus with a predilection for the palms and soles.
  • Pruritus precedes laboratory findings by a mean of 3 weeks and sometimes by months.
  • Jaundice is slight (Bilirubin levels rarely exceed 5 mg) and seen in 10% patients.
  • Cholestasis tends to recur in subsequent pregnancies (recurrence rate = 50%),estrogen-containing contraceptives\OCP’s are contraindicated in females with h/o cholestasis during pregnancy

Investigations:

  • Rise in S. bile acids is the earliest/the most consistent change/Best marker for cholestasis. There is a 10-100 fold increase in s. cholic acid followed by s. chenodeoxycholic
  • Serum bilirubin levels are increased (rarely more than 5 mg%) and increase is always in direct bilirubin.
  • Serum alkaline phosphatase is raised.
  • SGOT/SGPT levels are normal to moderately elevated (seldom exceed 250 U/L)
  • Symptoms disappear within two weeks postpartum. Jaundice usually disappears within weeks following delivery. Pruritus as a rule persists longer than jaundice.
  • Increase chances of PPH and cesarean section.
  • There is an increased incidence of prematurity, low birth weight babies, sudden IUD and meconium aspiration in the fetus.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 6/e, pg 291; Robbin's 7/e, pg 921; Williams Obs. 23/e, pg 1063, 1064.

question_text: All are the indications for termination of pregnancy in a woman with preeclampsia except
explanation:
Indications for termination of pregnancy irrespective of the weeks of gestation in case of preeclampsia are:

  • Severe preeclampsia, with impending eclampsia
  • Eclampsia (give MgSO4 first, followed by induction of labor)
  • HELLP syndrome.
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Significant renal dysfunction, coagulopathy
  • Abruption
  • Previable fetus
  • Fetal compromise

A woman with a past history of eclampsia is at increased risk for developing eclampsia again in subsequent pregnancies. However, this is not considered an indication for termination of pregnancy in and of itself.


Reference: Arias 5th edition pg no 197

question_text: The earliest sign of pregnancy on a transvaginal scan is?
explanation:
Explanation:

The gestational sac is the first structure visible on a transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) and can be seen as early as 4.5 to 5 weeks of gestation. It appears as a small, round, anechoic (dark) area within the endometrium (decidual reaction).

Explanation of other options:

Yolk sac (Option B): The yolk sac appears after the gestational sac and is usually seen by 5-6 weeks of gestation. It provides early nutrition to the developing embryo and confirms an intrauterine pregnancy.

Fetal pole (Option C): The fetal pole appears after the yolk sac, typically by 5.5-6 weeks of gestation. It represents the developing embryo and can be measured as crown-rump length (CRL).

Cardiac activity (Option D): Fetal cardiac activity is typically visible on ultrasound by 6 weeks of gestation, following the development of the fetal pole, and serves as confirmation of a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

A helpful mnemonic to remember the timeline of early pregnancy findings on ultrasound is:

G → Y → F → C

  • G: Gestational sac - appears at 5 to 5 weeks (first visible sign)
  • Y: Yolk sac - visible by 5 to 6 weeks
  • F: Fetal pole - seen by 5 to 6 weeks
  • C: Cardiac activity - typically detected by 6 weeks

Key Takeaway:

The gestational sac is the earliest sign of pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound, visible as early as 4.5-5 weeks of gestation.

question_text: A woman who is 3 months postpartum and regularly breastfeeding reports amenorrhea (no menstrual periods) since delivery. What is the most appropriate next step before considering surgical options?
explanation:
Explanation:

Amenorrhea in the postpartum period especially in breastfeeding women, a normal physiological condition known as lactational amenorrhea.

During breastfeeding, high prolactin levels suppress the release of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) from the pituitary gland, which in turn inhibits ovulation and menstruation.

This is a temporary and natural contraceptive effect that usually lasts until breastfeeding frequency reduces.

Hence, in this scenario, the best management is to reassure the mother that the amenorrhea is normal and self-limiting, rather than pursuing hormonal therapy or surgical intervention.

Lactational Amenorrhea

Explanation for other options:

Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (Option A): Used in PCOS to induce ovulation; not indicated in postpartum amenorrhea.

Contraceptives to be prescribed (Option B): Not immediately required unless contraceptive protection is desired. LAM provides natural contraception for the first 6 months if breastfeeding is exclusive.

Pulsatile GnRH for ovarian stimulation (Option C): Used for hypothalamic amenorrhea, not physiological postpartum amenorrhea.

Reference:

question_text: A prosthetic valve patient switches to heparin at which time of pregnancy?

Pregnancy following valve replacement:

Mechanical valve replacement is not preferred these days as anticoagulation is required throughout pregnancy.

Problem of anticoagulation: During pregnancy, the main problem is anticoagulation.

Warfarin is safe for the mother but can result in warfarin embryopathy of the fetus, miscarriage, IUGR and stillbirths. Heparin is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta, but is less effective than warfarin in preventing thromboembolic events. Low molecular weight heparin is inadequate and ACOG does not recommend its use in pregnant women with prosthetic heart valve.

Unfractionated heparin-Up Till 12 weeks

Warfarin-12-36 weeks

Heparin-36 weeks onwards and up till 6 hours before delivery For 6 hours after vaginal delivery and 24 hours after cesarean

question_text: Patient with 10 weeks of amenorrhea, size of uterus 12 to 14 weeks, with severe nausea and vomiting, snow storm appearance on ultrasound, Management?
explanation:
GESTATIONAL TROPHOBLASTIC DISEASE.

Definition

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease(GTD) encompasses a spectrum of proliferative abnormalities of trophoblasts associated with pregnancy. Persistent GTD(persistently raised beta hCG) is referred as gestational trophoblastic neoplasia(GTN).

  • Hydatidiform mole is a benign neoplasm of chorion with malignant potential.
  • It is the most common form of gestational trophoblastic disease.
  • It is an abnormal condition of the placenta where there are partly degenerative and partly proliferative changes in the young chorionic villi.
  • Grossly: It is characterised by multiple grape like vesicles filling and distending the uterus, usually in absence of an intact The vesicles are filled with interstitial fluid similar to ascitic or oedema fluid but is rich in hCG.
  • Microscopically it is characterised by :
    • Marked proliferation of the syncytial and cytotrophoblastic
    • Thinning of the stromal tissue due to hydropic degeneration(edema of villous stroma).
    • Avascular villi.
    • Maintenance of villus pattern.

INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE;

Partial mole:

  • On USG partial mole is often confused with missed

Complete mole

It gives the typical 'snow storm' appearance

Management of H. Mole

Spontaneous expulsion occurs at around 16 weeks and is rarely delayed beyond 28 weeks.

  • TOC in mole
    • Suction evacuation or curettage(It is the treatment of choice irrespective of uterine size) Suction evacuation is done first. After most of the molar tissue has been removed by aspiration, oxytocin is given. Once the myometrium has contracted, thorough but gentle curettage with a large sharp curette(10-12 mm) is performed. Intraoperative ultrasonographic examination may help document that the uterine cavity has been emptied.
  • Hysterectomy: It is indicated only in case of:
    • Female has completed her family irrespective of age
    • Age of patient - >35 years(as chances of malignancy are more).
    • Uncontrolled haemorrhage during suction evacuation
  • Hysterotomy: Indicated in cases complicated by haemorrhage.

question_text: Most common cause of platelet ↓ in pregnancy:
explanation:
Gestational thrombocytopenia/Benign Gestational Thrombocytopenia

It is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia accounting for 80-90% of all cases of thrombocytopenia occurring during pregnancy.

  • Exact cause is not known (may be due to hemodilution and increased platelet consumption)
  • Platelet count is rarely <70,000/mm3.
  • Women are asymptomatic and there is no H/O bleeding.
  • Condition is benign and has no risk to mother or infant.
  • The only problem associated with it is - that anaesthesiologists are reluctant to give epidural or spinal anaesthesia if platelet count is < 1 lakh/mm3.
  • Treatment with steroids and IgG or platelet transfusion before delivery is sometimes necessary.

Reference: Fernando Arias 3/e, p 475, Williams Obs, 23/e, p 1093

question_text: Concerning invasive cervical carcinoma all are correct except:
option_a: Radical hysterectomy is not indicated for stage Ia disease, if the excision margins are free of the disease
option_b: MRI imaging is safe for staging even during pregnancy
option_c: Radical trachelectomy and pelvic lymphadenec- tomy can be done for stage IIa disease
option_d: Pregnancy rate is about 35% within 1 year following +radical trachelectomy
explanation:
For stage I a, surgery of choice is conization in young females and simple hysterectomy in older females. Radical hysterectomy is not done in stage I a (i.e. option a is correct).

MRI is a safe investigation during pregnancy, hence in cancer cervix occurring during pregnancy, it can be done (i.e. option b is correct)

Laparoscopic assisted vaginal radical trachelectomy with pelvic and aortic lymphadenectomy (LAVRT) was designed (Daniel Dargent 1987) to treat early invasive cervical cancer. This is done in a young woman where childbearing function is to be preserved. Initially, pelvic and aortic lymph node dissection is done. Vaginal radical trachelectomy is done only when these nodes are negative. Vaginal part includes resection of cervical, vaginal, paracervical and paravaginal tissues. Vaginal cuff is resected circumferentially about 2 cm below the cervicovaginal junction. Ideally, the resected cervical tissue margins should be free of disease as evaluated by the frozen section.

Indications of trachelectomy are: (i) preservation of fertility, (ii) early stage disease (stage IA1, A2, IBI), (iii) small tumor volume (< 2 cm), (iv) no pelvic node metastasis, (v) cancer margin is at 1 cm below the internal os on MRI.

This trachelectomy is not done in stage IIA disease

Reference: Dutta Gynae 6th/ed pg 352

question_text: Which of the following cannot be used as an emergency contraceptive?
option_c: LNG 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours
explanation:
Explanation:

LNG 0.75 mg single dose given 72 hours after intercourse is not recommended as emergency contraception because this dose is designed to be taken within 72 hours, and a single 0.75 mg pill at the end of 72 hours is ineffective for reliable contraception.

Emergency Contraceptives:

  • Used to prevent unintended pregnancyafter unprotected or inadequately protected intercourse.
  • Includes Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs)and insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD).
  1. Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs):
  • Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg single dose (Option A ruled out):
    • Most effective within 72 hours, can be used up to 120 hours.
    • Commonly available in India.
  • Ulipristal Acetate (UPA) 30 mg single dose (Option D ruled out):
    • Effective up to 120 hours (5 days)post-intercourse.
    • Approved by US-FDA and European agencies; availability in India may be limited.
  • Centchroman (Option B ruled out):
    • Taken as two 60 mg tablets within 24 hours, effective as emergency contraceptive.
    • Requires adequate trials to establish emergency contraceptive effectiveness.
  1. Combined Hormonal Regimens (Yuzpe Method):
  • Two doses, 12 hours apart.
  • Each dose contains ≥100 μg ethinyl estradiol+ 500 μg levonorgestrel.
  1. Intrauterine Device (IUD):
  • Copper IUD:Most effective form of emergency contraceptive.
  • Can be inserted within 5 daysof unprotected intercourse.

 

References:

Emergency contraception - A review - PubMed

Emergency Contraception | Pediatrics

Overview of methods of Emergency Contraception

question_text: Which of the following features indicates the presence of heart disease in pregnancy and which is not seen in normal pregnancy?
explanation:
• Many of the physiological adaptations of normal pregnancy and physical findings resemble heart disease symptoms and signs, making the diagnosis of heart disease more difficult.
  • For example, in normal pregnancy, functional systolic heart murmurs are quite common; respiratory efforts are accentuated, at times suggesting dyspnea and edema in the lower extremities usually develops after midpregnancy.
  • It is important not to diagnose heart disease during pregnancy when none exists, and at the same time not to fail to detect and appropriately treat heart disease when it does

Clinical indicators of Heart disease during Pregnancy: Metcalfes criteria for Heart disease

question_text: Which of the following provides vaginal protection?
explanation:
Explanation:

The perineal body is a fibromuscular pyramidal mass located in the midline at the junction of the urogenital and anal triangles of the perineum. In nulliparous women, it clinically measures about 3.5-5 cm from the posterior hymenal margin to the mid-anal opening (a standard POP-Q landmark).

This structure is of major clinical importance because it provides significant support to the pelvic floor and vagina by serving as the point of convergence for several muscles:

  • Superficial layer: bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal, and external anal sphincter muscles.
  • Deeper layer: perineal membrane, pubococcygeus (part of levator ani), and internal anal sphincter.

During pregnancy, the perineal body lengthens slightly, and in the second stage of labor, it can stretch by more than 65%. Because of its central location and supportive role, it is commonly involved in obstetric interventions and injuries:

  • It is incised during an episiotomy.
  • It is frequently torn in 2nd-, 3rd-, and 4th-degree perineal lacerations.

Explanation for other Options:

pH 8 (Option A) is actually unfavourable (normal vaginal pH is acidic 3.8-4.5), so it does not protect.

Menstrual bleeding (Option B) is a physiological process, not a protective mechanism.

Oil glands (Option C) (sebaceous glands) are present in the vulva/labia majora, but they are not the main factor in vaginal protection.

question_text:
A woman presents at 6 weeks of gestation. Which of the following signs can be elicited at this gestation?
1. Goodells sign
2. Osiander sign
3. Internal ballotability
4. Lightening
explanation:
The Goodell sign refers to a probable sign of pregnancy, characterized by softening of the cervix. A positive Goodell sign occurs due to increased blood flow noticed in the cervix during the first 4 to 8 weeks of pregnancy, which can also give the vaginal part of the cervix a bluish appearance(Chadwick sign).

Osiander's sign

An early indication of pregnancy(at eight weeks) in which pulsation can be felt through the lateral vaginal fornix.

Internal ballottement can be elicited between 16-28th week. The fetus is too small before 16th week and too large to displace after 28th week. However, the test may not be elicited in cases with scanty liquor amnii, or when the fetus is transversely placed.

Lightening - At about 38th week, specially in primigravidae, a sense of relief of the pressure symptoms is obtained due to engagement of the presenting part.

The other signs observed in the 1st trimester are:

  • Isthmus softening: Hegar sign
  • Bluish discolouration of ectocervix: Chadwick sign
  • Regular rhythmic contraction: Palmer sign
  • Asymmetric growth of uterus due to lateral implantation: Piskacek sign

question_text: Which of the following, when used before conception, helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects?
explanation:
Explanation:

Folic acid intake before conception (and to a lesser extent after conception) effectively reduces the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs) in the fetus.

Folic acid (vitamin B9) is a water-soluble B vitamin found in foods as folate and in supplements as folic acid, which has higher bioavailability. Folate is crucial for DNA synthesis, repair, and cell growth. Adequate folate helps prevent NTDs by supporting thymidylate biosynthesis.

Recommended dosage is 2 to 4 mg daily before conception and during the first trimester, with a daily intake of 400 µg being effective.

Explanation for other options:

Iron (Option B) is important during pregnancy to meet increased demands, especially after 16 weeks, but it does not prevent neural tube defects.

Calcium (Option C) supplementation helps reduce risks of preeclampsia, preterm birth, and supports bone health but does not prevent neural tube defects.

Vitamin A (Option D) is fat-soluble and high doses are teratogenic, so it is contraindicated during pregnancy.

question_text: Dorsal lithotomy position contributes to hasten second stage of labour by which of the following methods
option_b: Increase in outlet diameter by 0.2 to 0.5 cm
option_c: Reducing diagonal conjugate by 1 to 1.5 cm
explanation:
Pelvic joints have a limited degree of mobility but can relax remarkably during pregnancy. At term, the sacroiliac joint can glide upward. This is greatest in dorsal lithotomy position and may increase the diameter of the outlet by 1.5 to 2.0 cm for delivery. Sacroiliac joint mobility also likely aids the McRoberts maneuver to release an obstructed shoulder in cases of shoulder dystocia. These changes may also contribute to the success of the modified squatting position to hasten second-stage labor. Squatting may increase the interspinous diameter and the pelvic outlet diameter.

Reference: williams obstetrics 26th edition chapter 2

question_text: The complication that can occur with internal podalic version for transverse lie:

Internal podalic version (IPV):

Prerequisites for IPV:

  • The membranes should be intact or very recently ruptured in other words liquor should be adequate.
  • The cervix should be fully dilated.

question_text: Which hormone is detected by home-based urine pregnancy tests?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Home pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in the urine.
  • hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the developing placenta after implantation, typically around 6-12 days post-ovulation.
  • Most tests detect beta-hCG, the unique subunit of hCG, with sensitivity around 20-25 mIU/mL, allowing for early pregnancy detection.

Explanation for other options:

FSH (Option B): Follicle-stimulating hormone regulates ovulation but is not a marker of pregnancy.

Estrogen (Option C): Estrogen rises during pregnancy but is not detected in home pregnancy tests.

Progesterone (Option D): Essential for pregnancy maintenance but not measured in urine tests.

Key Takeaways:

Home pregnancy tests detect β-hCG, which is produced by the placenta after implantation, making it the earliest marker of pregnancy.

question_text: Not true about clomiphene citrate
explanation:
Clomifene is one of several alternatives for ovulation induction in those who are infertile due to anovulation or oligoovulation. Evidence is lacking for the use of clomifene in those who are infertile without a known reason In such cases, studies have observed a clinical pregnancy rate 5.6% per cycle with clomifene treatment vs. 1.3%-4.2% per cycle without treatment.

Clomiphene citrate causes MULTIFOLLICULAR DEVELOPMENT in contrast to Letrozole which leads to monofollicular development. Hence Letrozole is the current drug of choice for follicle stimulation in case of PCOS.

Proper timing of the drug is important; it should be taken starting on about the fifth day of the cycle and there should be frequent intercourse.

The following procedures may be used to monitor induced cycles:

  • Follicular monitoring with vaginal ultrasound, starting 4-6 days after the last pill. Serial transvaginal ultrasound can reveal the size and number of developing follicles. question_text: What does the ferning pattern of drying cervical mucus indicate in terms of its mechanism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ferning pattern observed when cervical mucus dries on a glass slide is a microscopic indicator of estrogen activity.

During the follicular (pre-ovulatory) phase of the menstrual cycle, rising levels of estrogen cause the cervical mucus to become thin, watery, and stretchy (spinnbarkeit) - properties that facilitate the passage of sperm through the cervix into the uterus.

When this mucus dries, crystallisation of sodium chloride occurs in a distinctive fern-like pattern under the microscope. This phenomenon happens because estrogen increases the electrolyte and water content of cervical mucus, which leads to the formation of the branching crystal structures.

Hence, the presence of a ferning pattern indicates high estrogen levels and the ovulatory or pre-ovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle.

Explanation of Other Options:

Progesterone (Option B): Progesterone makes cervical mucus thick, sticky, and less permeable to sperm. This hormone dominates the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Under progesterone influence, the mucus loses its ferning pattern, as sodium chloride crystallisation does not occur.

Prolactin (Option C): Prolactin primarily functions to stimulate milk production in the mammary glands during the postpartum period. It has no direct role in altering the consistency or appearance of cervical mucus.

17-Ketosteroids (Option D): These are metabolic by-products of adrenal and gonadal androgens and are mainly used as a marker of adrenal function. They do not influence cervical mucus or reproductive tract physiology related to ovulation.

Reference:

question_text: Best test for estimating hCG:
explanation:
Before answering this questions, let us first understand what is bioassay, immunoassay and Radioimmunoassay

  • Bioassay – A Bioassay is a test that uses animals or live tissues to look for a response to the hormone that is injected.
  • Immunoassay – An Immunoassay is a test that uses antibodies detected against the hormone to “capture” the hormone. The test uses materials or substances that are related to or are a part of the immune system. To perform an immunoassay, cells are introduced from the immune system which may or may not have an antibody and cell clumping is observed.
  • Radioimmunoassay – An radioimmunoassay uses a radioisotope as the label to detect and measure the amount of hormone present in the sample.

Bioassay for detecting hCG was developed in the 1930's. wherein samples were injected in rabbits, frogs etc and ovulation was observed. These tests were expensive, slow and insensitive for hCG as they could not differentiate between LH and hCG.

Bioassay for hCG is an outdated test these days.

ELISA – It consists of immunosorbent assay of monoclonal antibodies to detect B-hCG. It forms the bases of home pregnancy tests. This is more sensitive and specific and can detect hCG in serum upto 1-2 mIU/ml. Radioimmunoassay and Radio receptor assay are more sensitive than ELISA and detect hCG Gupto .002 mLU/ml in serum (RIA) or .05 mLU/ml (IRMA)

But between the two, Radioimmunoassay is more specific as it does not cross react with luteinizing hormone and is the best test for detecting B-hCG

question_text: Use of folic acid to prevent congenital malformation should be best initiated:
explanation:
“Folic acid has been shown to effectively reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTD’s). A daily 4 mg dose is recommended for patients who have had a previous pregnancy affected by neural tube defects. It should be started at least 1 month (ideally 3 months) prior to pregnancy and continued through the first 6-12 weeks of pregnancy".

Reference: COGDT 10/e, p 197

Remember: Folic acid is used to reduce the risk of neural tube defects.

  • More than half of NTDs could be prevented with daily intake of 400 µg of folic acid throughout the periconceptional period.
  • Thus dose of folic acid which is given to all pregnant females = 0.4 mg, i.e. 400 mcg (also called as prophylactic dose).
  • A woman with a prior pregnancy complicated by a neural tube defect can reduce the 23% recurrence risk by more than 70% if she takes 4 mg of folic acid for the month before conception and for the first trimester of pregnancy. This is called a therapeutic dose of folic acid.
  • Therapeutic dose of folic acid (to be given in females with a previous history of baby with NTD)-4 mg.
  • Duration: It should be started 1 month before conception and continued till the first 6-12 weeks of pregnancy.
  • Dose of folic acid given to pregnant women with megaloblastic anemia = 1 mg day.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 409; COGDT 10/e, p 197

question_text: A 9-week primigravida presents with mild nausea and occasional vomiting that occurs throughout the day. She is otherwise healthy and has no signs of dehydration or weight loss. Which initial management strategy is most effective and safe for her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Dietary and Lifestyle Measures:

  • First-line therapy for mild nausea and vomiting in pregnancy
  • Mechanism:
    • Prevents prolonged fasting, which can trigger nausea
    • Maintains stable blood glucose levels
    • Reduces gastric irritability

Practical Recommendations:

  • Eat small, frequent meals every 2-3 hours
  • Avoid fatty, spicy, or overly sweet foods
  • Consume dry foods like biscuits or crackers before getting out of bed
  • Hydration should be maintained alongside meals
  • Safe, non-pharmacologic, and effective in first trimester

Explanation of Other Options:

Domperidone (Option B):

  • Dopamine antagonist, antiemetic
  • Not first-line due to safety concerns in pregnancy
  • Used only if dietary/lifestyle measures fail

Increase fluid intake (Option C):

  • Important for preventing dehydration
  • Alone, it does not address nausea triggers
  • Should complement, not replace, dietary modifications

Metoclopramide (Option D):

  • Dopamine antagonist
  • Reserved for moderate to severe nausea/vomiting
  • Used if first-line measures fail

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Morning sickness affects most women in the first trimester, usually resolving by 16 weeks.
  • Mild cases are managed conservatively with dietary and lifestyle modifications.
  • First-line approach: Eat small, frequent meals and avoid triggers.
  • Pharmacologic therapy reserved for moderate to severe symptoms or when lifestyle measures fail.

question_text: A woman presents with a twin pregnancy. On ultrasound, the estimated age of one fetus is 1 month more than the other fetus.
explanation:
Explanation:

Superfetation is the fertilization of two ova in different menstrual cycles, leading to a significant gestational age difference between twins.

  • Superfetation refers to the conception of a second fetus during an ongoing pregnancy, caused by ovulation and fertilization occurring in a separate menstrual cycle.
  • It is an extremely rare phenomenon in humans due to hormonal and physiological changes that usually prevent further ovulation and implantation once pregnancy begins.
  • In reported cases, it results in fetuses with a clear age gap, such as one fetus being a month older than the other, as described in this scenario.

Explanation of other options:

Superfecundation (Option B): Fertilization of two ova during the same cycle from separate acts of intercourse, possibly with different fathers. Twins are of the same gestational age.

Suppositious child (Option C): A fictitious or fraudulently presented child, often introduced to claim inheritance or lineage rights.

Posthumous child (Option D): A child born after the death of the biological father, but conceived while he was still alive.

question_text: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen in pregnancy?
option_a: Increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks
option_b: Peripheral resistance to insulin leading to hyperinsulinemia
option_d: Increased plasma volume and RBC mass
explanation:
Explanation:

An increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks is not a physiological change in pregnancy. Instead, blood pressure typically decreases during early gestation due to systemic vasodilation and decreased peripheral vascular resistance.

1. Cardiovascular Changes:

  • Blood Pressure:
    • Both systolic and diastolic pressures fall early in pregnancy, reaching their lowest levels at 24–26 weeks.
    • Diastolic pressure decreases more than systolic.
    • BP returns to pre-pregnancy levels by term.
    • Supine hypotensive syndrome may occur due to compression of the great vessels by the gravid uterus.

2. Blood Volume and Hematologic Changes:

  • Plasma Volume: Increases by 40-45% above nonpregnant levels by 32-34 weeks.
  • Erythrocyte Mass: Increases by ~450 mL due to elevated erythropoietin and enhanced erythropoiesis.
  • Hemodilution: Plasma expansion exceeds RBC increase, leading to a slight physiological anemia (Hb ≈ 12.5 g/dL at term). (Option D ruled out)

3. Metabolic and Endocrine Changes:

  • Insulin Resistance: Peripheral resistance to insulin develops due to placental hormones (progesterone, cortisol, placental growth hormone, prolactin) and cytokines (TNF-α, leptin), leading to compensatory hyperinsulinemia. (Option B ruled out)
  • Glucose Metabolism:
    • Fasting Hypoglycemia: Due to continuous glucose uptake by the fetus.
    • Postprandial Hyperglycemia: Due to insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose output. (Option C ruled out)

question_text: Following is true about halothane except?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Constricts bronchii Halothane It is a volatile liquid with sweet odour, nonirritating and noninflammable. It is a potent anaesthetic with poor analgesic and muscle relaxant properties. Halothane causes direct depression of myocardial contractility by reducing intracellular Ca. It causes fall in BP and CO. Heart rate decreases due to vagal stimulation. It tends to sensitize the heart to arrhythmogenic action of adrenaline → contraindicated in pheochromocytoma. It causes greater depression of respiration and ventilation perfusion mismatch. It dilates the bronchi → inhalation agent of choice in asthmatics (intravaneous anaesthetic of choice in asthmatics is ketamine). It is a hepatotoxic drug and can also cause malignant hyperthermia (Succinylcholine accentuate it). Recovery is smooth and reasonably quick. It causes postanaesthetic shivering and chills. It inhibits intestinal and uterine contractions → agent of choice for assisting external or internal version during late pregnancy. Because its uterine relaxant action it is contraindicated during labour. It is particularly suitable for induction and maintenance in children and as maintenance anaesthetic in adults.

question_text: In which phase of the menstrual cycle is vacuolation observed as a histological feature?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vacuolation is a histological characteristic observed during the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.

Secretory Phase:

The secretory phase begins around day 15 and continues until menstruation starts. During this phase, the epithelial cells of the endometrial glands develop clear, rounded areas called subnuclear vacuoles, located between the nuclei and the basement membrane. These vacuoles contain precursors of glandular secretions, such as mucin and glycogen, which provide nourishment to a potential fertilized ovum.

Explanation for other options:

Proliferative Phase (Option B): Starting from around day 5 or 6 and lasting until day 14, the proliferative phase is marked by rising estrogen levels. This causes the endometrial glands to become tubular, the epithelium to transform into a columnar shape, and the stromal cells to become spindle-shaped. Additionally, spiral arteries lengthen beneath the epithelium without branching.

Menstrual Phase (Option C): In the menstrual phase, a decline in estrogen and progesterone levels occurs due to the degeneration of the corpus luteum, leading to the shedding of the endometrial lining that was prepared for pregnancy.

question_text: The progesterone component of OCP acts by:
option_c: Bringing about alterations in cervical mucus
explanation:
Actions of the progesterone component of combined oral contraceptives:

  • Suppresses ovulation by its inhibitory action on the pituitary and the hypothalamus. This is predominantly achieved by estrogens but even by progesterone.
  • Causes atrophic changes in the endometrium and prevents nidation even if fertilization occurs.
  • Acts on the cervical mucus, making it thick and tenacious and impenetrable by sperms.

The third-generation progestogens have a higher affinity for progesterone receptor and have a role in inhibiting ovulation. The main function of progestogens in combined pills is to counteract the undesirable effects of estrogen such as endometrial hyperplasia and heavy withdrawal bleeding.

question_text: What is an abnormal cardiovascular system examination finding during pregnancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pregnancy leads to physiological cardiovascular changes, including increased cardiac output, plasma volume expansion, and decreased systemic vascular resistance.

Common normal findings in pregnancy include:

Soft systolic murmur (due to increased blood flow)

Physiological S3 (rapid ventricular filling)

Loud S1 (accentuated due to increased blood flow across valves)

Diastolic murmurs , however, are always abnormal and suggest underlying valvular pathology like mitral stenosis or aortic regurgitation, which require further evaluation.

Explanation of other options:

Soft Systolic Murmur (Option A): Common in pregnancy due to increased blood flow and cardiac output. Usually benign and functional (not associated with structural heart disease).

S3 (Option C): Physiological third heart sound (S3) occurs due to rapid ventricular filling from increased plasma volume. Commonly heard in pregnancy and not pathological.

Loud S1 (Option D): Due to increased blood volume and cardiac output, the first heart sound (S1) may be louder than usual. Considered a normal variant in pregnancy.

Key Takeaways:

Diastolic murmurs in pregnancy are always abnormal and warrant further investigation for underlying heart disease.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common site for uterine incision during cesarean delivery?
option_b: Just above the level of isthmus
option_c: In upper part of body of uterus
explanation:
Most common site for uterine incision during cesarean is lower segment of uterus.(LSCS)

The uterus is pear shaped and consists of two major but unequal parts.

The upper, larger portion is the body or corpus, whereas the lower smaller cervix projects into the vagina. The isthmus is the union site of these two.

It is limited above by the anatomical internal os and below by the histological internal os

It is of special obstetrical significance because it forms the lower uterine segment during pregnancy.

Reference: DC Dutta textbook of obstetrics, 8th edition; chapter 1

question_text: Which of the below is seen in the ovulatory phase?
option_a: Stimulation of continuation of reduction division of oocytes
option_c: FSH increases steroid synthesis in granulosa cells
option_d: Activin causes FSH to act on granulosa cells
explanation:
• Option a: Stimulation of continuation of reduction division of oocytes – correct During oogenesis the primary oocyte is arrested in prophase of meiosis 1. Just before ovulation, the LH surge initiates the continuation of meiosis, forming a secondary oocyte and 1st polar body.
  • The LH surge initiates the resumption of meiosis in the oocyte (meiosis is not completed until after the sperm has entered and the second polar body is released.
  • Option b: Inhibin A is increased in ovulatory phase – incorrect Levels of inhibin A are increased and reach peak in mid luteal phase, not in ovulatory phase. 
  • Option c: FSH increases steroid synthesis in granulosa cells— FSH acts on the granulosa cells to produce estrogen mainly in the follicular phase and not in ovulatory phase. 
  • Option d: Activin causes FSH to act on the granulosa cells— As discussed, activin does augment the action of FSH on granulosa cells but during early follicular phase and not during ovulatory phase.
  • In the granulosa of the early follicular phase, activin augments FSH activities: FSH receptor expression, aromatization, inhibin/ activin production, and LH receptor expression.
  • In the theca, activin suppresses androgen production, allowing the emergence of an estrogen microenvironment.

Reference: Speroff 8th edition, page 213,223,226,229.

question_text: Which one of the following is the best drug of choice for treatment of bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy?
explanation:
Bacterial Vaginosis:

  • It is an alteration in the normal vaginal flora (so, termed as vaginosis and not vaginitis)
  • Polymicrobial in nature
  • It is transmitted sexually
  • Infection is favoured by decrease in the number of protective bacteria of vagina (“Doderlein bacteria” which release hydrogen peroxide and help in maintaining the acidic pH of vagina)
  • Symptoms:
    • 50% are asymptomatic
    • Rest complain of malodorous vaginal discharge with no irritation.

Diagnosis: By Amsel's criteria.

  • Vaginal secretions are grey – white and thinly coat the vaginal walls
  • pH > 4.5 (≈ 5 – 5.5) (i.e. increased vaginal pH)
  • Whiff’s test/Amine test is positive, i.e. addition of 10% KOH to vaginal secretions produces Fishy odour
  • Presence of ‘clue cells’ (> 20% of epithelial cells).

CLUE CELLS: are epithelial cells with granular cytoplasm.

Microscopic examination shows:

  • Clue cells
  • Number of gardnerella vaginalis
  • Number of lactobacilli
  • Leucocytes (conspicuously absent).

Treatment:

  • DOC Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days

Treatment of male sexual partner does not improve therapeutic response and is not recommended

  • In pregnancy:
    • TOC is oral metronidazole after 1st trimester
    • Alternatively, clindamycin can be given

Topical application of metronidazole gel should be avoided during pregnancy.

Reference: Shaw 14/e, pg 118; COGDT 10/e, pg 601; Harrison 17/e, pg 827

question_text: What hormone is contained in the contraceptive depicted below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The hormone in the contraceptive called the Today sponge is nonoxynol-9.

The Today sponge is a vaginal barrier contraceptive that contains nonoxynol-9 as a spermicide. It can be inserted up to 24 hours before intercourse and must remain in place for at least 6 hours afterward to ensure maximum effectiveness. However, it should not be left in the vagina for more than 30 hours.

While it offers convenience, it is less effective compared to other barrier methods like diaphragms or condoms.

Mechanism of action:

  • Releases spermicide during intercourse, which damages the sperm cell membrane.
  • Absorbs the ejaculate.
  • Physically blocks the entrance to the cervix.

Note: To be effective, the sponge needs to stay in place for 6 hours after intercourse.

Side effects: Possible allergic reactions and vaginal dryness.

Octoxynol 8 (Option B), Menfegol (Option C), and Levonorgestrel (Option D) are not components of the Today Sponge.

question_text: All of the following may be observed in a normal pregnancy except:

In normal pregnancy – Since plasma volume increases more in comparison to Red cell volume so viscosity of blood decreases (not increases) i.e. option “c” is incorrect.

Therefore, option “d” is correct. In pregnancy hemoglobin mass increases(to the extent of 18-20%) but hemoglobin concentration decreases due to hemodilution.
  • Now let’s have a look at Iron metabolism in pregnancy.

    • Even an adequate diet cannot provide the extra demand of iron.

- Thus pregnancy is always a state of physiological iron deficiency.

question_text: Primigravida with full term, complains of faintness on lying down and se feels well when turns to side or sitting position. This is due to:
explanation:
SUPINE HYPOTENSION SYNDROME (POSTURAL HYPOTENSION): During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus produces a compression effect on the inferior vena cava when the patient is in supine position.

In 90% cases this, however, results in opening up of the collateral circulation by means of paravertebral and azygos veins.

In some cases (10%), when the collateral circulation fails to open up, the venous return of the heart may be seriously curtailed.

This results in production of hypotension, tachycardia and syncope called supine hypotensive syndrome.

The normal blood pressure is quickly restored by turning the patient to lateral position.

That is why pregnant females are advised to lie in lateral positions best being left lateral

question_text: The major contribution of the amniotic fluid after 20 weeks of gestation is

Source of Amniotic Fluid:

  • Main Source:
    • Fetal urine.
  • Second Most Important Source (2nd Half of Pregnancy):
  • Upto 12 Weeks:
    • Transudate from maternal plasma.
  • 12-20 Weeks:
    • Fetal skin.
  • After >20 Weeks:
    • Fetal urine becomes the primary source.

Drainage Mechanism:

  • Swallowing:
    • Most important drainage method.
  • Initiation:
    • Begins by 10-12 weeks, followed by intramembranous transfer.

Other Contributors to Amniotic Fluid:

  • Early Pregnancy:
    • Ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma.
  • Beginning of Second Trimester:
    • Extracellular fluid diffusion through fetal skin.
  • After 20 Weeks:
    • Cornification of fetal skin prevents diffusion, and amniotic fluid is mainly composed of fetal urine.

Minor Contributors:

  • Pulmonary fluid.
  • Fluid filtering through the placenta.

Fluid Replacement:

  • The water in the amniotic fluid is completely changed and replaced every 3 hours.

question_text: A pregnant woman developed idiopathic cholestatic jaundice. The following condition is not associated:
explanation:
In idiopathic cholestatic jaundice (intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy), serum bilirubin levels are often elevated, but they can sometimes remain below 5 mg/dl

Cholestatic jaundice of pregnancy/cholestatic hepatosis/icterus gravidarum

It is characterized by accumulation of bile acids in the liver with subsequent accumulation in the plasma causing pruritus and jaundice due to estrogen excess.

Clinical features:

  • Manifestations appear in the last trimester (beyond 30 weeks) and only occasionally in the late 2nd trimester.
  • The cardinal clinical finding/1st symptom to appear is severe generalized pruritus with a predilection for the palms and soles.
  • Pruritus precedes laboratory findings by a mean of 3 weeks and sometimes by months.
  • Jaundice is slight (Bilirubin levels rarely exceed 5 mg) and seen in 10% patients.
  • Cholestasis tends to recur in subsequent pregnancies (recurrence rate = 50%), estrogen-containing contraceptives\OCP’s are contraindicated in females with h/o cholestasis during pregnancy.

Investigation:

  • Rise in S. bile acids is the earliest/the most consistent change/Best marker for cholestasis. There is a 10-100 fold increase in s. cholic acid followed by s. chenodeoxycholic
  • Serum bilirubin levels are increased (rarely more than 5 mg%) and increase is always in direct bilirubin.
  • Serum alkaline phosphatase is raised.
  • SGOT/SGPT levels are normal to moderately elevated (seldom exceed 250 U/L).
  • Symptoms disappear within two weeks postpartum. Jaundice usually disappears within weeks following delivery. Pruritus as a rule persists longer than jaundice.
  • Increase chances of PPH and cesarean section.
  • There is an increased incidence of prematurity, low birth weight babies, sudden IUD and meconium aspiration in the fetus

Reference: Dutta Obs. 6/e, pg 291; Robbin’s 7/e, pg 921; Williams Obs. 23/e, pg 1063, 1064.

question_text: Treatment of red degeneration of fibroid in pregnancy:

  • If because of mistaken diagnosis laparotomy is done, abdomen is closed without doing anything
  • Myomectomy should never be contemplated during caesarean section as vascularity of fibroid is increased during pregnancy (due to increased estrogen) leading to increased blood loss during cesarean section.

question_text: Which of the following types of twin pregnancies does not occur?
explanation:
Explanation:

The type of twin pregnancy depends on when the zygote divides after fertilization.

  • Dichorionic diamniotic twins result when division occurs within the first 3 days. (Option C ruled out)
  • Monochorionic diamniotic twins occur when division happens between days 4-8. (Option B ruled out)
  • Monochorionic monoamniotic twins form when the split occurs between days 9-12. (Option A ruled out)

If separation occurs after day 12, conjoined twins may result.

A dichorionic monoamniotic combination does not exist, because if twins are dichorionic, each embryo must have its own amniotic sac.

Key takeaway:

The type of twin pregnancy is determined by the timing of zygotic division in monozygotic twinning.

question_text: Indication of classical cesarean section:
explanation:
Classical cesarean:

  • In classical cesarean section the uterine incision is made on the anterior uterine wall in the upper segment above the reflection of the uterovesical fold of the peritoneum.
  • The chances of rupture of the uterus are high with classical cesarean section therefore it is rarely used nowadays.
  • It is done only in cases where the lower segment is not approachable.

Also Know:

Classical cesarean section:

  • It is associated with the maximum incidence of rupture uterus (4-9%) .
  • Rupture can occur during pregnancy even prior to onset of labour.
  • Site of rupture - upper segment.

Lower segment transverse incision also called as MunroKerr incision:

  • It is the most common type of cesarean section practised.

Lower segment vertical incision:

Indications:

  • Constriction ring
  • Lower segment not formed as in transverse lie and prematurity.

Disadvantages:

  • Extension downwards can involve the cervix, the vagina and even the bladder.

Advantages of a Lower segment section over Classical cesarean section:

Healing of the lower segment incision is better as it is located in the lower segment which is quiescent. Hence tensile strength is more and so the chance of scar rupture in the next pregnancy is minimal.

Incidence of rupture

  • In women with uterine malformations who have undergone cesarean delivery, the risk for uterine rupture in a subsequent pregnancy may be as high as with a classical incision.

Cephalic index = BPD divided by occipito frontal diameter (OFD)

question_text: Wrong statement regarding POG calculation

question_text: Which of the following is not a complication of fibroid in pregnancy?
explanation:
Effects of Fibroid on Pregnancy

Infertility: It is either the cause or the effect of the fibroid:

  • Leiomyomas are a sole cause of infertility in less than 3% of cases.
  • It causes infertility by:
  1. Hindering the ascent of the spermatozoa by distorting the uterus and tubes
  2. By disturbances in ovulation and
  3. By interfering with implantation of the fertilized ovum
    • Pregnancy rate following myomectomy is 40%.

During Pregnancy:

  • Abortion, Placental abruption and Premature labour Occurs when fibroid interferes with enlargement of uterus, initiates abnormal uterine contractions or prevents efficient placentation.
  • Malposition and Malpresentation of Fetus: Occur as fibroid can prevent engagement of head.
  • Obstructed labour: It can be caused by cervical and broad ligament tumours which are fixed in the pelvis and by pedunculated subserosal leiomyomas which become trapped in the pouch of Douglas.

During Labour:

  • If fibroid is situated above the presenting part: uneventful vaginal delivery.
  • If fibroid is situated below the presenting part: trial for vaginal delivery should be given. Thus chances of cesarean sections are increased.
  • Postpartum Hemorrhage/Delayed Involution can occur if placenta is implanted over the leiomyoma.

Also Know:

question_text: A patient presents with a new 2 cm black nodular mass near an episiotomy scar that is painful and expands during menstruation. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Endometriosis involving a scar site presents as a painful nodular mass that enlarges cyclically with menstruation.

  • Endometriosis is defined as the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity.
  • When endometrial tissue implants in surgical scars-such as an episiotomy site-it can lead to scar endometriosis.
  • These lesions respond to hormonal changes, causing cyclical pain and swelling during menstruation.
  • On examination, they often appear as firm, pigmented nodules and may mimic other pathologies like tumors or granulomas.
  • Scar endometriosis should be suspected in any reproductive-aged woman with a history of obstetric or gynecologic surgery who presents with localized pain and a mass that fluctuates with her cycle.

Various sites where endometriosis can occur:

  • Diagnosis Guidelines:
    • Current guidelines do not require histologic confirmation to diagnose endometriosis, often based on clinical presentation and macroscopic findings during laparoscopy.
  • Macroscopic Findings:
    • Powder-burn or Gunshot Lesions: Dark, blackish-bluish puckered lesions on the peritoneal surface.
    • Clear Vesicles: Small, blister-like lesions on the ovarian surface or peritoneum.
    • Red Polypoidal Lesions: Red, polyp-like, vascularised lesions.
    • White Scarred Lesions: White, scar-like areas with fibrosis and few blood vessels.
    • Yellow-brown Peritoneal Discoloration: Indicates hemosiderin deposition and chronic endometriosis.
  • Correlation of Gross Appearance with Microscopic Findings
    • Red Lesions: Vascularized, indicating active endometriotic tissue.
    • White Lesions: Fibrosis with few vessels, suggesting chronic or scarred tissue.
  • Histologic Examination
    • Hemosiderin Deposition: Common in histologic samples, indicating prior bleeding within the lesion.
    • Histologic Diagnosis Criteria: The presence of both endometrial glands and stroma is required to confirm endometriosis.

Explanation of other options:

Melanoma (Option B): A pigmented, possibly nodular skin cancer, but it does not fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and is typically painless in early stages.

Foreign body granuloma (Option C): Results from retained suture or tissue, forming a firm, non-pigmented lump; typically non-cyclic and non-menstruation-related.

Inclusion cyst (Option D): A painless, smooth, epithelial-lined cyst resulting from trauma or surgery; does not enlarge or become painful during menstruation.

question_text: Young lady comes with mild erosion of cervix and pap smear shows dysplasia, next step is:

question_text: Variable decelerations observed on cardiotocography (CTG) are most commonly indicative of:
explanation:
Explanation:

Variable decelarations are the most frequent type of fetal heart rate (FHR) deceleration during labour, caused mainly by umbilical cord compression.


Explanation for other Options:

Head compression (Option A): This typically causes early decelerations that mirror uterine contractions, not the abrupt and variable changes seen here.

Fetal hypoxia (Option C): Prolonged or recurrent severe variable decelerations can cause hypoxia, but hypoxia itself is not the primary cause. Hypoxia is a consequence, not the initial trigger.

Uteroplacental insufficiency (Option D): This usually results in late decelerations, where FHR decreases after the peak of a contraction due to impaired oxygen exchange, not in the variable abrupt pattern.

question_text: Which of the following is not a typical characteristic of bacterial vaginosis (BV)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bacterial vaginosis is characterised by a thin, grayish-white, homogeneous vaginal discharge rather than a thick one. The discharge may have a subtle fishy odour, especially after sexual intercourse or when mixed with potassium hydroxide (KOH) during the Whiff test.


Pathophysiology:

BV occurs due to a reduction of protective lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Bacteroides. This shift in vaginal flora leads to changes in pH and the appearance of characteristic clue cells on microscopy.

Amsel Criteria for Diagnosis (at least 3 of 4 needed):

  • Thin, gray-white discharge (not thick)
  • Vaginal pH > 4.5
  • Positive Whiff test - fishy odour when KOH is added
  • Clue cells on wet mount - vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria

Normal Vaginal Microbiome


Explanation of Other Options:

Presence of clue cells (Option A): Clue cells are a hallmark of BV. They are vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria, giving a stippled appearance on microscopy. Their presence is essential for diagnosis.

Vaginal pH > 4.5 (Option C): In BV, the normal acidic vaginal environment (pH 3.8-4.5) is disrupted due to the loss of lactobacilli, resulting in a pH above 4.5. This is a reliable indicator used in clinical diagnosis.

Fishy odour (Option D): A characteristic symptom of BV, especially noticeable after intercourse or with the addition of KOH during the Whiff test. Theodor results from the breakdown of amino acids by anaerobic bacteria, producing amines.

Key takeaway:

question_text: A pregnant woman comes to the Gynaecology OPD with a positive urine pregnancy test (UPT). She already has twins delivered via normal vaginal delivery in a previous pregnancy. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Twin delivery counts as a single parity event, so with one previous twin delivery and a current pregnancy, the obstetric score is G2P1.

  • The obstetric score system includes Gravida (G) for the number of total pregnancies (including the current one) and Parity (P) for the number of pregnancies carried beyond the period of viability (≥28 weeks in India), regardless of the number of babies born.
  • In this scenario:
    • The woman is currently pregnant (1 gravida)
    • She had one prior pregnancy which resulted in twin live births through a normal vaginal delivery
    • Twin pregnancy counts as ONE in both gravida and parity
  • Thus:
    • Gravida = 2 (previous twin pregnancy + current pregnancy)
    • Parity = 1 (because the twin delivery counts as one delivery event)
    • Hence, her obstetric score is G2P1.

question_text: The appearance of an ovarian mass is given below. This is suggestive of:
explanation:
This is a gross specimen showing a cystic structure with hair and mucoid material suggestive of Mature cystic teratoma

Dermoid Cyst(Mature cystic teratoma)

  • Dermoidcyst is a benign
  • Teratomas are the most common germ cell neoplasm.

On the basis of maturity teratoma can be divided into:

A. Mature(Benign)teratoma = dermoid cystMost common benigntumor of ovary in reproductive age group.

  • Most common benign neoplasm diagnosed during pregnancy.
  • Most common Germ cell tumor.
  • It is the commonest tumor to undergo torsion.
  • It frequently arise in association with mucinous cystadenoma:
  • Age for combined tumor is 20-30 years.
  • Age for simple dermoid cyst is 40-50 years.
  • Bilateralin 10% to 15% of cases.
  • Lining epithelium is stratified squamous epithelium(if dermoid cyst undergoes malignant change - Squamous cell Ca is seen).
  • Dermoid cyst usually contain derivatives of ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm. Mostcommon tissue element in dermoid cyst is ectodermal.

It may attain a size of 20 cms(generally 15 cms)

  • On cross section - they typically show an area of localized growth from which hair projects, teeth and bone are seen. It is called as Rokitansky protuberance or dermoid process.
  • Malignant change in a dermoid cyst occurs in 0.5-2% cases in patients more than 40 Most common malignancy which develops is, squamous cell carcinoma.

B. Immature(Malignant)teratoma

  • Rare, mostly solid, differ from benign teratomas in the component tissue which resembles that observed in the fetus or embryo rather than mature adult tissue.
  • Tumor occur chieflyin prepubertal adolescents and young
  • Tumor grade is correlated with prognosis and extra-ovarian spread.

C. Gross Pathology of Mucinous Cystadenoma:

  • Size: Typically larger than serous cystadenomas, often reaching sizes of 15-30 cm in diameter or more.
  • External Surface: Smooth, often encapsulated with a thick outer wall.
  • Cyst Contents: Multiloculated (containing multiple cysts or chambers) filled with viscous, thick, gelatinous, or mucinous fluid.
  • Color: The fluid inside is usually clear, pale, or light yellow, sometimes with a jelly-like consistency due to mucin.
  • Location: Most commonly found in the ovaries.
  • Borders: Usually well-demarcated and benign, without invasion into surrounding tissue.

D. Gross Pathology of Serous Cystadenoma:

  • Size: Typically smaller than mucinous cystadenomas, often ranging from 5-15 cm in diameter.
  • External Surface: Smooth and thin-walled, usually less thick than mucinous cystadenomas.
  • Cyst Contents: Unilocular or multilocular, with clear, watery, or straw-colored fluid.
  • Color: The fluid is thin and transparent, resembling serum (hence the name "serous").
  • Location: Most commonly arises in the ovaries.
  • Borders: Well-circumscribed and benign, with no signs of invasion.

question_text: The image showing bimanual examination in early pregnancy, where the examiner's fingers in the anterior fornix and per abdomen seem to approximate easily due to softening at the uterine isthmus. Explanation:

Hegar's sign refers to the softening of the uterine isthmus felt during a bimanual examination in early pregnancy (around 6-8 weeks of gestation).

  • Because of this softening, the examiner's fingers in the anterior fornix and the hand palpating per abdomen seem to approximate easily.

Palmer's sign (Option C): Refers to regular, rhythmic uterine contractions felt during bimanual palpation in early pregnancy (around 6 weeks), not softening of the isthmus.

Piskacek's sign (Option D): Refers to asymmetrical uterine enlargement due to eccentric implantation of the embryo, where one uterine cornu enlarges more than the other.

question_text: A pregnant woman at 8 weeks of gestation presents with symptoms suggestive of hyperthyroidism. What is the drug of choice for treating hyperthyroidism during the first trimester of pregnancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

PTU is preferred in the first trimester as it carries less teratogenic risk compared to methimazole and carbimazole.

  • In pregnancy, managing maternal hyperthyroidism requires balancing maternal health and fetal safety.
  • During the first trimester (up to 12 weeks):
    • PTU is preferred because:
      • It is less teratogenic than methimazole/carbimazole.
      • It reduces the risk of congenital anomalies during organogenesis.
  • After the first trimester, the drug is usually switched to methimazole to avoid the risk of hepatotoxicity associated with long-term PTU use.

    • Fetal goiter or hypothyroidism

Clinical Approach to Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy:

Explanation of other options:

Carbimazole (Option C): A prodrug of methimazole with the same teratogenic risks. Not preferred in early pregnancy.

Propranolol (Option D): A beta-blocker used only for symptomatic relief (tachycardia, tremors) but not a definitive treatment for hyperthyroidism. It may be added temporarily but is not the drug of choice.

question_text: What is the primary cause of lactational amenorrhea?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • During lactation, prolactin levels are elevated to support milk production.
  • High prolactin suppresses GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, disrupting its pulsatile pattern.
  • This leads to reduced LH pulses from the pituitary.
  • Without sufficient LH pulses, ovulation does not occur, resulting in amenorrhea during breastfeeding.

Lactational Amenorrhea:

  • During breastfeeding, prolactin levels are elevated.
  • High prolactin levels cause:
    • Suppression of GnRH (Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone) release from the hypothalamus
    • Disruption of the pulsatile release pattern of GnRH
    • Reduction in LH (Luteinizing Hormone) pulses from the pituitary
  • Without proper LH pulses:
    • Ovulation doesn't occur
    • Regular menstrual cycles don't resume (amenorrhea)

Explanation of Other Options:

Increased progesterone (Option A): Progesterone levels are low during lactation because ovulation does not occur, and no corpus luteum forms to produce progesterone.

Increased GnRH secretion (Option B): Prolactin inhibits GnRH secretion; thus, GnRH levels are decreased, not increased.

Decreased prolactin secretion (Option C): Would restore GnRH pulses, ovulation, and menstruation, opposite to lactational amenorrhea physiology

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Lactational amenorrhea is caused by hyperprolactinemia interfering with the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.
  • Mechanism:
    • Elevated prolactin → suppresses hypothalamic Kiss1 neurons (Kisspeptin) → disrupts GnRH pulsatility.
    • Reduced GnRH pulsatility → decreased LH pulses.
    • Inadequate LH → failure of pre-ovulatory surge, anovulation, and amenorrhea.
  • FSH may remain sufficient for follicular growth, but estradiol production is inadequate.
  • Menstruation resumes when suckling frequency decreases, lowering prolactin.

Hormones that favor milk production: Prolactin, Insulin, Glucocorticoids, Growth hormone, Thyroxine

Hormones that inhibit milk production: Estrogen, Progesterone
