question_text: A 35-year-old primigravida comes to the labour room with an episode of bleeding. She is 32 weeks pregnant. She complains of mild vaginal bleeding which was painless in nature. On examination her pulse: 82/min, BP: 110/70mmHg. Fetus is in transverse lie with FHS: 130 bpm. She denies any abdominal pain and the uterus is relaxed. Most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Clinical features of previa

  • Painless, causeless and recurrent vaginal bleeding (fresh red)
  • Bleeding is always revealed proportionate to visible blood loss
  • Uterus proportionate to gestation age anterior
  • Abdomen is non tender, uterus relaxed (unless patient is in labour)
  • Foetus is not compromised (unlike abruption and vasa previa)

Reference:-Williams obstetrics 26thedition, chapter 43

question_text: A patient of 47 XXY karyotype presents with features of hypogonadism; likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
Klinefelter Syndrome

Genotype - 47 XXY

Clinical features

  • Klinefelter syndrome (KS) is the M/C cause of primary testicular failure, i.e. male hypogonadism affecting 1 in 1000 males.


Reference: Harrison 17th/ed p 2340-42

question_text: A 20-year-young female presented for antenatal checkup. She was in the Ist trimester and was diagnosed to have an ovarian cyst. Treatment of choice:
option_c: Termination of pregnancy and cyst removal
explanation:
• Patient is presenting in the first trimester with ovarian cyst.
  • The principle of treatment in case of ovarian tumour is to remove the tumour as soon as the diagnosis is made. But this principle should not be followed in the first trimester.
  • Surgery in the first trimester is best avoided, as during surgery a corpus luteal cyst or ovary might be removed which will be detrimental to the pregnancy, which may end up in a miscarriage.
  • Therefore, all such cases should be operated (ovariotomy/cystectomy) in the second trimester.
  • Therefore, the best time of elective operation for an ovarian tumor in pregnancy is between 14 to 18 weeks, as the chances of abortion are less and access to the pedicle is easy.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 310, Shiela Balakrishnan 1/e, pg 265

question_text: A woman presents with missed periods, headaches, blurred vision, and spontaneous milk secretion from the breasts. Which investigation is most appropriate to evaluate her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of amenorrhea, galactorrhea, headache, and visual disturbances strongly suggests hyperprolactinemia, commonly due to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Measuring serum prolactin is the most suitable first-line investigation. Elevated prolactin confirms the diagnosis and guides further management, including imaging of the pituitary if needed.

Explanation of other options:

LH (Option B): LH levels may be altered in pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction, but it is not the first-line test for hyperprolactinemia. Its measurement is more useful in evaluating ovulatory function or menstrual irregularities caused by other endocrine disorders.

FSH (Option C): FSH assessment is primarily used to evaluate ovarian reserve, primary ovarian insufficiency, or menopausal status. It does not specifically address the typical symptoms of hyperprolactinemia seen in this patient.

hCG (Option D): Serum hCG is mainly used to confirm pregnancy. Although amenorrhea can occur in pregnancy, the presence of galactorrhea, headaches, and visual disturbances points away from pregnancy as the primary cause.

question_text: 35 yr old with 4 months amenorrhea with increased FSH, decreased estrogen. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Ans. A. Premature ovarian failure It is a case of premature menoPause (premature ovarian failure)'

question_text: A female patient undergoes a methylene blue three-swab test, and the middle swab is stained blue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The staining of the middle swab in the methylene blue three-swab test indicates that urine is leaking from the bladder into the vagina, confirming a vesicovaginal fistula (VVF).

Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF):

  • An abnormal communication between the bladder and vagina, causing continuous urinary incontinence.
  • Symptoms:
    • Continuous dribbling of urine (true incontinence)
    • Genital area excoriation
    • Depression due to chronic incontinence
    • Secondary amenorrhea
    • Bladder stones due to chronic stasis
  • Classification:
    Simple fistulas:
    • Small (≤0.5 cm), single, non-radiated

Complex fistulas:

  • Large (≥2.5 cm), may result from chronic disease or prior radiotherapy
  • Often include previously failed fistula repairs
  • Diagnosis:
    Methylene Blue Three-Swab Test:
    • A catheter is inserted into the bladder via the urethra
    • Vaginal cavity is packed with three sterile swabs
    • Dilute methylene blue (50-100 ml) is instilled into the bladder
    • Interpretation:
      • Uppermost swab stained:Leak from ureter → ureterovaginal fistula (Option D ruled out)
      • Middle swab stained:Leak from bladder → vesicovaginal fistula
      • Lowermost swab stained:Leak from urethra → urethrovaginal fistula (Option A ruled out)
  • Other investigations:Urine culture, cystoscopy, intravenous pyelography (IVP), ureteric catheterization, and ultrasonography.
  • Management:
    Conservative:
    • Indwelling catheter and antibiotics for 3-4 weeks
    • Waiting period of ~3 months for tissue healing before surgery
  • Surgical repair:
    • Vaginal repair (e.g., Latzko procedure, Chassar-Moir technique) for most cases
    • Abdominal approach for large fistulasor failed vaginal repairs
    • In cases of extensive bladder lossor multiple failed repairs, urinary diversion techniques (e.g., sigmoid colon or ileal loop bladder) may be necessary

Explanation of Other Options:

Vesicouterine Fistulas (Option C): Occurs rarely, often after cesarean section. Patients may present with urinary incontinence, hematuria, or cyclical hematuria (menouria). Diagnosis is by cystoscopy or injecting methylene blue into the bladder; dye exits via the uterine cervix, not the vagina..

References:

Vesicovaginal Fistula: Diagnosis and Management - PMC

Early versus delayed repair of vesicouterine fistula - PMC

question_text: According to new WHO guidelines, what is the minimum number of antenatal visits recommended to have a positive pregnancy outcome?
explanation:
Recent evidence suggests that the focused antenatal care (FANC) model, which was developed in the 1990s, is associated with more perinatal deaths than ANC models that comprise at least eight contacts between the pregnant woman or adolescent girl and the health care provider.

Minimum number of visits as per MOHFW: 4

  • 2nd visit: 14-26 wks

question_text: Patient who was known to have graves- disease and on anti-thyroid medication delivers a baby with aplasia cutis. What is the medication she was taking in the antenatal period?
explanation:
Methimazole and Carbimazole has been associated with a 2-fold increased risk for aplasia cutis congenita, as well as choanal atresia and esophageal atresia. This constellation of findings has been termed methimazole embryopathy. Aplasia cutis is a rare abnormality characterized by a full-thickness skin defect, usually the scalp, occasionally with a defect of underlying bone.

Aplasia cutis congenita(ACC) has been observed after fetal exposure to the antithyroid drug methimazole/carbimazole (MMI), but not reported after propylthiouracil(PTU), the current antithyroid drug of choice during pregnancy.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with profuse vaginal discharge with a fishy odor. Microscopy of the vaginal smear reveals the cell shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of profuse, white, non-viscous vaginal discharge with a fishy odor, along with clue cells on microscopy, is characteristic of Bacterial Vaginosis (BV).

Explanation of Other Options:

Herpes (Option A): Typically presents with painful genital ulcers or blisters, not profuse discharge or clue cells.

Candida albicans (Option B): Causes thick, white 'cottage cheese' discharge with itching; shows pseudohyphae/yeast cells on KOH mount, but no fishy odor or clue cells.

question_text: A 23-year-old primigravida presents at 8 weeks of gestation for her antenatal check-up. On pelvic examination, a specific clinical sign is elicited. What is the name of this clinical sign?
explanation:
Explanation:

It is present in two-thirds of cases. It can be demonstrated between 6 and 10 weeks, a little earlier in multiparae.

This sign is based on the fact that:

  • Upper part of the body of the uterus is enlarged by the growing fetus
  • Lower part of the body is empty and extremely soft and
  • The cervix is comparatively firm

Because of variation in consistency, on bimanual examination (two fingers in the anterior fornix and the abdominal fingers behind the uterus), the abdominal and vaginal fingers seem to oppose below the body of the uterus (as shown in the image).

Explanation of other options:

Palmer's sign (Option B): Regular and rhythmic uterine contraction can be elicited during bimanual examination as early as 4-8 weeks. Palmer in 1949, first described it and it is a valuable sign when elicited. To elicit the test, the uterus is cupped between the internal fingers and the external fingers for about 2-3 minutes. During contraction, the uterus becomes firm and well defined but during relaxation, becomes soft and ill defined.

Internal Ballottement (Option C): Internal ballottement is a clinical sign performed during a vaginal examination, typically used to confirm pregnancy. During the procedure, the examiner gently presses a finger against the cervix, causing the fetus to float upward in the amniotic fluid and then return to its original position, producing a rebound effect. This sign is generally detectable between 16 and 20 weeks of gestation and is considered a probable sign of pregnancy.

External Ballottement (Option D): External ballottement is a clinical sign used to assess fetal presence and mobility during the later stages of pregnancy, typically in the third trimester. It is performed through the abdominal wall by placing one hand on one side of the uterus to gently push the fetus upward, while the other hand feels for the rebound movement as the fetus returns. This technique relies on the fetus being mobile in adequate amniotic fluid, making it challenging to elicit in obese patientsor in cases with oligohydramnios (scanty liquor amnii).

Key Takeaways:

Hegar's sign (softening of the lower uterine segment) is a clinical sign of early pregnancy detected between 6-10 weeks via bimanual examination.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the ultrasound finding in the given image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Anencephaly presents on ultrasound as absence of the cranial vault with exposed brain tissue and the classic "frog eye" sign, making it the most likely diagnosis.

  • Anencephaly is a lethal neural tube defect (NTD) resulting from failure of closure of the rostral (cranial) end of the neural tube around the 25th day of embryonic development.
  • Ultrasound Features:
    • Absence of cranial vault and calvarium
    • Absent cerebral hemispheres
    • Presence of bulging orbits, giving the classic "frog eye" appearance
    • Detected as early as 11-14 weeks in antenatal scans
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Failure of cranial neuropore closure → defective skull formation
    • Brain tissue is exposed and degenerates due to amniotic fluid exposure
  • Prognosis:
    • Lethal condition; most fetuses are stillborn or die shortly after birth

Explanation of other options:

Hydranencephaly (Option B): Cerebral hemispheres are replaced by CSF, but the skull and cranial bones are present. There is no frog eye appearance.

Spina Bifida (Option C): A neural tube defect affecting the spine, not the brain. It presents with signs like lemon sign (scalloping of frontal bones) and banana sign (curved cerebellum) on ultrasound, not absence of cranial vault.

Lissencephaly (Option D): A disorder of neuronal migration causing a smooth brain surface, seen later in gestation or postnatally; cranial bones are present, and there's no frog eye sign.

question_text: A 26-year-old woman with 12 weeks of amenorrhea undergoes a sonographic evaluation. Based on the image, what type of gestation is most likely observed?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ultrasound shows the lambda sign (twin peak sign), which is characteristic of a dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy. In this type of twin gestation, each fetus has a separate chorion and amniotic sac, and the lambda sign appears as a thick triangular projection of placental tissue between the two gestational sacs. This occurs when the zygote splits within the first 3 days after fertilisation, leading to dichorionicity. Dichorionic-diamniotic twins each have their own placenta and amniotic sac, which usually reduces the risk of complications compared to twins that share a placenta or amniotic sac.

Timing of Zygotic Cleavage and Twin Type


Explanations for Other Options:

Monochorionic diamniotic (option A): occurs when the zygote divides after 4-8 days post-fertilisation, resulting in twins that share a single placenta (chorion) but each has a separate amniotic sac. On ultrasound, these pregnancies show a T-sign at the interface between the intertwin membrane and the placenta rather than the lambda sign. Because the twins share a placenta, there is a higher risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and other vascular complications, which require careful monitoring throughout gestation.

Monochorionic monoamniotic (option C): arises when the division happens between 8-12 days after fertilisation, producing twins that share both the placenta and the amniotic sac. Ultrasound imaging in these cases reveals no membrane separating the fetuses, which is associated with a high risk of cord entanglement, fetal demise, and other perinatal complications. The lambda sign is absent, and these pregnancies are closely monitored with frequent ultrasounds and sometimes inpatient care in late gestation.

Conjoined twins (option D): result from a very late and incomplete division of the zygote, typically after day 13, causing physical fusion of the fetuses. Ultrasound shows a structural connection between the twins, which may involve shared organs or tissues depending on the type of conjoinment. Unlike dichorionic or monochorionic twins, conjoined twins do not have the lambda or T-sign, and they require highly specialised obstetric and postnatal management due to the complexity of their condition.

  • Government of India minimum standard: 4 visits.

6 visits (Option B), 8 visits (Option C), and 4 visits (Option D) are all inadequate according to the ideal recommendation of Indian health care guidelines, though they may represent minimum standards in different guidelines (WHO recommends 8, GOI recommends minimum 4).

question_text: A woman with an obstetric score of G2P1 presents at 14 weeks of gestation for her routine antenatal checkup. A uterine artery Doppler is suggested. What complication can this test help in detecting?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Uterine artery Doppler is a non-invasive screening tool performed in early pregnancy (11-14 weeks, sometimes repeated at 20-24 weeks) to evaluate uteroplacental blood flow.
  • It helps identify disorders due to defective trophoblastic invasion of maternal spiral arteries.

Key Mechanism:

  • Normally, trophoblasts invade maternal uterine vessels → low-resistance, high-flow circulation.
  • Failure of invasion → persistence of high-resistance uterine artery flow → detectable on Doppler.

Abnormal Doppler Findings:

  • Persistence of diastolic notch
  • High resistance index (RI) / pulsatility index (PI)
  • Predicts early-onset preeclampsia and placental insufficiency.

Explanation of other options:

Late-onset preeclampsia (Option B) is usually linked to maternal factors (e.g., obesity, diabetes, chronic HTN), not abnormal Doppler.

Fetal growth restriction (Option C) may also show abnormal Doppler, but the primary predictive value is for early-onset preeclampsia.

Placenta accreta (Option D) is diagnosed by USG or MRI, not by uterine artery Doppler.

Key Takeaway:

  • Uterine artery Doppler at 11-14 weeks → predicts early-onset preeclampsia

question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist complaining of curd-like white vaginal discharge. Upon examination, the physician observes that when attempting to remove the discharge, petechiae are seen. What condition is most likely causing these findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

Candidiasis:

  • A fungal infection caused by Candida albicans
  • Characteristic presentation includes:
    • Curd-like white discharge
    • Plaque on the vaginal wall that causes petechiae when removed
    • Out of proportion pruritus and splash dysuria are common symptoms

Risk Factors:

  • Diabetes
  • Pregnancy
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Combined oral contraceptives
  • Immunosuppression/steroids

Diagnosis:

  • KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and mycelia

Treatment:

  • Uncomplicated:
    • Clotrimazole 1-2% cream or vaginal suppositories
    • Fluconazole 150 mg orally single dose
  • Complicated:
    • Fluconazole 150 mg repeat dose after 72 hours
    • Topical steroid for external irritation
  • Recurrent:
    • Fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days ×3, then weekly maintenance ×6 months
    • Boric acid 600 mg vaginally for 2 weeks if resistant

Differential Diagnosis:

Trichomoniasis (Option B):

  • Presents with greenish-yellow, frothy discharge
  • Pruritus present
  • Does not cause petechiae on removal of discharg

Gardnella vaginalis (Option C):

  • Presents with thin creamy white discharge with fishy odour
  • No associated petechiae on examination

Gonorrhea (Option D):

  • Presents with purulent yellow-green vaginal discharge
  • No characteristic petechiae formation

Key Takeaway Points:

Recommended Regimens for Uncomplicated Vulvovaginal Candidiasis

  1. Clotrimazole
    • 1% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 7-14 days or 2% cream for 3 days
  2. Miconazole
    • 2% cream 5 g intravaginally daily for 7 days or 4% cream for 3 days
    • Vaginal suppository (one suppository daily): 100 mg for 7 days or 200 mg for 3 days, or 1,200 mg for 1 day
  3. Butoconazole 2% cream 5 g intravaginally in a single application
  4. Oral Agent - Fluconazole 150 mg orally in a single dose

Recommended Regimens for Complicated Vulvovaginal Candidiasis:

  • An additional 150 mg dose of fluconazole given 72 hours after the first dose.
  • Adjunctive treatment: 10-14 days of topical therapy.
  • A weak topical steroid, such as 1% hydrocortisone cream, for external irritative symptoms.

Treatment of Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis:

  • Fluconazole (150 mg every 3 days for three doses).
  • Maintenance: Fluconazole, 150 mg weekly for 6 months
  • Boric acid 600-mg vaginal suppository for 2 weeks if recurrence persists or in patients with non-albicans candida.

Reference:

Vulvovaginal Candidiasis - STI Treatment Guidelines

question_text: A woman presents for her first antenatal visit and reports that her LMP was approximately 2 months ago. Which ultrasound parameter is the most accurate for dating the pregnancy at this stage?
explanation:
Explanation:

At an estimated gestation of 2 months (approximately 8-9 weeks), the pregnancy is in the first trimester.

  • The Crown-Rump Length (CRL) is the single most accurate biometric parameter for determining gestational age in the first trimester (up to 13 weeks and 6 days).
  • It measures the length of the embryo from the top of its head (crown) to the bottom of its torso (rump).
  • During this period of organogenesis, there is very little biological variability in growth, making the CRL highly predictive of gestational age, with an accuracy of ± 5 to 7 days.

The Biparietal Diameter, Femur Length, and Abdominal Circumference are the primary biometric parameters used for dating and assessing growth in the second and third trimesters. (Options A, C & D ruled out)

question_text: A 26-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, right lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin, associated with nausea and vomiting. On examination, there is localized tenderness in the right adnexal region. The clinician suspects ovarian torsion. In a suspected case of ovarian torsion, which investigation provides the most rapid and reliable assessment of ovarian blood flow and morphology to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

USG Doppler is the first-line investigation for ovarian torsion. It is non-invasive, widely available, and can be performed rapidly.

  • Doppler ultrasound evaluates both ovarian morphology and vascular flow, which is crucial for early diagnosis.
  • Key sonographic findings include:
    • Enlarged, edematous ovary
    • Globular configuration
    • Disruption or absence of normal adnexal blood flow
    • Free fluid in the pelvis

Explanation of Other Options:

Clinical evaluation (Option B): While symptoms (sudden-onset unilateral pain, nausea, tenderness) are highly suggestive, they are non-specific and cannot definitively diagnose torsion. Imaging confirmation is required.

MRI (Option C): Provides detailed soft-tissue imaging but is time-consuming, less available in emergencies, and not first-line.

CT abdomen (Option D): Involves radiation, offers lower specificity for gynecologic emergencies, and is less ideal for acute ovarian torsion diagnosis.

question_text: A pregnant woman presents with passage of grape-like vesicles per vaginam. An ultrasound shows a snowstorm appearance. Which of the following hormone levels should be checked in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of grape-like vesicles and the ultrasound'snowstorm' appearance are classical for a hydatidiform mole. The hallmark investigation for diagnosis and monitoring is measurement of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).

  • hCG levels are typically markedly elevatedin molar pregnancy due to trophoblastic proliferation.
  • This measurement is also critical for diagnosis, baseline assessment, and long-term follow-upto detect persistence or transformation into gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN).

Follow-Up of Molar Pregnancy:

β-hCG Monitoring Protocol

  • Initial baseline test:within 48 hours after molar evacuation.
  • Subsequent follow-up:every 1-2 weeks until 3 consecutive normal values are obtained.
  • Post-normalization testing:monthly β-hCG for 6 months.

Median time for β-hCG resolution (GTD):

  • Partial mole: ~6 weeks
  • Complete mole: ~7 weeks

Timeline for β-hCG normalization:

  • 95% by 14 weeks
  • 99% by 25 weeks

Indicators of Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN):

  • Plateauing or rising β-hCG levels.
  • Persistence beyond expected resolution timeline.

Counseling on Conception After Mole:

  • Avoid pregnancy until follow-up is complete.
  • May conceive 6 months after β-hCG normalizationin uncomplicated mole.
  • If GTN develops→ delay pregnancy for 1 year after completion of therapy.
  • If metastasis present→ avoid pregnancy for 2 years after treatment.

question_text: A 22-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain. On pelvic examination, a mobile, non-tender adnexal mass is noted. An ultrasound image is shown below, demonstrating a complex ovarian mass with echogenic foci, calcifications, and areas of shadowing, suggestive of bone or teeth. Based on the clinical presentation and ultrasound findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is a 22-year-old woman presenting with lower abdominal pain and a mobile, non-tender adnexal mass. Ultrasound shows a complex ovarian mass with echogenic foci, calcifications, and shadowing, which are highly suggestive of bone or teeth.

These features are characteristic of a dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma):

Key Points Supporting Diagnosis:

  • Epidemiology:
    • Most common ovarian tumor in women of reproductive age, especially 10-30 years.
    • Predominantly benign; only 1-2% are malignant, usually in women >40 years.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Germ cell tumor containing elements from all three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.
    • Commonly contains hair, sebaceous material, bone, teeth, or neural tissue.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Often asymptomatic (50-60%), but can present with pain due to torsion (~10%) or mass effect.
    • Adnexal masses are usually mobile, unilateral, and <10 cm in most cases.
  • Imaging Findings:
    • Ultrasound: Complex mass with echogenic foci, calcifications, and acoustic shadowing, representing bone or teeth.
    • Calcifications are seen in 30-50% of teratomas.

Management:

  • Surgical excision is the treatment of choice, either via laparoscopy or laparotomy, depending on size and complexity.
  • Prognosis is excellent for benign dermoid cysts.

Endometrioma (Option A): Usually cystic with homogeneous low-level echoes ("chocolate cyst"), not calcified foci.

Serous cystadenoma (Option B): Typically unilocular, thin-walled, anechoic cyst.

Mucinous cystadenoma (Option D): Often multilocular with clear or mucoid fluid; calcifications or teeth are not seen.

question_text: A 16-year-old female with primary amenorrhea with her breasts are at Tanner 4 but she has no axillary or pubic hair. The most likely diagnosis from below:
explanation:
When a female presents with a complaint of primary amenorrhea, the first thing to do is to examine her secondary sexual characteristics.

  • In Turners Syndrome all secondary sexual characteristics are poorly developed where as in the question the female has proper breast development with absent axillary and pubic hair (therefore option ‘a’ ruled out).
  • In mullerian agenesis – Patient presents with primary amenorrhea with well- developed secondary sexual characteristics (both breast and pubic hair), e. option b ruled out.
  • In option d, i.e. premature ovarian failure – patient will have no secondary sexual characteristic, be it breast or pubic hair, i.e. this option is also incorrect.
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome-is a form of male pseudo hermaphroditism-gonadal sex is male with contrasting female phenotype.
  • It is the third most common cause of primary amenorrhea

question_text: A young primigravida at 32 weeks gestation was admitted with blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg and urine dipstick showing 2+ proteinuria during an antenatal checkup. On examination, she has pedal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Explanation of Other Options:

Placenta previa (Option A): Presents with painless vaginal bleeding; not associated with hypertension, proteinuria, or edema.

Placenta abruptio (Option B): Causes painful vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain from premature placental separation; not typically associated with proteinuria/edema.

question_text: What is the dose of folic acid in patients with sickle cell diseases?
explanation:
Management of sickle cell in pregnancy:

  • Folic acid supplementation 4 mg to 5 mg daily (ACOG 2013) is given to support rapid blood cell turnover.
  • Prophylactic penicillin (penicillin V 250 mg twice daily).
  • Prophylactic blood transfusions during pregnancy to maintain hematocrit above 25% and Hbs below 60% -are controversial.
  • Hydroxyurea is not recommended in pregnancy.
  • During every antenatal visit, Hb, hematocrit, platelet count, bilirubin, transaminase and lactose dehydrogenase levels should be checked (fortnightly).
  • Vaginal delivery is preferred.
  • Epidural analgesia is given during labor to relieve pain.
  • Postnatal thromboprophylaxis for upto 6 weeks may be needed

question_text:
A 23-year-old primigravida at 25 weeks gestation presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for the past two days. On examination, her blood pressure is 104/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and she has generalized edema. Laboratory findings show:
1. Leukocyte count: 10,500/mm³
2. Platelet count: 62,000/mm³
3. Hematocrit: 26%
4. AST: 90 IU/L
Peripheral smear reveals hemolysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

HELLP syndrome is a severe complication of pregnancy characterized by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets.

  • The patient has:
    • Hemolysis on peripheral smear
    • AST of 90 IU/L
    • Thrombocytopenia (62,000/mm³).
  • Classical presentation includes right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and laboratory evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
  • Importantly, hypertension may be absent, as in this case.
    Thus, this clinical picture fulfills the diagnostic criteria for HELLP syndrome.

Criteria for Diagnosis of HELLP Syndrome:

Another criterion, namely the Mississippi Triple Class System, further classifies HELLP Syndrome based on the platelet counts.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hepatitis B (Option B): Causes elevated liver enzymes but does not explain hemolysis or thrombocytopenia. Usually presents with jaundice.

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (Option C): Presents in late pregnancy with hypoglycemia, leukocytosis, more severe hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy. Hemolysis is less prominent initially.

Obstetric cholestasis (Option D): Presents primarily with intense pruritus and raised bile acids. Platelet count remains normal, and hemolysis is not a feature.

Key Take away points:

References:

The HELLP syndrome: Clinical issues and management.

Mississippi and Tennessee systems for diagnosis of HELLP syndrome

question_text: A woman presents six months after undergoing dilatation and curettage for a molar pregnancy with persistent abdominal pain and distension. Laboratory evaluation reveals persistently elevated β-hCG levels, and chest X-ray shows multiple well-circumscribed lesions ("cannonball" metastases). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), the malignant spectrum of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD), which can arise after a molar pregnancy. Features supporting this diagnosis include:

  • History of molar pregnancy
  • Persistently elevated β-hCG
  • Pulmonary metastases appearing as "cannonball" lesions on chest X-ray
  • Abdominal pain and distension due to uterine or metastatic involvement

GTN involves abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue, with potential for local invasion and distant metastasis, most commonly to the lungs.

Explanation of Other Options:

Endometriosis (Option B): Presents with cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. It does not cause elevated β-hCG or lung metastases.

Ovarian cyst (Option C): Can cause abdominal discomfort or distension but does not produce elevated β-hCG or pulmonary lesions.

Asherman's syndrome (Option D): Characterized by intrauterine adhesions after D&C causing amenorrhea or infertility; it does not cause elevated β-hCG or metastases

Key Take Away Points:

  • GTN should be suspected in persistent elevated β-hCG post-molar evacuation.
  • Cannonball pulmonary metastases are characteristic of choriocarcinoma.
  • Early diagnosis and chemotherapy are critical to prevent morbidity and mortality.

question_text: All are the laboratory investigations done in cases of pre eclampsia except
explanation:
In preeclampsia, the focus is on monitoring renal function (A), liver function (B), and urine analysis (C) to assess the severity of the condition and its impact on the body.

Anticardiolipin antibodies (D) are not typically part of the routine evaluation for preeclampsia; they are more relevant in the context of antiphospholipid syndrome.

Investigations to be done in case of pre eclampsia are hemogram, platelet count, hematocrit, RFT, LFT, coagulation profile, electrolytes, serum uric acid, ECG, echocardiogram

question_text: In a suspected case of ovarian cancer, imaging work up is required for all of the following except:
explanation:
"FIGO staging is based on finding surgical exploration." ... Novak 14th/ed p 1477

"Whenever malignancy is suspected, a staging laparotomy should be carried out." ... Jeffcoates 7th/ed p 550

Role of Imaging in Ovarian tumour:

  • Used for - delineating the site and size of lesion.
  • Characterization of lesion into benign or malignant. Detects early metastasis.
  • To asses resectability.
  • To exclude extraperitoneal metastasis( like liver parenchyma, enlarged pelvic and paraaortic nodes, hydroureter and hydronephrosis)

Imaging Modality of Choice is USG: for delineating the site and size of lesion, to devise scoring systems for differentiating benign from malignant tumours and for screening.

Other modalities: Regarding imaging used for ovarian Ca.

  • Direct radiological examination of abdomen: for evidence of fetal skeleton, calcification of leiomyoma or teeth in a dermoid cyst.
  • Colour flow imaging: to increase the specificity of diagnosis of malignant tumours.
  • CT and MRI: used to evaluate the tumour and the extent of spread but are more useful in monitoring the progress of the disease.

The risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) Scoring System

RMI score = Ultrasound score × Menopausal score × Ca 125 level in U/mL

The Risk of Malignancy Scoring System

There are 2 scoring systems, RMI 1 and RMI 2, each of which calculates scores by using ultrasound features, menopausal status, and pre-operative CA 125 level according to the equation:

RMI score = Ultrasound score × Menopausal score × Ca 125 level in U/mL

  • The RMI scoring system is the method of choice for predicting whether or not an ovarian mass in likely to be malignant.
  • Women with an RMI score> 200 have a high risk of ovarian cancer.

question_text: A 21-year-old female, who was 32 weeks pregnant is brought to the ER, with 1 week history of fever. She had been complaining of sever fatigue, decreased urine output and high coloured urine. This morning she developed two episodes of seizures and is unconscious. There were no focal deficits and both the plantar were extensor. Her investigations showed Hb: 6g/dL, Total Count of 20,000 cells/μL, Platelet of 10,000/μL, S. Cr was 4.5mg/dL. Her peripheral smear showed shistocytes. Her Prothrombin time and activated thromboplastin time were normal. Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: HELLP Syndrome can be a possible differential diagnosis.
option_b: TTP can be triggered by pregnancy
option_c: Renal impairment is life threatening in HELLP
option_d: ADAMTS 13 activity can be decreased in HELLP syndrome also.
explanation:
Renal failure is a common manifestation of HELLP but is not life threatening. Life threatening complications are neurological complications and hepatic hematoma.

HELLP syndrome is a Thrombotic Microangiopathy that occurs in pregnancy. It is usually associated with pre-ecclampsia. It is different from other TMAs by the presence of liver injury that defines its severity. Liver sub capsular hematoma can be life threatening as it can cause rupture of liver. Neurological complications include cerebral infarction, hemorthage in brainstem and cerebral edema.

aHUS and TTP can also be triggered by pregnancy and hence be a differential diagnosis of HELLP syndrome. In HELLP syndrome anti thrombin III will be decreased and D Dimer will be elevated. ADAMTS 13 activity may be reduced to 30-60%.

DIC can be considered as a DD, but it causes prolongation of PT and aPTT.

In TTP, there will be a classical pentad of fever, neurological symptoms, renal failure, thrombocytopenia and MAHA. It is due to decreased activity of ADAMTS 13 to < 10%, which results in accumulation of ultra large multimers of vWF, that clogs the microcirculation and causes MAHA. The low level of ADAMTS13 activity alone is not enough but TTP is usually triggered by pregnancy, pancreatitis or infection in such individuals.

Acquired TTP can occur due to antibodies to ADAMTS13 which inhibits its activity. It is common in females. It is very severe with mortality of >90% if untreated.

TRERATMENT OF TMAs:

Plasma infusion or plasma exchange is enough to treat congenital TTP.

Acquired TTP and DEAP HUS requires immunosuppression in addition to plasma exchange.

Caplacizumab is the monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of acquired TTP.

Atypical HUS is treated with Eculizumab

Neuraminidase associated HUS is treated with antibiotics and plasma exchange. Blood should not be given as it has IgM.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:317, Pg: 2365-2367.

question_text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination, there is no thelarche, but her stature is normal. Karyotyping shows a 46, XX genotype. What would be the next diagnostic investigation to guide treatment planning?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a young girl with primary amenorrhea, absent secondary sexual characteristics (no thelarche), and normal stature with a 46 ,XX karyotype, the most appropriate next step is to measure serum LH and FSH levels.

  • LH (Luteinizing hormone)and FSH (Follicle-stimulating hormone) are crucial in assessing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.
  • These hormone levels help determine whether the cause of amenorrhea is hypogonadotropic (central origin: hypothalamic/pituitary dysfunction)or hypergonadotropic (peripheral origin: ovarian failure).

Based on results:

  • Low LH and FSH→ Suggests hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as seen in Kallmann syndrome or functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
  • High LH and FSH→ Indicates hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, such as premature ovarian insufficiency or gonadal dysgenesis.

Since the patient has a normal stature and 46, XX karyotype (ruling out Turner's syndrome), a hormonal evaluation is the logical next step to classify the type of hypogonadism and guide therapy (e.g., hormone replacement).

Explanation of Other Options:

Diagnostic laparoscopy (Option A): This is an invasive procedure used to directly visualise pelvic organs to detect structural abnormalities like Müllerian agenesis or endometriosis.

However, it is not a first-line investigation in primary amenorrhea-hormonal assessment should precede imaging or invasive evaluation.

USG pelvis (Option B): Pelvic ultrasonography helps assess the presence and morphology of the uterus and ovaries, but it is not the priority when thelarche is absent.

Since this presentation points to a hormonal aetiology rather than an anatomical one, LH and FSH testing should be done first to confirm whether ovarian function is intact.

CT brain (Option D): A CT scan of the brain is indicated only if pituitary or hypothalamic lesions (such as a prolactinoma or craniopharyngioma) are suspected-usually when symptoms like headache, visual disturbances, or galactorrhea are present.
In this patient, there are no neurological signs, so a CT brain is not warranted at this stage.

question_text: Which cardinal movements occur during labour?
explanation:
Series of events that take place in the genital organs in an effort to expel the viable products of conception out of the womb through the vagina into the outer world is called Labour.

Mechanism of normal labour is defined as the manner in which the fetus adjusts itself to pass through the parturient canal with minimal difficulty.

There are 8 cardinal movements of the head in normal labour.

  • Every – Engagement (Synclitic or Asynclitic)
  • Decent – Descent
  • Female – Flexion
  • I – Internal rotation
  • Choose to – Crowning
  • Employ – Extension
  • Rises – Restitution
  • Extremely – External rotation

Mnemonic : Every Decent Female I Choose to and Employ Rises Extremely.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 128

question_text: The perineal injury can be prevented in normal labour by all except:
option_c: Slow delivery of the head in between contractions
explanation:
The perineal injury can be prevented in normal labor by all options except (B): Timely episiotomy as a routine. While episiotomies are sometimes performed, they are not recommended as a routine procedure and should be done judiciously based on specific indications.

A) Maintaining Flexion of the Head Keeping the fetal head flexed during delivery helps to reduce the diameter of the presenting part, which can minimize perineal stretching and injury. A well-flexed head facilitates a more controlled delivery and can help prevent tearing.

(C) Slow Delivery of the Head in Between Contractions Allowing the head to emerge slowly between contractions helps the perineal tissues to stretch gradually. This slow progression can significantly reduce the risk of tears and assist in the natural adaptation of the perineum to the baby's head.

(D) Effective Perineal Guard The perineal guard technique involves gentle support and manual pressure on the perineum during delivery. This can help to control the speed of delivery and assist in preventing tears by providing support to the perineal area.

Summary

Options (A), (C), and (D) all focus on techniques that support gradual stretching and controlled delivery, while (B) suggests a routine procedure that can potentially increase risk rather than decrease it.

Reference: Williams Obs. 23/e, pg 395 and Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 137

Course of Labour in Occipito Posterior Position

  • In 90% cases – if uterine contractions are good and the pelvis is favourable,the occiput rotates through 3/8th of a circle and the baby is born as occipitoanterior.
  • So, when diagnosis of occipito posterior presentation is made—labour is allowed to proceed in a manner similar to normal labour, in anticipation of normal vaginal delivery
  • So, a careful wait and watch policy should be adopted for the occipito posterior position

Indications of cesarean section in occipitoposterior position

  • Incoordinate uterine action
  • Fetal distress
  • Other obstetrical complications warranting cesarean.

question_text: A 45-year-old man goiter undergoes a thyroidectomy. One week later, he develops carpopedal spasms, muscle and abdominal cramps, and tingling of his lips and hands. Laboratory studies show a serum calcium of 6.2 mg/dL and serum phosphorous of 5.7 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs will most likely improve this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
• This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms highly suggestive of hypoparathyroidism, a condition that occurs most frequently after thyroidectomy or the removal of a parathyroid adenoma. Hypoparathyroidism is a condition of parathyroid hormone (PTH) deficiency leading to decreased calcium levels and other electrolyte abnormalities.
  • Normally a fall in extracellular fluid ionized calcium concentration leads to stimulation of PTH secretion. When released, PTH enhances active reabsorption of calcium and magnesium from distal tubules and the thick ascending limb in the kidney, enhances the release of calcium from bones and enhances the absorption of calcium in the intestine by increasing the production of activated vitamin D. However, in hypoparathyroidism, PTH levels are greatly reduced resulting in severe hypocalcemia.
  • There are three principal reasons for low Ca2+ in such cases
    • Low PTH reduces renal reabsorption of Ca++ but increases reabsorption of phosphate.
    • The resulting high plasma phosphate binds plasma Ca++ so plasma Ca++ decreases.
    • Low PTH causes low production of the active form of vitamin D, so Ca++ absorption in small intestine is decreased.
  • Hypoparathyroidism is characterized by severe hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, resulting in tetany, carpopedal spasms, muscle and abdominal cramps, and tingling of the lips and hands. A positive Chvostek sign (tapping the face in front of the ear elicits tetany) and Trousseau sign (abnormal muscular contractions elicited by applying a blood pressure cuff) will often be noted.
    • Since the blood calcium levels are often very low, either calcium gluconate or vitamin D preparations should be administered to correct the condition. Vitamin D preparations, such as Cholecalciferol, elevate calcium levels, and also increase phosphate levels. Another treatment option would be to use the vitamin D3 analog calcitriol. Calcitrol has a mechanism of action similar to that of cholecalciferol. Ergocalciferol is also used, but has shorter duration and lower potency than cholecalciferol. Although further elevation of serum phosphate would be undesirable, vitamin D analogues are front-line therapy for hypoparathyroidism; phosphate levels may be addressed with phosphate binders or other measures.

Reference: Basic & clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 15th Edition, pg no. 802-803

question_text: One of the following forms the basis for sex chromatin testing:
explanation:
Barr body forms the basis for sex chromatin testing.

Barr Body

When two X chromosomes are present in a cell (as in a normal female) one of them becomes inactivated and condensed on the nuclear membrane and is called the ‘Barr body’.

This process is termed as X chromosome lionization (inactivation) Presence or absence of Barr bodies helps in ascertaining the sex of an individuals

  • Absence of Barr body indicates that the patient has only one X chromosome (eg. Normal male XY or Turner’s syndrome (XO)
  • Nuclei of cells in females (XX) contain a darkly staining Barr body that is not present in the nuclei of cells in males.
  • Barr bodies are most easily seen in a smear of squamous epithelial cells obtained by scraping the buccal mucosa
  • Barr bodies react differently to histological stains and are best seen as dark staining bodies within the nucleus of non-dividing interphase cells.

Reference: Gamong 24/e p392-393

question_text: Which of the following is the ideal fixative used for a conventional Pap smear?
explanation:
Explanation:

For a Pap smear to be interpreted accurately, the cytopathologist needs a well-preserved sample. The critical step in ensuring cellular preservation is immediate fixation of the smear after collection.

  • Why fixation is important:
    • Prevents air-drying artifacts, which distort cells and obscure nuclear details.
    • Maintains the morphology of epithelial cells, which is essential for detecting precancerous or malignant changes.
  • Ideal fixative:
    • 95% ethanol is considered the gold standard for Pap smear fixation.
    • The smear should be placed immediately in 95% ethanol or sprayed with a fixative before drying.
    • This ensures uniform preservation of cells and prevents distortion.

Explanation for other Options:

Normal saline (Option A): Used for wet mount preparations, not for Pap smear fixation.

10% formalin (Option B): Preserves tissue for histopathology but not suitable for cytology smears, as it causes cellular shrinkage and artifact.

Acetone (Option D): Sometimes used for frozen sections, not for Pap smears.

question_text: A 16-year-old girl is brought by her mother for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. On examination, she has normal secondary sexual characteristics and normal axillary and pubic hair. However, ultrasound reveals the absence of a uterus. What should be the next diagnostic step?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient with primary amenorrhea, normal secondary sexual characteristics, normal pubic and axillary hair, and absence of a uterus, the two main differential diagnoses are:

  • Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, MRKH)- (46, XX)
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS)- (46, XY)

Both conditions present with primary amenorrhea and an absent uterus, but can be distinguished by:

Since the girl in this case has pubic and axillary hair, MRKH syndrome is more likely.

To confirm this and rule out AIS, the next diagnostic step is karyotyping - to determine whether the patient is 46, XX (MRKH) or 46,XY (AIS).

Explanation of Other Options:

Testosterone levels (Option A): Measurement of serum testosterone is useful if virilisation or ambiguous genitalia are present, or if AIS is strongly suspected (e.g., absent body hair).

Estrogen measurement (Option C): Estrogen levels reflect ovarian function and are usually normal in both MRKH and AIS. Therefore, measuring estrogen would not help differentiate between these two key causes of amenorrhea with an absent uterus.

LH and FSH measurement (Option D): LH and FSH levels are mainly used to evaluate ovarian failure or pituitary/hypothalamic causes of amenorrhea (when the uterus is present).

Key takeaway:

question_text: Identify the pattern in the image on CTG:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A mirror-image dip at the peak of contraction is characteristic of early decelerations.
  • Early decelerations are gradual, uniform decelerations that mirror uterine contractions, meaning the nadir (lowest point) of the deceleration aligns with the peak of the contraction, as shown in the CTG strip above.
  • They are benign and caused by fetal head compression, leading to vagal stimulation.

No intervention is required unless associated with abnormal labor progression.

Explanation of other options:

Late decelerations (Option C): Occur after the contraction peak and indicate uteroplacental insufficiency.

Normal CTG (Option B): Decelerations are not considered part of a normal CTG.

Key Takeaways:

Early decelerations are benign, uniform, and mirror uterine contractions, caused by fetal head compression during labor.

  • As an alternative to rotational forceps in occipito transverse or posterior position.
  • Delay in descent of the head in case of the second baby of twins.
  • Deep transverse arrest.

question_text: A woman currently receiving magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) therapy for eclampsia needs to be assessed before her next maintenance dose. Under which condition should the next dose of MgSO₄ be withheld?
option_b: Urine output of more than 45 mL/hr
explanation:
Explanation:

In the management of eclampsia, magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) is used to prevent and control seizures. However, excessive magnesium levels can depress the central nervous system and neuromuscular transmission, leading to magnesium toxicity.

The earliest and most reliable clinical sign of magnesium toxicity is the loss of deep tendon reflexes, especially the patellar (knee jerk) reflex. This occurs when serum magnesium levels exceed 9 mg/dL (≈7 mEq/L). Therefore, if the knee-jerk reflex is absent, the next dose of MgSO₄ must be skipped until the patient is reassessed and toxicity is managed.

Monitoring Parameters Before Each Maintenance Dose of MgSO₄:

Check the following before giving each maintenance dose:

  • Patellar reflex: Should be present.
  • Urine output: ≥ 30 mL/hour over the last 4 hours. (Option B ruled out)
  • Respiratory rate: ≥ 16 breaths per minute. (Option C ruled out)

If any of these are abnormal → withhold the next dose and evaluate for toxicity.

Absence of knee-jerk reflex = Early sign of magnesium toxicity → Skip next MgSO₄ dose immediately.

Serum Magnesium Levels and Their Effects:

Management of Magnesium Toxicity:

  • Immediately stop MgSO₄ infusion.
  • Administer 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly over 3 minutes to antagonise magnesium's effects.
  • Administer furosemide to enhance magnesium excretion.
  • Provide respiratory support (intubation, ventilation)if severe depression occurs.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: What is meant by co-testing in the context of cervical cancer screening?
explanation:
Explanation:

Co-testing refers to the combined use of HPV testing and cervical cytology (Pap test/Liquid-Based Cytology) for cervical cancer screening.

  • Between the ages of 30 and 65 years, guidelines allow for screening every 5 years with co-testing in women at low risk.
  • This strategy improves detection of high-risk HPV strains, identifies abnormal cytology earlier, and significantly reduces both incidence (>50% reduction) and mortality (>55% reduction) from cervical cancer.
  • Hence, co-testing (HPV + LBC/Pap test) is a widely accepted approach in routine cervical cancer screening.

Explanation for other Options:

Pap smear + VIA (Option B): VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic acid) is a low-cost screening tool used in low-resource settings, but it is not part of standard co-testing protocols.

Pap smear + Colposcopy (Option C): Colposcopy is a diagnostic procedure for women with abnormal cytology or HPV results, not a primary screening method.

HPV testing + Colposcopy (Option D): This is also diagnostic rather than screening; using colposcopy in all women would lead to unnecessary procedures.

question_text: Name the fistula indicated in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

The fistula depicted in the image represents an abnormal connection between the urinary bladder and the vagina, identifying it as a vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF):

  • An abnormal passage forms between the urinary bladder and the vagina.
  • Causes continuous, involuntary leakage of urine through the vagina.
  • Commonly results from prolonged obstructed labor, where sustained pressure from the fetal presenting part against the pelvic bones causes tissue necrosis between the bladder and vagina.

question_text: A Nursing assistant posted in obstetric care was asked to plot a partograph to monitor the progress of labour. After how much dilatation of the cervix, must she start plotting the graph?
explanation:
Partogram is the graphical recording of stages of labour including cervical dilatation, descent and rotation of the head.

  • It was introduced by WHO a part of the Safe Motherhood initiative.
  • The main purposeof the partogram is to avoid prolonged labour and intervene timely.
  • Once labour is diagnosed, its progress is charted on a partogram by abdominal and vaginal examination
  • The latent phase of labour is up to 3 cm dilatation, and should not be more than 8 In the active phase which extends from 3 cm to complete cervical dilatation, labour is expected to progress at the rate of at least 1 cm cervical dilatation per hour which corresponds to the alert line.
  • The action line is drawn 4 hours to the right and parallel to the alert line in the WHO partogram.
  • Labour is considered normal as long as the progress of cervical dilatation is to the left of the alert line.
  • Prolonged labour is diagnosed, once the alert line is crossed, e., there is a shift to the right. This is considered an indication for intervention.
  • If the patient is in a peripheral hospital, once the alert line is crossed, it is an indication for referral to a higher center.
  • If action line is crossed, it is an inducation for cesarean section.

Thus, the partogram can be used to identify an abnormal labour pattern and to indicate the correct time for intervention by means of the alert and action lines.

How to use it -

A partograph must be started only when a woman is in labor.

The partograph is used to plot the following parameters for the progress of labor:

  1. cervical dilatation,
  2. descent of fetal head, and
  3. uterine contractions. It will also be used for monitoring fetal conditions with the following parameters: fetal heart rate, membranes and liquor and moulding of fetal skull. Additionally, the partograph can be used to monitor maternal condition:

Cervical dilatation: The rate of dilatation of the cervix changes during labor, this is represented by the bold lines in the graph.

Dilatation of the cervix is measured by the diameter in cm. This is recorded with an X in the center of the partograph, at the intersection of vertical and horizontal lines. The vertical scale represents dilatation by 10 squares of 1 cm each. The horizontal scale represents time by 24 squares of one hour each.

question_text: A primigravida presents to the labor ward at 1 PM with cervical dilation of 5 cm. At 4 PM, her cervical dilation is noted to be 6 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient is in the active phase of labor (5 cm cervical dilation).
  • Over 3 hours, the cervical dilation increased only 1 cm, which is below the expected rate (normal: 1 cm/hour for primigravida).
  • Poor progress of labor requires prompt intervention to avoid maternal and fetal complications.

Management Principles:

Assess uterine contractions:

  1. Poor contractions + poor progress: Augment labor with oxytocin.
  2. Good contractions + poor progress: Consider cesarean section (possible cephalopelvic disproportion).

Explanation of Other Options:

Slow progress of labor (Option A):

  • Diagnoses the issue but does not provide a management plan.
  • Without intervention, labor may prolong, increasing maternal and fetal risks.

Wait for complete dilation (Option B):

  • Passive observation is inappropriate when labor progress is below normal.
  • Can lead to maternal exhaustion and fetal distress.
  • Active intervention is necessary.

Induce labor (Option C):

  • Induction is contraindicated in the active phase of labor.
  • May cause uterine hyperstimulation and fetal compromise.
  • Appropriate actions:
    • Augmentation with oxytocin if contractions are inadequate.
    • Consider cesarean section if cephalopelvic disproportion is suspected.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Normal active labor cervical dilation: 1 cm/hour
  • Poor progress is defined as slower than expected dilation or fetal descent
  • Active management is required to prevent prolonged labor complications
  • Oxytocin is used only when contractions are inadequate; otherwise, cesarean section may be indicated

question_text: The most serious complication of clomiphene therapy for induction of ovulation is:
explanation:
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) arises from the administration of exogenous gonadotropins or ovulation induction drugs like clomiphene citrate.

Following gonadotropin stimulation, multiple ovarian follicles develop, leading to increased vascular permeability and secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). This results in fluid shifts from the intravascular to the third space, causing ovarian enlargement and subsequent fluid accumulation in the peritoneal and occasionally pleural cavities.

Manifestations vary from mild abdominal discomfort and bloating to severe ascites, oliguria, electrolyte imbalances, and respiratory distress.

OHSS is categorized into mild, moderate, and severe forms based on clinical findings and the need for medical intervention.

Management involves symptomatic treatment for mild cases, including oral fluids and analgesia. Moderate to severe cases may necessitate hospitalization for intravenous fluids, electrolyte replacement, monitoring of renal function, and occasionally paracentesis or thoracentesis for symptomatic relief. Severe cases may require cessation of gonadotropin therapy and postponement of embryo transfer.

Reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 4th Edition, Page Number-315.

explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The partogram indicates prolonged labor with features suggestive of cephalopelvic disproportion and fetal distress, warranting an emergency Cesarean section.

  • The partogram reveals that labor has crossed the alert line, showing prolonged labor despite oxytocin augmentation.
  • Key findings include full cervical dilation, station at 3+, moulding 2+, meconium-stained liquor, and a fall in fetal heart rate — all suggestive of cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) with fetal distress.
  • Since oxytocin has already been administered and uterine contractions are adequate, further augmentation is not beneficial.
  • The presence of fetal distress and obstructed labor necessitates an emergency Cesarean section to prevent complications.

Explanation of other options:

Forceps-assisted delivery (Option A): Requires specific indications like prolonged second stage or maternal exhaustion with low station; not suitable here due to CPD and fetal distress.

Vacuum-assisted delivery (Option B): Also not indicated in suspected CPD with fetal distress; could worsen neonatal outcomes.

Oxytocin infusion (Option C): Already administered; since there's no progress, further oxytocin is not advisable in the setting of CPD and distress.

Reference:

https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/58903/WHO_FHE_MSM_93.8.pdf;jsessionid=14CEE7621A01932987688BA52AFE5736?sequence=1

question_text: The following are related to face presentation except:
option_c: The diameter distending the vulval outlet is mentovertical
explanation:
Face presentation:

  • The attitude of the fetus shows complete flexion of the limbs with extension of the spine. There is complete extension of the head so that the occiput is in contact with the back.
  • The denominator is mentum.
  • The commonest position is left mentoanterior (LMA).
  • Most common maternal cause is platypelloid pelvis and the most common fetal cause is anencephaly.
  • The engaging diameter of the head is submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm (3 3/4”) in fully extended head.
  • Engagement is delayed because of the long distance between the mentum and biparietal plane (7 cm).
  • The head is born by flexion: (11.5 cm).

Management

  • Vaginal delivery is possible in mentoanterior positions but not in persistent mentoposterior.
  • In mentoposterior during early stages of labor the policy of wait and watch should be adopted, in hope of mentoposterior getting converted to mentoanterior spontaneously. Persistent mentoposterior position is an indication for doing cesarean section.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 388

question_text: A 32-year-old multigravida with a history of two previous cesarean sections presents with massive hemorrhage during cesarean delivery. Intraoperatively, the placenta is found densely adherent to the uterus and has invaded through the myometrium into the bladder wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The finding of placental invasion into the bladder wall is diagnostic of placenta percreta.

Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS), formerly called morbidly adherent placenta, occurs due to failure of normal decidua formation and defective development of the Nitabuch's fibrinoid layer.

  • Placenta accreta (79%) → Villi adhere directly to the myometrium without invasion. (Option A)
  • Placenta increta (14%) → Villi invade into the myometrium. (Option B)
  • Placenta percreta (7%) → Villi penetrate through the myometrium and may invade adjacent organs, commonly the bladder.

Key risk factors present in this patient:

  • Previous cesarean delivery (risk increases with number; up to 6.7% with ≥5 C-sections).
  • Placenta previa is often associated (up to 70% if there is a prior cesarean).
  • Multigravidity and advanced maternal age (>35 years) also increase risk.

Clinical features:

  • Failure of normal placental separation at delivery.
  • Massive hemorrhage after attempted placental removal (life-threatening).
  • In cases of placenta percreta, the villi may invade surrounding structures such as the bladder, as in this case.

Workup and Evaluation:

  • Laboratory:
    • Complete blood count (CBC) after delivery to assess blood loss.
  • Imaging:
    • Ultrasonography, Doppler ultrasound, and MRI may help in prenatal diagnosis.
    • Absence of findings does not rule out abnormal placental attachment.
    • Low-lying placentas detected before 30 weeks may "migrate" in up to 90% of cases.
  • Special Tests:
    • None specifically indicated.
  • Definitive Diagnosis:
    • Usually made intraoperatively by failure of normal placental separation.
    • Confirmed histologically.

Pathological Findings

  • Absence of the decidua basalis, replaced by loose connective tissue.
  • Decidua parietalis may be normal or absent.
  • Placental villi may be separated from myometrial cells only by fibrin.

Explanation for other Options:

Placenta previa (Option D) is when the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment and covers (partially or completely) the internal cervical os.

question_text: Most common cause of vesicovaginal fistula in India is:

"In developing countries, 90% of genitourinary fistulas arise from obstetric trauma, specifically from prolonged or obstructed labor."

—William Gynae 1st/ed p 573

Most common Genital Fistula is vesico vaginal fistula and so the above statement holds good for VVF also.

The fistula resulting from pressure during long and difficult labour always involves the trigone of the bladder.

Whereas – "In developed countries, iatrogenic injury during pelvic surgery is responsible for 90% of VVF. In industrialized countries, hysterectomy is the most common surgical cause of VVF, accounting for approximately 75% of fistula cases. Laparoscopic hysterectomies were associated with the greatest incidence followed by abdominal and vaginal."

—Williams Gynae 1st/ed p 573 Extra Edge:

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed p 184; William Gynae 1st/ed p 573

question_text: Which among the following is an outlet forceps?
explanation:
Explanation:

Wrigley forceps is designed for outlet forceps delivery, which involves the fetal head being low in the birth canal and visible at the introitus.

Features of Wrigley Forceps:

  • Short, slightly curved blades
  • Fixed English-style lock
  • Ideal for low or outlet deliveries
  • Easy to manipulate when the fetal head is very low or visible

Criteria for Outlet Forceps Delivery:

  • Fetal scalp visible at the vaginal opening without separating the labia
  • Fetal head has reached the pelvic floor
  • Head is at or on the perineum
  • Occiput in anterior or posterior position, or rotated ≤45° from anterior/posterior

Explanation of Other Options:

Piper's forceps (Option A): These are highly specialized forceps featuring a distinct perineal curve, designed exclusively for delivering the after-coming head in a breech presentation.>

Das forceps (Option C): Shorter and lighter variant of long curved forceps. It is classified as a mid-cavity forceps, used when the fetal head is engaged but has not yet reached the pelvic floor, particularly in mothers with a narrow pelvis or low-birth-weight babies.

Kielland forceps (Option D): Classic rotational forceps with nearly straight blades and an adjustable pivot, used in the mid-pelvis to correct fetal head malpositions, such as deep transverse arrest, before applying traction.

question_text: Lochia in correct order: during puerperium:
explanation:
LOCHIA:

  • Depending upon the variation of the color of the discharge, it is named as:
    • Lochia rubra (red) 1-4 days.
    • Lochia serosa (5-9 days) - the color is yellowish or pink or pale brownish.
    • Lochia alba - (pale white) - 10-15 days.

Composition:

  • Lochia rubra consists of blood, shreds of fetal membranes and decidua, vernix caseosa, lanugo and meconium.
  • Lochia serosa consists of less RBC but more leukocytes, wound exudate, mucus from the cervix and microorganisms (anaerobic streptococci and staphylococci).
  • Lochia alba contains plenty of decidual cells, leukocytes, mucus, cholesterol crystals, fatty and granular epithelial cells and microorganisms.

Note:

  • The average amount of discharge for the first 5–6 days, is estimated to be 250 mL.
  • The normal duration may extend up to 24–36 days (Williams 24/e, p 670). The red lochia may persist for longer duration especially in women who get up from the bed for the first time in a later period.

Clinical importance:

  • The discharge may be scanty, especially following premature labors or in case of infection or may be excessive in twin delivery or hydramnios, or subinvolution of uterus and retained bits of conception.
  • If malodorous, indicates infection. Retained plug or cotton piece inside the vagina can also be a cause should be kept in mind.
  • Persistence of red color beyond the normal limit signifies subinvolution or retained bits of conceptus.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 146

question_text: All of the following statements are true for episiotomies except:
option_b: Can be either mild-line or mediolateral
option_c: Involvement of anal sphincter is classified 3rd-4th degree perineal tear
option_d: Midline episiotomies bleed less, are easier to repair and heal more quickly
explanation:
Episiotomy: is defined as a surgical incision made over the perineum and vulva during delivery to increase the diameter of the vulval outlet (and not the whole of birth canal) during child-birth and to prevent perineal tears. Thus episiotomy is a surgically given perineal tear of second degree.

Types of Episiotomy:

  • Median
  • Mediolateral
  • Lateral
  • 'J' shaped

Extra Edge: Structures cut in Mediolateral episiotomy (Very Important)

  • Posterior vaginal wall
  • Superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, bulbospongiosus and part of levator ani
  • Fascia covering those muscles
  • Transverse perineal branches of pudendal vessels and nerves
  • Subcutaneous tissue and skin.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 568, 569; Dewhurst 6/e, p 307

question_text: 24-year-old P2+0 woman presents to the emergency department complaining of pain in her right breast. The patient is postpartum day 10 from an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at 42 weeks. She reports no difficulty breast-feeding for the first several days postpartum, but states that for the past week her daughter has had difficulty latching on. Three days ago her right nipple became dry and cracked, and since yesterday it has become increasingly swollen and painful. Her temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Her right nipple and areola are warm, swollen, red, and tender. There is no fluctuance or induration, and no pus can be expressed from the nipple.
option_a: Continue breast feeding from both the breasts
option_c: Immediately start antibiotics and breastfeed only when antibiotics are discontinued.
option_d: Pump and discard breast milk till infection is over and then continue breastfeeding
explanation:
(A) Continue breastfeeding from both breasts

A postpartum lady coming with H/o pain in breast and fever and nipples being warm, red, swollen, with no induration, fluctuance and no pus extruding from them - leaves no doubt that the patient is having mastitis.

Mastitis is not a contraindication for breastfeeding. She should continue feeding from both the breasts.

Continuing to breastfeed is encouraged as it helps clear the infection, maintains milk supply, and provides comfort.

Antibiotics can be prescribed, but there is no need to stop breastfeeding during treatment, as breast milk remains safe.

Reference: Dutta Obs, 7/e, pg 439; William Obs, 22/e, pg 703, 23/e, pg 653; COGDT 10/e, pg 245

question_text: A woman has just delivered a healthy baby via normal vaginal delivery. You are considering the timing of IUCD insertion for contraception. What is the earliest time at which an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) can be inserted?
explanation:
Explanation:

An IUCD can be safely inserted within 48 hours of vaginal delivery, ideally immediately after placental expulsion, to reduce the chance of unintended pregnancy.

  • Postpartum IUCD (PPIUCD) insertion is a widely recommended and effective method of long-acting reversible contraception (LARC).
  • The earliest and commonly practiced insertion times are:
    • Postplacental insertion: Within 10 minutes of placental delivery, before uterine involution begins.
    • Early postpartum insertion: Within 48 hours after delivery. This window is considered safe and convenient, especially if the woman is motivated for contraception and already in a healthcare setting.
    • Interval IUCD: Done after 6 weeks postpartum when the uterus returns to its non-pregnant state.
  • Advantages of PPIUCD:
    • Convenient and acceptable (done before discharge)
    • Highly effective
    • Immediate protection
    • No interference with breastfeeding
    • Less perforation risk due to thick uterine wall
    • Cost-effective
  • Disadvantages:
    • Higher expulsion rate than interval insertion
    • Mild discomfort or bleeding

Explanation of other options:

After 6 weeks (Option B): A common alternative, especially when missed earlier, but not the earliest time.

After 3 months (Option C): Safe, but unnecessarily delayed if immediate postpartum contraception is desired.

After 6 months (Option D): Too delayed and not standard practice unless medically indicated.

question_text: A 26-year-old primigravida delivers vaginally at term. Soon after delivery of the placenta, she develops profuse postpartum hemorrhage and severe lower abdominal pain. On examination, a mass is seen protruding through the cervix into the vagina, and the uterus is not palpable abdominally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening postpartum complication where the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity and may even protrude through the cervix or vagina. Early recognition is crucial for successful management.

Key Features Supporting the Diagnosis:

  • Timing: Occurs immediately after delivery of the placenta.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Profuse postpartum hemorrhage
    • Severe lower abdominal pain
    • Palpable mass in the vagina
    • Absence of the uterus in the abdomen
  • Types: Complete inversion (fundus protrudes through cervix/vagina) or partial inversion (fundus remains in the uterine cavity).

Management Overview:

  • Immediate resuscitation: IV access, rapid fluid infusion, and blood products if needed.
  • Urgent manual replacement: Push the inverted fundus upward toward the normal position.
    • If the placenta is still attached, reposition with placenta in situ to reduce blood loss.
    • Tocolytic agents (e.g., terbutaline, nitroglycerin, magnesium sulfate) may be used to relax the uterus.
  • Surgical intervention: If manual replacement fails, laparotomy may be required.
    • Huntington procedure: Traction on round ligaments to reposition uterus.
    • Haultain procedure: Posterior incision through constriction ring if necessary.
  • Post-replacement care: Stop tocolytics, administer oxytocin and other uterotonics, and monitor for re-inversion.

Explanation for other Options:

Uterine rupture (Option A): Usually occurs during labor or delivery, with abdominal pain and fetal distress; uterus is palpable abdominally.

Retained placenta (Option C): May cause hemorrhage but does not produce a fundal mass protruding through the cervix.

Cervical polyp prolapse (Option D): Usually a slow-developing condition; presents as a small mass, not associated with acute hemorrhage.

question_text: A 30-year-old primigravida patient was admitted to the labor room with labor pain. During the second stage of labor she was exhausted so the obstetrician performed forceps delivery. Immediately after delivery she started bleeding with tachycardia and hypotension. Placenta did not deliver and there was shortening of umbilical cord. Obstetrician attempted manual removal of the placenta but could not reach the placental attachment. What would be the best step in management of this patient after initial resuscitation?
option_b: Manual removal of placenta under GA
explanation:
Rupture following manipulative or instrumental delivery:

Sudden deterioration of the general condition of the patient with varying amounts of vaginal bleeding following manipulative or instrumental delivery raises the suspicion. Exploration of the uterus to feel the rent confirms the diagnosis. Not infrequently, the diagnosis is not revealed until after varying intervals following development of shock or broad ligament hematoma or peritonitis. Shortening of the cord immediately following a difficult vaginal delivery is pathognomonic of uterine rupture, the placenta being extruded out into the abdominal cavity, through the rent in the uterus.

Reference: D C Dutta’s textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 29

question_text: In a primigravida, what is the satisfactory rate of cervical dilatation during the active phase of labor?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In nulliparous women (primigravida), the satisfactory rate of cervical dilatation during the active phase of labor is ~1.2 cm/hour.
  • In multiparous women, the rate is ~1.5 cm/hour.

Phases of Labor:

  1. Latent Phase
    • Duration:
      • Primigravida: 10-12 hours (should not exceed 20 hours)
      • Multigravida: 6-8 hours (should not exceed 14 hours)
    • Characteristics:
      • Interval from the onset of labor to the beginning of the active phase
      • Contractions start irregularly and become regular and stronger
      • Cervical effacement occurs, with dilation up to 6 cm
  2. Active Phase
    • Cervical Dilation: 6 cm → 10 cm (full dilation)
    • Characteristics:
      • Contractions are regular and stronger, leading to predictable cervical dilation
      • Cervical dilation rate:
        • Primigravida: ~1.2 cm/hour
        • Multigravida: ~1.5 cm/hour
  3. Protraction and Arrest of Labor
    • Protraction: Slower than expected cervical dilation ( <1.2 cm/hr in nulliparous; <1.5 cm/hr in multiparous).
    • Arrest: No cervical change for 2–4 hours despite adequate contractions

References:

Physiology, Cervical Dilation - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

Management of Normal Labor - Gynecology and Obstetrics - MSD Manual Professional Edition

question_text: 18 years old girl with  transverse vaginal septum presents to the hospital with dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. Which of the following is the most common complication?
explanation:
• Transverse vaginal septum is a rare Mullerian anomaly which is related to vertical fusion disorder. It is an uncommon anomaly that is not associated with a well-defined inheritance pattern.
  • The vast majority of these obstructed mullerian duct abnormalities are first seen at puberty.
  • Hematocolpos, hematometra, endometriosis and hematometrocolpos are some of its most common presentations.
  • Some authors have suggested that retrograde flow through the uterus and fallopian tubes could have ocurred earlier. It may even present before puberty.
  • Transverse vaginal septum is infrequently associated with genitourinary tract, gastrointestinal tract, musculoskeletal, and cardiac malformations. However, it is still prudent to work up patients of the possibility of having any concomitant anomaly.
  • The differential diagnosis of transverse vaginal septum includes imperforate hymen, Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome and vaginal agenesis.

question_text: Which of the following structures is attached at cervicovaginal junction
explanation:
Pelvic cellular tissue around the vaginalvault, supravaginal part of the cervix and into the layers of the broad ligament is called parametrium. Condensation occurs especially near the cervicovaginal junction to form ligaments which extend from the viscera to the pelvic walls on either side.

These are

  • Mackenrodt’s ligaments/ cardinal ligament,
  • uterosacral ligaments and
  • vesicocervical ligaments (fascia).

All these constitute important supports of the uterus to keep it in position.
