question_text: A 28-year-old married woman presents requesting termination of an unwanted pregnancy due to contraceptive failure. According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (India), up to what gestational age is MTP legally permitted in such cases?
explanation:
Explanation:

For cases of contraceptive failure, MTP can be performed for up to 20 weeks with approval from a single doctor.

Opinion requirement:

  • Up to 20 weeks → One Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP).
  • 20-24 weeks → Two RMPs required, but only under specific categories (rape survivors, minors, change in marital status, differently-abled women, etc.) → NOT contraceptive failure.
  • Beyond 24 weeks → Allowed only for substantial fetal abnormalities, after approval of a Medical Board.
  • At any gestational age, MTP can be done if continuation poses an immediate threat to maternal life.

Explanation of Other Options:

Option B (24 weeks): Allowed for rape survivors, minors, and specific categories, but contraceptive failure is excluded beyond 20 weeks.

Option C (32 weeks): Not legally permissible under routine circumstances. Only possible if life-saving for the mother or with major fetal anomalies.

Option D (12 weeks): Too restrictive; earlier law (1971 MTP Act) emphasized 12 weeks for medical opinion, but now legally extended.

Key Takeaway Points:

Who Can Perform Abortions:

  • Qualified Practitioners:
    • MBBS doctors with MD/DNB/DGO specialization
    • MBBS doctors with 6 months of training in gynecology
    • MBBS doctors who have performed 25 MTPs under supervision
  • Not Qualified to Perform Abortions:
    • Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA)
    • Practitioners of Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy (AYUSH)

question_text: Which of the following is legally required for termination of pregnancy at 21 weeks in a fetus diagnosed with meningomyelocele?
option_a: Consent of husband with opinion of one doctor
option_b: Her consent with opinion of 2 doctors
explanation:
Explanation:

At 21 weeks gestation, medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) is regulated under the MTP HypertensionAct, 1971 (amended in 2021).

  • For termination between 20-24 weeks, the law requires:
    • Pregnant woman's consent(her autonomy is central).
    • Opinion of two registered medical practitioners (RMPs)that termination is justified on legal grounds.

Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act (1971; Amended 2021):

  • Indications for MTP:
    • Maternal risk(physical/mental health).
    • Fetal risk(e.g., spina bifida, Down syndrome, meningomyelocele).
    • Eugenic reasons(grave anomalies).
    • Humanitarian reasons(pregnancy due to rape, incest, or marital rape - recognized after 2021 amendment).
    • Contraceptive failure(extended to both married and unmarried women after 2021 amendment).

Legal Requirements by Gestational Age:

  • ≤20 weeks:Woman's consent + opinion of one doctor.
  • 20-24 weeks:Woman's consent + opinion of two doctors.
  • >24 weeks:Allowed only if significant fetal anomalies are detected → requires state medical board approval (gynecologist + pediatrician + radiologist + others).

Qualifications to perform MTP:

  • MBBS doctors trained in obstetrics & gynecology.
  • MBBS with 6 months training in gynecology.
  • MBBS who has performed ≥25 MTPs under supervision.
  • Not permitted:AYUSH doctors, ASHAs, untrained practitioners.

Explanation of Other Options:

Consent of husband with opinion of one doctor (Option A): Not legally valid. The husband's consent is not required at any stage of pregnancy under the MTP Act. Only the woman's consent matters.

Opinion of 2 doctors (Option C): This alone is insufficient. Even with two doctors approving, termination cannot proceed without the woman's explicit consent.

All above (Option D): Incorrect because it includes the husband's consent, which is not a legal requirement.

question_text: A woman presents at 10 weeks of gestation and seeks medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). The appropriate choice would be?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of Mifepristone and Misoprostol is the safest and most effective method for medical abortion up to 10 weeks of gestation.

  • For first-trimester medical termination (up to 10 weeks POG), the standard regimen includes:
    • Mifepristone 200 mg orally: An antiprogesterone that sensitizes the myometrium to prostaglandins by blocking progesterone support to the pregnancy.
    • Followed by Misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally or sublingually 24-48 hours later: A prostaglandin E1 analogue that induces uterine contractions to expel the pregnancy.
  • Why this regimen?
    • High efficacy (>95%)
    • Non-invasive
    • Can be used safely in outpatient settings
    • Low complication rate

Medical Abortion Regimens Summary:

Explanation of other options:

Dinoprostone (Option B): Prostaglandin E2 is used mainly in second-trimester abortion or labor induction, not first-trimester MTP.

Oxytocin (Option C): Effective only in later gestation when oxytocin receptors are more abundant. Not used in the early first trimester for abortion.

Intrauterine Hyperosmolar Saline (Option D): Outdated method used for mid-trimester abortions; carries risk of complications like DIC and is not used today for early pregnancy termination.

Explanation:

  • For medical abortion up to 9 weeks of gestation, 800 mcg of misoprostol administered vaginally, buccally, or sublingually after 24-48 hours of mifepristone is the standard regimen.
  • This dosage ensures effective uterine contractions and nearly complete expulsion of the products of conception.
  • Success rates exceed 95% when this protocol is followed

Explanation of Other Options:

200 mcg (Option A): Too low a dose, ineffective for reliable uterine evacuation at 8 weeks.

600 mcg (Option B): Slightly more effective than 200-400 mcg but still inferior to 800 mcg in terms of complete abortion rates.

400 mcg (Option C): Sometimes used orally in very early pregnancies (<7 weeks) due to better tolerance, but has lower efficacy compared to 800 mcg via vaginal/buccal/sublingual routes.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Medical abortion protocol includes mifepristone followed by misoprostol 800 mcg.

Medical Abortion Protocol (up to 9 weeks gestation):

  • Step 1: Mifepristone (200-600 mg orally) → antiprogesterone, blocks pregnancy support.
  • Step 2: Misoprostol (800 mcg mucosal route: vaginal/buccal/sublingual) → prostaglandin E1 analog, induces uterine contractions.

Effectiveness:

  • 99% success within 7 weeks.
  • ~95% success up to 9 weeks.

Pre-requisites before MTP:

  • USG to confirm intrauterine pregnancy and rule out ectopic.
  • Counseling on procedure, expected bleeding, and need for follow-up.
  • Repeat USG after 1-2 weeks to confirm complete expulsion.

question_text: All are causes of Antepartum hemorrhage (APH) except:
explanation:
All of the listed conditions can contribute to antepartum hemorrhage (APH) except for D) Battledore placenta.

Battledore placenta, where the umbilical cord is inserted at the edge of the placenta, is generally not associated with significant bleeding. In contrast, placenta previa, abruptio placenta, and circumvallate placenta can all lead to APH.

Circumvallate placenta

  • It is an uncommon cause of antepartum hemorrhage.
  • In this condition, the chorionic plate which is on the fetal side of the placenta is smaller than the basal plate on the maternal side.
  • The fetal surface of the placenta presents a central depression surrounded by a thickened grayish white ring.
  • These pregnancies may be complicated by IUGR and an increased chance of fetal malformations.
  • Bleeding is usually painless.
  • Antenatal diagnosis is unlikely, and the diagnosis is usually made after examination of the placenta post-delivery.

Reference: Dutta Obs. Te, p 214, 216, 217; Textbook of Obs. by Sheila Balakrishnan, p 155.

question_text: Shoulder dystocia is defined as delay in delivery of shoulders after delivery of head by:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the anterior shoulder fails to deliver after the head due to impaction behind the maternal pubic symphysis.
  • It is clinically defined as failure to deliver the shoulders within 60 seconds after the head, or when additional maneuvers are required beyond gentle traction.
  • A delay beyond 60 seconds increases the risk of complications such as brachial plexus injury, fetal hypoxia, and postpartum hemorrhage.

Explanation of other options:

Option A, B, C are incorrect, as a delay beyond 60 secs is the correct answer.

Key Takeaways:

Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when the fetal shoulders fail to deliver within 60 seconds after the head, requiring additional maneuvers to complete the delivery.

question_text: With reference to fetal heart rate, a nonstress test is considered reactive when:
option_a: Two fetal heart rate accelerations are noted in 20 minutes
option_b: One fetal heart rate acceleration is noted in 20 minutes
option_c: Two fetal heart rate accelerations are noted in 10 minutes
option_d: Three fetal heart rate accelerations are noted in 30 minutes
explanation:
Non Stress Test: It is the most commonly used test for antepartum evaluation of the fetal status.

Principle : The test looks for the presence of temporary accelarations of fetal heart rate (FHR) associated with fetal movement. Presence of spontaneous fetal heart rate acceleration associated with fetal movements is an indicator of fetal well being, likewise the absence of fetal reaction suggests the possibility of fetal hypoxia.

Interpretation: Reactive/Positive NST-2 or more accelerations of at least 15 beats per minute, each lasting for at least 15 seconds and occurring within 20 minutes of the beginning of the test.

If in 20 minutes test is not reactive, do a 20 minute repeat test to account for fetal sleep cycle before concluding the test non reactive.

Reactive test means that the fetus is in no danger for at least 7 days.

Note : Most common condition for nonreactive NST - fetal hypoxia.

Time for performing these test:

  • Testing should begin by 32 weeks
  • In pregnancies with severe complications, begin at 26-28 weeks.

Note : In case test is being performed before 32 weeks, accelerations are defined as having 10 bpm or more above baseline for 10 seconds or longer:

  • Interval between NST testing
    • Ideally -repeated weekly
    • In high risk pregnancies like diabetes mellitus, IUGR and Gestational hypertension! twice weekly

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 108, 109; Williams Obs. 23/e, p 338; Fernando Arias 3/e, p 17

question_text:
A 30-year-old female patient is admitted to the Emergency Department with dyspnea, tachycardia, confusion, and other signs of hypoxia. The following laboratory data were obtained while the patient was breathing room air.
PaO2 = 67 mmHg
PaCO2 = 60 mmHg
pH = 7.27
[HCO3-] = 26 mEq/L
[Hb] = 15 g%
SaO2 = 90%
PvO2 = 30 mmHg
SvO2 = 55%
VO2 = 350 mL/min
CaO2-CvO2 = 7 mL O2/100 mL
Which of the following is the most appropriate classification of the patient's hypoxia?
explanation:
Alveolar hypoventilation (as evidenced by the higher than normal value of Paco2) is a type of hypoxic hypoxia or hypoxemia (as evidenced by the decreased PaO2).

Anemic hypoxia is characterized by a decreased concentration of hemoglobin (anemia) or a reduction in the saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen (SaO2) expected for a given Pao2, as would occur in carbon monoxide poisoning or methemoglobinemia.

Stagnant hypoxia is characterized by a decreased cardiac output; in this patient, cardiac output, calculated as (VO2/CaO2 - CvO2), is 5 L/min, which is normal. In histotoxic hypoxia, oxygen extraction is impaired, and thus CaO2 - CvO2 would be less than normal and Svo2 would be greater than normal.

Reference: Ganong, pp 683-691. Levitzky, pp 180-183.

question_text: A G2P1L1 woman with a previous LSCS presents with antepartum hemorrhage (APH) and required obstetric hysterectomy. A specimen (placenta invading uterine wall) is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis based on clinical history and the specimen image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Placenta accreta syndrome involves abnormal placental adherence to the uterine wall, often necessitating hysterectomy when separation fails, especially in scarred uteri from prior LSCS.

  • Placenta Accreta Syndrome (PAS) is a serious condition where the placenta invades too deeply into the uterine wall, often due to a defective decidua basalis and absence of the Nitabuch layer.
  • It is strongly associated with:
    • Previous cesarean section
    • Placenta previa
    • Uterine surgery/scarring
  • In PAS, manual separation fails, leading to massive hemorrhage, requiring life-saving obstetric hysterectomy.
    • Placenta Accreta Spectrum Variants:
    • Placenta accreta: Chorionic villi adhere to endometrium
    • Placenta increta: Invade into the myometrium
    • Placenta percreta: Penetrate through serosa, possibly bladder
  • Management:
    • Total PAS (e.g., increta/percreta): Immediate hysterectomy, especially in patients with completed family
    • Partial PAS: Attempt conservative management (oxytocics, embolization, MTX)
    • Complicated PAS (e.g., bladder invasion): Hysterectomy with partial cystectomy if needed

Explanation of other options:

Uterine inversion (Option B): Involves turning inside-out of uterus after delivery. Not related to LSCS history or hysterectomy specimens.

Abruptio placenta (Option C): Premature placental separation. Does not require hysterectomy, nor show placental adherence to the uterine wall.

Placenta previa (Option D): Placenta covers cervix → painless APH. Managed via cesarean, not typically associated with hysterectomy or placental invasion.

question_text: While conducting a delivery, you perform the maneuver shown below. Following this, there is incomplete separation of the placenta and massive hemorrhage. What is your next step in management?
option_a: Start oxytocin infusion and wait for spontaneous delivery of the placenta
option_c: Arrange for blood and use Crede's method for placental delivery
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The maneuver shown is the Brandt-Andrews maneuver (controlled cord traction).
  • In this case, incomplete separation of the placenta has led to massive postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to retained placental tissue.
  • The immediate next step is manual removal of the placenta under anesthesia, followed by inspection for retained fragments.

Retained Placenta

  • Definition: Failure to deliver placenta within 30 minutes after birth.
  • Causes:
    • Simple adherent placenta → failure of separation despite normal implantation.
    • Lower uterine segment constriction → placenta trapped.
    • Morbidly adherent placenta (placenta accreta, increta, percreta).

Immediate Action in Hemorrhage

  • Manual removal of placenta is life-saving.
  • Supportive care: blood transfusion, fluid resuscitation, uterotonics after removal.

Types of Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)

  • Primary PPH: Within 24 hours of delivery (most common cause: uterine atony).
  • Secondary PPH: 24 hours to 12 weeks (most common cause: retained placental tissue).

Explanation of other options:

Start oxytocin infusion (Option A): Helpful in atonic PPH, but not effective if mechanical cause (retained placenta).

Uterine massage (Option B): Useful for atonic uterus, not in retained placenta.

Crede's method (Option C): Obsolete and associated with complications; not recommended in modern obstetrics.

Key Takeaway:

  • In cases of incomplete placental separation with massive hemorrhage after Brandt-Andrews maneuver, immediate manual removal of the placenta is the correct management.

Here, the heart rate seems to be within 140-160 bpm, which is normal.(Option B ruled out)

Beat to beat variability can be appreciated here.(Option C ruled out)

question_text: A woman with eclampsia is started on magnesium sulphate. What is the first sign of MgSO<sub>4</sub> toxicity?
explanation:
Monitoring for magnesium toxicity

  • Urine output should be at least 30 ml/hr
  • Deep tendon reflexes(Patellar reflex) should be present
  • Respiration rate should be more than 14/min.
  • Pulse oximetry should be ≥ 96%

Remember

Repeat injection are given only if:

  • Knee jerks are present
  • Urine output > 30 ml/hour
  • Respiratory rate ≥ 14/min

Therapeutic range for MgSO4: 4-7 mEq/l

If MgSO₄ toxicity : Give Calcium Gluconate.

  • Knee Jerk lost >10meq/l(first sign).
  • Resp depression >12meq/l.
  • Resp paralysis >15meq/l.
  • Cardiac arrest >25meq/l.
  • Oliguria is not a sign of toxicity

"Tips & Tricks"

  • Knee Jerk lost >10meq/l(first sign).
  • Resp depression >12meq/l.

question_text: Identify the procedure shown in the image:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image demonstrates Intrauterine Balloon Tamponade for management of PPH.
  • Intrauterine balloon tamponade (IUBT) is used in cases of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony or placental site bleeding when uterotonics fail.
  • It involves inserting a balloon catheter (e.g., Bakri balloon, Sengstaken-Blakemore, or Foley catheter) into the uterus and inflating it with sterile fluid to apply direct pressure on the uterine walls, promoting hemostasis.

Explanation of other options:

Endometrial ablation (Option A): A procedure to destroy the endometrial lining for AUB, however the image shows balloon tamponade for managing PPH.

Cervical ablation (Option C): A treatment for cervical dysplasia, unrelated to uterine hemorrhage.

Punctate packing (Option D): A method of vaginal packing for hemorrhage, different from balloon tamponade.

Key Takeaways:

Intrauterine Balloon Tamponade is a life-saving procedure for PPH by applying direct pressure inside the uterus to control bleeding.

question_text: A female patient with postpartum hemorrhage has received oxytocin and ergometrine, but bleeding persists. Which prostaglandin derivative is appropriate to control the ongoing hemorrhage?
explanation:
Explanation :

Carboprost Tromethamine is a prostaglandin F2α analogue indicated for refractory postpartum hemorrhage after oxytocin and ergometrine. It stimulates strong tetanic uterine contractions, effectively controlling bleeding that persists despite first- and second-line therapy.

Dosage: 250 µg IM, repeatable every 15-90 min (maximum 8 doses)

Side Effects:

  • Diarrhea, vomiting, fever, flushing
  • Tachycardia, pulmonary constriction

Contraindications:

  • Asthma
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Severe renal, hepatic, or cardiac disease
  • Suspected amniotic fluid embolism

Uterotonic Agents for PPH Management

First-Line Agent:
Oxytocin

  • WHO recommended first-line prophylaxis for PPH
  • Dosage:20 units in 1000 mL crystalloid IV at 10 mL/min (200 mU/min)
  • IM administration alternative if IV access unavailable
  • Avoid undiluted IV bolus (risk of hypotension, arrhythmias)
  • Indicated for initiation or ongoing uterine atony

Second-Line Agents:
Ergot Alkaloids (Ergonovine / Methylergonovine - Methergine)

  • Induce rapid tetanic uterine contractions (~45 min)
  • Dosage:2 mg IM, repeatable every 2-4 h
  • Contraindications:Hypertension, preeclampsia, concomitant HIV protease inhibitors

Prostaglandins:

  • Carboprost:Effective in refractory PPH (see above)
  • Misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1 analogue):600-1000 µg rectally, orally, or sublingually; mainly prophylactic, limited role in treatment
  • Dinoprostone (Prostaglandin E2):20 mg rectally/vaginally every 2 h; hypotension risk; rarely used for PPH
  • Latanoprost:Ophthalmic prostaglandin F2α analogue; no role in PPH management

Explanation of Other Options:

Dinoprostone (Option A):Prostaglandin E2 derivative, mainly used for labor induction; hypotension risk limits its use in PPH.

Misoprostol (Option B): Prostaglandin E1 analogue; used prophylactically or for prevention of PPH but less effective for treatment after oxytocin and ergometrine.

Latanoprost (Option C): Prostaglandin F2α analogue designed for ophthalmic use (glaucoma); not used in PPH.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman who is 3 months' postpartum comes to the OPD complaining of tiredness, she has had no periods since the baby was born and she has been unable to breast-feed because of a lack of milk production. You notice in her case sheet that she required a blood transfusion after delivery for postpartum hemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Sheehan's syndrome is hypopituitarism following pregnancy complicated by hemorrhage at the time of delivery. The hemorrhage and associated hypotension is thought to cause pituitary infarction. Patients fail to lactate and remain amenorrhoeic post delivery, and also develop other pituitary hormone deficiencies of the thyroid and adrenal axis.
  • Nelson's syndrome is seen in patients with pituitary-driven Cushing's syndrome many years after bilateral adrenalectomy. Such patients are deeply pigmented.
  • Empty sella syndrome is associated with hypopituitarism, imaging of the pituitary fossa shows no obvious pituitary tissue. It is idiopathic.
  • Lymphocytic hypophysitis is an inflammation of pituitary gland occurring in the 3rd trimester or postpartum females. They tend to present with mass effects and features of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency commonly ACTH and TSH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2897

question_text: Which of the following is the correct definition of postpartum pyrexia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Postpartum pyrexia (puerperal fever) is defined as:

  • Temperature > 100.4°F (38°C)
  • Occurring from the first to the tenth day postpartum
  • Must be documented on at least two occasions
  • Excludes the first 24 hours postpartum, as early postpartum temperature rise can be physiological

Clinical Significance:

  • Early indicator of postpartum infections
  • Requires careful monitoring and evaluation
  • Early detection can prevent severe complications such as sepsis

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Option B (After 6 hours), Option C (After 3 hours), Option D (After 12 hours):
    • Incorrect because the first 24 hours postpartum are excluded when defining postpartum pyrexia.
    • Early postpartum temperature fluctuations are often physiological and not indicative of infection.

Key Takeaway Points:

Normal Puerperium:

  • Duration: Delivery → 42 days (6 weeks)
  • Woman remains immunocompromised, requiring careful monitoring

Common Causes of Puerperal Fever:

  • Endometritis - most common cause
  • Breast engorgement
  • Respiratory infection
  • Pyelonephritis
  • Thrombophlebitis

Postpartum pyrexia is a red flag for infection; investigation should follow after 24 hours if fever persists.

question_text: Which is not primary amenorrhea?
explanation:
• Kallmann’s syndrome is due to hypothalamic dysfunction characterised by a deficiency of gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) causing a hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. This is associated with anosmia. It can occasionally be associated with optic problems, such as color blindness or optic atrophy, nerve deafness, cleft palate, cryptorchidism, renal agenesis, and mirror movement disorder.
  • MRKH syndrome, also known as Mullerian agenesis, is due to anatomical absence of the uterus. This is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhea
  • Turner’s syndrome is a type of gonadal dysgenesis and is overall the most common cause of primary amenorrhea
  • Sheehan’s syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis. It leads to secondary amenorrhea and not primary amenorrhea.

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed, Page no:96-97

question_text: Which of the following statements is true about primary postpartum haemorrhage
option_b: Can only be diagnosed after delivery of placenta
option_c: Can be a consequence of antepartum haemorrhage
explanation:
C) Can be a consequence of antepartum hemorrhage.

Primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined as excessive bleeding occurring within the first 24 hours after delivery. It can result from various causes, including uterine atony (the most common cause), lacerations, and retained placental tissue. Antepartum hemorrhage (bleeding before delivery) can sometimes lead to complications during delivery, including an increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage, but PPH itself typically occurs after delivery.

Primary PPH: Hemorrhage occurs within 24 hours following the birth of the baby

  • Third stage haemorrhage: before delivery of placenta
  • True PPH: after delivery of placenta

Secondary PPH: after 24 hrs within puerperium

Option A is incorrect because PPH occurs within the first 24 hours after delivery, not 72 hours.

Option B is incorrect because PPH can be diagnosed and managed during and after the delivery of the placenta.

Option D is incorrect because the management of PPH may involve various approaches, and general anesthesia (GA) in the operating theater (OT) is not always required. The management depends on the cause and severity of the hemorrhage, and it may involve uterine massage, medications, or surgical interventions, among other measures.

Reference: D C Dutta's textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 28

question_text: Likely size of uterus at 8 weeks postpartum is:
explanation:
Weight of uterus :

  • Immediately after delivery - 1000 gm
  • At the end of 1 week - 500 gm
  • At the end of 2 weeks - 300 gm
  • At the end of 4 weeks it weighs - 100 gm (Pre-pregnant state).

Also Know :

  • Immediately following delivery, the fundus is just below the umbilicus (13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis/ 20 weeks gestational age size.)

Involution of the uterus

  • After 24 hours of delivery, height of uterus decreases by 1.25 cm/day.
  • Uterus is a pelvic to organ. by the end of 2 weeks.
  • Uterus returns almost to its normal size (pre pregnant size) by the end of 8 weeks.
  • The process by which the postpartum uterus returns to its pre pregnant state is called Involution.
  • Involution is achieved by decrease in the size of muscle fibres (and not in the number).

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 145; Williams Obs. 24/e, pg 669

question_text: The cause of 'postpartum blues' is:
explanation:
Puerperal Blues/3 Days Blues/Baby Blues

  • It is a transient state of mental illness observed 4-5 days after delivery in nearly 50% of postpartum women.
  • Postpartum blues occurs at the height of hormonal changes. -COGDT 10/e, pg 1025
  • Patients present with depression, anxiety, fearfulness, insomnia, helplessness and negative feelings towards infants.
  • It may last from a few days to 2-3 weeks.
  • Generally self limited, 20% of women may develop depression in the first postpartum year.

Treatment: Reassurance and psychological support of family members.

Postpartum Depression

  • It is observed in 10-20% of mothers.
  • It is more gradual in onset over the first 4-6 months following delivery or abortion.
  • Changes in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis may be a cause.
  • Manifested by loss of energy and appetite, insomnia, social withdrawal, irritability and even suicidal attitude.
  • Risk of recurrence 50-100% in subsequent pregnancies.

Treatment: Should be started early. Fluoxetine or paroxetine is effective and has fewer side effects.

Reference: Dutta Obs 7/e, pg 443; COGDT 10/e, pg 1020

question_text: What is the level of the uterus on postpartum day 2?
option_a: Two finger breadths below the umbilicus
option_b: One finger breadth below the umbilicus
option_c: Three finger breadths below the umbilicus
option_d: Four finger breadths below the umbilicus
explanation:
Explanation:

  • After delivery, the uterus begins involution, reducing in size day by day.
  • Immediately after delivery: Uterus is at or just below the umbilicus, corresponding to ~20 weeks gestation size.
  • By postpartum day 2: The fundus lies two finger breadths (≈2 cm) below the umbilicus.
  • Thereafter, the fundus descends about 1 finger breadth (≈1 cm) per day until it is no longer palpable abdominally by 2 weeks postpartum.

Key Takeaway:

  • On postpartum day 2, the uterus is two finger breadths below the umbilicus and continues to descend ~1 cm/day.

question_text: Primary amenorrhoea with anosmia is seen in:
explanation:
Laurence Moon Biedl Syndrome

It is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by GnRH deficiency (hypogonadism) (FSH < 40 mIU/ml) and associated with:

  • Obesity
  • Mental retardation
  • Polydactyly
  • Retinitis Pigmentosa

Sheehan's syndrome:

  • It is the syndrome which results from ischaemic necrosis of most of the anterior pituitary due to spasm in its arterioles occurring at the time of severe haemorrhage or shock complicating childbirth.
  • Only the anterior pituitary is affected because in parturient woman, blood supply to the pituitary gland is modified to the advantage of the posterior lobe and disadvantage of the anterior lobe so, when spasm occurs, the posterior lobe is protected.
  • When 75% of anterior pituitary is destroyed, manifestations of Sheehan's syndrome appear and when 95% is destroyed - fully developed Simmond's syndrome is seen.
  • Hormones of anterior pituitary are affected in order of frequency = GH, FSH, and LH, TSH and ACTH

Foster Kennedy Syndrome:

  • Do not get confused with this option: It is the same Foster Kennedy Syndrome as you have read in Ophthalmology, characterised by papilloedema in one eye and optic atrophy in the other. It results from raised intracranial pressure and simultaneous optic nerve compression secondary to tumor - classically, a meningioma of the olfactory groove, or more commonly, due to meningioma of the sphenoid wing.

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed, pg no: 70

question_text: Which of the following iron preparations cannot be used intramuscularly?
explanation:
Ferric carboxymaltose is a stable, non-dextran intravenous (IV) complex of ferric hydroxide and carbohydrate polymer.
It is designed specifically for intravenous use only due to its high molecular weight and poor intramuscular absorption.

  • Mechanism: When given IV, it releases iron slowly for uptake by reticuloendothelial macrophages, allowing large single doses (up to 1000 mg over 15 minutes) without anaphylaxis risk.
  • IM administration is contraindicated because:
    • It causes severe local pain and tissue necrosis.
    • The large molecular complex is not absorbed effectively from muscle tissue.
    • Risk of skin staining and abscess formation if injected intramuscularly.
  • Clinical use: Preferred for rapid iron repletion in CKD, IBD, postpartum anemia, or intolerance to oral iron.
  • Hence, ferric carboxymaltose is IV-only; it must not be used intramuscularly.

Iron Dextran (Option A): Can be given both IM and IV. IM route requires Z-track technique to prevent staining; test dose needed due to risk of anaphylaxis from dextran component.
Iron Sorbitol (Option B): Commonly used IM preparation (2 mL = 100 mg Fe). Usually given deep IM in the gluteal region. Less anaphylactic risk than dextran, but causes local pain and discoloration.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman undergoes a cesarean section for obstructed labour. Intraoperatively, she develops severe atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), which does not respond to uterotonics, including oxytocin and uterine massage. Her vitals are borderline stable. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

In cases of severe atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) unresponsive to uterotonics and uterine massage, surgical interventions are the next step before resorting to hysterectomy.

  • Uterine artery ligation can be performed unilaterally or bilaterally.
  • It is particularly effective for hemorrhage related to uterine incision lacerations and atony.
  • The mechanism is reduction of uterine arterial blood flow, lowering perfusion pressure and allowing clot formation.
  • Importantly, it is a fertility-sparing procedure, unlike hysterectomy, and is often chosen as the next line in borderline stable patients.

Thus, in this patient who is young, hemodynamically borderline stable, and desiring future fertility, uterine artery ligation is the next best step.

Explanation for other Options:

B-Lynch compression suture (Option A): Useful for atonic PPH, but typically done before opening additional vascular planes. Since the patient is already in laparotomy (cesarean), it can be considered, but ligation is usually more definitive in ongoing severe bleeding when conservative uterotonics fail.

Internal iliac artery ligation (Option C): Can reduce pulse pressure by 85% in distal vessels, but the procedure is technically difficult, with success in only ~50% of cases. It is usually reserved for refractory hemorrhage after uterine artery ligation or in cases like placenta previa/accreta.

Emergency hysterectomy (Option D):

This is the last resort, performed when conservative and fertility-sparing measures fail. Since the patient is young and vitals are borderline stable, less radical options (uterine artery ligation) are preferred first.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in a hypertensive woman with postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Methergine (Methylergometrine) is contraindicated in hypertensive patients because it causes intense vasoconstriction, which can significantly elevate blood pressure and increase the risk of cerebrovascular accidents (stroke).

Methergine belongs to the ergot alkaloid group and acts on alpha-adrenergic and serotonin receptors, producing powerful uterotonic and vasoconstrictive effects. While it effectively controls postpartum bleeding by contracting the uterus, its hypertensive potential makes it unsafe for women with pre-existing hypertension or preeclampsia.

Explanation for Other Options:

Carboprost (Option A): A prostaglandin F₂α analogue that promotes uterine contraction and is effective for managing PPH.
It is safe in hypertension, but should be used cautiously in patients with asthma due to risk of bronchospasm.

Oxytocin (Option B): The first-line drug for prevention and treatment of PPH.
It stimulates rhythmic uterine contractions and is safe in hypertensive patients.

Prostaglandins (Option D): Includes agents like misoprostol and carboprost, which help contract the uterus to reduce bleeding. They are not contraindicated in hypertension.

Key takeaway:

  • Methergine is a uterotonic agent used to manage postpartum hemorrhage, but it must not be given to hypertensive women because of its vasoconstrictive action.
  • Safe alternatives in hypertensive patients include Oxytocin and Prostaglandin analogues (e.g., misoprostol, carboprost).

Reference:

 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9941051/

question_text:
A 30-year-old woman with a previous history of dilatation and curettage (D&C) now presents with absence of menstruation. Her urine pregnancy test is negative, and hysterosalpingography (HSG) reveals a honeycomb-like pattern within the uterine cavity.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The woman has secondary amenorrhea following D&C, and the honeycomb appearance on HSG indicates intrauterine adhesions-a hallmark of Asherman syndrome. This condition arises due to the formation of fibrous scar tissue within the uterine cavity, most commonly after uterine procedures, infections, or trauma, leading to menstrual disturbances or infertility.

Explanation for other options:

Kallman syndrome (option B): This disorder is characterised by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia (loss of smell). Since the case lacks any mention of olfactory disturbance or pituitary hormone deficiency, this diagnosis is unlikely.

Sheehan syndrome (option C): Occurs after severe postpartum haemorrhage, causing ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary. It leads to hormonal insufficiency and amenorrhea. However, the patient's history does not include any postpartum haemorrhage, ruling out this possibility.

Stein-Leventhal syndrome (option D): Also known as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), it is associated with features such as hyperandrogenism, anovulation, and polycystic ovaries on imaging. The absence of these findings makes PCOS an incorrect diagnosis in this case.

question_text: Which of the following is NOT a complication of blood transfusion in a 25-year-old mother who developed acute postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), hypovolemic shock, and underwent major blood transfusion after delivering a baby boy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hypokalemia is not seen with blood transfusions. Stored blood undergoes a gradual leakage of potassium from red blood cells into the storage solution due to impaired cell membrane integrity over time. Consequently, transfused blood often has elevated potassium levels.
  • During a massive blood transfusion, the extracellular potassium that has leaked from stored red blood cells is directly infused into the recipient, significantly increasing the risk of transfusion-associated hyperkalemia, which can provoke dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.
  • Simultaneously, the citrate anticoagulant present in transfused blood binds to and chelates circulating calcium, leading to ionized hypocalcemia that may cause neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias, and hypotension.
  • Additionally, the rapid infusion of cold stored blood can induce hypothermia, further impairing coagulation, enzymatic function, and cardiac output.
  • Thus, the primary electrolyte and metabolic threats in this setting are hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia, accompanied by the risk of hypothermia.(Option A C and D are ruled out).

Key takeaways:

  • Complications of Massive Blood Transfusion

question_text: What is the purpose of this manoeuvre?
option_a: To rotate the fetal head during delivery
option_c: To prevent perineal trauma during delivery
explanation:
Explanation:

Ritgen's maneuver is used in the second stage of labor when the fetal head is crowning and the vaginal introitus is stretched to ≥5 cm. The technique involves placing gloved fingers behind the anus to apply upward pressure on the fetal chin, while the other hand exerts gentle counterpressure on the occiput.

  • This coordinated action helps control the speed of head delivery, preventing sudden expulsion.
  • By maintaining flexion of the head, it ensures that the smallest diameter of the fetal head passes through the birth canal.
  • The maneuver aims to minimize overstretching of the perineum, reducing the likelihood of third- or fourth-degree perineal tears (obstetric anal sphincter injuries, OASIS).
  • Although it helps in controlled delivery, studies show it does not significantly reduce the overall incidence of OASIS, but it still plays a role in perineal protection.
  • If expulsive efforts are weak or delivery needs to be expedited, Ritgen's maneuver can also assist in completing delivery quickly without aggressive traction.

Explanation for other Options:

To rotate the fetal head during delivery (Option A): This is incorrect because Ritgen's maneuver does not rotate the fetal head. Instead, it controls the flexion and gradual delivery of the head. Rotation maneuvers are used in malpositions or shoulder dystocia, not here.

To reduce postpartum haemorrhage (Option B): This is incorrect because postpartum hemorrhage is mainly related to uterine atony, trauma, or retained tissue. Ritgen's maneuver has no role in preventing uterine bleeding.

To manage shoulder dystocia (Option D): This is incorrect because shoulder dystocia requires maneuvers like McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, Rubin's, or Woods' corkscrew. Ritgen's maneuver is performed for controlled head delivery, not for shoulder release.

question_text: What is the typical duration of lochial discharge in a postpartum woman?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lochia is the vaginal discharge that occurs in the early postpartum period due to the shedding of decidual tissue. It typically lasts up to 35 days and has a characteristic offensive, fishy odor.

On average, lochial discharge continues for about 4 to 6 weeks, with the following phases based on color and duration:

  • Lochia rubra (reddish): Seen from day 1 to 4 postpartum
  • Lochia serosa (yellowish/pink/brown): Seen from day 5 to 9
  • Lochia alba (whitish): Seen from day 10 to 15, though it may persist longer in some women

So, the average duration of lochial discharge in a puerperal woman is up to 4-6 weeks, with lochia serosa and alba typically observed between day 5 and day 15. (Options B, C & D ruled out)

question_text: As a senior resident in obstetrics and gynaecology, in which of the following scenarios would uterine artery embolisation (UAE) not be an appropriate treatment option?
option_b: Before the removal of placenta accreta in a multiparous woman
option_c: Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
explanation:
Explanation:

Calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids are fibroids with a stalk projecting into the uterine cavity. These are better managed surgically, such as by hysteroscopic resection, rather than using UAE.

UAE is generally indicated for:

  • Large intramural fibroids
  • Multiple fibroids are causing menstrual bleeding or pelvic pain.

Fibroid (Uterine Leiomyoma)

  • Nature: Benign smooth muscle tumour of the uterus, estrogen-dependent
  • Common in: Reproductive-age women
  • Symptoms:
    • Menorrhagia
    • Dysmenorrhea
    • Pelvic pain/pressure
    • Dyspareunia
    • Urinary symptoms
    • Infertility or recurrent miscarriage
  • Complications:
    • Anaemia from chronic bleeding
    • Red degeneration
    • Torsion (pedunculated fibroids)
    • Rare malignant transformation (<1%)

FIGO Classification of Fibroids:



Pedunculated fibroids (Type 0) have a stalk and are prone to torsion or degeneration, requiring direct surgical removal.

  • UAE targets fibroids within the uterine wall, not those projecting into the cavity.

Explanation for other options:

Patient with postpartum haemorrhage (Option A): Controls bleeding by reducing uterine blood flow.

Before the removal of placenta accreta in a multiparous woman (Option B): Preoperative UAE reduces bleeding risk during surgical removal.

Multiparous woman with menorrhagia (Option D): Reduces fibroid size and alleviates symptoms.

question_text: Which of the following maternal conditions is not associated with preterm labor?
explanation:
Maternal risk factors

  2. Uterine anomalies: Cervical incompetence, malformation of uterus;

question_text: A 30-year-old G2P1 previous preterm delivery comes for an antenatal visit at 20 weeks of gestation. She denies having any abdominal pain or vaginal discharge. Her TVS done at 19 weeks of gestation reveals cervical length 2 cm and funneling of internal OS. On per speculum examination, herniation of membranes is seen from cervical OS. What would be the best management option for such a patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The best management for this patient is Cervical Cerclage.

Diagnosis: Cervical Incompetence (Insufficiency)

The clinical presentation is classic for cervical incompetence:

  1. History: Previous preterm delivery.
  2. Timing: Mid-trimester (20 weeks).
  3. Symptoms: Painless cervical dilation (no abdominal pain).
  4. Ultrasound Findings: Shortened cervical length (< 25 mm) and "funneling" of the internal os.
  5. Physical Exam: Dilated cervix with herniation of amniotic membranes.

Management:

Since the pregnancy is in the mid-trimester (typically 14-24 weeks) and the membranes are intact but bulging, a Rescue (Emergency) Cerclage is indicated to mechanically close the cervix and prolong the pregnancy.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Tocolytic drugs only (Option A): Tocolytics are used to stop uterine contractions in preterm labor. This patient has no pain or contractions, suggesting the pathology is structural weakness of the cervix, not active labor. Tocolytics may be used adjunctively after cerclage to prevent procedure-related contractions, but they are not the primary treatment for structural incompetence.
  • Tocolytic drugs and steroids (Option B) & Steroids only (Option C): Corticosteroids (e.g., Betamethasone) are administered to accelerate fetal lung maturity. Standard guidelines recommend administration between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation. At 20 weeks, the fetus is considered pre-viable, and lung maturity is not the immediate priority; mechanical retention of the pregnancy is.

Key Takeaway:

Cervical incompetence presents as painless cervical dilation in the mid-trimester. The diagnostic criteria include a cervical length < 25 mm and funneling. The treatment of choice for a dilated cervix with bulging membranes before viability is Rescue Cerclage.

question_text: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks of gestation presented to the OPD with laboratory findings showing LDH 700 IU/L, platelets 75,000/mm³, serum bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL, SGOT 200 U/L, SGPT 150 U/L, and blood pressure 140/96 mm Hg. Her coagulation profile and renal function tests were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient has:
    • High LDH → Hemolysis
    • Thrombocytopenia (platelets 75,000/mm³)
    • Elevated AST/ALT → Liver injury
    • Hypertension (140/96 mmHg)
  • Together, these are characteristic of HELLP syndrome, a severe complication of preeclampsia.

HELLP Syndrome

  • Definition: Rare complication of preeclampsia, usually in the 3rd trimester
  • Features:
    • H: Hemolysis
    • EL: Elevated liver enzymes
    • LP: Low platelets
  • Risk factors: Age >35, multiparity, diabetes, kidney disease, prior HELLP
  • Symptoms: RUQ/epigastric pain, headache, blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, edema
  • Maternal complications: DIC, liver failure, renal failure, pulmonary edema, eclampsia
  • Fetal complications: Growth restriction, preterm birth, respiratory distress
  • Treatment:
    • MgSO4 → Prevent seizures
    • Antihypertensives → BP control
    • <34 weeks: Corticosteroids for lung maturity
    • Definitive treatment: Termination of pregnancy

Explanation of other options:

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (Option B): Typically shows very high AST/ALT and normal LDH; hypertension is not common. Platelet count usually not as low as in HELLP.

Viral hepatitis (Option C): Transaminases are extremely high (2000+ U/L); platelet count usually preserved. No hypertension in typical viral hepatitis.

Intrahepatic cholestasis (Option D): Presents with pruritus and markedly elevated bile acids/bilirubin; LDH is normal, and no hypertension or hemolysis.

Key Takeaway:

  • HELLP syndrome = Hemolysis + Elevated Liver enzymes + Low Platelets, usually in the setting of preeclampsia.

Reference:

  1. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21637-hellp-syndrome

question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the fetal fibronectin (fFN) test?
option_a: In this test fFN is measured from maternal serum
option_b: Positive test in first trimester increases risk of abortion
option_c: Negative test means delivery will not occur in next 7 days
explanation:
Fibronectin is a glycoprotein that binds the fetal membranes to the decidua. Normally it is found in the cervicovaginal discharge before 22 weeks and again after 37 weeks of pregnancy. Presence of fibronectin in the cervicovaginal discharge between 24 weeks and 34 weeks is a predictor of preterm labor. When the test is negative it reassures that delivery will not occur within the next 7 days.

question_text: Which layer of myometrium is described as 'living ligature' of uterus
explanation:
3 layers of uterus

  • Endometrium
  • Myometrium
  • Perimetrium/serosal

Layers of myometrium

  • Outer longitudinal
  • Middle interlacing
  • Inner circular

The middle layer is the thickest of the three and consists of bundles of muscle separated by connective tissue. There is a tendency for the muscle bundles to interlace, and as the blood vessels which supply the uterus are distributed in the connective tissues, the caliber of the vessels is in part controlled by the contraction of the muscle cells. The purpose of this layer is therefore in part hemostatic. This layer is described as living ligatures of the uterus, and is responsible for control of bleeding in the third stage of labor.

Reference: Shaw’s textbook of gynecology, 16th edition, chapter 1

question_text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding obstructive uterine rupture?
option_a: Occurs in cases of obstructed labor
option_c: Margins of rupture are ragged and necrosed
option_d: FHS is absent in all cases
explanation:
Obstructive rupture-This is the end result of an obstructed labor. The rupture involves the anterior lower segment and usually extends through one lateral side of the uterus to the upper segment. The margins are ragged and necrosed.

Nonobstructive rupture-Grand multipara are usually affected and rupture usually occurs in early labor. Weakening of the walls due to repeated previous births as mentioned earlier may be the responsible factor. The rupture usually involves the fundal area and is complete.

question_text: The following statements are related to the management of obstructed labour except:
option_a: There is no place of wait and watch policy
option_b: Dehydration and ketoacidosis should be promptly corrected
option_c: Oxytocin has got a definite place in the management
explanation:
Management of obstructed labor:

  • Prompt Management of dehydration and ketoacidosis—by giving IV fluids
  • Antibiotics are given to prevent infection
  • Most important step is to relieve obstruction by either instrumental delivery or by doingLSCS. LSCS may even have to be done, if the baby is dead to relieve the obstruction otherwise uterine rupture can occur.

The two main principles in the management of obstructed labor are:

  • Never wait and watch
  • Never use oxytocin

Reference: Dutta Obs 7/e, p 59

question_text: Regarding use of glucocorticoid in preterm labor, which of the following statements is true?
option_a: It reduces incidence of IVH in preterm baby
option_b: Injection betamethasone is given as 6 mg IM 4 doses
option_c: Injection dexamethasone is given as 12 mg IM 2 doses
explanation:
Glucocorticoid therapy:

Maternal administration of glucocorticoids is advocated where the pregnancy is less than 34 weeks. This helps in fetal lung maturation so that the incidence of RDS, IVH and NEC are minimized. This is beneficial when the delivery is delayed beyond 48 hours of the first dose. Benefit persists as long as 18 days. Either betamethasone (Betnesol) 12 mg IM 24 hours apart for two doses of dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses is given. Betamethasone is the steroid of choice (RCOG – 2004).

Reference: D C Dutta’s textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 22

question_text: A 22-year-old primigravida patient came to hospital at 35 weeks of gestation complaining of abdominal pain. She denied having any vaginal discharge. She had regular uterine contraction and her cervical length was 2 cm in TVS. Obstetrician performed fFN test which was positive. What would be the most probable diagnosis for such a patient?
explanation:
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (2020e) defines preterm labor to be regular contractions accompanied by a change in cervical dilation, effacement, or both or to be regular contractions and cervical dilation of at least 2 cm at initial presentation.

fFN: Detected in cervicovaginal secretions in women who have normal pregnancies with intact membranes at term, fFN appears to reflect stromal remodeling of the cervix before labor.

Reference: Williams obstetrics 26th edition, chapter 45

question_text: Prolonged rupture of membrane is defined as:
option_a: Rupture of membrane 24 hr before delivery
option_c: Rupture of membrane before 37 completed week
option_d: Rupture of membrane before active stage of labor
explanation:
Spontaneous rupture of the membranes any time beyond 28th week of pregnancy but before the onset of labor is called prelabor rupture of the membranes (PROM).

When rupture of membranes occurs beyond 37th week but before the onset of labor, it is called term PROM and when it occurs before 37 completed weeks, it is called preterm PROM.

Rupture of membranes for > 24 hours before delivery is called prolonged rupture of membranes.

Reference: D C Dutta’s textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 22

question_text: 37 weeks presents with transverse presentation, TOC is:
explanation:
• ECV – provided there is a good amount of liquor with intact membrane, adequate size baby,not in active labour and there is no contraindication.
  • ECV should be tried in all cases.
  • LSCS – is the preferred method of delivery, if the version fails or is contraindicated.
  • Onset of active labor in a woman with a transverse lie is an indication for cesarean delivery.

Late labor:

  • Baby alive – If the baby is mature and the fetal condition is good, it is preferable to do LSCS in all cases.
  • Baby dead – LSCS even in such cases, is much safer in the hands of those who are not conversant with destructive operations. Following destructive operation, the uterine cavity is to be explored to exclude rupture of the uterus.
  • Before labor or early in labor, with the membranes intact, attempts at an external version are worth trying in absence of other complications that indicate cesarean section.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 397

question_text: MgSo₄ in preterm labor is given for:
explanation:
Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection: Very-low-birthweight neonates whose mothers were treated with magnesium sulfate for preterm labor or preeclampsia were found to have a reduced incidence of cerebral palsy at 3 years

question_text: Diagnostic criteria for preterm labor include all of the following except:
option_c: Regular uterine contraction without cervical changes
option_d: Length of cervix < 2.5 cm on TVS
explanation:
DIAGNOSIS OF PRETERM LABOR:

  1. Regular uterine contractions with or without pain (at least one in every 10 minutes);
  2. Dilatation (> 2 cm) and effacement (80%) of the cervix;
  3. Length of the cervix (measured by TVS) < 2.5 cm and funneling of the internal os and
  4. Pelvic pressure, backache and/or vaginal discharge or bleeding.

Reference: D C Dutta’s textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 22

explanation:
• Women who have a history of recurrent second-trimester loss and who are diagnosed with cervical insufficiency.
  • Woman identified during sonographic examination to have a short cervix. 
  • The third indication is a "rescue" cerclage, done emergently when cervical incompetence is recognized in women with threatened preterm labor.
