question_text: An asymptomatic 29 year old pregnant woman presents in the 1st trimester with urine culture showing >/= 10^5 CFU/ml E. coli. The most common complication associated with this is:
explanation:
Explanation:

Asymptomatic bacteriuria

  • >/= 10^5 CFU/ml of single uropathogen in a clean catch urine sample
  • Most common in High-risk women
    • Low socioeconomic status
    • Diabetes
    • Urinary tract anomalies
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Vesicoureteral reflux
    • Urinary stasis
  • Can cause pyelonephritis if left untreated
  • Associated complications:
    • Pyelonephritis (most common)
    • Preterm labor (2nd most common) (Option C)
    • Low birth weight
    • Preeclampsia
    • Perinatal mortality (Option D ruled out)
    • Abortions(Option B ruled out)
    • Chorioamnionitis (Option A ruled out)
  • Screening:
    • First prenatal visit, ideally 12-16 weeks POG
  • Diagnosis
    • Midstream fresh catch urine
    • Urine culture
    • Urine microscopy
  • Treatment:
    • Treat all cases to prevent progression for 1 week
    • Nitrofurantoin
    • Amocicillin-clavulanate
    • Cephalexin
    • Avoid: Fluoroquinolones – teratogenic (tendon rupture)

question_text: Mgso<sub>4</sub> false statement?
option_a: Mgso<sub>4</sub> causes uterine relaxation but dose dependant
option_b: Mgso<sub>4</sub> in renal failure loading dose can be given but maintenance dose should be adjusted based on renal function
explanation:
• MgSO₄ is the drug of choice for prevention and management of convulsions in eclampsia.
  • MgSO4 controls seizures but does not control hypertension.
  • MgSO4 is used as a tocolytic for uterine relaxation but this action is dose dependent.(Option A) The tocolytic of choice is Nifedipine.
  • MgSO4 acts as a neuroprotective agent and hence controls seizure in eclamptic patient and also used in preterm babies if born before 32 weeks POG.(Option D)

Mechanism of action:

  • It decreases the acetylcholine release from the nerve endings and decreases the sensitivity of motor end plate to Ach.
  • Blocks the calcium channel and decreases intracranial

Regimens for MgSO₄:

Therapeutic range - 4 to 7 mEq/L

  • There is a narrow range at which therapeutic effect and toxic effects of Magnesium occurs, therefore monitoring for magnesium toxicity is very important.
  • In patients with renal failure, Loading dose of MgSO4 can be given but the maintenance dose needs to be adjusted based on renal function(Option B)

Monitoring for magnesium toxicity

  • Urine output should be at least 30 ml/hr
  • Deep tendon reflexes (Patellar reflex) should be present
  • Respiration rate should be more than 14/min.
  • Pulse oximetry should be ³ 96%

Remember

Repeat injection are given only if:

  • Knee jerks are present
  • Urine output > 30 ml/hour
  • Respiratory rate ³ 14/min

MgS04 loading dose depends on volume of distribution whereas maintenance dose depends on clearance of the drug.

MgS04 in renal failure: loading dose can be given but maintenance dose should be adjusted based on renal function.

question_text: All the following are known causes of preterm labour except:
explanation:
The most important risk factor for preterm labour is a prior preterm birth.

History:

  1. Previous history of induced or spontaneous abortion or preterm delivery;
  2. Pregnancy following assisted reproductive techniques (ART);
  3. Asymptomatic bacteriuria or recurrent urinary tract infections;
  4. Smoking habits
  5. Low socioeconomic and nutritional status, and
  6. Maternal stress.

Fetal:

  • Multiple pregnancy, congenital malformations, and intrauterine death.

Placental:

  • Infarction, thrombosis, placenta previa or abruption.

Reference: D C Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics, 8th Edition, Chapter 22

question_text: A 28-year-old woman with a 10-week intrauterine gestation presents to the OPD with an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) in place. The IUCD thread is clearly visible. She expresses her desire to continue the pregnancy. What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Leave IUCD inside and continue pregnancy with prophylactic antibiotics
option_b: Leave IUCD inside and continue pregnancy
option_c: Remove IUCD immediately and continue with pregnancy
option_d: Termination of pregnancy due to risk of infection
explanation:
Explanation:

If the IUCD thread is visible and the woman wishes to continue the pregnancy, the IUCD should be removed immediately to reduce the risk of miscarriage and infection.

  • Pregnancy with an IUCD in situ carries significant risks including miscarriage, intrauterine infection, preterm labor, and intrauterine growth restriction.
  • When the IUCD thread is visible and easily accessible, removal during the first trimester is the recommended management.
  • This significantly improves pregnancy outcomes and reduces complications compared to leaving the IUCD in place.
  • Removal should be performed carefully to avoid disruption of the gestational sac.
  • If the IUCD cannot be safely removed (e.g., no visible thread or device embedded), options depend on IUCD position and patient preference.
  • If removal isn't feasible and the patient still wishes to continue the pregnancy, close monitoring is required.
  • Management algorithm:
    • Thread visible: Remove IUCD immediately.
    • Thread not visible, IUCD not fundal: Attempt ultrasound-guided removal or offer termination.
    • Thread not visible, IUCD in fundus: May consider continuation with IUCD in place under close surveillance.

Explanation of other options:

Leave IUCD inside and continue pregnancy with prophylactic antibiotics (Option A): Not routinely recommended. Antibiotics don't eliminate the risks of septic abortion, miscarriage, or preterm labor. Removal is preferred when the thread is visible.

Leave IUCD inside and continue pregnancy (Option B): Increases risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Since thread is visible, removal is feasible and thus preferred.

Termination of pregnancy due to risk of infection (Option D): Termination is not indicated if the patient wants to continue and the IUCD can be safely removed. It may be considered if IUCD cannot be removed or the patient opts for termination.

question_text: A 30-year-old female with a history of preterm delivery, comes now with 32 weeks of pregnancy and labour pains with OS dilated 2 cm. What would be the ideal management for such a patient?
explanation:
Principles of Management of Women with Preterm Labor:

  • Glucocorticoids to the mother to reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, BPD and PDA.
  • Antenatal transfer of the mother with fetus in utero to a tertiary center equipped with NICU.
  • Tocolytic drugs to the mother for a short period unless contraindicated .
  • Antibiotics to prevent neonatal infection with Group B Streptococcus (GBS) only in high risk cases not routinely recommended
  • Magnesium sulfate (neuroprotector) to the mother to reduce neonatal cerebral palsy when pregnancy is <34 weeks.
  • Careful intrapartum monitoring, minimal trauma and presence of a neonatologist during delivery. Vaginal delivery is preferred, unless otherwise indicated for cesarean birth.

Reference: D C Dutta’s textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 22

question_text: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks presents with severe abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements. On examination, her uterus is tender. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical triad of painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and loss of fetal movements is characteristic of abruptio placenta.

Abruptio Placenta

Definition: Premature separation of a normally situated placenta (partial or total) before delivery of the fetus.

Risk Factors:

  • Health history:Hypertension, preeclampsia, smoking, cocaine use, maternal age >35 years, previous abruption.
  • Pregnancy-related:Multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, short umbilical cord, sudden uterine decompression.
  • Trauma:Abdominal trauma (fall, motor vehicle collision, violence).

Clinical Features:

  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Vaginal bleeding(may be concealed or revealed)
  • Uterine tenderness / rigidity('woody hard' uterus)
  • Loss of fetal movements/ intrauterine fetal demise in severe cases

Classification (Page's classification):

  • Class 0 (Asymptomatic):Retrospective diagnosis; clot found after delivery.
  • Class 1 (Mild):Mild bleeding, minimal uterine tenderness, stable vitals, no fetal distress.
  • Class 2 (Moderate):Moderate bleeding, marked tenderness, maternal tachycardia / orthostatic hypotension, fetal distress, early coagulopathy.
  • Class 3 (Severe):Profuse bleeding (revealed/concealed), tetanic uterus, maternal shock, DIC, fetal death.

Explanation of Other Options:

Placenta previa (Option B) typically presents with painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester. The uterus remains soft and non-tender, and fetal movements are usually preserved.

Polyhydramnios (Option C) is characterized by excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid leading to maternal discomfort, abdominal distension, and sometimes preterm labor.

Preterm labor (Option D) is defined as the onset of uterine contractions leading to cervical changes before 37 weeks of gestation. While it may present with abdominal pain, it does not typically cause significant vaginal bleeding or uterine tenderness. Fetal movements are usually present.

Reference: Placental Abruption - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text:
A 22-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks gestation comes to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Nausea and vomiting began one day back, and now the patient is unable to tolerate fluids. She complains of pain in the right upper quadrant, which started a few hours back. On examination, her temperature is 100.2°F, pulse 119 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg. She has swelling of her lower limbs up to the ankles bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows a gravid uterus corresponding to 10 weeks of gestation and tenderness in the right upper quadrant with mild guarding.
Laboratory Findings:
1. Hemoglobin: 11 g/dl
2. Leukocytes: 13,000 cells/μl
3. Platelets: 150,000 cells/μl
4. AST: 40 U/L, ALT: 48 U/L
5. Urinalysis: Protein negative, pus cells 1-2/HPF, bacteria none
6. USG abdomen: 9.7 mm diameter, aperistaltic, non-compressible, dilated blind-ending structure arising from the cecum
What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has classic features of acute appendicitis:

  • Acute nausea, vomiting, right-sided abdominal pain.
  • Leukocytosis (13,000/μL).
  • Ultrasound showing non-compressible, dilated, blind-ending tubular structure (>6 mm).

Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in pregnancy.

  • Management = immediate appendicectomy regardless of gestational age.
  • Delay increases risk of perforation, peritonitis, maternal sepsis, abortion, or preterm labor.

Pre-operative care:

  • IV fluids and electrolyte correction.
  • GI decompression if needed.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics.
  • Analgesics after diagnosis.

Surgical approach: Laparoscopic or open appendicectomy, both safe in pregnancy.

Wait till 2nd trimester (Option B): Acute appendicitis is a surgical emergency and delay in a surgical emergency risks maternal and fetal morbidity/mortality

Conservative management (Option C): Conservative management is not recommended with clear appendicitis signs as there is risk of rupture.

Reassurance (Option D): Reassurance alone is inappropriate for suspected acute appendicitis as it is unsafe and can lead to perforation and peritonitis.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • In children: Ultrasound
  • In Adults, Gold standard: CECT

question_text: Most serious complication of PROM is:
explanation:
DANGERS OF PROM

(1) preterm labor and prematurity;

(2) Chance of ascending infection is more if labor fails to start within 24 hours. Liquor gets infected (chorioamnionitis) and fetal infection supervenes;

(3) Cord prolapse, especially when associated with malpresentation

(4) Continuous escape of liquor for long duration may lead to dry labor;

(5) Fetal pulmonary hypoplasia, especially in preterm PROM is a real threat when associated with oligohydramnios;

(6) Neonatal sepsis, RDS, IVH and NEC in preterm PROM;

(7) Maternal complications of PROM:Chorioamnionitis,placental abruption, retained placenta, endometritis, maternal sepsis and even death.

(8) Perinatal morbidities (cerebral palsy) are high.

Reference - D C Dutta's textbook of obstetrics 8th edition, chapter 22

question_text: Identify the type of uterus shown in the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

Didelphys uterus results from complete failure of Müllerian duct fusion, leading to two separate uterine cavities with individual endometrial linings and often two crevices.

  • A didelphys uterus arises due to complete non-fusion of the paired Müllerian ducts during embryogenesis.
  • It results in two entirely separate uterine horns, often with two separate endometrial cavities and two cervices, and occasionally a longitudinal vaginal septum as well.
  • This anomaly is best seen on imaging such as MRI or HSG, which shows two symmetric, widely spaced endometrial canals with no communication.
  • These findings, along with the presence of two distinct cervical canals, confirm the diagnosis.
  • Women with a didelphys uterus have an increased risk of miscarriage, preterm labor, and abnormal fetal presentations.
  • However, some can carry pregnancies to term.

Explanation of other options:

Bicornuate uterus (Option A): Incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts results in a uterus with two horns and a single cervix. The endometrial canals are partially joined and separated at the top with an external fundal indentation >10 mm and intercornual angle >105°.

Arcuate uterus (Option C): A normal variant with a mild concave indentation of the uterine fundus. The intercornual angle is >105°, and the depth of indentation is <10 mm, not associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Septate uterus (Option D): Caused by failure of resorption of the uterine septum. On imaging, the uterine fundus is normal (convex/flat), but the cavity is divided by a fibrous or muscular septum with an intercornual angle <75° and a fundal indentation depth >10 mm.

Hysterosalpingogram showing acute angle in a septate uterus (A) and wider angle in a bicornuate uterus (B).

question_text: A 36-week pregnant woman with chronic hypertension presents with complaints of headache and visual disturbances. What is the appropriate management in this situation?
option_a: IV Labetalol and deliver at 37 weeks
option_d: IV Labetalol + Magnesium sulfate and deliver
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct management for severe preeclampsia at 36 weeks includes controlling blood pressure with IV Labetalol and preventing seizures with Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄), followed by immediate delivery to avoid maternal and fetal complications.

Role of Magnesium Sulfate:

  • Prevents the onset and recurrence of seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia.
  • Has a mild tocolytic effect, delaying preterm labor.
  • Provides neuroprotection to the preterm fetus by reducing the risk of cerebral palsy.

Role of Labetalol:

  • Used as a first-line drug for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy.
  • Initial IV dose: 10-20 mg, followed by 20-80 mg every 10-30 minutes (maximum 300 mg), or continuous infusion at 1-2 mg/min.
  • Preferred due to fewer side effects and minimal tachycardia.
  • Contraindicated in patients with asthma, cardiac dysfunction, heart block, or bradycardia.

Explanation for incorrect Options:

IV Labetalol and delivery at 37 weeks (Option A): IV Labetalol and delivery at 37 weeks inappropriate, as immediate delivery is required in severe cases.

Give one dose of steroid (Option B): Steroid administration - indicated for fetal lung maturity only before 34 weeks.

I.V Labetalol + MgSO4 and deliver(Option C): IV Labetalol and immediately after delivery, is not recommended, as MgSO₄ is also necessary to prevent seizures.

Key takeaway:

Severe preeclampsia is a critical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy characterized by elevated blood pressure, proteinuria, and possible organ dysfunction.

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • Blood Pressure: ≥160/110 mm Hg on two readings at least 4 hours apart.
  • Proteinuria: ≥5 g/24 hr or ≥3+ on dipstick.
  • Symptoms: Severe headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, or altered liver enzymes.
  • Laboratory Findings: Thrombocytopenia, raised liver enzymes, and renal impairment.

Management Summary:

  • Hospitalization for intensive monitoring.
  • Antihypertensive therapy: IV labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine to maintain BP <160/110 mm Hg.
  • Seizure prophylaxis: Magnesium sulfate (4-6 g loading dose, followed by 1-2 g/hour).
  • Corticosteroids: For lung maturation if gestation is 24-34 weeks.
  • Fetal surveillance: Regular NSTs, BPP, and ultrasound evaluations.
  • Delivery: Indicated immediately after 34 weeks or earlier if maternal or fetal condition deteriorates.

question_text: What is the recommended dosage regimen of antenatal corticosteroids to promote fetal lung maturity?
option_a: Dexamethasone 6 mg every 12 hours for 4 doses
option_b: Betamethasone 6 mg every 12 hours for 2 doses
option_c: Dexamethasone 12 mg every 24 hours for 2 doses
option_d: Betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 4 doses
explanation:
Explanation:

Congenital Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation (CCAM) is identified by a well-circumscribed mass in the lung, which may present echogenic and solid or contain cysts of varying diameters. When the cysts are larger than or equal to 5 mm, the condition is described as macrocystic, while smaller cysts or solid lesions are classified as microcystic.

The CCAM Volume Ratio (CVR) is used to assess lesion size and predict the risk of hydrops. A CVR value greater than 1.6, or evidence of fetal hydrops, indicates the need for corticosteroid treatment. In such cases, dexamethasone (6 mg intramuscularly every 12 hours for four doses) or betamethasone (12 mg intramuscularly every 24 hours for two doses) is commonly prescribed.

A single course of corticosteroids resolves hydrops in approximately 80% of cases, with around 90% survival in treated fetuses. Some fetuses with large or progressive lesions may require two courses for optimal response.

While betamethasone (Option B ruled out) is an effective alternative, the standard dose is 12 mg, not 6 mg. Dexamethasone 12 mg every 24 hours for 2 doses (Option C ruled out) does not represent the conventional dosing schedule. Betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 4 doses (Option D ruled out) also deviates from the recommended regimen, as the accepted protocol involves two 12 mg doses given 24 hours apart.

Key takeaway:

Indications for Antenatal Corticosteroid Therapy:

  • Preterm labor between 24-34 weeks of gestation
  • Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) before 34 weeks
  • Expected preterm delivery due to maternal or fetal complications (e.g., preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction)

question_text: A primigravida in active labor was 4 cm dilated initially. After 4 hours, the cervical dilatation progressed to only 6 cm, with uterine contractions recorded as 3 in 10 minutes. Fetal heart rate is normal. The partograph shows the graph approaching the alert line but still left of the action line. What is the next best step?
option_c: Wait and watch for spontaneous progression
explanation:
Explanation:

The active management of labor, pioneered by O'Driscoll and later adapted at Parkland Hospital, emphasizes systematic intervention to prevent prolonged labor and unnecessary cesarean delivery:

  • In active labor, expected cervical dilatation is at least 1 cm/hr.
  • If progress is slower than this, the first step is amniotomy.
  • If, after amniotomy, cervical dilatation does not improve at the next assessment (≈2 hours), then oxytocin augmentation is added to strengthen contractions.
  • Cesarean section is considered only after oxytocin fails, with inadequate uterine activity (measured as <200 Montevideo units) despite 4 hours of augmentation.
  • Importantly, the partograph alert line signals the need for closer monitoring and interventions like augmentation, while the action line signals the need to evaluate for cesarean if labor fails to progress.

To perform an immediate cesarean section (Option B) is not correct, as the action line on the partograph has not been crossed, the fetal heart rate is normal, and stepwise measures like augmentation should be tried first.

To wait and watch for spontaneous progression (Option C) is not appropriate, since 4 hours have already passed with suboptimal cervical progress. Simply waiting further increases the risk of dystocia without improving outcomes.

To administer corticosteroids and delay labor (Option D) is incorrect, as corticosteroids are indicated in preterm labor to enhance fetal lung maturity, not in a term primigravida in active labor.

question_text: A 37-week primigravida presents with mild contractions for the past 20 hours. On examination, her cervix is only 1 cm dilated and not effaced. What is the most appropriate management in this situation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation suggests prodromal (false) labor rather than active labor, as evidenced by minimal cervical change despite prolonged mild contractions.

Observation and rest (sedation and waiting) is the appropriate approach because:

  • The patient is not yet in active labor despite experiencing contractions.
  • The cervix shows no effacement, indicating early or false labor.
  • Both mother and fetus are stable, and the pregnancy is at term.
  • This scenario is commonly seen in first-time mothers.

A cervical dilation of 1 cm signifies that the body is beginning to prepare for labor. Active labor may commence within hours, or it could take several days or weeks.

Note: Preterm labor occurs before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Tocolytic medications can be administered to delay contractions in women showing signs of preterm labor

Augmentation with oxytocin (Option B): Administering oxytocin is not appropriate when the cervix is unfavorable and the patient is not in active labor. Doing so may increase the risk of fetal distress.

Cesarean section (Option C): An emergency cesarean is not warranted in this case, as there are no maternal or fetal indications for surgical intervention.

Amniotomy (Option D): Artificial rupture of membranes should be avoided when the cervix is not favorable and labor is not active. Performing an early amniotomy can raise the risk of infection and umbilical cord prolapse without improving labor progress.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Bishop Score is used to assess cervix and station of the fetal head before inducing labor.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman, G2P1L1, presents in labor with complaints of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and loss of fetal movements. She has a history of occasional smoking, but no alcohol or recreational drug use. On examination, her pulse is 80 bpm, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, and abdominal palpation reveals a tense, rigid uterus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture strongly suggests a diagnosis of placental abruption (abruptio placentae). This condition is characterized by the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta, and one of its known risk factors is smoking, which leads to vasoconstriction of placental blood vessels and reduced uteroplacental blood flow.

Explanation for other options:

Placenta Previa (Option B): Presents with painless, bright red, recurrent vaginal bleeding. The uterus is soft, non-tender, and fetal heart sounds are usually present. This does not match the tense abdomen and pain in the current case.

Polyhydramnios (Option C): Refers to excessive amniotic fluid (>2000 ml). Smoking is not a direct cause, and it typically doesn't present with such acute symptoms or fetal demise.

Preterm Labor (Option D): Smoking is associated with preterm labor, but patients typically present with regular uterine contractions, progressive cervical dilatation, and intact fetal movements (depending on gestational age). The tense abdomen and loss of fetal movement here suggest something more severe.

question_text: A 35-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents for delivery. In which of the following conditions is the use of oxytocin contraindicated?
option_b: Induction of labor in post-term pregnancy
option_c: Augmentation of labor in case of slow progress
option_d: Preterm labor with cervical dilation of 3 cm
explanation:
Explanation:

Placenta previa, where the placenta partially or completely covers the internal cervical os, is a contraindication for oxytocin use. Administering oxytocin in such cases can precipitate severe maternal hemorrhage, endangering both mother and fetus.

Oxytocin:

Indications:

  • Antepartum (FDA-approved):
    • Labor induction in cases of preeclampsia, maternal diabetes, or premature rupture of membranes
    • Stimulation of inactive uterus to initiate labor
    • Management of inevitable or incomplete second-trimester abortion
  • Postpartum (FDA-approved):
    • Facilitate placental delivery during the third stage of labor
    • Control postpartum hemorrhage
  • Non-FDA-approved:
    • Treatment of delayed orgasm
    • Inducing sexual arousal
    • Investigational use in autism (social skills improvement)

Contraindications:

  • Hypersensitivity to oxytocin
  • Vaginal delivery-specific:
    • Placenta previa
    • Vasa previa
    • Active genital herpes infection
    • Invasive cervical cancer
    • Umbilical cord prolapse or malpresentation
  • Fetal considerations:
    • Abnormal fetal position (e.g., transverse lie)
    • Fetal distress when delivery is not imminent
  • Maternal/pelvic issues:
    • Inadequate pelvic size for vaginal delivery
    • Hyperactive or hypertonic uterus

Explanation of Other Options:

Induction of labor in post-term pregnancy (Option B): Safe and common indication; oxytocin helps initiate contractions in pregnancies beyond 40 weeks.

Augmentation of labor in slow progress (Option C): Standard use; oxytocin strengthens contractions and promotes labor progression unless contraindicated.

Preterm labor with cervical dilation of 3 cm (Option D): Can be used for augmentation if labor is inevitable and deemed safe by the provider.

question_text: A 40-year-old G2P1 woman at 18 weeks of gestation presents with a dilated cervix. Cervical length is 15 mm. Despite understanding the risks, she insists on cerclage. Which of the following is a contraindication for cervical cerclage?
option_b: Prolapse of membranes into the vagina
explanation:
Explanation:

Cervical cerclage is contraindicated in ruptured membranes.

Cervical Cerclage:

  • A surgical procedure to reinforce a weak or incompetent cervix, aimed at preventing preterm birth or mid-trimester loss.

Timing of Cerclage:

  • Prophylactic: ~14 weeks gestation
  • Emergency: When cervical dilation or membrane prolapse occurs
  • Removal: Typically at 37 weeks, or earlier if labor begins

Types of Cerclage:

  • McDonald (simpler, most common)
  • Shirodkar (requires dissection of cervical tissue for suture placement)

Indications:

  • Short cervix (<25 mm) on ultrasound
  • Cervical dilatation with or without bulging membranes
  • History of prior mid-trimester losses

Contraindications:

  • Ruptured membranes (risk of infection and preterm labor)
  • Active uterine infection
  • Significant vaginal bleeding
  • Severe uterine irritability
  • Cervical dilation >4 cm
  • Intrauterine fetal demise

Explanation of other options:

Prolapse of membranes into the vagina (B): This is often an indication for emergency cerclage to prevent further damage.

Fetal fibronectin positive (C): Indicates risk of preterm labor but is not a contraindication. Cerclage may still be considered if cervical insufficiency is present.

Advanced maternal age (D): Increases pregnancy risk but does not contraindicate cerclage.

Key Takeaway:

  • Cervical cerclage is contraindicated in the presence of ruptured membranes.

Reference:

  1. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229469261_The_effect_of_advanced_maternal_age_on_pregnancy_outcome.
  2. https://fogsi.org/wp-content/uploads/fogsi-focus/fogsi-focus-maternal-fetal-and-neonatal-medicine-2020.pdf.

question_text: Which complication is specific to monochorionic twins?
explanation:
• In almost all MC twins, there is a shared circulation in the placenta with different anastomoses. These could be arterial to venous (A-V), venous to venous (V-V) and arterial to arterial (A-A) anastomoses. It has been increasingly known that sharing placenta between twins is not equal.
  • Combination of placental vascular anastomoses and unequal placental sharing predispose MC twins to specific complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) and the consequence of co-twin death.

question_text: In which of the following cases is the drug given below contraindicated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The drug is oxytocin, which is contraindicated in malpresentation of the fetus (e.g., transverse lie, breech) because stimulating uterine contractions can cause obstructed labor or fetal injury.

Explanation of Other Options:

Heart disease (Option A): Not an absolute contraindication. In fact, low-dose synthetic oxytocin is often considered a safe and effective alternative for patients with heart disease in cases where elective delivery is warranted.

Premature labor (Option C): This is not a contraindication. Oxytocin can be used to induce labor in preterm pregnancies when continuing the pregnancy poses a greater risk to the mother or fetus (e.g., severe preeclampsia, chorioamnionitis).

Hypothyroidism (Option D): Hypothyroidism does not affect the action of oxytocin on the uterus, and its use is considered safe in these patients.

Reference: Oxytocin - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: Not a criterion for preterm labour
option_b: Contractions 8 Contractions in 60 mins with cervical changes
explanation:
Posterior cervix is an unfavourable factor for labour and hence this is easily ruled out.

Diagnostic criteria of preterm labour:

question_text: MgSO<sub>4</sub> have no role in prevention of?
explanation:
Uses of MgSO4:

Magnesium sulfate infusions have been a common practice on obstetrical floors for more than 60 years. It's a well-studied drug, so doctors know very well how it affects moms and babies. Here is how it is used:

  • In Preterm Labor: To Allow Time For Steroids

Magnesium sulfate is a tocolytic that has been used to slow or stop premature labor.

Doctors may treat preterm labor with 48 hours of magnesium sulfate, hoping to buy enough time to complete a course of steroids to help the baby's lungs develop.

  • In Preeclampsia: To Prevent Seizures

Preeclampsia is a common complication of pregnancy that causes high blood pressure and protein in the urine. If not treated, preeclampsia can develop into eclampsia, a seizure disorder.

The only cure for preeclampsia and eclampsia is delivery of the baby, but magnesium sulfate can help prevent seizures in women with severe preeclampsia.

  • In Preterm Babies: To Protect Newborn Brains

Premature babies, especially those who are born before about 32 weeks gestation, have immature brains at birth. As they grow, they are at risk for cerebral palsy, a disorder that affects movement and intelligence.

Short-term (24 hours or less) infusions of magnesium sulfate have been shown to help protect the baby's brain by reducing the incidence of cerebral palsy.

question_text: A 32-year-old woman with an obstetric score of P2L2 presents with 6 months of secondary amenorrhea. Laboratory evaluation shows FSH 36 mIU/mL, LH 56 mIU/mL, and anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) 0.05 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation:

question_text: Newer progestational contraceptives primarily act by:
explanation:
FOGSI is Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecological Societies of India and the highest governing body in Obs and Gynae in India.

Progesterone only pills

Mechanism of action of POP’s is mainly on cervical mucus-

"All Estrogen free pills except the newer desogestrel pill primarily rely on changes in cervical mucus as they do not inhibit ovulation consistently."

The cervical mucus effect peaks within 3–4 hours after taking the tablet and lasts for about 22 hours. Hence the next tablet must be taken within 27 hours of the preceding tablet or else the contraceptive benefit of the cervical mucus effect will decrease and finally subside.

  • Unlike COC’s that almost always prevent ovulation, traditional POP’s (progesterone only pills) inhibit ovulation in 40–50% of cycles. "A randomized double blind study, performed over 13 cycles showed that 75 mg desogestrel daily was sufficient to inhibit ovulation in 97% of cycles. Hence for newer POP’s containing desogestrel the primary mode of action is inhibition of ovulation". FOGSI Focus Jan 06 issue on Modern pill, Chapter Estrogen free pill p 41

Thus, for newer progestational agents the main mechanism of action is by inhibition of ovulation. Remember

  • Traditional POP’s are also known as Low-dose progestogen only pills. —Shaw 14th/ed p 210
  • Main progesterone used are: – Norethisterone 350 mcg
    • Norgestrel 75 mcg
    • Levonorgesterel 30 mcg
  • Their main mechanism of action (as discussed earlier) is thickening of cervical mucus.

They also:– Render endometrium unsuitable for implantation

  • Accelerate tubal motility
  • Disturb corpus luteal function.

A word of caution to all of you out there: Be careful in reading the question - whether question is on Low dose progestins (Traditional pills) or on newer progestins containing desogestrel

question_text: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, presents at 32 weeks of gestation. She underwent a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), which revealed a fasting glucose of 110 mg/dl and a 2-hour glucose of 180 mg/dl. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
option_d: Induce labour due to risk of fetal macrosomia
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient meets the criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), as her fasting glucose exceeds 92 mg/dl. The preferred management is insulin therapy, because it does not cross the placenta, allowing safe and effective maternal glucose control while minimising fetal risk. Admission enables close monitoring of maternal blood sugar and proper adjustment of insulin doses, reducing the chances of complications such as macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and preeclampsia.

Explanation of Other Options:

Start oral hypoglycemics (Option A): Oral agents like metformin or glyburide are generally not first-line for GDM, especially in cases with significant hyperglycemia. These drugs can cross the placenta, potentially causing fetal hypoglycemia or other adverse effects, making them less safe than insulin.

Reassurance (Option B): Simply reassuring the patient is inadequate, as GDM requires active monitoring and intervention. Ignoring elevated blood sugar can lead to maternal and fetal complications, including macrosomia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycemia, and preeclampsia.

Induce labor due to risk of fetal macrosomia (Option D): Inducing labour at 32 weeks is premature. At this gestational age, the fetal lungs and organ systems may not be fully developed, posing a high risk for respiratory distress and neonatal morbidity. The immediate priority is to control maternal blood glucose, not early delivery.

question_text: A 30-year-old female, P2L2, with a history of infravaginal cervical lengthening, is considering surgical options.
explanation:
Explanation:

Fothergill surgery (also known as Manchester repair) is ideal for young women under 40 years with cervical elongation and uterine prolapse who wish to preserve fertility.

  • Fothergill surgery is specifically indicated in women with uterine prolapse who desire uterine conservation, especially when associated with infravaginal cervical elongation.
  • It is appropriate for younger women (typically <40 years) who have completed their families or wish to preserve reproductive potential.
  • The procedure involves:
    • Amputation of the elongated cervix
    • Plication of the Mackenrodt's (cardinal) ligaments to support the uterus
    • Anterior colporrhaphy and colpoperineorrhaphy for vaginal wall support
  • This combination restores normal anatomy while retaining the uterus, which aligns with the needs of a young woman with cervical elongation.
  • Complications include:
    • Cervical stenosis
    • Fibrosis
    • Cervical incompetence (if future pregnancy occurs)
    • Urinary retention

Explanation of other options:

McCall culdoplasty (Option B): Used to prevent enterocele by suspending the vaginal apex, typically performed during or after hysterectomy-not suitable for patients needing cervical correction or uterine conservation.

LeFort's repair (Option C): A partial colpocleisis reserved for elderly women with advanced prolapse who are unfit for more extensive surgery and do not desire future sexual activity or fertility.

Hysterectomy (Option D): Although definitive, it's inappropriate here given the patient's age and her need for uterine preservation due to prior cervical surgery and reproductive considerations.

question_text: Which vaccine is not safe in pregnancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Live attenuated vaccines like Varicella are contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal infection and congenital varicella syndrome. Pregnant women should receive the vaccine postpartum if they are non-immune.

Explanation of other options:

Influenza (Option B): The inactivated influenza vaccine is safe and recommended in all trimesters of pregnancy to protect both the mother and fetus from severe influenza complications. However, the live attenuated nasal spray vaccine is not recommended in pregnancy.

Rabies (Option C):Rabies vaccine (inactivated) is safe in pregnancy and should be given if there is exposure or a high risk of exposure to rabies.

Td (Option D):Tetanus-diphtheria (Td) and Tdap (Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis) vaccines are safe and recommended during pregnancy (preferably between 27-36 weeks) to provide passive immunity to the newborn.

Key Takeaways:

Live vaccines, including varicella, are contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal infection.

question_text: Surgical management of ruptured uterus include:

Chance of injury to the ureters or bladder is thereby minimized. However, if the condition permits and/or there is colporrhexis, a total hysterectomy may be done.
  • Repair: This is mostly applicable to a scar rupture where the margins are clean. Repair is done by excision of the fibrous tissue at the margins. question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents with chronic dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and cyclical pelvic pain unresponsive to medical therapy. explanation:
Explanation:

  • HPE remains the gold standard for confirming endometriosis, demonstrating endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity, often with hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
  • Provides definitive diagnosis and guides further management, including surgical excision or hormonal therapy

Investigations for Endometriosis:

  • Ultrasonography (TVS and ERUS) (Option C ruled out): Initial investigation, where endometrioma appears as ground glass opacities and hemorrhagic cysts appear as thread-like structures.
  • Laparoscopy (Option B ruled out): Investigation of choice, with new lesions visualised as red flame-like and chronic lesions as powder-burnt appearance.
  • Histopathology: Gold standard for confirming the diagnosis, showing blood-filled macrophages (hemosiderophages).
  • MRI (Option D ruled out): This is not routinely done but is accurate for diagnosing deep-infiltrating endometriosis (DIE), such as Bowel, Thoracic, Bladder, and Rectovaginal endometriosis, and is done before laparoscopy.
  • CA 125 Assay: Non-specific marker, often elevated in endometriosis.
  • Laparotomy: Not done for confirmatory purposes due to its invasiveness and higher risk of complications.

question_text: A 75-year-old woman presented with a mass protruding per vaginum, as seen in the image provided, and was scheduled for surgical correction. However, during the pre-anaesthetic evaluation, she was deemed unfit for major surgery. Which of the following procedures would be the most appropriate alternative in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Le Fort's Repair is a vaginal surgical procedure primarily used to manage complete uterine prolapse in elderly women, particularly those who are medically unfit for prolonged surgeries and have completed their childbearing.

Le Fort's Operation Overview:

  • Indication: Ideal for elderly patients with procidentia (complete uterine prolapse) who have multiple comorbidities and cannot tolerate major surgery.
  • Procedure: The operation involves partially closing the vaginal canal by suturing the anterior and posterior vaginal walls This supports the prolapsed uterus and limits further descent. It is typically performed under local anaesthesia with sedation or epidural anaesthesia, making it suitable for high-risk surgical candidates.
  • Preoperative Requirements: The patient must have no evidence of uterine or pelvic malignancy (e.g., endometrial or cervical cancer). Cervical cytology (Pap smear) must be normal before proceeding.
  • Complications: May include pyometra (uterine infection due to blocked drainage) and urinary stress incontinence.
  • Contraindications: Not suitable for reproductive-age women, menstruating women, or those with cervical/uterine pathology.

Explanation for other options:

Abdominal Wall Cervicopexy (Option A): Also called the sling procedure, it is preferred in nulliparous women or congenital prolapse cases without associated cystocele.The cervix is suspended and fixed to the anterior abdominal wall and sacrum using a sling to restore pelvic support.

Shirodkar's Sling Operation (Option B): Also referred to as anterior colporrhaphy, it is performed in young women under 40 who wish to preserve fertility. The cervix is attached to the lumbosacral fascia using Mersilene tape, preserving uterine function and reducing the risk of pregnancy-related complications.

Khanna's Sling Operation (Option D): Involves placing a mesh sling beneath the cervix, anchored to the pubic bones bilaterally, providing support through the Mackenrodt's ligaments. It is indicated in women with grade 2 or 3 uterine prolapse who still desire to maintain menstrual and reproductive functions.

question_text: Dose of aspirin for prevention of pre eclampsia is
explanation:
The action of low-dose aspirin in the prevention of preeclampsia involves its effects on blood clotting and vascular function:

  1. Antiplatelet Effect:Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation by blocking the enzyme cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), which reduces the production of thromboxane A2. This helps to prevent excessive blood clotting and improves blood flow.
  2. Vascular Protection: By inhibiting thromboxane A2, aspirin also helps to reduce endothelial cell activation and vasoconstriction, which can lower the risk of placental insufficiency and the development of preeclampsia.

Overall, these effects contribute to improved placental blood flow and reduced risk of the complications associated with preeclampsia.

As per ASPREE trial, 150 mg of aspirin is given from 12-36 weeks of pregnancy in patients with high risk of developing preeclampsia for prevention.

question_text: A 36-week pregnant woman with a prosthetic mitral valve on warfarin presents with an INR of 3. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
option_d: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin
explanation:
Explanation:

In this clinical scenario, the patient is on warfarin during pregnancy, but as she approaches term, the anticoagulation is switched to LMWH until after delivery.

Warfarin Use in Pregnancy:

  • Warfarin is the most effective anticoagulant for preventing valve thrombosis but is teratogenic, especially in the first trimester (risk of embryopathy, miscarriage, stillbirth).
  • Risk of fetal malformations is dose-dependent:
    • If ≤5 mg/day, fetal risks are lower and comparable to LMWH.
    • If >5 mg/day, risk of embryopathy exceeds 8%.
  • Anticoagulation Strategy:
    • First trimester: Often switch to LMWH or UFH to reduce teratogenicity.
    • Second trimester: Some switch back to warfarin if dose is ≤5 mg/day.
    • Near term (around 36 weeks): Switch from warfarin to LMWH to allow better control around delivery and reduce bleeding risks.
  • Monitoring:
    • LMWH requires anti-Xa level monitoring (target: 0.8-1.2 U/mL 4-6 hrs post-dose).
    • Warfarin requires INR monitoring (target based on valve type).
  • Delivery Planning:
    • Anticoagulation is paused pre-delivery to reduce bleeding and allow for possible regional anesthesia.
    • Anticoagulants (warfarin or heparin) can be resumed 6-24 hours postpartum, depending on delivery type and bleeding.

Heparin-both unfractionated (UFH) and low-molecular-weight (LMWH)-is preferred during pregnancy due to its safety profile, as it does not cross the placenta.

However, UFH, even at therapeutic doses, is generally ineffective in preventing valve thrombosis in women with mechanical heart valves.

LMWH poses a lower thrombotic risk than UFH, making it the preferred anticoagulant during pregnancy for many women with mechanical valves.

Regular monitoring is crucial:

  • PT-INR is used for warfarin,
  • Anti-Xa levels, though not routinely measured with LMWH, become essential in pregnancy to ensure effective anticoagulation.

Explanation for other options:

Stopping warfarin and starting aspirin (Option B) is not advisable because high-dose aspirin in the last trimester can cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, pulmonary hypertension, and kernicterus in the fetus. Therefore, aspirin is generally avoided during pregnancy.

Continue Warfarin (Option C) : its not recommended because it is teratogenic, potentially causing miscarriages, stillbirths, and a constellation of birth defects known as fetal warfarin syndrome.

Stopping warfarin and starting both LMWH and aspirin together (Option D) is also not recommended, as using two anticoagulants simultaneously increases the risk of severe maternal bleeding and can lead to life-threatening complications for both mother and baby.

question_text: A pregnant woman at 35 weeks gestation with a history of a classical cesarean section in her previous pregnancy presents with a breech fetus. What is the next step in management?
option_b: Advice ultrasound and visit after 2 weeks
option_c: Internal podalic version followed by vaginal delivery
explanation:
Explanation:

A classical cesarean section involves a vertical incision on the upper segment of the uterus, which carries a high risk of uterine rupture in subsequent pregnancies. Because of this, vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) is contraindicated, especially when the fetus is in a breech presentation.

  • Planned cesarean at 37 weeks is recommended to:
    • Minimize the risk of spontaneous labor and uterine rupture
    • Ensure fetal maturity
    • Optimize maternal and fetal safety

Contraindications for TOLAC / Indications for Cesarean Delivery:

  1. Previous classical or inverted T-shaped uterine incision
  2. Prior extensive myomectomy involving the uterine cavity
  3. More than two previous lower segment cesarean sections (LSCS)
  4. Pelvic abnormalities or suspected cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
  5. Other obstetric complications such as:
    • Pre-eclampsia or eclampsia
    • Malpresentation (breech, transverse lie)
    • Placenta previa or accreta
  6. Medical complications limiting safe labor
  7. Limited availability of resources for emergency cesarean (anesthesia, surgical team, blood transfusion)
  8. Patient refusal to undergo TOLAC
  9. History of prior uterine rupture

Explanation of other options:

Advice ultrasound and visit after 2 weeks (Option B): Performing an ultrasound at this stage will not alter the management decision. The history of a prior classical cesarean section is the critical factor, and cesarean delivery remains the safest option. Monitoring alone would put the patient and fetus at risk of uterine rupture.

Internal podalic version followed by vaginal delivery (Option C): Internal podalic version is a technique primarily used for the second twin in a transverse lie. It is not indicated for a singleton breech pregnancy and is contraindicated in women with a prior classical cesarean due to high risk of uterine rupture.

External cephalic version at 36 weeks (Option D): External cephalic version (ECV) is performed to turn a breech fetus into cephalic presentation. It is contraindicated in patients with a previous classical cesarean section because abdominal manipulation can precipitate uterine rupture and endanger both mother and fetus.

Key Takeaway:

  • A prior classical cesarean is an absolute contraindication for VBAC.

Reference:

  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507844/

explanation:
Anisocytosis is variation in size of the red blood cells.

The patient in the question has hypochromic anemia along with anisocytosis which can be seen in case of

  • Iron deficiency anemia -Harsh Mohan 5/e, p 372

Blood picture:

  • Red cells are hypochromic and microcytic
  • There is anisocytosis and poikilocytosis
  • In severe cases target cells, elliptical forms and polychromatic cells are present.

Dimorphic anemia

Blood picture:

  • Cells may be normocytic, microcytic or macrocytic (i.e. anisocytosis is seen)
  • Hypochromia or Normochromic.

Therefore in both iron deficiency anemia and dimorphic anemia anisocytosis with hypochromia may be seen.

But since dimorphic anemia is the commonest type of anemia seen in tropics, we are taking it as the correct answer.

Dimorphic anemia:

  • It is the commonest type of anemia seen in the underprivileged sections of society especially in the tropics.
  • It results either from dietary inadequacy or intestinal malabsorption and thus anemia is associated with deficiency of iron as well as vitamin B12 and folic acid.
  • Bone marrow is predominantly megaloblastic (as folic acid is required for the development of the red cell precursors).

Treatment consists of prescribing both iron and folic acid in the diet.

question_text: Acute PID is treated by all except;

Management of PID

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (oral or IV)
  • If tubo-ovarian mass/abscess is present - it should be treated medically but, if there is no response, drainage should be done.
  • Drainage of a pelvic abscess by colpotomy may occasionally be needed

question_text: Surgical staging of ovarian Ca all done except:
explanation:
Surgical staging is done in all cases of ovarian cancer.

  • Typically, the abdominal incision must be adequate to identify and resect any disease that may have been missed on physical examination or imaging tests.
  • The operation begin by aspirating free ascitic fluid or collecting peritoneal washing followed by visualization and palpation of all peritoneal surfaces and viscera proceeding in a clockwise manner from cecum.
  • Next an extrafascial (simple) hysterectomy and BSO are performed and infracolic omentectomy done.
  • In the absence of gross extraovarian disease, peritoneal biopsies are obtained, along with a biopsy or scraping of the right diaphragm.
  • Finally, a pelvic and infrarenal para-aortic lymphadenectomy is complete.

Note: Infracolic omentectomy is done: Not omental biopsy

Reference: Williams Gynae 1st/ed pg 729; Novak 14th/ed pg 1478

question_text: What is the appropriate management for an 8 cm endometrial cyst?
explanation:
Explanation:

Endometriomas larger than 4 cm typically require laparoscopic cystectomy, as they are often associated with adhesions to surrounding pelvic organs.

Surgical removal helps reduce recurrence, alleviates pain, and increases the chances of spontaneous conception.

For endometriomas smaller than 3 cm, laparoscopic aspiration followed by irrigation with saline is usually sufficient.

Explanation for other options:

Needle aspiration (Option A) is suitable only for cysts under 3 cm. In this case, since the cyst measures 8 cm, aspiration is not appropriate.

GnRH analogues (Option C) can shrink endometriomas by lowering estrogen levels but are not curative and often result in regrowth after stopping treatment. Long-term use beyond 6 months is not recommended.

Conservative management (Option D) is not advisable for an 8 cm cyst, even if asymptomatic, due to the risk of adhesions and potential complications. Cystectomy is preferred for cysts larger than 4 cm.

question_text: Identify the condition shown in the image below:
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts Condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts), which are:

  • Caused by:Human Papillomavirus (HPV), mainly types 6 and 11.
  • Transmission:Predominantly through sexual contact.
  • Risk Factors:Multiple partners, unprotected sex, age, and immunosuppression.
  • Histopathology:Shows acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and koilocytosis(keratinocytes with perinuclear halo and pyknotic nuclei).

Clinical Features:

  • Asymptomatic in many cases, but may cause pruritus, bleeding, or pain.
  • Morphology:Raised, flesh-colored papules that can be flat, broad, pedunculated, or cauliflower-like.
  • Distribution:Commonly seen in the anogenital region; rarely in the oral cavity.
  • Lesions often appear in multiplesand may coalesce.

Management:

  • Observation:Small lesions may regress spontaneously.
  • Medical therapy:Podophyllotoxin, Imiquimod, or Trichloroacetic acid (TCA).
  • Procedures:Cryotherapy, electrosurgery, laser ablation, or surgical excision for refractory cases.

Explanation of Other Options:

Condyloma lata (Option A):Seen in secondary syphilis. Presents as broad, flat, moist, painless lesions in the genital/perianal area.;

Molluscum contagiosum (Option B):Viral infection by poxvirus. Produces small, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication; commonly painless.

question_text: How is the contraceptive device shown in the image inserted into the female reproductive system?
explanation:
Explanation:

The device shown is the Essure coil, which is a permanent, non-surgical sterilisation method for women. It is inserted using a hysteroscopic approach, meaning a thin, flexible hysteroscope is passed through the vagina and cervix into the uterus. Through this device, a small coil is placed into each fallopian tube. Over the next few months, fibrosis forms around the coils, causing permanent occlusion of the tubes and preventing sperm from reaching the eggs.

Explanation of Other Options:

Abdominal (Option B): This refers to procedures involving an incision in the abdominal wall, such as a traditional tubal ligation via laparotomy. Essure does not require abdominal surgery.

Laparoscopic (Option C): Laparoscopy involves inserting instruments and a camera into the abdominal cavity through small incisions. While laparoscopic tubal ligation is a common permanent contraceptive method, Essure is specifically inserted hysteroscopically.

Oral (Option D): Oral contraception involves taking pills containing hormones to prevent ovulation. The Essure device is a mechanical, permanent method.

Key takeaway:

  • Procedure Duration: Typically 10-20 minutes under local anaesthesia with sedation.
  • Recovery: Most women can resume normal activities within a day or two.
  • Effectiveness: The contraceptive effect is achieved after 3 months, when a hysterosalpingogram (HSG) confirms tubal occlusion.
  • Advantages: Non-surgical, avoids general anaesthesia, minimal recovery time.
  • Possible Complications: Mild pelvic pain, cramping, vaginal bleeding, infection, coil migration, or rarely, perforation of the uterus or tubes.

question_text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic mitral valve is on warfarin therapy. Her INR is 3. What is the appropriate next step in management?
option_d: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves require ongoing anticoagulation to prevent thrombosis.
  • Warfarin is effective but crosses the placenta and is teratogenic (especially in first trimester) and can cause hemorrhagic complications near term.
  • At 36 weeks, warfarin increases the risk of fetal intracranial hemorrhage and maternal peripartum bleeding.
  • LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin) does not cross the placenta, making it safer for the fetus while maintaining anticoagulation for the mother.

Clinical Protocol:

  • Stop warfarin 2-3 weeks before delivery.
  • Switch to therapeutic LMWH, adjusted by anti-Xa levels, until labor or delivery.

Explanation of Other Options:

Stop warfarin and start heparin (Option B): Unfractionated heparin can be used but is less effective than LMWH for thromboprophylaxis in mechanical valves and requires continuous IV infusion or frequent monitoring, making it less practical near term.

Continue warfarin (Option C): Continuing warfarin near term increases the risk of fetal hemorrhage, particularly intracranial bleeding, and maternal bleeding during delivery.

Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin (Option D): Adding aspirin increases the risk of maternal and fetal bleeding without additional benefit for valve thrombosis prevention in this setting.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Warfarin in pregnancy: Avoid in first trimester (teratogenic) and near term (risk of hemorrhage).
  • LMWH: Preferred in late pregnancy due to placental safety.
  • Heparin: Effective but less convenient, requires close monitoring.
  • Transition strategy for mechanical valves:
    • First trimester → LMWH
    • Mid-pregnancy → Warfarin (if dose <5 mg/day, some protocols allow)
    • Late pregnancy → LMWH/UFH near term

It should be started at least 1 month (ideally 3 months) prior to pregnancy and continued through the first 6-12 weeks of pregnancy."-COGDT 10/e, p 197

Remember:

  • Therapeutic dose of folic acid (to be given in females with a previous history of baby with NTD) - 4 mg.
  • Prophylactic dose of folic acid = 0.4 mg i.e., 400 mg
  • Duration: It should be started 1 month before conception and continued till 3 months of pregnancy.

Note: Women with insulin dependent diabetes mellitus and those with seizure disorders treated by valproic acid and carbamazepine are also at greater risk for NTD's and should be given therapeutic dose of folic acid i.e 4 mg.

question_text: Definitive treatment for pre eclampsia is
explanation:
• The definitive treatment for preeclampsia is delivery of the baby and placenta. This is because preeclampsia is caused by the placenta, and it cannot be cured until the placenta is removed.
  • Anti-hypertensives, MgSO4, and aspirin are all used to manage the symptoms of preeclampsia and prevent complications, but they cannot cure the disease.
  • Anti-hypertensives are used to lower blood pressure, which is one of the main symptoms of preeclampsia.
  • MgSO4 is used to prevent seizures, which can be a serious complication of preeclampsia.
  • Aspirin is used to lower blood pressure and prevent preeclampsia in women who are at high risk.
  • However, none of these treatments can cure preeclampsia. The only way to cure preeclampsia is to deliver the baby and placenta.
  • The timing of delivery will depend on the severity of the preeclampsia and the health of the mother and fetus. In mild cases, delivery may be delayed until the baby is more mature. In severe cases, delivery may be necessary immediately to prevent complications.

Reference: Arias 5th edition pg no 193

question_text: A woman with 35 + 5 wks gestation complains of epigastric pain, headache and blurring of vision. Her BP- 170/110. She is in labor pains. Examination shows 3 cm dilatation, bag of liquor. What is the management?
option_b: Administer tocolytics and deliver at 37 wks
option_c: Treat hypertension, administer MgS04 and consider termination of pregnancy
option_d: Give steroid cover and wait until steroid cover is complete
explanation:
This is a case of severe pre eclampsia with features of impending eclampsia:

  • Epigastric pain
  • Headache
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • New onset visual disturbances

Management of PIH/eclampsia

Mild PIH

  • Anti-hypertensive: Role is doubtful. No proven efficacy. Generally bed rest and some diet restrictions are done.
  • Definitive management(as discussed earlier will always be): Termination of pregnancy done at 37 completed weeks of pregnancy.

Severe PIH

  • 1st step in management is seizure prophylaxis-MgSO4
  • Antihypertensives should be given to decrease BP in a controlled manner without compromising the utero-placental perfusion. Aim-Systolic BP should be between-140 to 155 mm of Hg and Diastolic BP should be between 90 to 105 mm of Hg
  • Glucocorticoids-for lung maturation
  • Definitive management is - termination of pregnancy at 34 completed weeks.(Option B and D ruled out) If a pregnant woman comes with severe PIH before 32 weeks = terminate immediately.
  • No role of conservative management(Option A ruled out)

Timing of termination of pregnancy:

  • Mild preeclampsia: >=37 wks
  • Severe pre eclampsia: >=34 wks
  • Impending eclampsia: Terminate immediately
  • Eclampsia: Terminate immediately
  • HELLP syndrome: Terminate immediately

question_text: A 4th gravida patient of 30-week pregnancy came to LR with complaint of painful bleeding PV with reduced fetal movement. On examination, uterus is tonically contracted. Uterus has size of 34 weeks. FHR absent. BP-166/110 mmHg. She had wet undergarments but bleeding has stopped now. On P/V examination, cervix 6 cm dilated, 70% effaced. Next step?
explanation:
This seems to be a case of antepartum haemorrhage with hypertension and probable intrauterine fetal death. Most probably, a case of Abruptio placenta with preeclampsia. Management includes:

  • Abruptio: Definitive management is by vaginal delivery using ARM followed by Oxytocin(Emergency LSCS in case of fetal distress)
  • If the fetus has died, vaginal delivery preferred.

->Early amniotomy in the management of abruption is needed. It achieves better spiral artery compression to diminish implantation site bleeding and reduce thromboplastin infusion into the maternal vascular system.

->Membrane rupture may hasten delivery.

->If rhythmic uterine contractions are not superimposed on baseline hypertonus, oxytocin is given in standard doses.

->No data indicate that oxytocin augments thromboplastin escape into the maternal circulation to worsen coagulopathy.

Options A: Emergency LSCS is indicated in cases of fetal distress and in this case fetus is already dead.

Option B: Tocolytics won't help here as we need to expedite the delivery of the dead fetus

Option D: Observation won't suffice as mother can go into DIC if not managed immediately

question_text: Which of the following is contraindicated in pregnancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Enalapril (ACE inhibitor) is contraindicated in pregnancy due to its fetotoxic effects, particularly in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. It can cause oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia, and skull hypoplasia. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should be strictly avoided in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal growth restriction, neonatal hypotension, and renal dysgenesis.

Explanation of other options:

Alpha-methyl dopa (Safe in pregnancy) (Option A): First-line drug for hypertension in pregnancy. Has a long safety record and does not harm the fetus.

Nifedipine (Safe in pregnancy) (Option B): A calcium channel blocker used for hypertension and tocolysis (preterm labor inhibition). Recommended as a first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy.

Labetalol (Safe in pregnancy) (Option C): Beta-blocker with alpha-blocking effects, used as a first-line agent for hypertensive disorders in pregnancy. Preferred over other beta-blockers due to minimal fetal side effects.

Key Takeaways:

Enalapril (ACE inhibitor) is contraindicated in pregnancy due to its fetotoxic effects, while methyldopa, nifedipine, and labetalol are safe and commonly used antihypertensives in pregnancy.

question_text: A hypertensive pregnant lady presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding and loss of fetal movements. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypertension in pregnancy is the most important predisposing factor. Preeclampsia, gestational hypertension and essential hypertension, all are associated with placental abruption.

The association of preeclampsia in abruptio placentae varies from 10% to 50%.

The mechanism of the placental separation in preeclampsia is: Spasm of the vessels in the utero-placental bed (decidual spiral artery) → anoxic endothelial damage → rupture of vessels or extravasation of blood in the decidua basalis (retroplacental hematoma).

Abruptio placenta is defined as haemorrhage occurring in pregnancy due to the separation of a normally situated placenta. It is also called accidental haemorrhage or premature separation of placenta.

Clinical Features

Management

  • In case of abruption: The abruptio delivery interval is
  • Do not prolong this interval as complications like DIC/Renal failure(acute cortical necrosis) can

explanation:
Explanation:

  • She also has asthma, which contraindicates the use of non-selective beta-blockers like labetalol (both IV and oral).
  • Calcium channel blockers, such as nifedipine, are safe in asthmatic patients and effective for BP control in pregnancy.

  • Hydralazine
  • Methyldopa
  • Prazosin

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Labetalol IV (Option A) / Oral Labetalol (Option D):
    • Non-selective beta-blocker; may trigger bronchospasm in asthmatics.
    • IV labetalol is commonly used for acute severe hypertension, but contraindicated here.
  • ACE inhibitors (Option C):
    • Contraindicated during pregnancy due to fetal risks, including:
      • IUGR
      • Renal dysgenesis
      • Oligohydramnios

Key Takeaway Points:

Antihypertensive Treatment During Pregnancy

First-line drugs:

  • Labetalol commonly treats acute severe hypertension in pregnancy.
  • Initial IV dose: 10-20 mg, then 20-80 mg every 10-30 mins up to 300 mg.
  • Continuous IV infusion: 1-2 mg/min.
  • Fewer side effects than alternatives; less tachycardia.
  • Avoid in asthma, heart disease, compromised heart function, heart block, or bradycardia.
  • Methyldopa, an alpha agonist, is less effective in severe hypertension and has sedative side effects. It acts centrally and by reducing sympathetic outflow to affect a generalized decreased vascular tone.

Second-line drugs:

Contraindicated drugs:

Pre-existing Medication Management:

  • ACE Inhibitors/ARBs: Discontinue immediately upon pregnancy recognition.
  • Other Antihypertensives:
    • Mild/Moderate Hypertension: Some guidelines suggest discontinuation in the first trimester and restart if BP approaches a severe range.

question_text: All are true about biophysical profile(BPP) except:
option_a: Includes breathing, movements, tone and Amniotic fluid volume
option_b: Can tell us about fetal outcome and fetal pH
option_c: Score is inconsistent with fetal pH at different gestational ages
option_d: Score <4: fetal pH <7.2; Score 0: 100% fetal acidemia
explanation:
A Biophysical Profile (BPP) is a prenatal test used to assess the well-being of a fetus, as well as its pH(Option B) typically during the third trimester. It combines an ultrasound evaluation with a non-stress test (NST) to monitor several parameters that indicate the health and functioning of the baby. BPP is often performed if there are concerns about the baby's well-being, such as in high-risk pregnancies, to help assess whether the baby might need early delivery.

Components of Biophysical Profile:

The BPP assesses five key parameters, each scored on a scale of 0 to 2, for a total possible score of 10 points(Option A):

  1. Fetal Heart Rate (Non-Stress Test):
    • Monitors the baby's heart rate in response to its movements.
    • A reactive (normal) result scores 2 points, while a non-reactive result scores 0.
  2. Fetal Breathing Movements:
    • Observation of rhythmic breathing movements in the fetus for at least 30 seconds.
    • Presence of breathing movements scores 2 points; absence scores 0.
  3. Fetal Movement:
    • The baby's body movements (e.g., limb or trunk movements).
    • At least 3 discrete movements in 30 minutes scores 2 points; fewer than 3 scores 0.
  4. Fetal Muscle Tone:
    • Evaluation of the baby's muscle tone by observing flexion and extension of limbs or trunk.
    • Normal muscle tone (e.g., flexion/extension movements) scores 2 points; abnormal or absent tone scores 0.
  5. Amniotic Fluid Volume:
    • Assessment of the amount of amniotic fluid surrounding the fetus.
    • An adequate fluid pocket (at least 2 cm) scores 2 points; insufficient fluid scores 0.

Scoring and Interpretation:

  • 8-10 points: Considered normal, indicating that the baby is likely in good health.
  • 6 points: Borderline; may require further monitoring or follow-up testing.
  • 4 points or lower: Considered abnormal, often prompting immediate intervention, such as additional testing or even delivery if necessary.It is suggestive of acidemia if fetal pH < 7.2(Option D)

Purpose:

The BPP is typically used when there are concerns about fetal distress or complications, such as:

  • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
  • Diabetes or hypertension in the mother
  • Post-term pregnancy (beyond 40 weeks)
  • Decreased fetal movements

It provides a comprehensive assessment of the baby's well-being and helps guide decisions regarding delivery or further monitoring.

Note: A BPP score of 0 was almost invariably associated with significant fetal acidemia, whereas a normal score of 8 or 10 was associated with normal pH. An equivocal test result-a score of 6-was a poor predictor of an abnormal outcome. A drop in the BPP score from 2 or 4 down to 0 more accurately predicted an abnormal fetal outcome.

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia of 2 months duration. He has been on a chronic medication for last 15 years. The urine is hypoosmolar. His blood sugars are normal. Which could be the drug?
explanation:
Polyuria, polydipsia with large volume of hypoosmolar urine suggest the diagnosis of Diabetes insipidus. Among the following, Lithium therapy causes nephrogenic diabetes.

Other drugs causing Diabetes Insipidus: Lithium, Demeclocycline, Methoxyflurane, Amphotericin B, Aminoglycosides, Cisplatin, Rifampin, Foscarnet.

Lithium causes DI by entering the Collecting Duct via the ENaC, where it down regulates the Aquaporin channels.

Lithium also causes Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disease.

Amiloride can be used to prevent and treat Lithium induced Diabetes Insipidus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch: 316, Pg: 2363.

question_text: A 16-year-old boy is being treated with desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. His plasma glucose level (fasting) is 108 mg/dl, sodium 139 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 4.5 mmol/l (3.5-4.9) and calcium 10.9 mg/dl. He still has complaints of polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia. What could be the most probable cause?
explanation:
• This boy most probably has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus due to hypercalcemia. In this condition, renal tubules are resistant to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is due to a receptor defect of vasopressin-2 receptor or a post-receptor defect in an ADH-sensitive water channel called aquaporin-2.
  • Central DI (ADH deficiency) show good response to desmopressin (V2 agonist) administration.
  • The findings do not suggest diabetes mellitus, which is also associated with these symptoms.
  • In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH), low sodium levels are the hallmark.

Metabolic causes of Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus:

  • Chronic Hypokalemia
  • Chronic Hypercalcemia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2920

A 16-year-old boy is being treated with desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. His plasma glucose level (fasting) is 108 mg/dl, sodium 139 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 4.5 mmol/l (3.5-4.9) and calcium 10.9 mg/dl.
He still has complaints of polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia. What could be the most probable cause?
explanation:
• This boy most probably has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In this condition, renal tubules are resistant to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is due to a receptor defect of vasopressin-2 receptor or a post-receptor defect in an ADH-sensitive water channel called aquaporin-2.
  • The findings do not suggest diabetes mellitus, which is also associated with these symptoms. In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH), sodium levels are usually low.

question_text: A 54-year-old chronic smoker presents with polyuria, polydipsia and altered sensorium for the past 2 days. He is known to be suffering from squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination he is lethargic and confused. ECG shows a narrowed QT interval. What is the most probable metabolic abnormality?
explanation:
• Paraneoplastic syndromes in bronchogenic carcinoma can cause several electrolytes abnormalities. The features in this case are suggestive of hypercalcaemia. This occurs due to parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) production.
