question_text: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated in the endocrinology clinic for increased urine output. She weighs 60 kg and has a 24-hour urine output of 3500 ml. Her basal urine osmolality is 210 mOsm/kg. She undergoes a fluid deprivation test and her urine osmolality after fluid deprivation (loss of weight 3 kg) is 350 mOsm/kg. A subsequent injection of subcutaneous DDAVP (desmopressin acetate) did not result in a further significant rise of urine osmolality after 2 hours (355 mOsm/kg). Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Diabetes insipidus (DI) is suspected when the urine output is > 50 ml/kg per day . If the basal urine osmolality is > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests an osmotic diuresis (due to glucose / mannitol).
  • If fluid deprivation causes a urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests psychogenic (primary) polydipsia as in this patient.
  • If not, it is either pituitary or nephrogenic DI. These are differentiated by the administration of subcutaneous DDAVP which causes an increased urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg in pituitary DI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2921-22

question_text: Which of the following statements about urinary tract infection (UTI) in pregnancy is true?
option_a: The prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is 50%
option_b: It is lower in people with sickle cell trait
option_c: The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin
option_d: If ASB is not treated, 75% of them will develop symptomatic infection
explanation:
Explanation:

If asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is left untreated during pregnancy, about 75% of affected women may develop symptomatic UTI or pyelonephritis. This can lead to serious maternal and fetal complications such as preterm labour, low birth weight, and sepsis. Hence, routine urine screening and early treatment during pregnancy are strongly recommended.

Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB):

  • Defined as ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism in urine without urinary symptoms.
  • Common organisms: coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, and Enterococcus.

Risk Factors:

  • Female sex
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Pregnancy
  • Urinary tract abnormalities or catheter use
  • Immunosuppression

Diagnosis:

  • Urine culture showing ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single bacterial species in two consecutive specimens.

Management:

  • Pregnant women: Always treat (e.g., nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, or amoxicillin based on culture results).
  • Non-pregnant women:Only treat if symptomatic.
  • Elderly/catheterised patients:Treat only if symptomatic.

Complications:

  • Pyelonephritis
  • Preterm delivery
  • Low birth weight
  • Septicemia

Screening:

  • Routine urine culture between 12-16 weeks of gestation.

Explanation for other Options:

The prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is 50%(Option A): The prevalence of ASB in pregnancy is 5-10%, not 50%.

It is lower in people with sickle cell trait (Option B): Sickle cell trait actually increases susceptibility to UTIs due to renal medullary dysfunction.

The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin (Option C). While amoxicillin is safe, nitrofurantoin or cephalexin are more commonly preferred due to resistance concerns; antibiotic choice should be guided by culture and sensitivity.

Reference: Medscape - Workup of Uterine Anomalies

question_text: At what gestational age is screening for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) recommended in India?
explanation:
Explanation:

In India, screening for GDM is recommended between 24-28 weeks of gestation using a one-step approach, as recommended by WHO and IADPSG (International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Group).

One-step approach:

  • Applicable to all pregnant womenat 24-28 weeks.
  • Serves both screening and diagnostic purposes.
  • Preparation:Unrestricted diet for 72 hours followed by overnight fasting.
  • Procedure:Administration of 75 g oral glucose.
  • Sample collection:
    • Fasting sample
    • 1 hour after 75 g glucose
    • 2 hours after 75 g glucose
  • Interpretation:If any one value is abnormal, GDM is diagnosed.

Note:

  • The two-step approachrecommended by ACOG is not preferred in India.
  • Two-step details:
    • Oral Glucose Challenge Test (OGCT):50 g glucose, non-fasting.

    • Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT):Confirmatory test with 100 g glucose after 8 hours fasting.

Reference:

International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups Recommendations on the Diagnosis and Classification of Hyperglycemia in Pregnancy - PMC

question_text: About Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy management, false statement is
option_a: Elective LSCS has no effects on reducing incidence of brachial plexus injury
option_b: GDM female can use insulin on the night before and on morning of IOL
option_c: In active labour, if RBS is <70 mg/dl, 5% dextrose is given
option_d: Capillary blood glucose are maintained at FBS: 95 mg/dl and PPBS: 120 mg/dl
explanation:
Morning dose of insulin is skipped on the day of labour

Antepartum Management

  • Diet: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT): It is the cornerstone of treatment of diabetes in Caloric requirement is 25-35 kcal/kg body weight/ day according to body mass index. It is advisable to take 3 major and 3 minor meals so that there is no intermittent hypoglycemia and still ideal blood sugars are maintained.

Diet composition should be 45% of carbohydrates, 30% proteins and 25% fats

  • Excercise :Planned physical activity for 30 minutes/day is recommended.

Metabolic Goals during Pregnancy:

  • Premeal value- 70-90 mg/dl > (95 mg/dl)
  • Postmeal 1 hr PP = < 148 mg/dl, 2 hr PP < 120 mg/dl
  • HbA1c <6%.
  • If these goals are not achieved patient should be put on
  • Oral hypoglycemics are not advised during pregnancy as they can cross the placenta and cause fetal hypo- glycaemia.The only oral hypoglycemic drug approved for use in pregnancy is Glyburide and metformin.

Diet and exercise should be continued for at least 2-3 weeks with the aim to achieve the following metabolic goals.

  • Insulin: is the drug of choice for management of DM/GDM in pregnancy as it does not cross the placenta.

-Patient should be advised self checking of Glucose.

Indication for starting insulin in pregnancy:

  • If FBS is more than 95 mg/dL or if 1 hour postprandial value is more than 140 mg/dL or 2 hour postprandial value is more than 120 mg/dL.
  • Dose = 7 to 1 units per kg/day in divided doses.
  • Rapid acting insulin NPH (aspart and lispro), and intermediate acting insulin are safe in The total daily requirement of insulin = 2/3 in morning + 1/3 at Night such that
  • Morning dose = 2/3 NPH + 1/3 short acting
  • Pre dinner dose = ½ NPH + ½ short acting

Intrapartum Management

Time of delivery

  • Low risk patients-wait for spontaneous labor till maximum 40 weeks
  • High risk patients-38 weeks- induce labor as IUD occurs mostly in last 2 weeks of pregnancy.
  • Mode of delivery -vaginal delivery.(Option A)

Indications of Elective LSCS in GDM Patients

  • Macrosomia with weight > 5 kg (for predicting macrosomia, shoulder width > 14 cm, EFW > 4.5 kg on ultrasound)
  • Demonstrable fetal compromise (Severe IUGR)
  • Bad obstetric history
  • Other obstetric indications
  • Elderly primigravida

Note:

  • Suspected macrosomia is not a C/I for VBAC.
  • Insulin requirement decrease during labor and since patient is on liquid diet-insulin is stopped during labour

Precautions During Caesarean:

Elective caesarean for macrosomia is recommended in a diabetic pregnancy if the estimated fetal weight is .4.5kg (ACOG).

  • Anaesthetist must be consulted prior to elective surgery.
  • After appropriate consent and blood availability, a light meal and night dose of insulin are given.
  • Elective section of a diabetic patient should preferably be performed as the first case in the morning as the patient is fasting and also there is availability of all the necessary personnel.
  • Morning insulin dose is omitted and fasting glucose level done.
  • If required sliding scale of insulin can be started and continued in the postoperative period.
  • Severely obese may require thromboprophylaxis.

Postpartum Management

Revaluation of glycemic status using 75 g oral GTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum.

question_text:
A 28-year-old female sustained a minor head injury, was seen in the emergency department with headache and was discharged following a normal computed tomography of the head, She presented again 2 months later with polyuria and polydipsia. She has a 2-year history of recurrent pyelonephritis and is under investigation by the urologists. A water deprivation test was performed:
Water deprivation phase: Plasma osmolality 295 mOsmol/kg (NR: 275 - 295 mOsmol/kg), Urine osmolality 220 mOsmol/kg
Desmopressin (DDAVP) phase (after administration of 2 pg desmopressin): Plasma osmolality 300 mOsmol/kg Urine osmolality 250 mOsmoL/kg. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the water deprivation test after overnight fast shows the maximal osmolality of urine is abnormally low < 750 mOsmol/ kg, After administration of exogenous vasopressin (DDAVP), there is only slight increase in urine osmolality In cranial diabetes insipidus, DDAVP produces a rise in urine osmolality of about 50%. In psychogenic polydipsia, a low initial plasma and urine osmolality.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:381 Pg: 2920

question_text: A 29-year-old woman came to the diabetes clinic with her two children. This is her third pregnancy and although not normally diabetic, she was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus. Recent fasting plasma glucose levels have been in the range of 80-90 mg/dl and she is taking BD mixed insulins. Later that evening she collapses while shopping and is brought to the Emergency Department with blood glucose of 56 mg/dl. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this patient?
option_a: Reduce her dose of BD mixed insulin by 50%
option_b: Reduce her dose of BD mixed insulin by 20%
option_c: Check a random cortisol to rule out Addison's disease
option_d: Change her to a basal bolus regime
explanation:
• This lady's fasting plasma glucose levels are appropriate, but taking a BD mixed insulin regime is probably not appropriate to her lifestyle where her mealtimes and portion sizes may be slightly irregular given the fact that she has two other children to manage.
  • A basal bolus regime would give her more flexibility in varying insulin dose.
  • The coexistence of Addison's is unlikely and increasing the size of her meals would only promote more excess weight gain and worsening insulin resistance.

Reference: ADA Standards of Diabetes Care - 2023

question_text: A 30-year-old primigravida at 18 weeks of gestation presents for her antenatal check-up. Her random plasma glucose level was 243 mg/dL, and further tests revealed fasting blood glucose 146 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.6%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_a: Maturity onset diabetes of the young
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In this case:
    • Fasting glucose: 146 mg/dL
    • Random glucose: 243 mg/dL
    • HbA1c: 7.6%
    • Meets criteria for overt diabetes
  • Overt diabetes in pregnancy is hyperglycemia first recognized during pregnancy that meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes in non-pregnant adults.
  • ADA Diagnostic Criteria for Overt Diabetes in Pregnancy:
    • Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L)
    • 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) after OGTT
    • Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms
    • HbA1c ≥ 5% (48 mmol/mol)

Explanation of Other Options:

Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) (Option A): Usually presents at a younger age with a strong family history; rare during pregnancy and not consistent here.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) (Option C): GDM is mild hyperglycemia first detected in pregnancy, usually FPG < 92 mg/dL and HbA1c 5.7-6.4%; the patient's levels exceed these thresholds.

Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA) (Option D): Requires autoantibody testing; not indicated in this scenario.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Overt diabetes in pregnancy = meets adult diabetes criteria, discovered during pregnancy
  • Early recognition is important to prevent maternal and fetal complications
  • GDM = milder form, typically later onset and does not meet adult diabetes thresholds

question_text: Following is the emergency management of bleeding vulvar varices during pregnancy:
explanation:
Varicosities (lower leg, vulva, rectum) may appear for the first time or aggravate during pregnancy usually in later months.

  • It is due to obstruction in the venous return by the pregnant uterus
  • Specific treatment is better to be avoided
  • Varicosities usually disappear following delivery
  • Valvular varicosities may be aided by application of a foam rubber pad suspended across the vulva by a belt used with a perineal pad
  • Rarely large varicosities may rupture leading to profuse hemorrhage.

A) Pressure: Applying gentle pressure to varicose veins, such as using support garments or compression stockings, can help alleviate discomfort associated with varicosities. This option aligns with the conservative approach recommended during pregnancy.

B) Cautery: Cautery or surgical procedures are generally not the first-line approach for managing vulvar varicosities during pregnancy. Specific treatment is usually avoided during this time to minimize risks.

C) Simple vulvectomy: Simple vulvectomy, a surgical removal of the vulva, is not a standard treatment for vulvar varicosities during pregnancy. It is a more invasive procedure that is typically reserved for other medical conditions.

D) Observation only: This option is in line with the approach recommended for managing varicosities during pregnancy. Observation and conservative measures are often preferred, as varicosities tend to resolve on their own after childbirth.

In summary, during pregnancy, it is generally advisable to opt for conservative management (Option A) and observation only (if not bleeding) rather than more invasive measures like cautery or surgery.

question_text: Which of the following tests is not required for Turner mosaic syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Turner's syndrome is caused by monosomy of the X chromosome; therefore, the ANA test is not appropriate for its diagnosis.
  • ANA (antinuclear antibody) testing is used for autoimmune diseases such as SLE, scleroderma, and rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Autoimmune conditions linked with Turner's syndrome include autoimmune thyroiditis, celiac disease, and occasionally Type 1 diabetes.

Turner mosaic syndrome:

  • Turner's syndrome results from the deletion or non-functioning of one X chromosome in females and is a genetic condition.
  • About 50% of affected individuals have a mosaic chromosomal pattern (45,X mosaicism).
  • Mosaic Turner syndrome is not inherited but occurs due to a random event during early fetal cell division.
  • This causes some cells to have the normal two sex chromosomes, while others have only one X chromosome.

Explanation for other options:

Echocardiography (Option A) is an imaging technique used to detect cardiovascular abnormalities in Turner's syndrome, such as bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.
Although milder forms can occur in Mosaic Turner syndrome, regular screening with echocardiography is recommended.

Periodic audiometry (Option B) is advised every 3-5 years to screen for sensorineural hearing loss, as hearing loss and cholesteatoma are associated with Turner's syndrome.

Oral glucose tolerance test (Option C) is performed since most patients with Turner's syndrome have glucose metabolism abnormalities, including insulin resistance. Screening for diabetes can be done with HbA1c or oral glucose tolerance test, with the latter being more sensitive.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554621/

question_text: A 26-year-old P1L1 woman presents with abdominal pain. She has a history of rheumatic heart disease and mitral valve replacement and is on Warfarin 3 mg OD. On examination, a 14-week-sized abdominal mass is palpable. Ultrasound shows an 8 �� 6 cm unilocular left ovarian cyst with a reticular pattern. What is the next line of management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with a functional-appearing ovarian cyst. Unilocular ovarian cysts with a reticular pattern in reproductive-aged women are usually benign and often resolve spontaneously. The next appropriate step is to repeat ultrasound in 6-12 weeks to monitor for changes in size or morphology.

Functional Ovarian Cysts:

  • Origin: Arise during follicle maturation and ovulation
  • Types:
    • Single cysts: Follicular or corpus luteum cysts (most common)
    • Multiple cysts: Seen in PCOS, OHSS, FSH-secreting pituitary adenomas
  • Features:
    • Usually 3-7 cm, unilocular, filled with clear fluid
    • Often asymptomatic and benign
    • May cause mild abdominal pain

Management:

  • Observation: Most cysts resolve within 4-6 months
  • Follow-up: Ultrasound after 6-12 weeks
  • Symptomatic treatment: Pain relief or hormonal therapy (COCs)
  • Surgery: Indicated only for:
    • Cysts >10 cm
    • Persistent or enlarging cysts
    • Acute complications (torsion, rupture)

Explanation of Other Options:

Measure CA-125 (Option A): CA-125 is primarily useful in postmenopausal women for suspected malignancy. It can be elevated in benign conditions (menstruation, endometriosis, PID) and is not indicated for a simple functional cyst in a young woman.

Surgical intervention (Option C): Immediate surgery is not required for a simple ovarian cyst. Surgery is reserved for persistent, enlarging, symptomatic, or complex cysts.

MRI pelvis (Option D): Transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging. MRI is only indicated for complex or uncertain cases, which is not necessary here.

question_text: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes an ultrasound that identifies a unilocular ovarian cyst measuring 6 cm. Her serology is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient most likely has a functional ovarian cyst, which arises due to normal ovulatory activity. Functional cysts include follicular cysts (failure of follicle rupture) and corpus luteum cysts (persistent luteal activity). These cysts are usually unilocular, thin-walled, and asymptomatic, and they often resolve spontaneously within 1-2 menstrual cycles.

Management guidelines for asymptomatic ovarian cysts in premenopausal women:

  • Size <7 cm, simple, unilocular, negative tumour markers: Conservative management is appropriate. Follow-up with ultrasound after 1-2 menstrual cycles is recommended. Oral contraceptives may be given to suppress ovulation and reduce recurrence.
  • Persistent, complex, multilocular, or symptomatic cysts: Surgical intervention (laparoscopy or laparotomy) may be warranted.
  • Postmenopausal women: Any cyst >5 cm or with suspicious features often requires surgical evaluation due to higher malignancy risk.

Explanation for Other Options:

Laparotomy (Option A): Laparotomy is a major surgical procedure involving a large abdominal incision. It is reserved for large, persistent, or suspicious ovarian masses. Performing a laparotomy on a small, benign, functional cyst would be unnecessary and expose the patient to surgical risks.

Ovariotomy (Option C): Ovariotomy involves removing the affected ovary. This is not indicated for simple functional cysts, as fertility preservation is important in premenopausal women. Ovariotomy is reserved for ovarian torsion, malignancy, or complicated cysts with haemorrhage rupture.

Follow-up with CA-125 (Option D): CA-125 is a tumour marker that can be elevated in epithelial ovarian cancers but also in benign conditions like endometriosis. Routine CA-125 testing is not necessary for simple functional cysts, especially in premenopausal women, because it has low specificity and may lead to unnecessary anxiety or interventions.

Reference:

https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9133-ovarian-cysts

question_text: In which of the following conditions is tandem radiotherapy commonly used?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Tandem radiotherapy refers to the use of intracavitary brachytherapy in which a tandem applicator (inserted into the uterine cavity) and ovoids or ring applicators (placed in the vaginal fornices) are used.
  • This technique allows high-dose localized radiation to the cervix and adjacent parametrial tissues while minimizing exposure to surrounding organs (bladder, rectum).
  • It is a cornerstone of treatment in locally advanced cervical cancer (Stage IB3 onwards), typically in combination with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) and concurrent cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Ovarian Cancer (Option B):

  • Main treatment: cytoreductive surgery + platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin, paclitaxel).
  • Radiotherapy has no major role and tandem brachytherapy is not used.

Choriocarcinoma (Option C):

  • Highly chemosensitive tumor.
  • Treated with methotrexate, actinomycin D, or multi-agent chemotherapy (EMA-CO regimen) depending on FIGO risk scoring.
  • Radiation therapy, including tandem, is not standard.

Endometrial Cancer (Option D):

  • Managed primarily with surgery (TAH + BSO ± pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy).
  • Adjuvant radiotherapy may involve EBRT or intravaginal brachytherapy using a vaginal cylinder, but tandem + ovoids are not typically employed.

question_text: Which of the following conditions present with both Mullerian and Wolffian duct structures?
explanation:
Anti Mullerian hormone deficiency = persistent mullerian duct syndrome = uterine hernia syndrome

Karyotype is 46 XY

Since the Y chromosome is present, gonads are testis, i.e. they are males. In this syndrome, in males – sertoli cells fail to secrete Mullerian inhibiting substance and Mullerian duct is present.

Since Leyding cells are also present, they secrete testosterone normally, thus Wolffian duct is also present. So in antiMullerian hormone deficiency both mullerian and wolffian ducts are present.

Ovotestis: It is seen in true hermaphroditism. Both ovaries and testis are present. There is ambiguity of external genitalia. The internal structures depend on the degree of differentiation of the gonads.

Mixed Gonadal dysgenesis Karyotype = 45XO/46XY.

In this situation, the gonadal pattern on one side is streak gonad ovary (corresponding to karyotype 45 XO) and a normal testis on the other side (corresponding to karyotype 46 XY)

Mullerian duct and Wolffian duct development correlates with the character of ipsilateral gonad,

Thus, both Mullerian duct and wolffian ducts are present in AMH DEFICIENCY . In case of FSH receptor mutation in females, Mullerian ducts develop normally, the problem is in the binding of FSH to its receptors.

The patient presents with primary or early secondary amenorrhea, variable development of secondary sexual characters and high levels of FSH and LH.

Thus only mullerian duct would be present as the karyotype of females is normal i.e. 46(XX).

question_text: A woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents with a heart rate of 120 bpm and blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg. She has pedal edema and proteinuria and is diagnosed with eclampsia. She is started on the Pritchard regimen with magnesium sulfate. Under which of the following conditions should the treatment be stopped?
option_d: Urine output of less than 60 ml in 4 hours
explanation:
Explanation:

Urine output less than 30 ml/hour (i.e., <60 ml in 4 hours) indicates possible magnesium accumulation and impending toxicity, necessitating cessation of magnesium sulfate.

  • Magnesium sulfate is the first-line drug for seizure prophylaxis in eclampsia.
  • The Pritchard regimen involves a loading dose of 4 g IV and 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock), followed by a maintenance dose of 5 g IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks.
  • Before giving each dose, three parameters must be confirmed:
    • Respiratory rate ≥ 16/min
    • Patellar reflexes present
    • Urine output ≥ 30 ml/hr
  • If urine output is <60 ml in 4 hours, magnesium excretion is reduced, increasing the risk of toxicity (due to renal clearance dependency).
  • In such cases, withholding the next dose and close monitoring is essential.
  • If signs of toxicity appear (respiratory depression, areflexia), 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate IV is the antidote.

Explanation of other options:

Respiratory rate (RR) < 18 breaths per minute (Option A): While a low RR (<12/min) is a classic sign of toxicity, 18/min is not a cutoff to stop the drug. A RR <16/min should raise concern, but <12/min mandates immediate discontinuation and treatment.

Visual disturbances start (Option B): This is a feature of worsening preeclampsia or impending eclampsia, not magnesium toxicity. It is not an indication to stop magnesium sulfate.

Knee jerk reflex is present (Option C): Presence of patellar reflex is reassuring and required before giving each dose. Loss of reflex would indicate magnesium toxicity and is a contraindication to further dosing.

Reference:

https://www.bioline.org.br/pdf?am09018 page 78

question_text: According to WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), which of the following is classified as MEC Category 1 for the use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Women with HIV infection, however, can safely use combined oral contraceptives without restriction. This makes it MEC Category 1.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have developed the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) to guide safe contraceptive use in women with various health conditions.

  • The MEC uses a 1-4 category system:
    • Category 1: No restriction for use of the contraceptive method.
    • Category 2: Advantages generally outweigh theoretical or proven risks.
    • Category 3: Risks usually outweigh advantages (method not recommended unless other methods are not available/acceptable).
    • Category 4: Unacceptable health risk (method should not be used).

When applying this to combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs):

  • Women with diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), or hyperlipidemia have increased cardiovascular risks. For these conditions, combined OCPs fall into higher risk categories (MEC 2, 3, or 4 depending on severity). (Option A, B, and C ruled out)

question_text:
Arrange the steps of D&C in order:
1. Serial dilation
2. Curettage
3. Uterine sound
4. Assessment of uterine size and direction
explanation:
Dilation and Curettage (D&C) is a medical procedure in which the cervix is dilated (opened) and the lining of the uterus is scraped or suctioned to remove tissue. It is commonly performed to diagnose or treat certain uterine conditions, such as abnormal bleeding, or after a miscarriage. Here's a brief overview of the steps involved:

Steps of D&C:

  1. Preparation:
    • The patient is positioned on an exam table, typically in the lithotomy position (lying on the back with legs in stirrups).
    • Local or general anesthesia is administered to manage pain and discomfort.
  2. Assessment of uterine size and direction:
    • Using palpation methods
    • Using Uterine sound
  3. Cervical Dilation:
    • The healthcare provider uses a speculum to open the vaginal walls and access the cervix.
    • The cervix is gradually dilated using a series of increasingly larger dilators to allow access to the uterus.
  4. Curettage:
    • A curette (a small, spoon-shaped instrument) or suction device is inserted into the uterus.
    • The provider gently scrapes or suctions the uterine lining to remove tissue.
  5. Tissue Collection:
    • The tissue removed from the uterus is collected and may be sent for laboratory examination if the procedure is done for diagnostic purposes.
  6. Post-procedure:
    • After the procedure, the patient is monitored while the effects of anesthesia wear off.
    • Mild cramping and spotting are common after the procedure.

Recovery:

  • Most patients can go home the same day and resume normal activities after a few days.
  • Follow-up care includes monitoring for any signs of infection or complications.

D&C is often a safe and quick procedure with a relatively short recovery time.

question_text: Which of the following procedures is done with the instrument shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The instrument shown is a curette, used to collect tissue from the uterine lining. Endometrial sampling (or endometrial biopsy) involves obtaining a small tissue sample from the endometrium for microscopic examination to detect abnormalities or assess uterine conditions.

Endometrial Sampling/Endometrial Biopsy:

  • Performed outpatient, typically using a thin, flexible tube (Pipelle) or Sharman's curette.
  • Pipelle biopsy is preferred for initial evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding suspicious for malignancy.
  • Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is performed if the biopsy result is insufficient or bleeding persists.
  • Hysteroscopy-guided biopsy allows direct visualization and targeted sampling; more sensitive for focal lesions, but may increase positive peritoneal cytology in endometrial cancer without worsening prognosis.

Indications for Endometrial Sampling:

  • Abnormal uterine bleeding
  • Evaluation for endometrial neoplasia or precancerous hyperplasia
  • Surveillance of previously diagnosed endometrial hyperplasia or cancer
  • Assessment of uterine response to hormone therapy

Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS) Findings Suggesting Biopsy:

  • Diffuse or focal heterogeneity of the endometrium
  • Endometrial thickness > 4 mm
  • Inadequate visualization of the endometrium

Explanation of Other Options:

Hysterosalpingography (Option A): Imaging procedure using X-rays and contrast dye to assess the uterus and fallopian tubes. The Leech-Wilkinson cannula injects dye; does not involve tissue sampling.

Dilatation and curettage (Option B): Surgical procedure involving dilation of the cervix and removal of uterine tissue. Broader in purpose (e.g., post-miscarriage); endometrial sampling is focused on obtaining lining tissue for diagnosis.

Cervical sampling (Option C): Collection of cells from the cervix using a brush or spatula during a Pap smear; curette is not used.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541135/

question_text: A pregnant woman with no other comorbid conditions develops preeclampsia. She enquires about the cause of her condition. The doctor explains that it is due to the failure of the invasion of:

Explanation:

  • In normal pregnancy, extravillous trophoblasts invade maternal spiral arteries and remodel them into low-resistance, high-capacitance vessels, ensuring adequate uteroplacental blood flow.
  • First wave (10-12 weeks): invasion up to decidua.
  • Second wave (16-18 weeks): invasion into myometrium.
  • In preeclampsia, this second wave fails → spiral arteries remain narrow and muscular → placental ischemia.
  • Placental ischemia triggers release of anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1, sEng) → systemic endothelial dysfunction → hypertension, proteinuria, and organ involvement.

Explanation of other options:

Spiral artery by villous trophoblasts (Option A): Villous trophoblasts form chorionic villi for maternal-fetal exchange, not for spiral artery remodeling.

Radial artery by cytotrophoblasts (Option B): Radial arteries are upstream uterine arteries, not directly remodeled by cytotrophoblasts.

Arcuate artery by extravillous trophoblasts (Option D): Arcuate arteries supply radial arteries; they are not the target of trophoblast invasion.

Key Takeaway:

  • Preeclampsia results from failure of spiral artery remodeling by extravillous trophoblasts, leading to placental ischemia and systemic maternal endothelial dysfunction.

question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with oligohydramnios?
explanation:
Explanation:

Renal agenesis is a congenital anomaly where one or both kidneys fail to develop. By around the 13th week of gestation, the fetal kidneys normally begin producing urine, which forms a significant component of the amniotic fluid. In renal agenesis, urine production is impaired, resulting in oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid). This condition is often detected on ultrasound and is strongly suggestive of bilateral renal agenesis.

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Potter facies: low-set ears, beaked nose, epicanthic folds, downward-slanting eyes
  • Pulmonary hypoplasia → respiratory distress at birth
  • Limb deformities and contractures due to fetal compression
  • Intrauterine growth restriction
  • High perinatal mortality

  • Management:
    • Ultrasound every four weeks
    • Fetal monitoring weekly
    • Delivery between 36-37 weeks if diagnosed early

Explanation of Other Options:

Neural tube defect (Option B): Associated with polyhydramnios due to impaired swallowing of amniotic fluid.

Esophageal atresia (Option C): Leads to polyhydramnios, since the fetus cannot swallow and absorb amniotic fluid.

Premature birth (Option D): A complication resulting from oligohydramnios but not a direct cause of it.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Amniotic fluid increases until 34-36 weeks (~400 mL).
  • Kidneys form urine by 12 weeks; bilateral agenesis → severe oligohydramnios (fatal).
  • Unilateral renal agenesis may be asymptomatic and compatible with life.
  • Complications: pulmonary hypoplasia, growth restriction, deformities, fetal death.

question_text: A patient diagnosed with breast cancer in one breast is started on tamoxifen therapy. The use of this medication is associated with an increased risk of which of the following conditions?
option_c: Breast cancer in the opposite breast
explanation:
Explanation:

Tamoxifen, prescribed for the treatment of hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, increases the risk of developing endometrial cancer.

While tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue (acting as an antagonist), it stimulates estrogen receptors in the uterus (acting as an agonist). This estrogen-like activity in the uterus can lead to abnormal endometrial growth, raising the risk of endometrial cancer.

Explanation for other options:

Ovarian Cancer (Option A): Tamoxifen is not linked to a higher risk of ovarian cancer. However, individuals with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are at greater risk for both breast and ovarian cancers. In such cases, tamoxifen may be recommended as a preventive therapy.

Contralateral Breast Cancer (Option C): Tamoxifen does not increase the risk of cancer in the opposite breast. In fact, due to its estrogen-blocking effects in breast tissue, it helps reduce the chance of recurrence in the other breast in hormone receptor-positive cases.

Cervical Cancer (Option D): There is no established association between tamoxifen use and an increased risk of cervical cancer.

question_text: Ovarian drilling is done in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) is a surgical procedure used in the management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), particularly in women with infertility who do not respond to medical therapy (e.g., clomiphene citrate or letrozole).

PCOS (also called Stein-Leventhal syndrome)

  • A multisystem endocrinopathy seen in reproductive-age women.
  • Characterized by ovulatory dysfunction, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology.

Diagnostic Criteria - Rotterdam (2003): At least 2 of the following:

  • Hyperandrogenism - clinical (hirsutism, acne) or biochemical (↑ testosterone).
  • Ovulatory dysfunction - oligo/amenorrhea.
  • Polycystic ovarian morphology on USG - ≥12 small follicles (2-9 mm) or ovarian volume ≥10 cm³, with "string-of-pearls" appearance.

Clinical Features:

  • Menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea)
  • Infertility
  • Obesity, insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans
  • Hirsutism, acne

Management of PCOS involves:

  • Lifestyle modification: Weight loss, diet, exercise, smoking cessation
  • Pharmacological treatment:
    • Oral contraceptives for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenic symptoms
    • Anti-androgens (spironolactone, ketoconazole)
    • Metformin for insulin resistance and fertility improvement
  • Ovulation induction: Clomiphene citrate (first-line), Letrozole (for resistant cases)
  • Surgical treatment: LOD indicated when:
  • Medical therapy fails
  • Persistent anovulation with infertility
  • History of failed ovulation induction
  • Associated with recurrent pregnancy loss

Explanation of Other Options:

Ovarian tumor (Option A): Managed by surgical excision or oncological treatment, not ovarian drilling.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) (Option C): A complication of ovulation induction; managed conservatively or with supportive care, not drilling.

Endometriosis (Option D): Treated with medical therapy (OCPs, GnRH agonists) or surgical excision/ablation, not drilling.

After evacuation of the mole, persistent rise or plateau of hCG may indicate persistent GTD or choriocarcinoma.

question_text: What is the single most common cause of spontaneous abortions in the first trimester?
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct answer is Chromosomal abnormalities. Fetal genetic defects are the most common cause of first-trimester miscarriages, accounting for at least 50% of all cases. These are typically sporadic, non-inherited errors that occur during gametogenesis or fertilization, leading to a non-viable embryo.

  • The most frequent type of chromosomal anomaly found in abortus specimens is autosomal trisomy.
  • The single most common specific aneuploidy is Monosomy X (Turner Syndrome, 45,X).

Causes of Spontaneous Abortion by Trimester:

Explanation of Other Options:

Syphilis (Option B): Maternal infections like syphilis are a recognized cause of pregnancy loss, but typically in the second trimester or later, not the first.

Cervical incompetence (Option C): This is a classic cause of recurrent second-trimester loss, characterized by painless cervical dilation, not first-trimester miscarriage.

Rhesus isoimmunization (Option D): While Rh isoimmunization can lead to fetal hydrops and demise, this is a complication of the late second and third trimesters, not the first trimester.

question_text: A 26-year-old woman comes with irregular vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain over the past 4 days. Physical examination shows a friable cervix, and cervical and adnexal tenderness. You prescribe doxycycline and a second medication. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the most appropriate second drug used to treat this infection?
option_a: Binding at the D-ala-D-ala muramyl pentapeptide to prevent transglycosylation reactions
option_b: Binds to microtubules and causes mitotic arrest in metaphase
option_c: Inhibits DNA synthesis in virally infected cells
option_d: Inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis through the blockade of transpeptidation enzymes
explanation:
• This patient has signs of pelvic inflammatory disease, and since distinguishing diagnostic clues are not provided here, the answer should pertain to the most common causes, which include Chlamydia and gonococcal infection.
  • Infections of the cervix may present as an erythematous, edematous, and friable cervix, but most often are without obvious signs or symptoms. Early signs and symptoms of a chlamydial infection in women tend to be mild and include pain during urination, frequent urination, and low-grade fever.
  • Later symptoms can be more intense and include nausea, fatigue, and abnormal discharge from the vagina. Other symptoms include abdominal pain, lower back pain, irregular menstrual bleeding or spotting, and pain during sex.

question_text: True about fatty liver of pregnancy:
option_b: Due to accumulation of shortchain fatty acid
explanation:
The correct answer is (A): Common in third trimester.

Fatty liver of pregnancy, also known as acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP), typically occurs in the third trimester. The condition is associated with the accumulation of long chain fatty acids. It is related to mitochondrial dysfunction and not primarily due to lysosomal injury or alcohol consumption.

  • Acute fatty liver of pregnancy/Acute yellow atrophy of the liver

It is a rare condition occurring in third trimester

It is the M/C cause of acute liver failure during pregnancy.

Aetiology:

It is associated with disorders of fatty acid transport and oxidation-deficiency of LCHAD enzyme, i.e. long chain hydroxyl acetyl coenz A dehydrogenase accumulation of long chain fatty acid

Risk factors:

First pregnancymale fetuses, preeclampsia, maternal obesity and multiple pregnancy

Histology: Pathology

Liver is yellow, soft and greasy:

  • Swollen hepatocytes with central nuclei and cytoplasm filled with microvesicular fat
  • Periportal sparing

Clinical features

  • Patients present in the third trimester (generally at 37 weeks) with nonspecific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia, vague abdominal discomfort and malaise.
  • In many women, persistent vomiting is the main symptom.
  • AFP should also be suspected in any woman who presents with new onset nausea and malaise in third trimester.
  • This is followed by jaundice (progressive in nature) after about one week
  • In almost all severe cases, there is profound endothelial cell activation with capillary leakage causing hemoconcentration, hepatorenal syndrome, ascites, and sometimes pulmonary edema. Fetal death is more common in cases with severe hemoconcentration.
  • The syndrome typically continues to worsen after diagnosis. Hypoglycemia is common, and obvious hepatic encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy, and some degree of renal failure develop in approximately half of women

Management:

  • Rapid delivery is essential
  • Mode of delivery – Induction of labor followed by vaginal delivery

Reference: Williams Obs 23/e, pg 1065, 1066; COGDT 10/e, pg 382

question_text: The first step in the management of hirsutism due to Stein-Leventhal syndrome is:
explanation:
Medical Treatment of Hirsutism

Drug therapy : If a patient has hirsutism the primary goal is lowering androgen levels to halt further conversion of vellus hairs to terminal ones.

Drugs used are :

  • OCPs -

Basis of using OCPs for hirsutism

  • The progestin component suppresses LH, resulting in decreased ovarian androgen production.
  • The estrogen component increases hepatic production of SHBG (sex hormone bonding globilin), resulting in decreased free testosterone concentration.
  • Circulating androgen levels are reduced.

Estrogen decreases conversion of testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone in some by inhibition of 5-alpha reductase

"OCPs are the first line of management of oligomenorrhea caused by PCOS. Progestins decrease total androgen level by reducing the activity of 5-alpha reductase. OCP usage results in an overall decrease in the formation of new androgen dependant hair growth and androgen stimulated acne. All low dose OCP preparations are believed to have similar results. If therapy with OCPs is suboptimal , addition of an antiandrogen , such as spironolactone or finasteride, is recommended."

Reference: Novak 14th/ed pg no: 1082-1083

question_text: Which of the following statement is correct about acute fatty liver of pregnancy?
option_c: Common if female fetus is present
option_d: May be associated with decreased uric acid
explanation:
• Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is a rare condition that typically occurs in the third trimester of pregnancy.
  • It is more common in the third trimester but can also occur in the second trimester.
  • It is associated with disorders of fatty acid transport and oxidation, often related to a deficiency of the LCHAD enzyme.
  • AFLP is a serious condition that requires prompt recognition and intervention as it can lead to acute liver failure.
  • It is not specifically associated with the gender of the fetus (Option C ruled out) or a particular level of uric acid (Option D ruled out).
  • The incidence is estimated to be around 1 in 7,000 to 1 in 15,000 pregnancies rather than 1 in 1000 (Option A ruled out).

Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP) / Acute Yellow Atrophy of the Liver:

Aetiology:

  • Rare condition occurring in the third trimester (mean gestational age of 37.5 weeks).
  • Most common cause of acute liver failure during pregnancy.

Associated Risk Factors:

  • Disorders of fatty acid transport and oxidation, particularly deficiency of LCHAD enzyme (long-chain hydroxyl acetyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase).
  • Increased risk in first pregnancies, male fetuses, preeclampsia, maternal obesity, and multiple pregnancies.

Histology:

  • Liver appears yellow, soft, and greasy.
  • Swollen hepatocytes with central nuclei and cytoplasm filled with microvesicular fat.
  • Periportal sparing acute yellow atrophy.
  • Minimal hepatocellular pathology.

Clinical Features:

  • Typically presents in the third trimester (around 37 weeks) with nonspecific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia, vague abdominal discomfort, and malaise.
  • Persistent vomiting may be a prominent symptom.
  • AFP should be suspected in any woman with new-onset nausea and malaise in the third trimester.
  • Progresses to jaundice over about one week.
  • In 50% of cases, features of preeclampsia such as hypertension, proteinuria, and edema are present.
  • Severe cases may lead to endothelial cell activation, hemoconcentration, hepatorenal syndrome, ascites, and sometimes pulmonary edema.
  • Maternal leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia may occur.

Investigations:

  • Abnormal liver function tests:
    • Rise in serum bilirubin (usually less than 10 mg/dL).
    • Increased SGOT and SGPT (less than 1000 IU/L).
    • Moderately increased alkaline phosphatase.
    • Prothrombin time may be increased.
    • Prolonged clotting time.
  • Severe cases may exhibit disseminated coagulation failure.
  • Abnormal renal function tests, including elevated serum creatinine and uric acid levels.
  • Other abnormalities: Hypoglycemia, decreased platelet count, and low fibrinogen levels.

Management:

  • Rapid delivery is essential.
  • Mode of delivery: Induction of labor followed by vaginal delivery.
  • Cesarean section is avoided if possible due to coagulopathy but is still common in practice.

Complications:

  • Maternal mortality ranges from 10% to 75%.
  • Hepatic dysfunction typically resolves postpartum.
  • Postpartum complications may include transient diabetes insipidus and acute pancreatitis.

Fetal Prognosis:

  • Generally poor.
  • Surviving fetuses may develop a Reye-like syndrome with hepatic encephalopathy and severe hypoglycemia due to a defect in beta-fatty acid oxidation.

explanation:

Management of Intrahepatic Cholestasis – Medical Management

The most troublesome feature of intrahepatic cholestasis is pruritus (and pruritus is due to bile acid in blood):

  • Ursodeoxycholic acid (10-15 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses) relieves pruritus decreasing in the concentration of bile acid in blood and it also improves biochemical abnormalities.

In patients of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy – there is increased perinatal mortality. Hence fetal surveillance is done with biweekly NST. Conventional antepartum testing, does not predict fetal mortality as there is sudden death in choletasis due to acute hypoxia, hence delivery is recommended at 37-38 weeks.

Causes of premature ovarian insufficiency (failure)

question_text:
28-year-old woman, at 30 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for the management of elevated blood pressures. Treatment with an intravenous drug is initiated. Physical examination shows pitting edema of both lower extremities that was not present on admission.

This patient was given a drug most likely that predominantly acts by which of the following mechanisms?
option_a: Increases the intracellular concentration of cGMP in smooth muscle
explanation:
• This woman has likely been treated with intravenous hydralazine, a first-line treatment for severe hypertension during pregnancy.
    • Hydralazine is a direct peripheral vasodilator that preferentially affects arteriolar smooth muscle and increases the intracellular concentration of cGMP, which reduces afterload and blood pressure.
    • Common adverse effects of hydralazine therapy include headache (due to direct vasodilation), tachycardia (due to reflex sympathetic activation), and peripheral edema (due to increased hydrostatic pressure, retention of sodium and water, and fluid extravasation). To reduce these adverse effects, direct arteriolar vasodilators are often co-administered with a β-blocker and/or a diuretic.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 176

question_text: All are used in treating spasmodic dysmenorrhea except:
explanation:
Spasmodic dysmenorrhoea is another name for primary dysmenorrhoea.

The etiology of primary dysmenorrhea includes excessive amount of prostanoids secreted from the endometrium during menstruation. The prostanoids result in increased uterine contractions with a dysrhythmic pattern, increased basal tone, and increased active pressure.

Pain is spasmodic in nature

Pain of primary dysmenorrhea usually begins a few hours before or just after the onset of a menstrual period and may last 48 to 72 hours.

Characteristics of spasmodic dysmenorrhoea

  • Seen in adolescent girls
  • Pain begins few hours before a rest of menstruation and lasts for 12–24 hours, but never 48 hours more than
  • Management: NSAIDs, OCP’s can be used for management.

question_text: A 16-year-old girl presents to the OPD with primary amenorrhea (no onset of menstruation) and cyclical lower abdominal pain. On examination, the following image is observed. What is the most likely underlying cause of this presentation?
option_a: Transverse septum in the proximal vagina
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of primary amenorrhea with cyclic pain suggests cryptomenorrhea, a condition in which menstrual blood accumulates due to an obstruction in the genital outflow tract. The visible vaginal bulge further supports this diagnosis.

The most common cause of cryptomenorrhea is an imperforate hymen, where the hymenal membrane completely covers the vaginal opening, preventing menstrual blood from exiting. This leads to the collection of blood within the vagina (hematocolpos) and uterus (hematometra), resulting in pain and a tense, bulging perineal mass.

Management involves a cruciate (X-shaped) incision on the hymen to drain the retained blood and relieve the obstruction.

Explanation of Other Options :

Transverse septum in the proximal vagina (Option A): This is a congenital anomaly where a horizontal septum of tissue forms within the vaginal canal, partially or completely obstructing menstrual flow. While it can also cause cryptomenorrhea, it usually occurs higher up in the vagina and does not cause a visible bulge at the vaginal opening, unlike an imperforate hymen. Diagnosis often requires imaging, like MRI or ultrasound, to locate the septum precisely.

Complete vaginal atresia (Option B): In this condition, the vagina fails to develop properly, leading to the absence of the vaginal canal. Patients present with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pain, but since there is no vaginal opening, no perineal bulge is seen. On examination, only a blind perineum is noted. Surgical creation of a vaginal canal (vaginoplasty) is needed for management.

Cervical agenesis (Option D): Cervical agenesis refers to the congenital absence of the cervix, which blocks menstrual outflow at a higher level. Patients may present with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pain, but there will be no bulge or distension at the vaginal opening, since the blockage is above the vagina. It often coexists with uterine or vaginal anomalies, and management is complex, sometimes requiring hysterectomy if reconstruction is not feasible.

Key takeaway:

question_text: A 28-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks gestation presents in labor for the past 18 hours. On examination, the uterus appears tonically contracted, and a transverse groove is visible across the abdomen, just above the pubic symphysis. The fetal head is high and not descending, despite strong uterine contractions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient is a 28-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks, in labor for 18 hours.
  • On examination, the uterus is tonically contracted with a transverse groove seen above the pubic symphysis.
  • This groove represents the pathological retraction ring of Bandl, which forms between the thickened upper uterine segment and the excessively thinned lower uterine segment.
  • Obstructed labor leads to progressive stretching and thinning of the lower segment when fetal descent is blocked, causing the pathological retraction ring to become visible externally.
  • The fetal head remains high and fails to descend despite strong contractions, confirming obstruction.

Explanation for other Options:

Uterine rupture (Option A): Presents with sudden severe abdominal pain, cessation of contractions, vaginal bleeding, and loss of fetal station. In this case, the uterus is intact but overstretched, with a visible Bandl's ring.

Prolonged latent phase (Option C): Characterized by delayed cervical dilatation in early labor, not by a visible uterine groove or obstructed descent.

Cord prolapse (Option D): Would present with sudden fetal distress (bradycardia) and cord felt on vaginal examination, not with a pathological retraction ring.

question_text: A 37-week pregnant woman with a breech presentation is being evaluated for external cephalic version (ECV). Which of the following is not a contraindication for ECV?
explanation:
Explanation:

Primigravida is not a contraindication for ECV; the procedure can be safely attempted in first-time mothers under appropriate clinical settings.

  • External Cephalic Version (ECV) is a procedure used to turn a fetus from breech to cephalic presentation by manual manipulation through the maternal abdomen.
  • It is generally attempted around 37 weeks of gestation when the baby is mature, but before labor begins.
  • Prerequisites for ECV:
    • Singleton pregnancy
    • Adequate amniotic fluid
    • Intact membranes
    • Reactive NST (Non-stress test)
    • No contraindications to vaginal delivery
  • Contraindications for ECV include:
    • Absolute:
      • Placenta previa (risk of hemorrhage)
      • Previous classical cesarean scar or uterine rupture risk
      • Multiple pregnancy (e.g., twins)
    • Relative:
      • PROM (risk of infection and cord prolapse)
      • Oligohydramnios
      • Fetal compromise
      • Uterine anomalies
  • Being a primigravida is not a contraindication.
  • While multiparous women generally have higher success rates, ECV is routinely and safely attempted in primigravidas as well.

Explanation of other options:

Placenta previa (Option A): Absolute contraindication due to risk of bleeding when manipulating the uterus.

Twin pregnancy (Option B): Contraindicated as manual rotation of one fetus may affect the position of the second, increasing risk.

PROM (Option D): Contraindicated due to risks of cord prolapse, infection, and reduced amniotic fluid, which hinders manipulation.

question_text: McCall's culdoplasty is performed in which of the following surgical procedures?
explanation:
Explanation:

McCall's culdoplasty is specifically performed during enterocele repair. It involves reinforcing the uterosacral and Mackenrodt's ligaments to the vaginal vault and the peritoneum of the pouch of Douglas, thereby obliterating the cul-de-sac and preventing recurrence of the enterocele.

Enterocele:

  • Definition:Herniation of the pouch of Douglas into the rectovaginal septum, frequently associated with uterine prolapse.
  • Location:
    • Upper one-third of the posterior vaginal wall → Enterocele
    • Lower two-thirds → Rectocele
  • Clinical Features:
    • Pelvic discomfort or pressure
    • Descending vaginal mass
    • Bowel symptoms: constipation or diarrhea
    • Bowel incontinence
    • Sexual dysfunction

Surgical Procedures in Enterocele:

  1. McCall Culdoplasty:
  • Reinforces the uterosacral and Mackenrod's ligaments to the vaginal vault and pouch of Douglas peritoneum
  • Commonly performed during abdominal or vaginal hysterectomy with enterocele repair
  • Prevents prolapse recurrence
  1. Moschcowitz Repair:
  • Obliterates the cul-de-sac of the pouch of Douglasvia multiple purse-string sutures
  • Often performed during abdominal surgery
  1. Halban's Procedure:
  • Obliteration of the peritoneal sacusing vertical sutures
  • Can be performed via transvaginal or abdominal route

Explanation of Other Options:

Rectocele repair (Option B): Rectocele involves herniation of the anterior rectal wall into the lower two-thirds of the posterior vaginal wall. McCall's culdoplasty is not indicated; repair usually involves posterior colporrhaphy.

Urethrocele repair (Option C): Urethrocele is prolapse of the urethra into the anterior vaginal wall. Surgical repair focuses on anterior vaginal wall reinforcement, not culdoplasty.

Vault prolapse surgery (Option D): While culdoplasty can be part of vault suspension in some procedures, McCall's technique specifically targets the enterocele portion rather than isolated vault prolapse.

question_text: In sacrocolpopexy (sacrocolposuspension), which is the correct site of attachment of the mesh?
explanation:
Explanation:

In sacrocolpopexy, the mesh is anchored to the anterior longitudinal ligament over the sacral promontory to provide durable support to the vaginal vault or uterus.

  • Sacrocolpopexy is a surgical procedure performed for vault prolapse or uterine prolapse, particularly when uterine preservation is desired or following hysterectomy.
  • It is often performed abdominally or laparoscopically.
  • In this procedure, a synthetic mesh is used to suspend the vaginal apex (or uterus) to the anterior longitudinal ligament over the sacral promontory-a strong anchoring point on the anterior surface of the sacrum at the lumbosacral junction.
  • This provides physiologic and durable support, preserving the axis of the vagina and minimizing prolapse recurrence.
  • It is preferred in sexually active women and those desiring anatomical and functional restoration.

Explanation of other options:

Ischial spine (Option B): While it's an anatomical landmark for procedures like uterosacral ligament suspension, it is not the site for mesh attachment in sacrocolpopexy.

Pubic symphysis (Option C): Lies anteriorly and has no role in pelvic organ prolapse surgeries involving vault suspension.

Ischial tuberosity (Option D): Serves as the origin for hamstring muscles and is unrelated to any pelvic organ prolapse surgical mesh fixation.

question_text: Miss Uma, a 52-year-old multiparous woman, reports a sensation of a vaginal mass that has been progressively descending for the last 6 months. On examination, she is found to have grade 3 uterovaginal prolapse with a decubitus ulcer over the prolapsed tissue. What is the most likely cause of this ulcer, and what is the appropriate management?
option_b: Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient is presenting with a decubitus ulcer, which commonly develops in individuals with uterovaginal prolapse. The ulcer forms due to localized tissue injury and impaired venous return in the exposed prolapsed tissue.

Management:

Treatment typically involves moist vaginal packing, using acriflavine and glycerin-soaked roller gauze to promote healing and prevent infection.

Other potential complications of uterovaginal prolapse include:

Decubitus Ulcer:

Occurrence:

  • Complication of advanced pelvic organ prolapse, especially long-standing uterovaginal prolapse.
  • Women may be concerned about both prolapse and the ulcer.

Pathophysiology:

  • Venous congestion in the prolapsed organ leads to local tissue edema.
  • Edema reduces tissue strength, making the vaginal tissue more friable.
  • Friction between the prolapsed organ and clothing contributes to ulcer formation.

Surgical Implications:

  • Friable tissue can complicate vaginal hysterectomy or other corrective surgeries.
  • Presence of ulcer may delay surgery, prolonging physical and psychosocial discomfort.

Associated Risks:

  • Possible association with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or cervical malignancy.
  • Ulcer may serve as a source of infection, increasing risk of postoperative complications.

Management:

  • Reduce prolapsed organ back into the vagina.
  • Daily vaginal packing with glycerin and acriflavine to promote healing.

Explanation of Other Options:

Malignancy and excision (Option A): Decubitus ulcers in prolapse are not caused by malignancy and excision is not a standard treatment.

Infection and antibiotics (Option C): While infection can complicate a decubitus ulcer, it is not the primary cause. Therefore, antibiotics alone are not the appropriate treatment in this case.

Trauma and dressing (Option D): Trauma can contribute to the development of a decubitus ulcer, but it is not specified in the given scenario. Dressing alone would not address the underlying cause of venous congestion in uterovaginal prolapse.

question_text: What is this grid system used for?
explanation:
Explanation:

The POP-Q grid system is a standardized method used to assess the severity and classification of pelvic organ prolapse.

  • The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the most widely accepted and standardized method for evaluating and documenting pelvic organ prolapse.
  • It uses specific reference points on the vaginal walls and cervix in relation to the hymen to assign a prolapse stage from 0 to IV.
  • The system allows objective, reproducible measurements that help clinicians compare prolapse severity over time or pre- and post-treatment.
  • POP-Q Staging:
  • Stage 0: No prolapse.
    • Stage I: Most distal portion of prolapse is >1 cm above the hymen.
    • Stage II: Leading edge of prolapse is ≤1 cm above or below the hymen.
    • Stage III: Leading edge is >1 cm below hymen but not complete eversion.
    • Stage IV: Complete eversion of the total vaginal length.
  • This system improves communication between providers and guides surgical or conservative management of prolapse.

Explanation of other options:

Vulvar cancer (Option B): This is staged using FIGO or TNM systems, not POP-Q.

Endometrial cancer (Option C): Endometrial cancer staging is done surgically based on FIGO criteria, not prolapse quantification systems.

Abruption placenta (Option D): Abruptio placentae is a clinical obstetric emergency assessed based on symptoms and imaging, not by any pelvic organ measurement grid.

Key Features of Pedunculated Submucosal Myoma:

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with chronic lower abdominal pain that worsens during menstruation. An ultrasound (USG) shows a cystic ovarian mass with a "ground glass" appearance. Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with these findings?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Endometriomas are cystic ovarian lesions associated with endometriosis and show a characteristic "ground glass" appearance on ultrasound.

  • Endometriosis is a chronic gynecological condition where ectopic endometrial tissue is found outside the uterus, commonly on ovaries.
  • When endometriosis involves the ovaries, it leads to the formation of endometriomas-also called "chocolate cysts" due to the presence of altered blood.
  • Ultrasound (USG) findings show a cystic mass with homogeneous low-level internal echoes, termed a "ground glass" appearance.
  • This is typical of endometriomas and helps distinguish them from other adnexal masses.
  • Associated diagnostic points:
    • Laparoscopy is the investigation of choice.
    • Histopathology confirms the diagnosis, showing hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
    • MRI helps with better characterisation, showing hyperintense T1 and "shading" on T2.

Explanation of other options:

Intramural fibroid (Option A): Solid masses within the uterine wall; do not appear cystic or have ground glass appearance.

Adenomyoma (Option B): Appears as a heterogeneous mass in the myometrium, not as a cystic ovarian lesion.

Myomatous polyp (Option D): Pedunculated, solid uterine masses; not associated with ovarian cysts or ground glass appearance.

Reference:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10120420/

question_text: Which of the following is NOT associated with fibroids?
explanation:
Explanation:

Amenorrhea, or the complete absence of menstrual bleeding, is not a characteristic feature of uterine fibroids.

Fibroids typically cause excessive or prolonged menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia or polymenorrhagia) due to their interference with uterine contractility and distortion of the endometrial cavity. However, they rarely cause the cessation of menstruation altogether. If a patient with fibroids presents with amenorrhea, another underlying condition-such as premature ovarian failure, Asherman's syndrome, or hypothalamic dysfunction-should be considered.

Explanation of Other Options:

Pelvic mass (Option A): Fibroids are among the most common causes of a pelvic mass in women of reproductive age.

They can enlarge the uterus and give it an irregular, firm, "bosselated" (knobby) contour. On bimanual examination, the uterus is often enlarged, irregular, and non-tender. Large fibroids may even cause abdominal distension, mimicking pregnancy or ovarian tumours.

Infertility (Option C): Fibroids, particularly submucosal or intramural types that distort the uterine cavity, can contribute to infertility and recurrent miscarriages.

They can interfere with sperm transport, embryo implantation, and uterine contractility. Removal of such fibroids (myomectomy) can improve fertility outcomes in affected women.

Menstrual irregularity (Option D): Menstrual disturbances are the hallmark symptom of uterine fibroids. They can manifest as menorrhagia (heavy bleeding), metrorrhagia (intermenstrual bleeding), or polymenorrhea (frequent periods). This occurs due to increased endometrial surface area and congestion caused by the fibroid mass.

Uterine i.e. endometrial calcification from chronic endometritis

Although alkylating agents may be used for most types of cancer, they are generally of greatest value in treating slow-growing cancers. Alkylating agents are not as effective on rapidly growing cells. Examples of alkylating agents include chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, thiotepa, and busulfan.

question_text: A pregnant woman with a fibroid uterus develops acute pain in abdomen with low grade fever and mild leucocytosis at 28 weeks. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
Red degeneration of fibroid

  • The myoma suddenly becomes acutely painful, enlarged and tender
  • It is an aseptic condition
  • It is seen mostly during mid pregnancy (but can occur at other times, as well as in nonpregnant females also)
  • Patient presents with:
  • Acute abdominal pain
  • Vomiting
  • Malaise
  • Slight fever

Lab investigations:

  • Moderate leukocytosis
  • Raised ESR

Pathological changes in the tumour:

  • Fibroid becomes soft, necrotic or homogenous especially in its centre
  • It is stained Salmon pink, or red (due to diffusion of blood pigments from the thrombosed vessels)
  • It has fishy odour (due to secondary infection with coliform organisms)
  • Histologically: There is evidence of thrombosis in some vessels
  • Pathogenesis: There is subacute necrosis of the myoma caused by an interference in blood supply (aseptic infarction).

Diagnosis is by ultrasound.

Differential diagnosis:

  • Appendicitis, Twisted ovarian cyst, Pyelitis and Accidental hemorrhage
  • So amongst the above options — Red degeneration is the correct answer.

Management:

  • Conservative management
  • Patient is advised rest
  • Analgesics are given to relieve the pain

The acute symptoms subside in 3-10 days and pregnancy proceeds uneventfully.

question_text: A 45-year-old female presenting with dysmenorrhea rhoea and menorrhagia most probably has:

So, option “a” is ruled out.

Option “b”: Endometriosis

  • Dysmenorrhea (secondary and progressive in nature) and menstrual irregularities including menorrhagia are specifically seen in endometriosis.
  • As far as age is concerned.

“Active endometriosis is seen most commonly between the ages of 30 and 40 years. It can however occur at any time between the menarche and the menopause, even before the age of 20 years.” So, endometriosis is one of the possible differential diagnoses.

Fibroid

Fibroid uterus causes menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea. So, the possibility of fibroid is high

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with bleeding following sexual intercourse. On per vaginal examination, a lesion is noted that bleeds upon gentle touch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of post-coital bleeding along with a vascular, easily bleeding cervical lesion is highly indicative of a cervical polyp. These are benign growths arising from the mucosal lining of the cervical canal and are common in women between 30 and 50 years of age. They can present with intermenstrual bleeding, post-coital bleeding, or vaginal discharge.

Diagnosis is usually confirmed via colposcopy, Pap smear, or biopsy, and management involves polypectomy followed by histopathological examination to confirm the benign nature of the lesion.

Key Features of Cervical Polyps:

  • Origin: Typically from the endocervical canal; occasionally from the ectocervix.
  • Size and Shape: Usually small, 0.5-2 cm, pedunculated, finger-like projections.
  • Colour: Red to purplish (vascular) or pale (fibrous).
  • Symptoms: Often asymptomatic; can present with post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, or discharge.
  • Diagnosis: Colposcopy, Pap smear, or direct biopsy to exclude malignancy.
  • Management: Polypectomy followed by histopathological examination is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is rare but may occur if the base of the polyp is not completely removed.

Explanation for Other Options:

Hemorrhagic cyst (Option A): These are fluid-filled sacs within the ovary and are typically not associated with cervical lesions or post-coital bleeding. They usually present with pelvic pain or are found incidentally on ultrasound.

Cervical cancer (Option C): Cervical carcinoma can cause irregular or post-coital bleeding; however, lesions in cancer are usually firm, friable, and may not bleed easily with light touch. They are often associated with other symptoms like abnormal discharge, pelvic pain, or weight loss in advanced stages. A biopsy is required to confirm malignancy.

Cervical fibroid (Option D): Fibroids arising from the cervix are rare and generally present with mass effects, such as urinary symptoms or pelvic pressure. They are less likely to cause bleeding simply upon touch, unlike vascular cervical polyps.

question_text: During the removal of a submucosal fibroid by hysteroscopy, a deficit of 2000 mL is estimated in a patient. What is the immediate complication of this?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Excessive absorption of hypotonic distension media during hysteroscopy can lead to pulmonary edema due to fluid overload.

  • Hysteroscopy, both diagnostic and operative, requires the use of distension media to visualize the uterine cavity.
  • During hysteroscopic myomectomy, especially when submucosal fibroids are involved, electrolyte-free hypotonic solutions like 1.5% glycine or 3% sorbitol are often used with monopolar electrosurgery.
  • These solutions can be absorbed systemically through open venous sinuses.
  • A fluid deficit >1000 mL (for hypotonic solutions) or >2500 mL (for isotonic solutions) raises significant concern for intravascular absorption.
  • A 2000 mL deficit indicates that the patient has likely absorbed a dangerous volume of hypotonic fluid.
  • This leads to fluid overload and dilutional hyponatremia, both of which predispose to pulmonary edema, the most immediate life-threatening complication.
  • Additional complications include hyponatremia, cerebral edema, heart failure, and even death in extreme cases.

Explanation of other options:

Acute tubular necrosis (Option A): ATN is a late complication caused by ischemia or nephrotoxicity; it is not the immediate effect of fluid overload during hysteroscopy.

DIC (Option B): Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation may occur in settings of massive trauma, sepsis, or obstetric catastrophes-not as an immediate result of fluid absorption.

Thromboembolism (Option D): While thromboembolism is a risk in postoperative patients, it is not the direct or immediate outcome of excessive distension fluid absorption during hysteroscopy.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6676032/

question_text: During your clinical rotation, you observe a senior resident using an instrument in the gynecology ward. Which of the following is not an appropriate use of this instrument?
option_a: To differentiate between chronic inversion and fibroid polyp
option_b: It is used to diagnose cervical stenosis
option_c: It is used in fallopian tube recanalization
option_d: It is used to measure the uterine cavity and the cervical length
explanation:
Explanation:

The instrument shown is a Sims uterine sound. It is not used for fallopian tube recanalization, which requires specialized hysteroscopic or laparoscopic instruments with fine catheters.

Explanation of Other Options:

To differentiate between chronic inversion and fibroid polyp (Option A): Sims uterine sound helps differentiate between chronic inversion and fibroid polyp by assessing continuity with the uterine cavity.

It is used to diagnose cervical stenosis (Option B): Resistance felt while passing the sound can help diagnose cervical stenosis.

It is used to measure the uterine cavity and the cervical length (Option D): The instrument is routinely used to measure uterine cavity length and cervical length before procedures such as D&C or IUD insertion.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Sims uterine sound is primarily used for:
    • Measuring uterine and cervical length
    • Diagnosing cervical stenosis
    • Differentiating chronic inversion from fibroid polyp
    • Assessing uterine tilt/position
    • Guiding D&C and IUD insertion
  • It is not used for fallopian tube recanalization.

question_text: Best Investigation to assess tubal patency:
explanation:
The gold standard / best investigation to asses tubal patency is laparoscopic chromotubation.

Laparoscopy enables one to look at the external condition of the uterus, tubes and pelvis and at the same time the patency of tubes can be seen. Methylene blue/indigo carmine dye is injected through a cannula attached to the cervix to visualize the free spill or absence of spill. It can also demonstrate peritubal adhesions and unsuspected endometriosis.

The greatest advantage of laparoscopy is therapeutic procedure can be performed if adhesions or fimbrial block is recognized in one sitting.

Also known: Other questions frequently asked on tubal patency tests.

  • Time for performing tubal patency tests: Day 7 - Day 10 of cycle
  • No anesthesia is required for tube testing
  • First test to assess tubal patency is HCG
  • HSG is not the best test because it cannot differentiate between cornual spasm and cornual blockage.
  • Obsolete method of testing tubal patency - Rubins test / CO2 Insufflation test(in preovulatory phase)
  • Best test as discussed is laparoscopic chromopertubation.
  • Other tests are:
    • Sonosalpingography is a method of assessing tube patency. It was popularized by G.Allahabadia and is also called the Sion test. Under USG guidance, a slow and deliberate injection of 200 ml of physiological saline into the uterine cavity is accomplished via a foley's catheter, the inflated bulb of which lies above the internal os and prevents leakage. It is possible to visualize the flow of saline along the tube and observe it coming out as a shower at the fimbrial end.

question_text: Endometriosis is explained by:
explanation:
Endometriosis is the occurrence of ectopic endometrial tissue (both glands and stroma) outside the cavity of the uterus.

Several theories have been propounded to explain endometriosis

Sampson’s implantation theory

-Endometriosis occurs as a result of reflux of menstrual endometrium through the fallopian tubes and its subsequent implantation

metaplasia Coelomic (Meyer and Ivanoff)

-Endometriosis arises as a result of metaplastic changes in embryonal cell rests of embryonic mesothelium, which are capable of responding to hormone stimulation.

Metastatic theory (Halban)

-Explains occurrence of endometriosis at less accessible sites like umbilicus, pelvic nodes, ureter, etc. The theory suggests embolization of menstrual fragments occurs through vascular or lymphatic channels. This leads to launching of endometriosis at distant sites.

Histogenesis by induction

-Proposes that an endogenous (undefined) biochemical factor can induce undifferentiated peritoneal cells to develop into endometrial tissue.
