question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. She is diagnosed with endometriosis and undergoes a laparoscopy, which reveals dense pelvic adhesions, the bowel adherent to the uterine fundus, and bilateral cystic ovaries stuck to each other. What should be the next step in management?
option_b: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
explanation:
Explanation:

The most appropriate management for a woman with severe endometriosis, dense pelvic adhesions, and ovarian endometriotic cysts (endometriomas) is laparoscopic cystectomy with adhesiolysis.

  • Cystectomy(removal of endometriomas) helps reduce recurrence, relieve pain, and improve fertility outcomes by restoring normal ovarian anatomy and function.
  • Adhesiolysis(surgical release of adhesions) restores pelvic anatomy, reduces pain, and enhances the chances of conception by freeing the ovaries and tubes.

This conservative surgical approach is ideal for women who desire future fertility, as it treats the underlying pathology while preserving reproductive organs.

Following surgery, medical therapy (e.g., GnRH agonists, progestins) may be used to prevent recurrence.

Explanation of Other Options:

LUNA for chronic pelvic pain (Option A): Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) involves destroying the uterosacral nerves to alleviate chronic pelvic pain.

However, LUNA is not effective for endometriosis with dense adhesions and ovarian cysts, as it only addresses pain, not the underlying disease. Moreover, studies show limited benefit compared to targeted surgical excision.

Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge (Option B): Gestrinone is a synthetic steroid with anti-progestogenic and anti-estrogenic properties that suppresses ovulation and reduces endometrial growth.

It may help in mild to moderate endometriosis, but in this case, with extensive adhesions and endometriomas, surgical management is necessary to restore anatomy and fertility-drug therapy alone is inadequate.

Hysterectomy and oophorectomy (Option D): Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a radical treatment reserved for women with severe, recurrent, or refractory endometriosis who have completed their family and no longer desire fertility.

question_text: Which is false regarding retroverted uterus:
option_c: It is a cause of infertility
explanation:
The usual position of the uterus is one of anteversion and anteflexion, in which the body of the uterus is bent forward at its junction with the cervix.

Retroversion

Symptoms:

  • Mobile retroversion is usually symptomless, main disadvantage being increased risk of perforation of the uterus at the time of instrumentation.

Symptoms which can be seen are:

  • Spasmodic dysmenorrhea
  • Pelvic congestion syndrome causing:
    • Congestive dysmenorrhea
    • Polymenorrhagia
    • Premenstrual low backache
    • Dyspareunia (it is the most specific and genuine complain in case of retroversion)
    • Leucorrhoea
  • Infertility: as the cervix is directed forward away from the seminal pool.

To implicate retroversion as a cause of infertility, it is necessary to perform Sims-Huhner test (postcoital test). Abundant motile sperms are seen in the vaginal pool but their failure to show up in the cervical canal indicates that the cervical canal is away from the seminal pool and is not accessible to the motile sperms. In such a case, retroversion is the case of infertility. Surgical correction of the retroversion should result in conception.

  • Abortion: can cause abortion between 10th to 14th

Treatment:

  • If retroversion is mobile no treatment is required.
  • In patients complaining of dyspareunia and backache with retroverted uterus : Hodge pessary may be used to keep the uterus in an anteverted position.
  • Surgical management: – Modified Gilliam's operation
  • Plication of round ligament

Baldy webster operation

Reference: Dutta Gynae 4th/ed p 193; Novak 14th/ed p 898.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhea, persistent acne, and progressive facial and body hair growth over the past year. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum insulin and total testosterone levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient demonstrates the classic features of PCOS, the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age. PCOS, also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome, is a multisystem endocrinopathy with ovarian expression of metabolic disturbances.

Clinical features:

  • Irregular menstrual cycles (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea)
  • Hyperandrogenism: Hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia
  • Metabolic features: Insulin resistance, obesity in some cases
  • Laboratory findings: Elevated serum testosterone and insulin levels

PCOS is the leading cause of hirsutism in women and should be suspected in any reproductive-aged woman with menstrual irregularities and hyperandrogenic signs.

Explanation of Other Options:

Endometriosis (Option B):

  • Presents mainly with dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and infertility.
  • Does not cause hyperandrogenism or elevated testosterone/insulin levels.
  • The absence of pelvic pain and infertility makes this diagnosis unlikely.

Ovarian Tumor (Option C):

  • Can cause hormonal imbalance but usually presents with rapid-onset symptoms, pelvic mass, or bloating.
  • The gradual, chronic presentation with classic PCOS features makes ovarian tumor less likely.

Hypothyroidism (Option D):

  • Typically causes fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and hair thinning, not excessive hair growth.
  • Does not elevate testosterone, so androgenic symptoms are absent.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • PCOS prevalence: Most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age
  • Classic triad: Menstrual irregularity, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
  • Metabolic risk: Insulin resistance → risk of type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome
  • Management: Lifestyle modification, hormonal therapy, insulin sensitizers (e.g., metformin) for metabolic control

question_text: Ideal contraceptive for lactating mother is:
explanation:
For newly married couples oral contraceptive pills are the method of choice provided there are no contraindications.

It has many noncontraceptive benefits along with effective contraception.

Barrier and Natural methods have a high failure rate.

IUCD are not prescribed in nulliparous females due to increase risk of PID and infertility

In a couple who are living separately in two cities and meet only, occasionally contraception of choice is a barrier method.

"Condoms are suitable for use in old age for couples who have infrequent coitus, during lactation, during holidays, subjects who can not tolerate OCP, IUCD".

Reference: Practice of fertility control S.K. Chaudhuri 7th/ed p 71

In Breastfeeding Females

For lactating mothers, contraceptives should be chosen in such a way that in addition to providing effective contraception, they do not adversely affect the success of lactation or the health of the infant. Barriers have a high failure rate of 4–14% and are not reliable for long-term control.

As estrogens decrease the quality and quantity of milk, COC pills are absolutely contraindicated in lactating mothers.

Lactation Amenorrhea Method (LAM)

  • Excessive secretion of prolactin, which controls lactation, inhibits the pituitary. Prolactin inhibits luteinizing hormone (LH) but has no effect on follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). However, it partially inhibits ovarian response to both of these gonadotropins. As a result, while the prolactin level remains high, the ovary produces little estrogen and no progesterone. Hence, ovulation and menstruation are affected.
  • LAM is effective only till 6 months postpartum. Beyond this, it is not a reliable method.
  • Even for 6 months, it is effective only if there is exclusive breastfeeding.
  • If at any time in the first 6 months the menses starts, then it cannot be used as birth control.
  • POPs are safe with breastfeeding and very effective. They were mainly designed especially for lactating mothers.

Reference: Shaw 14th/ed p 208.

question_text: A woman treated for infertility, presents with 6 week amenorrhea with urinary retention. The most likely etiology :
explanation:
The patient in the question:

  • Was being treated for infertility.
  • Now H/O 6 weeks of amenorrhea.
  • Presents with urinary retention.

The first diagnosis which comes to mind is retroverted gravid uterus.

Points which favour the diagnosis are: The woman is pregnant and has complained of urinary retention.

But friends, here it is important to understand that retroverted gravid uterus causes urinary retention at 14–15 weeks of gestation (not 6 weeks). —Jeffcoate 7th/ed p 299

So Option 'a' is ruled out

Option 'b' Pelvic hematocele

"Pelvic hematocele is formed in a patient complaining of 6 weeks amenorrhea in case of ectopic pregnancy."

—Jeffcoate 6th/ed p 212

Though pelvic hematocele causes urine retention but then other symptoms (pain) and signs of ectopic pregnancy should be present.

Option 'c' Impacted cervical fibroid

"A cervical fibroid impacted in the pouch of Douglas can cause retention of urine. The onset of retention is acute and usually occurs immediately before menstruation, when the uterus is further enlarged by congestion or during early pregnancy."

Reference: Jeffcoate 7th/ed p 493

question_text: A 20-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles. Based on the ultrasound image below, what is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely cause of the irregular menstrual cycles is Polycystic Ovary Disease (PCOD). The ultrasound shows multiple peripheral ovarian follicles arranged in a "necklace pattern", which is characteristic of PCOD. This condition commonly affects young women and results from hormonal imbalance, leading to anovulation and menstrual irregularities.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome, is a multisystem endocrinopathy involving ovarian, metabolic, and reproductive dysfunction.

Key Components of PCOS

  • Increased androgens
  • Ovulatory dysfunction
  • Polycystic ovarian morphology

Clinical Features

  • Seen in young women of reproductive age
  • Menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea)
  • Infertility
  • Hirsutism and acne due to hyperandrogenism
  • Central obesity (BMI >30 kg/m², waist >88 cm)
  • Acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance

Rotterdam Diagnostic Criteria (Any 2 of 3 required)

  • Hyperandrogenism: Clinical (hirsutism, acne) or biochemical (raised testosterone).
  • Ovulatory dysfunction: Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea due to lack of ovulation.
  • Polycystic ovaries on USG: ≥12 follicles (2-9 mm) and/or ovarian volume ≥10 cm³.

Typical USG finding: Multiple small cysts along the periphery ("necklace pattern") with an increased central stromal component that produces excess androgens.

Explanation for other options:

Obesity (option B): Although obesity can aggravate hormonal imbalance and menstrual irregularity, it is not the primary cause here. The ultrasound pattern specifically indicates PCOD.

Hirsutism (option C): Hirsutism is a symptom of elevated androgens, often seen in PCOD, but it is not a cause of irregular periods. The underlying condition is PCOD itself.

Turner's syndrome (option D): Turner's syndrome causes primary amenorrhea due to streak ovaries (nonfunctional ovaries). Since the patient experiences irregular periods, not a complete absence of menses, Turner's syndrome is ruled out.

question_text: Clomiphene citrate is indicated in:
explanation:
Clomiphene Citrate

  • Was first used in gynecology in 1956
  • It is non steroidal triphenylethylene compound related to diethylstilbestrol (DES).
  • It is an isomer of cis and trans form. Enclomiphene is more potent isomer and anti estrogenic whereas zuclompiphene is weak antiestrogenic
  • It binds to estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, so the negative feedback of estrogen on FSH is prevented resulting in increased pulsatile GnRH frequency and rise in FSH and LH.
  • The antiestrogenic effects of Clomiphene are seen on the cervix and endometrium.

Indications

  • Anovulation, PCOS.
  • Anovulatory DUB with infertility.
  • Amenorrhea and anovulation following the use of OCP's (Post pill amenorrhea).
  • In vitro fertilization, GIFT technique and assisted reproduction technique.
  • Male infertility (Role doubtful).

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed p 314

option_c: May be associated with abnormal glucose
explanation:
As discussed in the preceding text PCOD

question_text: In an infertile woman, endometrial biopsy reveals proliferative changes. Which hormone should be preferred ?
explanation:
In the question, the infertile woman's endometrial biopsy shows proliferative changes. Endometrial biopsy for infertility is taken on D 25 of cycle with the aim to rule out anovulation. Normally on these days, endometrial biopsy should show secretory changes (as ovulation occurs on D-14 and subsequently there is an increase in progesterone levels in the body). But in case of anovulation, endometrial biopsy shows proliferative changes.

The hormone which should be administered here is obviously progesterone, but that derivative of progesterone which has a weak antiovulatory effect so that it would not further inhibit ovulation.

Synthetic progesterones :

So, according to this our answer is Medroxy Progesterone Acetate (MDPA).

Besides the above reasoning - another reason for using medroxy progesterone acetate is that it can be given intramuscularly. 'In treatment of LPD (Luteal phase defect) - Intramuscular progesterone in oil produces higher plasma concentration, which is sustained for a longer period. Hence the intramuscular route of progesterone administration is considered the 'gold standard.'-Advanced infertility management by Mehroohansotia

Since, medroxy progesterone acetate can be given intramuscularly so it is the preferred agent.

Reference: KDT 6th/ed p 307

question_text: Sperm count on a seminormal is 16 million/ml, with 40% motility and <1% of sperm with normal morphology. What is the term for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The sperm count of 16 million/ml and motility of 40% fall within borderline normal limits according to WHO 2021 guidelines. However, <1% normal morphology is markedly abnormal. Since abnormal morphology is the defining feature here, the condition is classified as Teratospermia.

Semen Analysis:

Semen analysis is the first-line investigation for male infertility, typically performed:

  • After 1 year of unprotected intercoursewithout conception, or earlier if risk factors exist.
  • Following 2-7 days of abstinence.
  • On liquefied semen analyzed within 1 hour(liquefaction takes 20-30 min).

Normal Semen Analysis Parameters (Normozoospermia)- WHO 2021 Guidelines:

  • Volume:>1.4 ml
  • pH:2-8.0
  • Sperm concentration:≥16 million/ml
  • Total sperm count:≥39 million/ejaculate
  • Total motility:≥42%
  • Progressive motility:≥30%
  • Morphology:≥4% normal forms
  • Pus cells (WBC):1–2 million/ml
  • Viability:≥54%

Reproductive Terms Related to Semen Analysis:

  • Normospermia:Normal sperm count, motility, and morphology (Option B ruled out)
  • Aspermia:Complete absence of semen
  • Azoospermia:Absence of sperm in semen
  • Oligospermia:Low sperm count (Option A ruled out)
  • Asthenospermia:Reduced or absent sperm motility (Option C ruled out)
  • Necrospermia:Presence of dead sperm
  • Teratospermia (Correct Answer):Abnormal sperm morphology

References:

 

Comparison of the WHO reference manual for semen analysis as per the 5th & 6th edition 

Demographics of infertility and management of unexplained infertility - ScienceDirect

question_text: A couple presents to the infertility clinic with normal HSG and a semen analysis report with azoospermia. Which of the following test is useful to differentiate between testicular cause and obstructive vas deferens
explanation:
• In testicular cause there is decreased or no production of testicular hormones which in turn have negative feedback on FSH.
  • In obstructive vas deferens the FSH levels are normal as the testicular hormone production is not affected.

question_text: A young girl presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and hirsutism. Ultrasound shows multiple ovarian follicles. Which of the following would be increased in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture described is consistent with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome.
PCOS is a multisystem endocrinopathy in reproductive-age women, characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries.

  • In PCOS, serum testosteroneand other androgens (androstenedione, DHEA-S) are elevated.
  • This hyperandrogenism explains the hirsutism, acne, and menstrual irregularities.

Clinical & Endocrinological Features of PCOS:

  • Core Components:
    • ↑ Androgens(biochemical or clinical)
    • Ovulatory dysfunction(oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility)
    • Polycystic ovaries(≥12 follicles, ≥10 cm³ volume)

  • Clinical Findings:
    • Menstrual irregularity (oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea)
    • Infertility
    • Hirsutism
    • Acne
    • Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance)
    • Central obesity (BMI > 30, waistline > 88 cm)

  • Endocrinological Changes:
    • ↑ Estrone (peripheral conversion of androgens)
    • ↑ LH (>10 IU/mL)
    • Normal FSH
    • ↓ FSH/LH ratio
    • ↓ SHBG
    • ↑ Testosterone & ↑ DHEA-S
    • ↑ Insulin & Insulin Resistance
    • ↑ Triglycerides, ↓ HDL
    • Mild ↑ Prolactin (in 15% cases)
    • Tendency toward hypothyroidism

  • Biochemical Ranges in PCOS:
    • Testosterone may exceed 2 ng/mL(normal 0.2–0.8 ng/mL).
    • Free testosterone > 2 pg/mL.
    • Fasting insulin > 10 mIU/Lin ~50 70% cases.
    • ↑ DHEA-S; normal androstenedione.

Rotterdam Criteria (Diagnosis of PCOS):

At least 2 of 3 criteria required:

  1. Hyperandrogenism(clinical or biochemical).
  2. Ovulatory dysfunction(oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea).
  3. Ultrasound evidenceof polycystic ovaries (>12 follicles or ≥10 cm³ volume). The cysts appear in a characteristic "necklace pattern" along the periphery, with prominent central stromal tissue responsible for androgen production.

Management of PCOS:

  • Lifestyle modification: Weight reduction, Diet & exercise, Smoking cessation
  • Pharmacological treatment:
    • OCPs→ regulate cycles, treat acne/hirsutism.
    • Anti-androgens(spironolactone, ketoconazole).
    • Metformin→ reduces insulin resistance & androgen levels, improves fertility.
    • Dexamethasone→ reduces adrenal androgen production.
  • Infertility management:
    • Clomiphene citrate→ first-line ovulation induction.
    • Letrozole→ for clomiphene-resistant cases.
  • Surgical: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling(if medical management fails or persistent infertility).

Explanation of Other Options:

SHBG (Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin) (Option A): SHBG levels are decreased in PCOS due to hyperinsulinemia and hyperandrogenism, leading to increased free testosterone.

FSH levels (Option C): FSH is usually normal or low-normal. It does not rise significantly in PCOS.

FSH/LH ratio (Option D): In PCOS, LH is elevated, while FSH remains normal → thus the FSH/LH ratio decreases, not increases.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for primary infertility. Her hysterosalpingogram (HSG) reveals bilateral fluid-filled, convoluted, S-shaped structures adjacent to the uterine cavity. Which of the following best describes this finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hydrosalpinx is the distension of the fallopian tube with serous fluid due to distal tubal obstruction.
  • On HSG, the tubes appear dilated, tortuous, and S-shaped or serpentine.
  • Can be unilateral or bilateral.
  • Represents a significant cause of infertility as it prevents gamete transport.

Hydrosalpinx:

  • Definition: Distention of fallopian tube with fluid
  • Appearance: Characteristic S-shaped or serpentine structure
  • HSG finding: Dilated, convoluted fallopian tubes
  • Distribution: Can be unilateral or bilateral

Hysterosalpingography

  • It is a radiographic imaging technique.

Indication:

  • Infertility evaluation
  • To assess the endocervical canal, the endometrial cavity, and the fallopian tube lumina and patency.

Procedure:

  • Radiopaque contrast material is injected through the cervical canal.
  • It is performed between cycle days 5 and 10.

Normal findings:

  • The spill of contrast from the tubes into the peritoneal cavity suggests patency of the fallopian tubes.
  • The endometrial cavity is usually triangular and has a smooth contour.

Contraindications:

  • Acute pelvic infection
  • Active uterine bleeding
  • Pregnancy
  • Iodine allergy

Normal HSG (Option A): In a normal HSG, fallopian tubes appear as thin, linear structures with free spillage of contrast into the peritoneal cavity. The S-shaped dilated appearance is not seen in normal tubes. The radiograph below shows normal HSG.

Bilateral cornual block (Option B): Cornual block shows complete obstruction at the proximal fallopian tubes with no filling of the tubes beyond the cornual region. This would not show S-shaped fluid-filled structures.

Extravasation into venous system (Option C): Venous extravasation appears as irregular, thin channels with rapid dissipation of contrast material. It does not present as bilateral S-shaped structures and is typically seen as a complication during HSG.

Key Takeaway Points:

HSG Images of Uterine Anomalies

A: Unicornuate uterus with a single fallopian tube.

B: Didelphys uterus (two separate uterine cavities and two separate endocervical canals).

C: Bicornuate uterus (Angle formed by the medial borders of two hemicavities >105°).

D: Septated uterus (Angle formed by the medial borders of two hemicavities <60°).

E: Arcuate uterus.

F: DES (Diethylstilbestrol) exposed uterus appearance in hysterosalpingography.

a: Right hydrosalpinx b: Block at right cornua (No distention of the tube)

question_text: The following are the contraindications of tubal reconstructive surgery except:
option_d: Reversal done after 5 years of sterilization
explanation:
Tubal reconstruction surgery can be done for a number of reasons including for reversal of sterilisation procedure. The most favourable outcome is seen when it is done for reversal of sterilisation procedures.

Factors for Poor Outcome Following Tuboplasty

  • Dense pelvic adhesions.
  • Loss of fimbriae.
  • Bilateral hydrosalpinx > 3 cm.
  • Length of the reconstructed tube < 4 cm.
  • Reversal done after 5 years of sterilization operation.

Presence of other factors for infertility

question_text: A 28-year-old woman developed secondary amenorrhea for 9 months following a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure. Both the progesterone challenge test and estrogen-progesterone challenge test were negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions following uterine instrumentation).

  • The patient is a 28-year-old woman with secondary amenorrhea for 9 months after undergoing a dilation and curettage (D&C)
  • In such cases, damage to the endometrium can cause intrauterine adhesions and scarring, leading to failure of endometrial proliferation.
  • The progesterone challenge test is negative, which indicates either inadequate estrogen priming or an unresponsive endometrium.
  • The estrogen-progesterone challenge test is also negative, which rules out estrogen deficiency and points toward an absent or scarred endometrium.

Asherman syndrome

  • Definition: Condition characterized by intrauterine adhesions or scarring, usually following uterine curettage, especially after septic abortion or in the postpartum period.
  • Symptoms: Amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea, infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, and cyclic pelvic pain.
  • Diagnosis: Best made by hysteroscopy (direct visualization of intrauterine adhesions). Imaging alternatives include sonohysterography or hysterosalpingography.
  • Management: Hysteroscopic resection of adhesions, followed by intrauterine device or balloon placement plus estrogen therapy to promote endometrial healing.
  • Prevention: Avoid excessive curettage, treat intrauterine infections promptly.
  • Outcome: Many women regain normal menstruation and fertility after appropriate treatment.

Explanation for other Options:

Sheehan syndrome (Option A): Occurs after severe postpartum hemorrhage with pituitary infarction → features include failure of lactation and other pituitary hormone deficiencies, not just isolated amenorrhea.

Premature ovarian failure (Option C): Ovarian estrogen production stops early, but the endometrium can still respond to exogenous estrogen-progesterone; withdrawal bleeding would occur after the combined challenge test.

Hypothyroidism (Option D): Can cause menstrual irregularities, but the endometrium remains intact and will respond positively to the estrogen-progesterone test

question_text: A Patient at 24 weeks gestation is diagnosed as having IUD which occurred at 17 weeks but did not have a miscarriage. This patient is at increased risk for:
explanation:
Dead fetuses, if retained for more than 4 to 5 weeks, release thromboplastin which leads to DIC (consumptive coagulopathy). In the question, the fetus has been dead and has been retained for five weeks so there are increased chances of DIC.

Reference:: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 325

question_text: For which of the following diagnoses in the given OT list would hysteroscopy be the preferred procedure?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Asherman syndrome involves intrauterine adhesions best visualized and treated using hysteroscopy.

  • Hysteroscopy is the procedure of choice for evaluating and managing intrauterine adhesions, which are characteristic of Asherman syndrome.
  • It allows direct visualization of the uterine cavity and enables both diagnostic and therapeutic interventions such as adhesiolysis.
  • Asherman syndrome may present with infertility, amenorrhea, or recurrent miscarriage.
  • Hysteroscopy offers the advantage of real-time imaging and treatment in such cases.
  • Indications of hysteroscopy:
    • Diagnostic: AUB, infertility, recurrent miscarriage, uterine anomalies, evaluation of intrauterine pathology (e.g. Asherman syndrome).
    • Therapeutic: Adhesiolysis, polypectomy, fibroid resection (<5 cm), septal resection, endometrial ablation, foreign body removal, and hysteroscopic sterilization.
  • Contraindications include:
    • Active genital tract infection, large uterine cavity (>10 cm), known cervical/endometrial cancer, and pregnancy.

Explanation of other options:

Tubal ligation (Option A): Performed to block fallopian tubes and does not require uterine cavity visualization; hysteroscopy is not preferred.

Cervical polyp (Option C): Arises from the cervix and typically managed via speculum examination or simple removal; hysteroscopy is not indicated.

Subserosal fibroid (Option D): Grows on the outer surface of the uterus and is not accessible via hysteroscopy, which is only useful for intracavitary fibroids.

Reference:

NIH.gov Link

Medscape Link

question_text: A couple presents with inability to conceive. The husband's semen analysis is normal. The wife reports excessive menstrual bleeding, and a hysterosalpingogram (HSG) reveals distal tube dilatation resembling a "tobacco pouch appearance." What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tubal salpingitis (specifically Salpingitis Isthmica Nodosa, SIN) is characterized by chronic inflammation of the fallopian tubes, leading to mucosal outpouchings and distal dilatation visible on HSG.

Key Features:

  • "Tobacco pouch appearance" on HSG: Distal tube fimbrial end is dilated with patent orifice; resembles a pouch.
  • Chronic infection causes granulomas, which may ulcerate, leading to mucosal irregularity.
  • Can result in hydrosalpinx, beaded or rigid tubes, and bilateral involvement.

Pathophysiology:

  1. Endosalpingitis: Inflammation starts in the mucosa.
  2. Granuloma formation: Caseous necrosis leads to nodularity (SIN).
  3. Adhesions and fimbrial distortion: Produce the "tobacco pouch" or retort-shaped appearance.

Clinical Features:

  • Infertility (most common)
  • Dysmenorrhea or menorrhagia (in some cases)
  • Recurrent pelvic infections

Diagnosis:

  • HSG: Shows tubular irregularity, diverticular outpouchings, hydrosalpinx, and beaded tubes.
  • Ultrasound / Sonohysterography: Can detect hydrosalpinx.
  • Laparoscopy: Confirms tubal patency and adhesions.

Management:

  • Antibiotics: Treat acute infection.
  • Surgical intervention: Salpingostomy or adhesiolysis for hydrosalpinx.
  • Assisted reproductive techniques (ART): IVF is often needed if tubes are damaged.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tubal endometriosis (Option B): Characterized by endometrial tissue implantation on the tubal wall; does not produce tobacco pouch appearance on HSG.

Tubal polyp (Option C): Appears as smooth, rounded, or oval filling defect on HSG, unlike the irregular outpouchings seen in salpingitis.

Tubal spasm (Option D): Occurs due to transient muscular contraction during HSG; usually resolves with repeat injection or antispasmodics and does not cause permanent dilation or pouching.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3901176/

question_text: A 14-year-old girl presents with recurrent cyclical lower abdominal pain and a midline hypogastric mass. She has not yet attained menarche. On per-vaginal examination, a bluish bulging swelling is observed. What is the most probable underlying cause of her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical Case:

  • Age: 14-year-old girl
  • Symptoms:
    • Cyclical abdominal pain (suggests functioning endometrium with obstructed outflow)
    • Midline hypogastric lump (due to collected menstrual blood → hematometra)
    • Primary amenorrhea (has not achieved menarche)
  • Exam finding: Blush-colored swelling at the introitus on per-vaginal exam

The presentation is consistent with imperforate hymen, a condition where the vaginal opening is obstructed by a membrane, leading to cryptomenorrhea.

Pathophysiology:

  • Imperforate hymen → congenital anomaly (failure of complete canalization of vaginal plate).
  • Leads to obstruction to menstrual flow → accumulation of blood:
    • Hematocolpos = blood in vagina
    • Hematometra = blood in uterus
    • Hematosalpinx = blood in fallopian tubes (in long-standing cases)

Clinical Features:

  • Pubertal girl, primary amenorrhea
  • Cyclical lower abdominal pain (monthly)
  • Midline pelvic/abdominal lump
  • Bulging bluish membrane at introitus (tense imperforate hymen with collected menstrual blood)
  • Urinary retention / constipation may occur due to mass effect

Differential Diagnosis:

  • Transverse vaginal septum - similar presentation, but no bluish bulge at introitus
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) - primary amenorrhea with normal breast, absent uterus (not a midline lump with bulge)

Management:

  • Definitive treatment = Cruciate incision of hymen (hymenectomy) to drain collected blood.
  • Early treatment prevents complications like endometriosis and infertility.

Explanation of other options:

Bartholin cyst (Option A):

  • Presents as labial swelling not a midline hypogastric lump.

Transverse vaginal septum (Option B):

  • Causes obstructive symptoms but it is not visible externally.

Endometrioma (Option D):

  • Occurrence of Endometrioma is unlikely before menarche.

question_text: A 14-year-old girl presents with acute urinary retention, cyclic abdominal pain, and absence of menarche. On genital examination, a bluish bulge is seen at the vaginal introitus. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of cyclic abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea, acute urinary retention, and a bluish bulging membrane at the vaginal introitus are classical features of imperforate hymen.

This congenital anomaly occurs due to failure of the hymenal membrane to perforate during embryonic development, leading to accumulation of menstrual blood (hematocolpos) behind the intact hymen.

Imperforate Hymen is a congenital obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract presenting in adolescence with primary amenorrhea, cyclic abdominal pain, urinary retention, and a bluish bulging hymen.

Prompt diagnosis and surgical correction (hymenectomy) are essential to prevent complications like endometriosis, infertility, and urinary obstruction.

Clinical Features:

  • Primary amenorrhea with cyclic pelvic/abdominal pain
  • Urinary retention or frequency due to compression of the urethra by the distended vagina
  • Bluish bulging hymen seen on inspection, caused by retained blood
  • May lead to hematometra or hematosalpinx if untreated

Complications:

  • Urinary tract obstruction → hydronephrosis or acute renal injury
  • Retrograde menstruation → endometriosis or infertility
  • Risk of pelvic infection if blood becomes infected

Management:

  • Hymenectomy - Cruciate or annular incision under anesthesia to drain hematocolpos and relieve obstruction.

Explanation for Other Options:

Transverse vaginal septum (Option A): This congenital anomaly also causes primary amenorrhea and cyclic abdominal pain due to vaginal outflow obstruction, but the obstruction is higher in the vagina, not at the hymenal level. Hence, no bluish bulge is seen on perineal examination.

MRKH syndrome (Option C): Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome presents as primary amenorrhea but normal secondary sexual characteristics. It results from agenesis of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina, so no cyclic pain or bluish bulge is present since there is no menstrual blood accumulation.

OHVIRA syndrome (Option D): Obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal anomaly presents with cyclic pain after menarche due to obstruction of one vaginal canal. It may cause a lateral vaginal bulge, not a midline bluish bulge. It is also associated with a renal anomaly on the same side as the obstruction.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560576/

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5798792/

question_text: A 29-year-old woman presents with a history of infertility and chronic pelvic pain. A transvaginal ultrasound is performed, which reveals an adnexal mass characterized by incomplete septations and a cogwheel appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A cogwheel appearance with incomplete septations on ultrasound is most characteristic of hydrosalpinx, especially in chronic cases with inflammation.

  • Hydrosalpinx refers to the accumulation of serous fluid within a fallopian tube due to distal tubal obstruction.
  • This chronic condition often results from pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or tubercular salpingitis.
  • Over time, the inflamed and damaged tubal epithelium leads to loss of fimbrial architecture, forming a smooth, clubbed end filled with fluid.
  • On transvaginal ultrasound, the hallmark features include:
    • A thin-walled, cystic tubular or fusiform structure.
    • Incomplete septations due to residual endosalpingeal folds.
    • Cogwheel or beads-on-a-string appearance, particularly in chronic inflammation, reflecting thickened longitudinal mucosal folds.
  • These sonographic findings are highly suggestive of hydrosalpinx, especially in the context of infertility or pelvic pain.
  • Hydrosalpinx impacts fertility and may significantly reduce IVF success rates by 50% due to toxic fluid and embryo washout.
  • Surgical resection before IVF improves outcomes.

Explanation of other options:

Follicular ovarian cyst (Option B): These are simple, thin-walled, anechoic cysts formed from unruptured follicles. They do not exhibit incomplete septations or cogwheel appearance.

Endometriosis (Option C): Endometriomas typically show homogeneous, "ground-glass" internal echoes. They are not associated with incomplete septations or cogwheel patterns.

Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst (Option D): These may show internal echoes or fibrin strands but the cogwheel sign is not typical. Although septations may appear due to clots, the structure is usually not tubular or fusiform as in hydrosalpinx.

question_text: The use of combined OCPs is associated with an increased incidence of:
explanation:
This is a tricky question as some believe Option "b" i.e. chlamydial endocervicitis should be the answer while others believe Option "c" i.e. vaginal warts should be concerned. As far as candidial (monilial) vaginitis is concerned, OCP’s use increases their incidence. But for Chlamydial infections: CGDT 9th/ed p 727 says:

“Persons who use barrier contraception are less frequently infected by C. trachomatis than those who use no contraception, and women who use oral contraceptives may have a higher incidence of cervical infection than women not using oral contraceptives”.

As if replying to CGDT Novak 13th/ed p 259; 14th/ed p 275 says:

"Chlamydial colonization of the cervix appears more likely in OC users than in non-users, but despite this, there is a 40–50% reduction in risk for Chlamydial PID"

I then had to confirm the answer from Clinical gynaecologic endocrinology and Infertility 7th/ed by Leon Speroff (It is the most authentic and reliable book for all problems related to Endocrinology, Contraception and Infertility)

“Fifteen of the Seventeen published studies reported a positive association of oral contraception with lower Genital tract infections caused by Chlamydial cervicitis. Because lower genital tract infection are on the rise (now the most prevalent STI in the US) and the rate of hospitalization for PID is also increased, it is worthwhile for both patients and clinicians to be alert for symptoms of cervicitis or salpingitis in women on oral contraceptives who are at high risk of sexually transmitted infections.” —Leon Speroff 7th/ed p 905

As far as HPV infection i.e. Vaginal warts is concerned

'The viral sexually transmitted infections (STI’s) include HIV, human papilloma virus (HPV), herpes simplex virus (HSV) and hepatitis B (HBV). At the present time, no known associations exist between oral contraception and the viral STDS' So, now we can be sure that the answer is Chlamydial endocervicitis.

Also know:

Infections and Oral contraception:

Note:

  • If question says PID and does not specify any organism—Then OCP’S overall not only decrease the incidence of PID but also risk of hospitalisation and severity of the disease is decreased.
  • For protection against PID, at least 12 months of continuous use is necessary and this protection is limited only to current users.

Reference: Novak 14th/ed p 275; CGDT 9th/ed p 727; Leon Speroff 7th/ed pp 904-905

question_text: A male patient presents for infertility evaluation. He has a history of recurrent hospitalizations for infections since the age of 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Recurrent respiratory infections since childhood combined with male infertility strongly suggest Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, a genetic disorder affecting motile cilia and sperm motility.

Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia:

  • Definition:A genetically heterogeneous, autosomal recessive disorder affecting motile cilia, leading to respiratory, otologic, and fertility issues, with organ laterality defects in ~50% of cases.
  • Respiratory distress in term neonates:>80% of full-term neonates show early respiratory distress, often misdiagnosed as transient tachypnea or pneumonia.
  • Oto-sino-pulmonary manifestations:
    • Early signs: nasal congestion, chronic wet cough, recurrent sinus infections, chronic otitis media
    • Progression: Persistent infections may cause bronchiectasisand progressive lung function decline.
  • Non-pulmonary manifestations:
    • Situs inversus:Present in ~60% of pediatric patients
    • Congenital heart disease:More common in situs ambiguus
    • Fertility issues:Male infertility due to impaired sperm motility; females may have reduced fertility or ectopic pregnancies
    • Skeletal anomalies: Pectus excavatum (~10%), scoliosis (5-10%)

Explanation of Other Options:

Celiac disease (Option A): Autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten causing malabsorption (diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain). Respiratory infections are not a feature.

Cystic fibrosis (Option B): Autosomal recessive disorder due to CFTR mutations. Diagnostic criteria include:

  • One of:
    • Sweat chloride concentration > 60 mmol/l on at least two occasions
    • Two CF-causing mutations
    • Abnormal chloride transport (nasal PD)

and

  • One of:
    • Clinical characteristics, typical for CF
    • Sibling with CF
    • Positive newborn screening

COPD (Option D): Chronic lung disease seen in adults, usually related to smoking/environmental exposure; presents with chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea.

References:

Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia. Recent Advances in Diagnostics, Genetics, and Characterization of Clinical Disease 

https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Cystic-fibrosis-in-adults.-Diagnostic%2C-and-aspects-Gilljam/aea5f2ba241d602af32f1a04cdf15a6a728eec8c

question_text: Intrauterine insemination is done for all except:
explanation:
Indication

Intrauterine insemination is done in males with:

  • Severe hypospadias
  • Retrograde ejaculation (Immediate postcoital urine is taken and sperms are extracted from it.)
  • Neurogenic impotence
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Oligospermia
  • Asthenospermia
  • Low ejaculate volume

In female infertility IUI is useful in:

  • Cervical infertility–Antisperm antibodies are present in cervix
  • Vaginismus (involuntary contraction of perineal muscles during intercourse)
  • Unexplained infertility.

question_text: A 38-year-old multigravida presents with 2 years of infertility, dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea. She has a retroverted uterus and adnexal tenderness. What would be the initial investigation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The scenario involving dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea with adnexal involvement suggests endometriosis and requires a transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) for detailed anatomic assessment of adnexal structures.
  • Ultrasound is the first-line investigation for pelvic pathology, performed either transabdominally (TAS) or transvaginally (TVS).
  • Adnexal tenderness necessitates precise anatomic detail, best provided by transvaginal ultrasound.
  • A vaginal probe acts as an extension of bimanual palpation with enhanced resolution of pelvic findings.
  • Advantages of TVS over TAS include:
    • No need for a full bladder
    • Superior image resolution
    • Better imaging in obese women
  • The investigation of choice is laparoscopy, with histopathological examination (HPE) as the gold standard for diagnosis.

Explanation for other options:

Laparotomy (Option A) can confirm the diagnosis made by ultrasound and clarify the lesion's origin if uncertain, but because it is invasive, it is not preferred over ultrasound.

Colposcopy (Option C) is useful for identifying vaginal and cervical abnormalities, but transvaginal ultrasound is preferred for evaluating adnexal pathology.

Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound (Option D) is the first-line investigation; however, the transvaginal ultrasound route is preferred due to its superior detailed imaging and other advantages.

option_b: Chance of pregnancy is three fold as compared to placebo
option_d: It can also be used for male infertility with oligozoo- spermia
explanation:
Clomiphene citrate :

  • Clomiphene citrate is the first line intervention for medical induction of ovulation in almost all circumstances, clomiphene acts purely as an antagonist or antiestrogen.


Thus clomiphene is used for anovulation and is the DOC for PCOS patients.

Clomiphene is a racemic mixture of zuclomiphene enclomiphene. Hence, all actions of clomiphene will be the actions of both these isomers.

Indications :

  • Anovulatory infertility in case of PCOS (Stein-Leventhal syndrome), Chiari frommel syndrome.
  • Amenorrhea and anovulation following the use of OCP's (Post pill amenorrhea).
  • In vitro fertilization, GIFT technique and Assisted Reproduction Technique.

'It is the usual first choice for ovulation induction in most patients because of relative safety, efficacy, route of administration and relative low cost'.-Novak 14th/ed p 64

Results : 80-85% treated women ovulate and 40-50% conceive after the use of Clomiphene-Novak 14th/ed p 1064; Shaw 14th/ed p 284

Side effects :

Clomiphene and multiple pregnancy

'Multiple ovulation and multiple pregnancy in (case of clomiphene) is 10%' -Shaw 15th/ed p 314.

'Multi follicular development is relatively common and the overall risk of multiple pregnancy is increased approximately 7-10%' -Leon speroff 8th/ed p 1302

Novak 14th/ed, p 1064 says- 'Incidence of multiple pregnancies ranges from 6.25 to 12.3%.' -Jeffcoates 7th/ed, p 105 says

'Pregnancy occurs in 40 - 50% of women following treatment and even though the dosage is carefully monitored, 5-10% of the conceptions are multiple.'

Clomiphene for the management of oligospermia in males with idiopathic male infertility.- Leon speroff 8th/ed p 1281

  • Most infertile men are eugonadotropic, normally virilized, and otherwise normal, but have low sperm density. Empiric treatment with either clomiphene citrate or tamoxifen is commonly offered to stimulate increased pituitary gonadotropin secretion and spermatogenesis in men with idiopathic infertility. Whereas treatment appears to benefit some men, there is no reliable method for identifying those who might respond. Overall antiestrogenic treatment is not effective.

'A randomized clinical trial conducted by WHO involving nearly 200 men and over 1300 couple months of observation found no differences among men treated with clomiphene or placebo. Moreover a meta analysis including 10 randomized trials involving over 700 men concluded that evidence is inefficient to indicate that anti estrogen treatment improves semen quality or male fertility.'-Leon speroff 8th/ed p 1281

From the above lines it is clear - It has shown to increase fertility in oligospermic males in randomized controlled trials is incorrect.

Reference: Novak 15th/ed pp 1153-1154; Shaw 15th/ed p 314; Jeffcoates 7th/ed pp 104-105;

Reference: Leon speroff 8th/ed, pp 1294-1295, 1281

question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with primary infertility. On pelvic ultrasound and MRI, she is found to have a unicornuate uterus. This congenital uterine anomaly results from defective formation or fusion of which embryological structure?
explanation:
Explanation:

The unicornuate uterus is specifically linked to defective formation or failure of fusion of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts.

Congenital uterine anomalies such as unicornuate uterus, septate uterus, bicornuate uterus, or uterine didelphys arise due to abnormal development, fusion, or resorption of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts during embryogenesis.

  • Normally, the Mullerian ducts fuse around the 10th week of gestation, and the central septum is resorbed between the 10th-20th weeks to form a single uterine cavity.
  • In a unicornuate uterus, one Mullerian duct fails to develop, leading to a single-sided uterus. Often, the ipsilateral kidney and ureter are absent due to associated mesonephric anomalies.
  • These anomalies may cause infertility, recurrent abortion, preterm labor, abnormal presentations, or dysmenorrhea.

Explanation for other Options:

Mesonephric duct (Option A): These ducts contribute to the male reproductive tract (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles) and are not primarily responsible for uterine development.

Wolffian duct (Option C): Another name for the mesonephric duct; same reasoning applies-not the source of uterine anomalies.

Urogenital sinus (Option D): Forms structures such as the lower vagina, bladder, and urethra, but not the uterus.

question_text: A male was referred to the urology OPD for evaluation of infertility. Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype. Which of the following statements is not true about this condition?
option_a: Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient's XXY karyotype is consistent with Klinefelter syndrome, the most common sex chromosome disorder in males.

  • Hormonal Findings:
    • FSH and LH:Elevated (not reduced), due to testicular failure
    • Testosterone:Reduced
    • Estradiol:Increased (Option C ruled out)
  • Clinical Features:
    • Hypogonadism:Characterized by small testes and reduced testicular function, often associated with decreased virilization such as sparse facial and pubic hair and lack of normal deepening of the voice. (Options B & D ruled out)
    • Body Habitus:Tall, elongated body with eunuchoid proportions
    • Gynecomastia:Common
    • Cognitive Profile:Average to below-average intelligence, verbal/language deficits
  • Genetic & Pathological Findings:
    • Classic karyotype: 47,XXY (90%)
    • Mosaic patterns: e.g., 46,XY/47,XXY (10-15%)
    • Positive sex chromatin (Barr bodies) due to extra X chromosome
    • Testicular biopsy: Hyaline degeneration of seminiferous tubules, prominent Leydig cells due to gonadotropin elevation

question_text: Treatment for Cervical infertility can be all except:
explanation:
Cervical factor infertility can be due to abnormal or deficient mucus ... William Gynae 1st/ed p 460

  • Infection
  • Prior cervical surgery
  • Use of antiestrogens (e.g. clomiphene citrate) for ovulation induction (so clomiphene is a cause of cervical factor infertility rather than management)
  • Sperm antibodies

The treatment of cervical factor thus depends on the cause:

  • If it is due to chronic cervicitis/infection - Treatment of infection by antibiotics is the cure.
  • If it is due to decreased mucus volume - Treatment includes short term supplementation with exogenous estrogen like ethinyl estradiol and use of mucolytic expectorant like guaifenesin. However, their value has not been confirmed.
  • If it is due to antisperm antibodies. Treatment options include:
    • Use of condom or diaphragm as a barrier method for 3 months. During this period, the antibodies will disappear and conception may occur then.
    • Corticosteroids given to female partners can also help in getting rid of these antibodies
  • Intrauterine insemination at the time of ovulation (most acceptable method for cervical factor infertility) or GIFT (Gamete intrafallopian transfer) are very useful techniques in such cases.
  • IUI is the best method for treating cervical factor infertility and unexplained infertility. So many clinicians forgo cervical mucus testing and proceed directly to IUI treatment in absence of tubal disease.

Reference: Dutta Gyane 5th edition, page 241; Williams Gynae 1st edition, page 460

question_text: A 24-year-old married life of 4 years, visits infertility clinic with history of recurrent abortions. On further workup, she is found to be having 'septate uterus'.  Which surgery has better reproductive outcome?
explanation:
The treatment of choice for Septate uterus is Transcervical hysteroscopic septal resection.

Option A,D were earlier used to treat septate uterus but could leave a scar on the uterus hence making LSCS a necessity. Hence, these procedures are replaced by Hysteroscopic septal resection.

Option B: Straussman metroplasty is a procedure for bicornuate pr didelphys uterus and is used as an unification surgery.

A procedure called hysteroscopic metroplasty is the most common treatment for a septate uterus. It's an outpatient procedure that takes about an hour. First, surgical instruments are inserted through the cervix and into the uterus.

The rate of miscarriage in the general population is around 10 to 20 percent in women who know they are pregnant. The estimated rate of miscarriage in women with septate uteri is thought to be between 20 and 25 percent. Some research shows it may be as high as forty percent.

question_text: A 23-year-old woman, accompanied by her mother-in-law, visits the infertility clinic. She has been having regular unprotected intercourse for the past 6 months but has not been able to conceive. What is the next step in management?
option_b: Reassure and review the couple after 6 months
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after at least 1 year of unprotected intercourse; hence, reassurance is appropriate at 6 months.

  • Infertility is clinically defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse.
  • Since this couple has only been trying for 6 months, the appropriate next step is to reassure them and plan a follow-up after 6 more months of attempts.
  • Early evaluation may be considered if there are known risk factors, but none are mentioned here.
  • If the couple fails to conceive after 1 year, further evaluation is indicated and is guided by suspected causes, including:
    • Ovulatory dysfunction: AMH levels, early follicular FSH ± estradiol, ovulation kits, antral follicle count
    • Tubal/pelvic disease: Hysterosalpingography, laparoscopy with chromopertubation
    • Uterine factors: TVS, saline infusion sonography, MRI, hysteroscopy ± laparoscopy
    • Male factors: Semen analysis

Explanation of other options:

Semen analysis for husband (Option A): Important in infertility workup but premature before 1 year of trying unless risk factors are present.

Hysterolaparoscopy (Option C): Invasive diagnostic procedure reserved for suspected pelvic or tubal pathology or after a longer duration of infertility.

Diagnostic hysteroscopy (Option D): Useful to evaluate intrauterine abnormalities but not indicated this early in the infertility workup.

question_text: A lady with primary infertility was diagnosed to have 2 uterine fibroids in the cornual region. Right side is 7 x 5cms and left side is 5 x 4cms. On HSG both the tubes are found to be blocked. What is your management if you are told that the woman is ovulating and the semen analysis of her partner is normal?
explanation:
Uterine fibroids can potentially cause infertility by blocking the fallopian tubes or stopping a fertilized egg from implanting in the uterus.

In addition, large fibroids may prevent a fetus from growing fully due to decreased space in the uterus.

When fibroids do contribute to infertility, it's often because of their size. Anything over six centimeters may cause problems. The ideal management in such condition is myomectomy/hysterectomy.

This choice depends on the age and if childbearing is complete or not.

  • Menopausal or childbearing complete: Hysterectomy
  • Pre menopausal or childbearing not complete: Myomectomy

question_text: An athlete with a BMI of 17.5 kg/m<sup>2</sup> presents with secondary amenorrhea and primary infertility. Laboratory investigations reveal FSH 2 mIU/mL, LH 0.3 mIU/mL, TSH 1.2 μIU/mL, and prolactin 20 ng/mL. What is the underlying cause of her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's low FSH and LH, along with a history of low BMI and athletic activity, indicate reduced GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (HH).

Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (HH):

  • Cause: Dysfunction at the hypothalamic or pituitary level → inadequate gonadotropin (LH & FSH) secretion
  • Types:
    • Congenital HH:
      • Kallmann syndrome: Anosmia with absent/abnormal olfactory bulbs
      • Normosmic isolated HH: Normal sense of smell
    • Acquired HH:
      • Causes: Excessive exercise, low body weight, stress, systemic illness, medications, tumors, trauma

Clinical Features:

  • Hypogonadism: Amenorrhea, infertility, low libido, delayed/absent secondary sexual characteristics
  • Other: Decreased bone density, low estradiol/testosterone, mood changes

Diagnosis:

  • Low FSH & LH
  • Low estradiol (females) or testosterone (males)
  • GnRH stimulation test may confirm hypothalamic/pituitary origin
  • MRI for structural anomalies if congenital (e.g., Kallmann syndrome)

Management:

  • Address underlying cause: Nutritional support, reduce excessive exercise, treat systemic illness
  • Hormonal therapy: To restore menstrual cycles and secondary sexual characteristics
  • Fertility treatment: Ovulation induction with GnRH or gonadotropins if pregnancy desired

Explanation of Other Options:

Primary ovarian failure (Option A): Characterized by high FSH and low estradiol, indicating a primary ovarian defect. Not consistent with low FSH/LH in this patient.

Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (Option C): Seen in ovarian failure, with elevated FSH and LH due to absent negative feedback. This patient has suppressed gonadotropins, so this is incorrect.

Normogonadotropic normogonadism (Option D): FSH and LH are normal, often seen in PCOS or structural causes of amenorrhea. Does not match suppressed gonadotropins in this patient.

question_text: A woman has 2 kids. She presents with galactorrhea and amenorrhea for 1 year. The most probable diagnosis is:
option_d: Metastasis to pituitary from another carcinoma
explanation:
The female in the question is presenting with galactorrhea and amenorrhea for 1 year which raises the suspicion for pituitary tumor i.e. prolactinoma/pituitary adenoma.

Pituitary Adenomas:

  • Most common Pituitary adenoma is Prolactinomas.

Presentation:

Women present with:

  • Galactorrhea
  • Features of hypogonadism:
    • Amenorrhea/ Oligomenorrhea (as prolactin inhibits GnRH) – Delayed puberty, Anovulation
    • Infertility

In both sexes, they can cause symptoms due to mass effects of the tumor:

  • Cavernous sinus syndrome consisting of: – Headaches
  • Visual defects (Most common Bitemporal hemianopsia)
  • Cranial nerve palsies especially III, IV, and VI
  • Raised serum prolactin levels
  • X-Ray sella shows space occupying lesions.

Investigations:

  • In all cases of hyperprolactinemia:
    • MRI should be performed
    • TSH levels should be measured

Management:

Microadenoma with no desire of fertility:

  • Asymptomatic patients with microadenomas rarely progress to macroadenomas and are managed conservatively.
  • If a patient has osteopenia, (due to hypoestrogenemia caused by ↑ Prolactin levels) = estrogen replacement or OCP's.
  • Monitor patients with regular serial prolactin levels and MRI (every 12 months).

For symptomatic microadenomas:

  • Medical management by dopamine agonists viz bromocriptine and cabergoline (which increase dopamine levels, thus decreasing prolactin levels) are the mainstay of therapy.
  • Other dopamine agents like pergolide, lisuride (both ergot derivatives) and quinagolide (non ergot derivative) can also be used.
  • Macroadenomas: Long-term Bromocriptine therapy with periodic serum prolactin measurements (6 monthly) and MRI (6 monthly).

Surgery indications:

  • Tumors unresponsive to Bromocriptine
  • Tumors causing persistent visual field loss

Reference: Novak 14th/ed, pg 1104, 1109;

Reference: Harrison 17th/ed, pg 2205-2206;

Reference: Williams Gynae 1st/ed, pg 338.

question_text: A 24-year-old woman undergoing infertility treatment with human menopausal gonadotropin presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness. Ultrasound reveals a characteristic "spoke-wheel" appearance in the ovaries.
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The clinical presentation following hMG stimulation and the classical "spoke-wheel" USG appearance is diagnostic of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

  • Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a serious iatrogenic complication of ovulation induction, especially with gonadotropins like hMG.
  • It results in exaggerated ovarian response with multiple cystic enlargements and increased vascular permeability.
  • This leads to third-spacing of fluid causing ascites, pleural effusion, hemoconcentration, and even thromboembolism.
  • Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles arranged in a spoke-wheel pattern.
  • Management is supportive-paracentesis for relief of discomfort, fluid monitoring, and thromboprophylaxis.

Explanation of other options:

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Option B): Typically presents with chronic menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, and multiple small peripheral cysts on USG-not acute symptoms or spoke-wheel appearance post-ovulation induction.

Theca lutein cysts (Option C): Usually seen with high β-hCG levels, such as in molar pregnancy or multiple gestations-not commonly in OHSS-like acute settings.

Granulosa cell tumor (Option D): A rare estrogen-secreting ovarian tumor, presents more gradually with hormonal symptoms, unrelated to ovulation induction or spoke-wheel pattern.

question_text: A 16 year old presents with absent menses. Examination shows widely spaced nipples, webbed neck, Tanner grade 1 breast development. US shows streak ovaries. Investigation shows- raised FSH, raised LH, reduced estradiol. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis is Turner syndrome

Turner Syndrome

Genotype: Most common = 45 XOQ (Loss of one X chromosome is due to Non- dysjunction during meiosis, the X chromosome retained is maternal in origi in most cases).

Mosaics = 45 XO/46 XX or 45 XO/46 XY

  • Gonads: B/L Streak Gonads.(since one single X chromosome is present, so ovaries are not properly formed).
  • Associated with low E2 and high FSH, LH

Other options:

B. Kallmann Syndrome:

Kallmann syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by a failure to start or fully complete puberty, combined with an impaired sense of smell (anosmia). It results from the failure of the hypothalamus to produce sufficient gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which is essential for the development of secondary sexual characteristics and reproductive function. The condition affects both males and females, leading to delayed or absent puberty and infertility.

  • Key Features: Delayed or absent puberty, infertility, lack of or reduced sense of smell.
  • Cause: Genetic mutations affecting the development and migration of neurons that produce GnRH.
  • Treatment: Hormone replacement therapy (testosterone for males, estrogen and progesterone for females) to induce puberty and maintain secondary sexual characteristics. Fertility treatments may be required to conceive.

C. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS):

Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a genetic condition in which a person who is genetically male (XY chromosomes) is unable to respond to male sex hormones (androgens). As a result, individuals with AIS develop female physical traits despite having male genetics. There are two types: Complete AIS (CAIS), where the body is entirely unresponsive to androgens and results in a female appearance, and Partial AIS (PAIS), where there is some sensitivity to androgens, leading to varying degrees of masculinization.

  • Key Features: Individuals with complete AIS often have a female appearance, undescended testes, and are typically infertile. In partial AIS, genital ambiguity may occur.
  • Cause: Mutations in the gene responsible for the androgen receptor.
  • Treatment: Management includes hormone therapy, surgery (e.g., for undescended testes), and counseling. Fertility treatments are typically ineffective for CAIS.

D. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) Syndrome:

MRKH syndrome is a congenital condition in females where the uterus and the upper part of the vagina are underdeveloped or absent, but the external genitalia are normal. It affects the reproductive tract but does not impair the development of secondary sexual characteristics such as breast development or pubic hair. Girls with MRKH typically discover the condition when they do not start menstruating during puberty (primary amenorrhea).

  • Key Features: Absent or underdeveloped uterus and vagina, normal ovaries and external genitalia, primary amenorrhea, and infertility.
  • Cause: The exact cause is unknown, but it is believed to involve disruptions in the development of the Müllerian ducts during embryonic development.
  • Treatment: Management may include surgical creation of a functional vagina (vaginoplasty) and psychological support. Although natural conception is not possible, fertility options like surrogacy using a woman's own eggs can be considered.

question_text: A 26-year-old with married life of 2year visits infertility clinic. She was put on HMG. On treatment, she developed dyspnea, abdominal pain. Her USG reports shows following image. What is the condition called
explanation:
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a condition that can occur in women who are undergoing fertility treatments, particularly those that involve stimulating the ovaries, such as in-vitro fertilization (IVF). It happens when the ovaries become swollen and painful due to an exaggerated response to fertility drugs, especially those used to induce ovulation.

Key points about OHSS:

  1. Causes: OHSS is typically triggered by the use of hormones like human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which stimulates the ovaries to produce multiple eggs. Also ovulation induction drugs like Clomiphene citrate are causative of this condition. Women with higher sensitivity to these medications are at greater risk.
  2. Symptoms: OHSS can range from mild to severe.
    • Mild symptoms: bloating, mild abdominal pain, nausea, and weight gain.
    • Severe symptoms: significant weight gain, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, shortness of breath, and fluid buildup in the abdomen or chest. In rare cases, it can lead to blood clots, kidney failure, or other serious complications.
  3. Risk Factors: Women who are younger and thin have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or have had OHSS in the past are at a higher risk.
  4. Treatment: Mild cases usually resolve on their own with rest and hydration. Severe cases may require hospitalization for monitoring, fluid drainage, or medication to prevent complications.
  5. Prevention: Adjusting the dosage of fertility drugs, using a lower dose of hCG, or using alternative medications can reduce the risk of developing OHSS. Monitoring the ovaries through ultrasound during treatment is also crucial to prevent it.

question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with complaints of painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea), painful intercourse (dyspareunia), and infertility. On pelvic examination, the uterus is retroverted, fixed, and tender, with tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Endometriosis is the most probable diagnosis in this case. The triad of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility, along with a fixed, tender, retroverted uterus and nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments, is are classic feature of this condition. Endometriosis occurs when endometrial-like tissue grows outside the uterus, responding to hormonal changes and leading to cyclic bleeding, inflammation, scarring, and adhesions - all of which cause pain and infertility.


Explanation for other options:

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (option A): Usually presents with fever, vaginal discharge, and a history of infection. The absence of infectious symptoms makes PID unlikely here.

Pelvic Tuberculosis (option C): May cause pelvic pain and infertility, but tenderness and uterosacral nodularity are uncommon. It typically presents as a non-tender pelvis with menstrual irregularities.

Leiomyoma (option D): Commonly presents with menorrhagia (heavy bleeding) rather than dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia. The findings of uterine fixation and ligamentous nodularity are not characteristic of fibroids.

question_text: A nulliparous woman with a BMI of 23 presents with complaints of hirsutism. An ultrasound was performed, and the image is provided below. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

PCOS is a multisystem endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age, characterized by oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries.

Ultrasound Findings in PCOS

  • Ovarian enlargement with volume >10 mL.
  • ≥12 small peripheral follicles (2-9 mm in size) in a "string of pearls" pattern.
  • Increased ovarian stroma (central echogenic area).
  • Performed ideally in early follicular phase (Day 2-;5 of cycle).
  • Doppler may show increased blood flow.
  • Only one ovary may show these features in some cases.
  • Not reliable in women taking combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs).
  • Also used to monitor response to treatment and exclude ovarian tumors.

Etiology & Pathogenesis

  • Exact cause unknown
  • Contributing factors:
    • Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors
    • Insulin resistance → hyperinsulinemia → increased ovarian androgen production
    • Obesity exacerbates hormonal imbalance
    • Raised LH, low/normal FSH → anovulation

Clinical features

  • Menstrual disturbances: Oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea
  • Infertility due to anovulation
  • Hyperandrogenism: Hirsutism, acne, alopecia
  • Obesity, acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance)
  • Metabolic syndrome risks: Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, CVD
  • Long-term risk of endometrial cancer

Diagnosis (Rotterdam Criteria - 2 out of 3):

  1. Oligo/anovulation
  2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
  3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound:
    1. ≥12 follicles (2-9 mm) or ovarian volume >10 cm³

Investigations:

  • Transvaginal USG: Diagnostic; shows "string of pearls" appearance
  • Hormonal profile:
    • ↑ LH, ↑ androgens (testosterone, DHEAS)
    • ↓ SHBG, altered LH:FSH ratio
    • Fasting insulin/glucose (<4.5 suggests insulin resistance)
    • Rule out: Cushing's, CAH, adrenal/ovarian tumors
  • Thyroid function, Prolactin, 17-OH progesterone if indicated

Explanation for other options:

Tubal block (Option B) is typically diagnosed using a hysterosalpingogram (HSG). Common causes include salpingitis, benign intraluminal polyps, tubal endometriosis, tubal spasm, and intratubal mucus debris.

Multiple fibroids (Option C) are identified on transvaginal ultrasound as an enlarged, distorted uterus with homogeneous echogenic regions corresponding to the fibroids. While most cases are asymptomatic, some women may present with menstrual irregularities, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, pelvic pressure, lower abdominal pain, or recurrent miscarriage.

Mesenteritis (Option D) on ultrasound typically shows a thickened, distorted root of the mesentery with a characteristic hypoechoic "halo" around the mesenteric vessels. Clinically, it often presents with abdominal pain and fever, and may be accompanied by signs of intestinal obstruction. In certain cases, a palpable abdominal mass may be noted.

question_text: A patient exhibits physical characteristics as shown in the image given below. Identify the underlying genetic disorder.
explanation:
Explanation:

Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder resulting from the loss or structural abnormality of one X chromosome (45, XO). It primarily affects females and is characterised by distinctive physical and reproductive traits. The typical clinical signs include short stature, webbing of the neck (pterygium colli), a low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples, and streak ovaries leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility. These patients also show a lack of secondary sexual characteristics due to gonadal dysgenesis. Turner's syndrome is thus identified by the combination of these phenotypic and chromosomal features.

Explanation of Other Options :

Testicular feminising syndrome (Option A): Also known as androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), this condition occurs in genetically male individuals (46, XY) who are resistant to the effects of androgens. As a result, they develop a female external appearance, with normal breast development but absent uterus and undescended testes.

Kallmann syndrome (Option B): This disorder is marked by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (loss of sense of smell) due to defective migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons. Affected individuals typically have delayed or absent puberty. Since the patient in question does not present with anosmia and has features consistent with gonadal dysgenesis rather than GnRH deficiency, Kallmann syndrome is unlikely.

Klinefelter syndrome (Option D): Klinefelter syndrome occurs in males with an extra X chromosome (47, XXY). Such individuals are usually tall, have small testes, reduced facial and body hair, gynecomastia, and infertility. It affects males, not females, and does not cause features like a webbed neck or streaked ovaries. Therefore, it can be ruled out in this scenario.

question_text: Based on the following findings in the USG, what is the most likely diagnosis for a woman who has a previous infertility history and is currently undergoing HMG treatment?

Explanation:

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a clinical condition marked by ovarian enlargement following exogenous gonadotropin therapy.

question_text: On cytological examination of somatic cells, a Barr body is observed in the nucleus. Which of the following syndromes is associated with this false positive Barr body?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Barr bodies are inactivated X chromosomes in cells of individuals with more than one X chromosome.
  • Formula: Number of Barr bodies = Number of X chromosomes - 1.

Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY):

  • Male with extra X chromosome → 1 Barr body present in somatic cells.
  • This is a false positive Barr body, because normally males (46, XY) do not have a Barr body.
  • Clinical features of Klinefelter syndrome:
  • Tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, hypogonadism, infertility.

Explanation of Other Options:

Turner's syndrome (45, XO)(Option B):

  • Only one X chromosome → no Barr bodies.
  • Female phenotype, short stature, streak ovaries, primary amenorrhea.

Down's syndrome (Trisomy 21)(Option C):

  • Extra autosome (chromosome 21) → does not affect X chromosomes.
  • Females with Down syndrome (46, XX + 21) → 1 Barr body (normal for female).

Edward's syndrome (Trisomy 18) (Option D):

  • Extra autosome (chromosome 18) → X chromosome count unaffected.
  • Females with Edwards syndrome → 1 Barr body, males → no Barr body.

Key Takeaway Points:

1. Barr Body Patterns in Chromosomal Disorders

2. Clinical Correlation:

  • False positive Barr body in males: Strong indicator of Klinefelter syndrome.
  • Barr body detection: Seen as dense chromatin near nuclear membrane in somatic cells.
  • High-yield for FMGE: Any male with a Barr body → consider Klinefelter syndrome.

3. Learning Points:

  • Barr bodies reflect X inactivation, not the Y chromosome.
  • Useful in diagnosing sex chromosome abnormalities cytologically

Bar Body Patterns:

  • 47 XXX Female: 2 Barr bodies

question_text: A 25-year-old man is evaluated for primary infertility. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. A testicular biopsy is done, and the histology image is provided. The finding is consistent with which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

Sertoli cell-only syndrome (Germ cell aplasia):

  • Seminiferous tubules contain only Sertoli cells, with absence of germ cells.
  • Tubular basement membrane appears thickened.
  • Patients present between 20-40 years with primary infertility and azoospermia.
  • Hormonal profile: ↑ FSH (no feedback from sperm production), normal LH and testosterone (Leydig cells unaffected).
  • Testes are usually normal-sized, with no secondary sexual abnormalities.

Explanation of other options:

Testicular atrophy (Option B): Seen in cryptorchidism, atherosclerosis, cachexia, or chronic orchitis. Shows hyalinized, shrunken seminiferous tubules, often with reduced testosterone (Leydig cell loss). Not isolated Sertoli cells.

Benign testicular neoplasm (Option C) includes Sertoli cell tumors and Leydig cell tumors. Sertoli or Leydig cell tumours present as mass lesions. Histology shows tumor cells, not empty seminiferous tubules lined only by Sertoli cells. Leydig cell tumors characteristically show Reinke crystals.

Orchitis (Option D): Inflammatory infiltrates (neutrophils, lymphocytes) with possible abscess formation. Biopsy would show inflammation, not isolated Sertoli cells.

Key Takeaway:

  • In a young man with azoospermia, normal secondary sexual features, elevated FSH, and biopsy showing seminiferous tubules with only Sertoli cells, the diagnosis is Sertoli cell-only syndrome.

Reference:

  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534293/
