question_text: A patient with carcinoma of the endometrium is treated with external beam irradiation to the whole pelvis. Which of the following pelvic organs is most radiosensitive?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The ovaries are the most radiosensitive organs in the pelvis due to the presence of rapidly dividing granulosa cells, which are highly susceptible to radiation-induced damage.
  • Radiation can lead to:
  • Decline in endocrine function → decreased estrogen production
  • Loss of oocytes and follicle reserve → infertility and premature menopause
  • Radiosensitivity depends on age, irradiation dose, and field of treatment.

Vagina (Option B), bladder (Option C), and rectum (Option D), These tissues are less radiosensitive compared to ovaries. Although they may suffer radiation effects, they are not the primary concern for fertility preservation.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Granulosa cells in the ovary are most radiosensitive, particularly during mid-folliculogenesis, because they are rapidly dividing and essential for oocyte maturation.
  • Primordial follicles are relatively resistant as they are arrested in meiosis.
  • Radiation toxicity leads to infertility (loss of functional oocytes) and premature menopause (loss of estrogen secretion).
  • Fertility may be temporarily preserved if developed oocytes survive due to their independence from granulosa cell proliferation.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman reports severe dysmenorrhea, painful intercourse, and infertility. She has been diagnosed with endometriosis and scheduled for laparoscopic surgery. During the operation, dense pelvic adhesions were found, with the bowel adherent to the uterine fundus and cystic ovaries adhered to one another. What should be the next step in her management?
option_b: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
explanation:
Explanation:

When dense adhesions and cystic ovaries are identified during laparoscopy, the most appropriate course of action is to perform cystectomy along with adhesiolysis.

  • Adhesiolysis helps restore normal pelvic anatomy and can significantly reduce pain symptoms associated with endometriosis.
  • Cystectomy is important for removing endometriotic cysts and improving fertility outcomes.

Explanation for other options:

Laparoscopic uterine nerve ablation (LUNA) (Option A) is a surgical technique that involves severing uterine nerves in an effort to alleviate chronic pelvic pain. However, it is not commonly used for managing endometriosis and may not provide effective relief for all patients.

Gestrinone (Option B) is a synthetic hormone that works by lowering luteinising hormone (LH) levels, which can help suppress ovulation and reduce the growth of endometrial tissue. Despite this, it is not generally considered a first-line treatment for endometriosis.

Hysterectomy and oophorectomy (Option D) involve surgical removal of the uterus and ovaries, respectively. This approach is more radical and typically reserved for individuals with severe, treatment-resistant endometriosis or for those who have completed their families and do not wish to conceive in the future.

question_text: A patient complaints of post coital bleed; no growth is seen, on per speculum examination; next step should be:
explanation:
Colposcopic Directed Biopsy

Colposcopy is the Gold standard technique for evaluation of an abnormal cervical cytology smear/pap smear.

  • It is an outpatient procedure that is simple, quick and well tolerated.
  • It allows examination of the lower genital tract and anus with a microscope (magnification = 30 times).

Method

  • The first step to visualize the cervix under magnification.
  • Leukoplakia must be looked for before applying acetic and otherwise it gets confused with acetowhite areas. Biopsy sample should be taken
  • Biopsy samples should also be taken from any rough area or raised area of the cervix.
  • Any abnormal blood vessel pattern viz reticular blood vessels, comma-shaped blood vessels or punctate blood vessels should be biopsied.
  • Then 3-5% acetic acid should be applied on the cervix gently but liberally.

Principle

  • Application of acetic acid to normal epithelium: Glycogen producing epithelium of the cervix does not produce any effect and it appears pink during colposcopy.
  • Application of acetic acid to dysplastic epithelium: When acetic acid is applied to dysplastic epithelium which have large nuclei with abnormally large amounts of chromatin (i.e. protein), acetic acid coagulates the proteins of the nucleus and cytoplasm, making the proteins opaque and white, therefore, dysplastic cells and cancerous cells appear white (known as Aceto white areas)
  • Application of acetic acid to metaplastic epithelium: The immature metaplastic cells have large nuclei and also show some effects of the acetic acid. Since metaplastic epithelium is very thin, it does not appear white but instead appears grey and filmy.

Indications of Colposcopy ... Shaw 14th/ed p 362

  • Abnormal pap smear cytology
  • To locate abnormal areas
  • To obtain directed biopsies
  • Conservative therapy under colposcopy guidance
  • For follow up of cases treated conservatively

Abnormal findings on colposcopy indicative of dysplasia are:

  • Aceto white epithelium: Dysplastic epithelium turns white after application of acetic acid and is called aceto white epithelium.
  • Leukoplakia or hyperkeratosis: It is an area of white, thick epithelium which is appreciated prior to application of acetic acid and may indicate HPV infection/ Keratinizing CIN, Keratinizing carcinoma, Chronic trauma from diaphragm, pessary and radiotherapy.
  • Mosaicism or punctuation: Reflecting abnormal vascular pattern of surface capillaries.
  • Atypical vessels: With bizarre capillaries in corkscrew, comma shape or spaghetti like configuration. (They suggest early stromal invasion).

Reference: Novak 15th/ed pg 1306

Metropathia Hemorrhagica

It is a specialized form of DUB.

Mostly seen in premenopausal women.

Maximum age incidence: Between ages 40-45 years.

Pathology


Changes in the Uterus: Symmetrical enlargement of the uterus to a size of 8 - 10 weeks due to hypertrophy of muscles.

Microscopic appearance:

  • Intense cystic glandular hypertrophy.

  • Glands are empty and lined by columnar epithelium.
  • Secretory changes are absent. (no corkscrew glands seen)
  • Follicular cysts containing estrogen present on ovaries.

Signs and Symptom: Patient complains of prolonged amenorrhea (of 6-8 weeks) followed by excessive painless bleeding (anovulatory bleeding).

question_text: In cervical cancer treatment, which therapy is given together with radiotherapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is the standard radiosensitizer used in concurrent chemoradiation.
  • In the management of locally advanced cervical cancer (Stage IB3-IVA), concurrent chemoradiation (CCRT) is the standard treatment.
  • Platinum-based chemotherapy (Cisplatin) is given along with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) to enhance the effectiveness of radiation by sensitizing cancer cells.

Explanation of other options:

Immunotherapy (Option A): Immunotherapy (e.g., Pembrolizumab) is used in advanced or recurrent cases, not routinely with radiotherapy.

Hormone therapy (Option C): Not used in cervical cancer, as it is not hormone-dependent like breast or endometrial cancer.

Targeted therapy (Option D): Targeted agents like Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) are used in metastatic cases, not as part of primary radiation therapy.

Key Takeaways:

Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is the standard radiosensitizer used in concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced cervical cancer, improving treatment efficacy.

question_text: Recombinant HPV Vaccine is made from?
explanation:
Currently, three HPV vaccines are FDA approved for prevention of incident HPV infection and cervical neoplasia.

They use recombinant technologies for the synthetic production of the L1 capsid proteins of each HPV type included in the vaccine.

The resultant virus-like particles are highly immunogenic but are not infectious as they lack viral DNA.

question_text: A 26 years old female suffers from PPH on her second postnatal day. Her APTT and PTT are prolonged while BT, PT and platelet counts are normal. Likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
This means the patient is suffering from hemophilia. The question now arises whether it is acquired or inherited/congenital hemophilia.

Inherited congenital hemophilia:

  • Is extremely rare in females.
  • It is an x linked disorder seen mainly in males.

Acquired hemophilia

  • It is a disorder in which antibodies develop against coagulation factors.
  • Antibodies can develop against one coagulation factor or several factors.
  • The most common target protein is factor VIII.
  • Anti-factor VIII antibodies are seen in:
    • Hemophiliacs (apart from the congenital factor VIII or IX deficiency)
    • Postpartum females
    • Due to drugs
    • SLE
    • Normal elderly individuals
  • The patient in the question is a post –partum female who has developed antibodies against factor VIII (i.e. she is a case of Acquired hemophilia).
  • The patients coagulation profile matches exactly with that of acquired hemophilia confirming our diagnosis.

Reference: Ghai 6/e, p 322, 323; Harrison 16/e, p 342, 685

question_text: A 48-year-old postmenopausal female presents with irregular uterine bleeding. Endometrial biopsy reveals endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the most appropriate treatment option?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Systemic progesterone therapy (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate, norethisterone acetate) is an effective first-line treatment for endometrial hyperplasia without atypia.
  • It counteracts unopposed estrogen stimulation, leading to endometrial regression and reducing progression to carcinoma.
  • It is especially useful in postmenopausal women who are not candidates for LNG-IUS or prefer oral/IM therapy.

Explanation of other options:

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCPs) (Option A): COCPs contain both estrogen and progestin, which are primarily used for menstrual cycle regulation in premenopausal women. In postmenopausal women, COCPs are not preferred due to the risk of unopposed estrogen exposure, which can worsen endometrial hyperplasia.

LNG-IUS (Levonorgestrel intrauterine system) (Option B): LNG-IUS is a highly effective treatment for endometrial hyperplasia without atypia, as it provides localized progestin with minimal systemic effects. However, in postmenopausal women, its use may be limited if there are contraindications or patient preference for systemic therapy.

Danazol (Option C): Danazol, an androgenic agent, induces endometrial atrophy by inhibiting ovarian function. However, due to its significant androgenic side effects (weight gain, acne, hirsutism), it is not commonly used in the treatment of endometrial hyperplasia.

Key Takeaways:

Progesterone is the first-line treatment for endometrial hyperplasia without atypia, especially in postmenopausal women.

References: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 149 (2015) - Management of Endometrial Hyperplasia

question_text: A 26-year-old woman, G2P2, arrives at the emergency department with severe, sudden pelvic pain and heavy bleeding following a home delivery. She is diagnosed with secondary postpartum hemorrhage. At what time frame does secondary postpartum hemorrhage typically occur?

Explanation:

Clinically significant uterine bleeding affects approximately 1% of women, most commonly within 1 to 2 weeks postpartum.

Types of PPH:

  • Primary PPH: Within 24 hours of delivery
    • Most common cause: Atonic PPH
  • Secondary PPH: After 24 hours of delivery to 12 weeks
    • The most common cause: Retained bits of placenta

Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

question_text: A postpartum woman diagnosed with Plasmodium vivax malaria requires therapy to prevent relapse. Which antimalarial drug is recommended for preventing postpartum relapse in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Primaquine targets hypnozoites, the dormant liver forms of vivax and P. ovale, and is therefore essential for preventing relapse.
  • Safe to use postpartum, particularly in non-lactating women (caution advised if breastfeeding).
  • Timing:
    • Primaquine is not given during pregnancy due to potential hemolytic risk in G6PD-deficient fetuses.
    • In the postpartum period, it is the drug of choice to eliminate residual liver forms and prevent relapse.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Preventing relapse reduces maternal morbidity, prevents repeated hospitalizations, and lowers risk to the neonate indirectly by preventing maternal anemia or fever.

Explanation of Other Options:

Artemether (Option A):

  • Used mainly in combination with lumefantrine for acute treatment of P. falciparum malaria.
  • Acts on blood-stage parasites only; does not target hypnozoites, so it cannot prevent relapse in vivax.

Quinine (Option C):

  • Effective against blood-stage parasites and safe in pregnancy but does not prevent relapse.
  • Primarily used for acute malaria episodes when other drugs are contraindicated.

Artesunate (Option D):

  • Preferred for severe or complicated malaria, particularly falciparum.
  • No activity against liver hypnozoites, so it cannot prevent vivax relapse.

Key Takeaway Points:

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532739/

question_text: Which of the following options can help lower the risk of endometrial cancer in a postmenopausal woman receiving hormone replacement therapy (HRT)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Adding progesterone to estrogen in hormone replacement therapy (HRT) lowers the risk of endometrial cancer.

HRT is prescribed to postmenopausal women to ease symptoms such as:

  • Hot flushes
  • Night sweats
  • Palpitations
  • Sleep disturbances

Estrogen effectively relieves these symptoms and, with long-term use, helps delay osteoporosis and reduces cardiovascular disease risk. However, estrogen alone can cause increased endometrial proliferation, raising the risk of endometrial cancer. Therefore, progestogen is added or its dose increased to control this proliferation. Note that the progestogen component may increase breast cancer risk.

Explanation for other options:

Combined oral contraceptive pills (Option A) contain both estrogen and progestin but are not typically used in postmenopausal women to reduce endometrial cancer risk due to different hormone concentrations.

Clonidine (Option B) is primarily used to treat high blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels and slowing heart rate; it does not reduce endometrial cancer risk.

Vitamin E (Option C) is an antioxidant with some health benefits but has not been proven to significantly impact endometrial cancer risk.

Cervical cancer screening is an important part of women's health care. You should start having screening at age 21, regardless of when you first start having sex. How often you should have cervical cancer screening and which tests you should have depend on your age and health history:

question_text: What is the ideal treatment for a 55-years-female with Simple hyperplasia of endometrium with Atypia?
explanation:
Management of Atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia:

“Hysterectomy is the best treatment for women at any age with atypical endometrial hyperplasia because the risk of concurrent subclinical invasive disease is high.”

  • Williams Gynae 1st/ed p 691

“In presence of atypia, response to progesterone therapy is poor and relapse rate is high. Nearly one-third of them will progress to cancer and one-fourth may already have associated undiagnosed cancer. In women approaching or past menopause, hysterectomy is a safer choice in those with complex or atypical hyperplasia.”

  • Jeffcoate 7th/ed p 425

So Remember: Best management of atypical hyperplasia is hysterectomy. Also Know: Management of Endometrial Hyperplasia:

Management depends on the patient’s age and the presence or absence of cytological atypia.

Non atypical hyperplasia:

  • Premenopausal women: Progesterone therapy-

Options: – Medroxyprogesterone acetate for 21 days a month daily for 3 months.

– Progesterone containing IUCD.

  • Postmenopausal women

Simple hyperplasia without atypia – Generally followed without therapy.

Complex hyperplasia without atypia – Cyclical/continuous progesterone therapy. These patients should be followed annually by endometrial biopsy.

Atypical hyperplasia:

  • Ideal treatment is hysterectomy
  • Premenopausal women willing to preserve fertility – High dose progesterone therapy after full information of risk of an undiagnosed cancer or progression to cancer. In these cases, periodic TVS and endometrial biopsy is necessary.

Reference: Jeffcoate 7th/ed p 425; Williams Gynae. 1st/ed p 691

  • Small urinary fistulas may heal spontaneously during the first few weeks.
  • For established fistulas, it's advisable to wait for about 3 months for all tissue inflammation to subside.
  • In cases of fistulas following surgery, the waiting period is 3–6 months.
  • For fistulas following radiation, 6 months to 2 years may be needed before inflammation subsides.

Techniques of Repair:

  • Layer technique
  • Latzko procedure (for fistulas following hysterectomy)
  • Chassar Moir technique

Post-operative Management:

  • Continuous bladder drainage for 14 days.
  • Antibiotic coverage.
  • Avoid vaginal examination, P/S (per speculum), intercourse for 3 months.
  • Avoid pregnancy for 2 years.
  • In pregnancy after repair of vaginal fistula, elective cesarean section is performed.

Additional Information:

  • Traditional teaching recommended delayed repair of fistulas at 3–6 months after injury. However, recent practices suggest that waiting is not necessary unless there is severe infection or acute signs of inflammation.
  • Early surgical intervention for uncomplicated fistulas does not affect closure rates and may reduce social and psychological distress for the patient.
  • Fistulas identified within the first 24–48 hours postoperatively can be safely repaired immediately, with success rates of 90–100%.

Reference:

  • Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th Edition, Page 187.
  • Williams Gynecology, 1st Edition, Pages 575-576.

question_text: A postmenopausal woman presented with pain in her lower abdomen for the past 4 months. She has had fibroids for a long time. What is the type of degeneration that occurred in this patient in the radiological investigation is shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical vignette shows a calcified fibroids

  • Long standing fibroid
  • The X-ray shows dense, well-defined calcified masses in the pelvic region
  • These appear as bright white, radio-opaque structures

Calcific degeneration occurs when calcium deposits form within a fibroid, typically after menopause when fibroids involute.

  • Clinical features: Long-standing fibroids may become painful due to degenerative changes.
  • Radiological appearance:
    • Dense, well-defined radio-opaque masses on X-ray or CT scan
    • Often described as "popcorn-like" calcifications
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Fibroids (leiomyomas) undergo secondary degenerative changes over time: hyaline, cystic, fatty, myxoid, red, or calcific degeneration.
  • Calcification is common in postmenopausal women, representing the end stage of fibroid involution.

Explanation of Other Options:

Fatty degeneration (Option A):

  • Smooth muscle cells replaced by mature fat; may be seen histologically.
  • Not visible as dense radio-opaque masses on X-ray.

Hyaline degeneration (Option B):

  • Most common type (~60% of cases)
  • Homogeneous eosinophilic material in the extracellular space
  • Not visible on plain radiographs.

Cystic degeneration(Option D):

  • Liquefaction of fibroid tissue forming fluid-filled cavities
  • Appears as lucent or hypodense areas, not dense calcifications

Key take away points:

  1. Secondary Degenerative Changes in Fibroids

  2. Clinical Pearls:
    • Calcific degeneration = late-stage involution, usually postmenopause
    • Hyaline degeneration = most frequent overall but radiographically occult
    • Imaging clue: "Popcorn-like" appearance on X-ray or CT = calcific degeneration

References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4318819/

question_text: A 24-year-old lactating woman with an 18-month-old child presents with irregular, heavy bleeding and seeks contraceptive advice. Which contraceptive is the most appropriate choice?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Mala N is a combined oral contraceptive (COC) containing ethinylestradiol 30 µg + levonorgestrel 0.15 mg.
  • Best suited here because:
    • Provides reliable contraception.
    • Regulates cycles and helps control irregular heavy bleeding (polymenorrhea, menorrhagia).
    • Safe to start >6 weeks postpartum. Since this patient is 18 months postpartum, estrogen use is no longer a concern for lactation suppression.

Explanation of other options:

Progestasert (Option A): Hormone-releasing IUCD → increases bleeding tendency → unsuitable in heavy menstrual bleeding.

Copper-T 380A (Option B): Non-hormonal IUCD; highly effective but may worsen menorrhagia and anaemia → contraindicated in this scenario.

Norethisterone enanthate - depot injection (Option D): Progestin-only method, safe in lactation, but commonly causes menstrual irregularities (spotting, unpredictable bleeding), which would worsen the patient's complaint.

Key Takeaway:

  • In lactating women >6 months postpartum with heavy, irregular bleeding, combined oral contraceptives (Mala N) are preferred because they provide both effective contraception and cycle regulation.

question_text: Investigation of choice in a 55-year-old post-menopausal woman who has presented with postmenopausal bleeding:
explanation:
Fractional curettage is the gold standard investigation for endometrial carcinoma.

In a woman with postmenopausal bleeding chances of endometrial carcinoma are very high. Therefore, such a patient should be evaluated so as to rule out endometrial carcinoma. Hence fractional curettage should be done.

Investigations for endometrial carcinoma- Novak 15th/ed p 1257

  1. Endometrial Aspiration Biopsy: "It is the accepted first step in evaluating a patient with abnormal uterine bleeding or suspected pathology. The diagnostic accuracy of an office based endometrial biopsy is 90-98% when compared with subsequent findings at dilatation and curettage (D and C)". -Novak 15th/ed p 1257
    1. "Endometrial sampling should be performed in any woman with irregular or heavy bleeding older than age 35. Although a formal dilatation and curettage has been the standard technique for diagnosis, outpatient endometrial biopsy has replaced it in most situations"
  2. Dilatation and Fractional Curettage: "Fractional curettage is not only the definite method of diagnosis but can detect the extent of growth." -Dutta Gynae 5th/ed p 344
  3. Hysteroscopy and biopsy: It is nowadays the investigation of choice for endometrial cancer but most of the cancers are detected easily by endometrial aspiration biopsy and it is reserved for those cases where there is cervical stenosis or patient cannot tolerate endometrial aspiration, bleeding recurs after a negative endometrial biopsy or specimen is inadequate.
  4. Transvaginal ultrasound: May be useful adjunct to endometrial biopsy for evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding and selecting patients for additional testings.
    1. If endometrial thickness is > 4 mm, a polypoid endometrial mass is present or a collection of fluid is present within the uterus, in postmenopausal females always follow up with histopathological diagnosis.
  5. Pap smear: It is not a reliable test for diagnosis of endometrial carcinoma. Only 30-50% patients with endometrial carcinoma have positive pap test and they are women with advanced disease.

Reference: Novak 14th/ed p 1350; Dutta Gynae 5th/ed p 344

question_text: A 35-year-old lady with post coital bleeding management is:

question_text: A 55-year-old pre-menopausal woman is diagnosed with early-stage invasive breast carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry shows strong estrogen receptor (ER+) and progesterone receptor (PR+) positivity. Axillary lymph node biopsy confirms metastatic involvement. Considering her hormonal receptor status and pre-menopausal state, which adjuvant therapy is most appropriate for reducing recurrence?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that competitively inhibits estrogen binding to its receptor in breast tissue, preventing estrogen-driven tumor proliferation.
  • Effective in both pre-menopausal and post-menopausal women with ER+ breast cancer.
  • Used as adjuvant therapy, especially in lymph node-positive cases, to reduce recurrence risk by approximately 25%.
  • Standard duration is 5-10 years depending on risk factors and patient tolerance.

Explanation of Other Options:

Anastrozole (Option B):

  • Aromatase inhibitor that reduces peripheral estrogen synthesis.
  • Effective only in post-menopausal women; not recommended for pre-menopausal patients due to ovarian estrogen production overriding its effect.

Trastuzumab (Option C):

  • Monoclonal antibody targeting HER2/neu receptor.
  • Indicated only for HER2-positive breast cancers.
  • Not effective for hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative tumors.

All of the above (Option D):

  • Incorrect because only Tamoxifen is indicated in pre-menopausal ER+/PR+ breast cancer without HER2 positivity.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Tamoxifen is an antiestrogen used in treating ER +ve pre-menopausal patients with breast cancer.
  • It is used as adjuvant chemotherapy and reduces the recurrence rate 25%

question_text: A 55-year-old post-menopausal woman presents to the OPD for a routine BP checkup. Her BP was 170/100 mmHg. She also complains of a blood-stained discharge per vagina. What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Reassure her that some discharge is normal at this age
option_b: Immediate referral to a cardiologist before any further evaluation
option_c: Immediate pelvic examination, transvaginal sonography (TVS), and Pap smear
option_d: Start antihypertensive medication and observe for 1 week
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB), including any blood-stained discharge, is considered endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.
  • The most important cause to rule out is endometrial carcinoma.
  • The mandatory next step is a thorough gynecological evaluation:
    • Pelvic examination (speculum + bimanual): To identify lesions of cervix or vagina.
    • Pap smear: To screen for cervical cancer/pre-cancer.
    • TVS: To measure endometrial thickness (>4 mm is abnormal in PMB).
  • If endometrial thickness is >4 mm, endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy is warranted.
  • Although the patient has hypertension, this does not take priority over ruling out malignancy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Reassure her that some discharge is normal at this age (Option A): Any bleeding or blood-stained discharge in a postmenopausal woman is abnormal and requires urgent investigation.

Immediate referral to a cardiologist before any further evaluation (Option B): While the hypertension must be addressed, delaying the urgent investigation of PMB is inappropriate. The gynecological workup for potential cancer should be initiated immediately and can occur concurrently with the management of her blood pressure.

Start antihypertensive medication and observe for 1 week (Option D): This is incorrect because it ignores and dangerously delays the evaluation of the PMB, which is a significant red flag for malignancy.

question_text: Hormone Replacement Therapy is truly associated with which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hormone replacement therapy in females is associated with a decreased risk of colon cancer.
  • This treatment is used for menopausal symptoms.
  • It usually involves estrogen and sometimes a combination with progesterone.
  • HRT lowers the risk of colon cancer because of estrogen's protective effects.
  • Therefore, colon cancer is less common in women of reproductive age compared to men of the same age group.
  • Indications of HRT:
    • Therapeutic:
      • Symptomatic menopausal women
      • Gonadal dysgenesis in adolescents
    • Prophylactic:
      • Patients at high risk for menopausal complications like cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, stroke, colon cancer, etc
      • Premature menopause: Spontaneous following surgery or cancer therapy

Explanation for other options:

Breast cancer risk (Option A) is increased by hyperestrogenism. Breast cancers that develop following HRT tend to be low-grade and have a good prognosis.

Estrogen replacement therapy (Option B) can increase the risk of well-differentiated endometrial carcinoma; adding progesterone to estrogen therapy reduces this risk.

After menopause, bone density decreases yearly, leading to osteopenia and eventually osteoporosis (Option C). Osteoporosis commonly results in fractures of the vertebrae, femur, and wrist. HRT containing estrogen protects against osteoporosis and lowers fracture risk.

The most common causes are: inflammation and thinning of the vaginal lining (atrophic vaginitis) or womb lining(endometrial atrophy) caused by lower oestrogen levels. cervical or womb polyps - growths that are usually non-cancerous.

For any patient above 45 years it is necessary to perform endometrial biopsy to rule out endometrial cancer.

Options B,C,D are methods for screening and diagnosis of cervical Ca.

question_text: What is the leading cause of bleeding after menopause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The primary cause of postmenopausal bleeding is cervical cancer

Cervical Cancer

  • Most common gynecological tumor in women

Risk Factors:

  • High-risk HPV infection (e.g., HPV types 16, 18)
  • Early onset of sexual activity
  • Multiple sexual partners
  • Use of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
  • Multiparity
  • Increasing age
  • Low socioeconomic status

Symptoms:

  • Irregular vaginal bleeding
  • Postcoital bleeding
  • Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
  • Pelvic pain
  • Uremic symptoms

On Examination:

  • Cervix may appear normal
  • May present with:
    • Exophytic (outward-growing) or endophytic (inward-growing) lesions
    • Barrel-shaped cervix (suggestive of adenocarcinoma)
    • Cervical ulcer (in adenocarcinoma)

Explanation for other options:

Uterine atrophy (Option A) occurs after menopause as a result of reduced estrogen levels. However, it does not typically lead to postmenopausal bleeding.

Endometrial cancer (Option C) is a potential cause of uterine bleeding in postmenopausal women, but it is not the most frequent cause.

Hormone replacement therapy (Option D), which is prescribed to manage or prevent postmenopausal symptoms, can lead to bleeding-especially if initiated within the first year after menopause. This bleeding may persist for up to six months, though HRT is not the most common reason for postmenopausal bleeding.

  • There is adequate endogenous estrogens (serum E2 level more than 40 pg/ml) to promote progesterone receptors in the endometrium,
  • Anatomically patent outflow tract and
  • Endometrium is responsive.
  • The defect lies in production of progesterone (as when progesterone is supplemented from outside, it results in withdrawal bleeding) and since progesterone is produced mainly by corpus luteum, so, the defect is anovulation.

question_text: A 46-year-old nulliparous woman presents with delayed cycles and heavy bleeding for the past 1 year. Transvaginal ultrasonography reveals an endometrial thickness of 18 mm. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In women >45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), the primary concern is endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
  • Endometrial thickness >12 mm in a perimenopausal woman is considered abnormal and requires evaluation.
  • The gold standard first-line diagnostic step is endometrial sampling/biopsy (methods: Pipelle, D&C, hysteroscopy-guided biopsy).
  • Biopsy confirms whether the cause is benign hyperplasia, atypical hyperplasia, or carcinoma.

Clinical rule:

  • Any woman >45 years with AUB, OR
  • Any younger woman with AUB + risk factors (obesity, PCOS, chronic anovulation, family history, tamoxifen use, etc.) + thickened endometrium
  • Must undergo endometrial biopsy to rule out malignancy.

Endometrial Thickness Cut-offs (TVUS) for Biopsy:

  • Premenopausal AUB: ≥12 mm
  • Postmenopausal bleeding: ≥4 mm

Explanation of Other Options:

Start combined oral contraceptive pills (Option A): While OCPs can be used to manage AUB in younger women after pathology has been ruled out, prescribing them without a tissue diagnosis in this high-risk patient would be inappropriate, as it could mask or delay the diagnosis of a malignancy

Schedule hysterectomy (Option B): Hysterectomy is definitive treatment for confirmed atypical hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma. It is not the initial step before establishing a tissue diagnosis.

Wait and watch for 6 months (Option C): Delaying biopsy risks missing endometrial carcinoma in a perimenopausal woman with AUB and thickened endometrium.

question_text: Which of the following is a cause of secondary amenorrhoea?
explanation:
Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses for three cycles or six months in women who previously had regular menstruation. Identifying the underlying cause typically requires a combination of history, physical examination, and diagnostic testing.

  1. Physiological Causes
    • Pregnancy (most common cause)
    • Breastfeeding (lactational amenorrhea)
    • Menopause or perimenopause
  2. Hypothalamic Causes
    • Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: Often due to stress, weight loss, excessive exercise, or eating disorders.
    • Chronic Illnesses: Conditions like celiac disease or chronic kidney disease can impact hypothalamic function.
    • Infiltrative Disorders: Tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma), sarcoidosis, or other infiltrative diseases affecting the hypothalamus.
  3. Pituitary Causes
    • Hyperprolactinemia: Can be caused by pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas), medications (e.g., antipsychotics), or hypothyroidism.
    • Pituitary Tumors: Growths that interfere with hormone production, such as non-prolactin-secreting adenomas.
    • Sheehan's Syndrome: Postpartum pituitary necrosis due to severe blood loss during or after childbirth.
    • Empty Sella Syndrome: Pituitary gland is either flattened or small.
  4. Ovarian Causes
    • Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): Common cause, associated with irregular menstruation, hirsutism, and metabolic issues.
    • Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI): Premature ovarian failure, often due to autoimmune factors, genetic issues (e.g., Turner syndrome mosaicism), or chemotherapy/radiation exposure.
    • Ovarian Tumors: Granulosa cell tumors or other hormone-producing ovarian neoplasms.
  5. Uterine Causes
    • Asherman Syndrome: Intrauterine adhesions or scarring, often secondary to uterine surgeries like dilation and curettage (D&C) or infections.
    • Endometrial Atrophy: Often due to long-term use of hormonal contraception or other endometrial damage.
  6. Endocrine Causes
    • Thyroid Disorders: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can disrupt menstrual cycles.
    • Adrenal Disorders: Conditions like Cushing's syndrome or adrenal tumors that cause excess androgens.
    • Diabetes Mellitus: Poorly controlled diabetes can impact menstrual regularity.
  7. Medications and Lifestyle Factors
    • Medications: Antipsychotics, chemotherapy agents, hormonal contraception, antidepressants, and certain antihypertensives can affect menstrual cycles.
    • Lifestyle: Severe stress, extreme exercise, malnutrition, and rapid weight changes.

Options A,B,C are causes of primary amenorrhea

question_text: The following statements are related to Krukenberg tumour except:
option_b: The most common primary site is pylorus of the stomach
explanation:
• Krukenberg tumor is generally a metastatic tumor to the ovary. But "krukenberg tumor may be a primary tumor"
  • The most common primary sites from where metastases to the ovaries occur are gastrointestinal tract (pylorus, colon and rarely small intestine), gallbladder, pancreas, breast and endometrial carcinoma.
  • These are usually bilateral tumors which maintain the shape of the ovary. Histologically 'signet ring’ looking cells are characteristic of krukenberg tumor.
  • In most patients with Krukenberg's tumors, the prognosis is poor. Median survival being less than a year. Rarely, no primary site can be identified and the Krukenberg's tumor may be a primary tumor.

Also know: Metastatic tumors from the GI tract can be associated with sex hormone (estrogen and androgen) production. Patient may present with postmenopausal bleeding.

Reference: Dutta Gynae 6th/ed pg 387

question_text: Before menarche corpus to cervix ratio is:
explanation:
The relationship between the length of the cervix and that of the body of the uterus varies with age.

  • Before puberty, the cervix to corpus ratio is 2:1.
  • At puberty, this ratio is reversed to 1:2,
  • During the reproductive years, the cervix to corpus ratio may be 1:3 or even 1:4.
  • After menopause (1:1), the whole organ atrophies and the portio vaginalis may eventually disappear.

Reference: Shaw’s textbook of gynecology, 16th edition, chapter 1

question_text: A female patient has adenocarcinoma uterus along with sarcoma of uterus. It is known as:
explanation:
Mixed mullerian carcinoma is a mixture of both carcinomatous and sarcomatous elements.

  • Represent 50% of all uterine sarcoma.
  • Most common combination is serous carcinoma with endometrial sarcoma.
  • Most commonly occur in postmenopausal women.

Remember:

  • Most common histologic type of uterine sarcoma is carcinosarcoma.
  • Most common symptom of uterine sarcoma is bleeding.
  • Surgery is the mainstay of treatment followed by chemotherapy.

Also know:

Heterologous tumors: If the sarcoma component of mixed mullerian tumors mimic extra uterine tissue (viz – striated muscle cell, cartilage, adipose tissue and bone) it is known as Heterologous tumor.

Homologous tumor: If the mesenchymal/sarcomatous component of mixed mullerian tumor consists of malignant endometrial or smooth muscle differentiation, the term homologous is used.

Reference: COGDT 10th/ed pg 866.

question_text: Which of the following is true about Brenner's tumour?
option_c: Accounts for 20% of all ovarian tumors
explanation:
Brenner tumour is also called as Transitional cell tumour:

  • It is a rare epithelial neoplasm of the ovary resembling a fibroma.
  • It is an essentially benign tumour.
  • Tumour is generally seen in women around menopause and is generally unilateral.
  • Causes menopausal bleeding and Pseudo Meigs syndrome (ascites and hydrothorax).
  • Malignant change is very rare.
  • Histologically, it shows Walthard cell rests of transitional cells, cells have coffee bean nuclei, cut sections are gritty.

Reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th Edition, Page Number-376.

question_text: Characteristic feature of carcinoma fallopian tube:
explanation:
• Fallopian Tube Carcinoma accounts for 0.3% of all cancers of the female genital tract.
  • Most common site is the ampulla of the tube.
  • Most common type is adenocarcinoma.
  • The fallopian tube is frequently involved in secondary to carcinoma of ovary, endometrium, gastrointestinal tract, breast and peritoneum.
  • Women with mutation in BRCA I and BRCA II have higher risk of developing fallopian tube carcinoma (therefore, a prophylactic surgery in these women should include a complete removal of both tubes along with the ovaries).
  • Most common symptom is Vaginal discharge (prominent watery vaginal discharge called Hydrops tubae profluens). Later due to ulceration – watery discharge becomes blood stained and may take the form of perimenopausal/ postmenopausal bleeding.

Always remember:

  • In perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with unusual, unexplained or persistent vaginal discharge, even in absence of bleeding, the clinician should always keep the possibility of occult tubal cancer in mind.

Reference: Novak 14th/ed pg 1562

question_text: A pregnant woman with bronchial asthma develops postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) during delivery of her first child. Which drug is contraindicated?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma due to its bronchoconstrictive properties, which can trigger life-threatening asthma exacerbations.

  • Carboprost is a synthetic analogue of Prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α), used in the management of refractory PPH due to uterine atony.
  • However, it induces bronchial smooth muscle contraction, making it dangerous in patients with asthma.
  • Dose: 250 µg IM every 15-90 mins, up to a maximum of 2 mg.
  • Efficacy: Very effective in controlling uterine bleeding (~88%).
  • Side effects: Bronchospasm, diarrhea, hypertension, fever, nausea, vomiting.
  • Absolute Contraindications: Asthma, pulmonary hypertension, amniotic fluid embolism.
  • Relative Contraindications: Cardiac disease, liver/renal dysfunction, preeclampsia.
  • In asthmatic patients, using carboprost could lead to bronchoconstriction and respiratory distress, which can be fatal.

Explanation of other options:

Methyl ergometrine (Option A): Causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertension, not asthma. It’s relatively safe in asthmatic patients if blood pressure is controlled.

Misoprostol (Option C): A Prostaglandin E1 analogue. It does not cause bronchoconstriction, making it safe in asthma. Used rectally, orally, or sublingually for PPH.

Oxytocin (Option D): First-line agent for PPH. Promotes uterine contraction by acting on oxytocin receptors. It’s safe in asthma, with no bronchial side effects.

Reference:

question_text: False about Anti-D postpartum prophylaxis:
option_a: Given to the newborn within 72 hrs of birth
option_b: Required when baby is Rh+ and mother Rh-
option_c: Can be helpful in ABO incompatibility
option_d: Can be given upto one month of age of baby
explanation:
The correct answer is (C): Can be helpful in ABO incompatibility.

Anti-D postpartum prophylaxis is specifically designed to prevent Rh sensitization in Rh negative mothers with Rh-positive infants. It is not effective for managing ABO incompatibility, which involves different blood group antigens and does not benefit from Anti-D administration. The other statements regarding the timing and necessity of Anti-D in Rh incompatibility are accurate.

Option B: If the baby is Rh positive and mother Rh negative, 300 µg of Anti D immunoglobulin (IgG) is given to the mother and not infant (provided maternal antibody screening is negative).

Option A,D: Postpartum prophylaxis is best given within 72 hours after delivery but it can be given till 28 days after delivery.

Also Know:

Role of postpartum prophylaxis:

Anti D immunoglobulin given postpartum binds to antigen sites on the fetal red cells so that these cells cannot mount an immune response and thus prevent future sensitisation and
next pregnancy.

If after delivery, the fetus has a positive direct Coombs test, it means that the mother is already immunized. In such cases, there is no point in giving anti D.

Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 334; COGDT 10/e, pg 284

question_text: A woman presents 5 days postpartum with smelly greenish vaginal discharge. What should be the initial investigation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The first step in evaluating postpartum abnormal vaginal discharge is a per vagina (PV) examination. This allows the clinician to:

  • Assess the appearance, amount, and odor of the discharge
  • Identify signs of infection or inflammation.
  • Collect samples for microscopy, culture, or swab tests to guide treatment.t

Common Causes of Postpartum Vaginal Discharge

Trichomonas Vaginitis:

  • Caused by vaginalis, sexually transmitted
  • Symptoms: Frothy yellow-green discharge, foul odour, vulvar irritation, dysuria, dyspareunia
  • "Strawberry cervix" may be seen on the PV exam.
  • Diagnosis: Wet mount microscopy, elevated vaginal pH, NAAT (gold standard)
  • Treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole for both patient and partner

Explanation for other options:

CBC (Option A): Can detect infection (e.g., elevated WBC) but is not first-line for discharge evaluation.

USG (Option B): Useful if retained products of conception or uterine infection are suspected, but not the initial step for discharge.

Urine analysis (Option C): Relevant only if urinary symptoms are present; discharge-focused symptoms need PV exam first.

question_text: A 55-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, distension, ascites and dyspnea. Her CA 125 levels are elevated. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
• M/c age incidence for primary ovarian neoplasms is 40-60 years, peak age incidence being 55–60 years.
  • Ovarian malignancies generally present with vague symptoms like abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and patients may also experience irregular menses and if pelvic mass compresses the bladder or rectum she may have urinary frequency or constipation.
  • In advanced stages patients have symptoms related to presence of ascites, omental metastasis or bowel metastasis like abdominal distension, dyspnea, bloating, nausea, anorexia or early satiety.
  • In the patient given in the question all these symptoms are present (which could be seen in other cancers as well) plus her Ca 125 levels are raised, which favors the diagnosis of ovarian cancer in her.

Remember

  • The most important sign of epithelial ovarian cancer is the presence of a pelvic mass on physical examination.
  • For postmenopausal patients with an adnexal mass and a very high serum CA125 level (>200U/ml), there is 96% positive predictive value for ovarian malignancy.

Reference: Jeffcoates 7th/ed pg 543; Novaks 15th/ed pg 1366.

question_text: A type 1 diabetic mother is on magnesium sulfate infusion post-cesarean section for preeclampsia. She develops delirium and drowsiness. She has a respiratory rate of 10/min, a random blood glucose level of 240 mg/dL, oliguria, and bilaterally absent knee reflexes. What is the cause of her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture points to magnesium sulfate toxicity, not diabetic or eclamptic complications:

  • Absent deep tendon reflexes (knee reflexes) → classic early sign of magnesium toxicity
  • Respiratory rate of 10/min → respiratory depression (seen when serum magnesium ~12 mEq/L)
  • Oliguria → reduced renal excretion → drug accumulation
  • Blood glucose (240 mg/dL) is elevated but not sufficient to explain the CNS depression seen

Magnesium Sulfate Toxicity

Monitoring:

  • Observe deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output
  • Reflex loss at ~9 mg/dL, respiratory depression at ~12 mEq/L (14.4 mg/dL), cardiac arrest >30 mg/dL

Serum Magnesium Levels:

  • 5-9 mg/dL → therapeutic
  • 9 mg/dL → loss of patellar reflexes
  • ~12 mEq/L → respiratory depression
  • 30 mg/dL → cardiac arrest

Management:

  1. Stop magnesium infusion immediately
  2. Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% IV over 3 minutes → antidote
  3. Furosemide for enhanced excretion (if renal function allows)
  4. Intubation & ventilation if severe respiratory depression

Explanation of other options:

Diabetic ketoacidosis (Option B): Presents with dehydration, Kussmaul respiration (not hypoventilation), and altered sensorium. Here, absent reflexes point away from DKA.

Eclampsia (Option C): Involves seizures and hypertension-related complications, but drowsiness with absent reflexes and low RR strongly indicate drug toxicity.

Diabetes insipidus (Option D): Causes polyuria, polydipsia, and hypernatremia, not oliguria and CNS depression.

Key Takeaway

  • Absent reflexes + oliguria + respiratory depression in a preeclamptic woman on magnesium sulfate = magnesium sulfate toxicity.

Reference:

  1. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32443079/

question_text: Vaginal defence is lost:
explanation:
Vaginal defence is lost 10 days after birth. The maternal estrogen circulating the newborn maintains the vaginal defence for 10 days. Thereafter it is lost upto pre-puberty and after menopause. High levels of circulating estrogen increase the vaginal defence during puberty, pregnancy and in the premenstrual phase.

  • Squamous epithelium is resistant to gonococcal infection hence theoretically gonococcal vaginitis can occur in newborn females
    • Vagina does not have any mucus-secreting glands.
  • Since vagina does not have any glands, vaginal discharge is not derived from vagina.
  • The components of vaginal secretion are derived from:
    • Endocervical glands
    • Endometrial glands
    • Bartholin’s glands
    • Vagina does not have any serosal covering except for the area covered by cul de sac posteriorly.
    • Apart from Doderlein’s bacilli, it contains many other pathogenic organisms including Cl. welchii.

Reference: Dutta Gynae 6th/ed p 5.

question_text: Causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding can be:
explanation:
-DUB is defined as a state of abnormal uterine bleeding without any clinically detectable organic pelvic pathology.

DUB is of 2 types:

  1. Anovulatory (80%)
  2. Ovulatory (20%)

Anovulatory (80%):

  • Threshold bleeding of puberty menorrhagia
  • Metropathia haemorrhagica cystic glandular hyperplasia
  • Premenopausal DUB (Atrophy of endometrium).

Ovulatory (20%):

  • Irregular ripening of corpus luteum
  • Irregular shedding of corpus luteum
  • IUD insertion
  • Following sterilisation operation.

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed pp 301-302.

question_text: The commonest cause of occipitoposterior position of fetal head during labour is:
explanation:
In vertex presentation when the occiput is placed posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint or directly over the sacrum. It is called the occipitoposterior position.

Causes of Occipitoposterior Position:

Most common cause of occipitoposterior position is anthropoid pelvis:

  • In the anthropoid pelvis, the AP diameter of the brim exceeds the transverse diameter. This pelvis is usually of high assimilation type with an extra vertebrae in the sacrum. Therefore, inclination of the pelvis is increased and this favours occipitoposterior.
  • In android pelvis the inlet is wedge shaped and so the bulky occiput cannot find space in the narrow forepelvis. This predisposes to occipitoposterior.
  • Primary brachycephaly cause marked deflexion of the head.
  • Attachment of placenta on anterior wall of uterus cause marked deflexion of the head.
  • Abnormal uterine contraction leads to deflexion and persistent occipitoposterior position.
  • At the onset of labor — 15–20% cases are occipitoposterior
  • At the end of labor—5% cases are occipitoposterior
  • M/C position in OP = is Right occiput posterior position.

Reference: Dutta Obs 7/e, p 365

question_text: A 50-year-old woman, who had her last pregnancy 20 years ago, presents with heavy bleeding and a mass felt on the perineum. A smooth, round, globular structure is observed on examination. On bimanual examination, the uterus is firm, and the cervix admits one finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A myxomatous (fibroid) polyp is a benign leiomyoma that can prolapse through the cervix, presenting as a smooth mass with a firm uterus and abnormal bleeding years after delivery.

  • Myxomatous polyps (also called fibroid polyps or prolapsed submucous fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus that can protrude through the cervix and present as a mass at the introitus or perineum.
  • In this case, the key findings include:
    • Smooth, round, globular mass on perineal examination
    • Palpable, firm uterus on bimanual exam
    • Cervix admitting one finger (suggesting something protruding through the cervix)
  • This constellation strongly suggests a prolapsed submucous fibroid (i.e., a myxomatous polyp), especially in a woman long past childbearing age.

Leiomyoma:

  • Leiomyomas are non-cancerous tumors composed of smooth muscle cells that arise from the myometrium.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Asymptomatic in ~75%: Often discovered incidentally
    • Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) in ~30%: Includes menorrhagia and metrorrhagia
    • Pelvic pain symptoms: Dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia
    • Reproductive issues: Infertility
    • Pressure effects: Increased urinary frequency or retention, constipation
    • Sensation of heaviness: Lower abdominal or pelvic discomfort

Explanation of other options:

Uterine Inversion (Option B): Occurs acutely postpartum, not decades after delivery. It presents with severe pain, hemorrhage, and shock-not seen here.

Placental Polyp (Option C): Retained placental tissue occurs shortly after delivery or abortion. It is highly unlikely 20 years post-childbirth.

Hypertrophied Cervix (Option D): Refers to generalized cervical enlargement, not a discrete globular mass at the perineum. The presence of a protruding mass with a separate firm uterus rules this out.

question_text: In the anteroposterior measurements of the pelvic inlet, what defines the true conjugate?
option_a: The distance from the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the uppermost margin of the symphysis pubis
option_b: The shortest distance between the sacral promontory and the symphysis pubis
option_c: The distance from the lowest margin of the symphysis to the sacral promontory
option_d: The distance from the posterior margin of the sacral promontory to the symphysis pubis
explanation:
Explanation:

The true conjugate (conjugata vera) is defined as the distance from the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the upper border of the pubic symphysis. This measurement is essential for evaluating the adequacy of the pelvic inlet for vaginal delivery. A true conjugate of less than 9.5 cm may indicate a risk of cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD), where the fetal head may not pass through the pelvis easily.



Explanations for Other Options:

Distance from the posterior margin of the sacral promontory to the symphysis pubis (option D): It is sometimes cited as another description of the true conjugate. However, it is less precise, because the true conjugate is specifically measured from the midpoint of the sacral promontory, not its posterior edge. This distinction is important for accurate obstetric assessment.

question_text: A pregnant female was given indomethacin for treatment of pain. Which of the following can be likely outcome in the baby?
explanation:
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus is a rare phenomenon. It is thought to be caused by one of three things: abnormal levels of produced and circulating prostaglandin, maternal ingestion of prostaglandin synthase inhibitors or it can be idiopathic.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) have been associated with premature closure of the ductus arteriosus(DA). Ibuprofen is a member of the NSAID class with potential obstetric treatment advantages despite a 40-fold decreased potency compared to indomethacin.

question_text: A 65-year-old postmenopausal female presents with a chief complaint of vaginal bleeding for the past three months. She undergoes a hysterectomy, and the gross specimen is shown below. Based on the image and clinical scenario, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is endometrial cancer based on the patient's age, clinical presentation, and the appearance of the gross specimen.

  • Clinical Clue: The patient is a 65-year-old postmenopausal female with vaginal bleeding. This is a classic presenting symptom of endometrial carcinoma and should always prompt an investigation to rule out this diagnosis.
  • Gross Specimen Findings: The image of the hysterectomy specimen reveals a large, bulky, and irregular mass filling the endometrial cavity. The mass has a friable and necrotic appearance, and it appears to be infiltrating the underlying myometrium. These features are highly characteristic of a malignant neoplasm, probably an endometrial adenocarcinoma.

Explanation of Other Options:

Fibroid (Leiomyoma) (Option B): This is a benign smooth muscle tumor of the uterus. On gross examination, fibroids typically appear as firm, well-demarcated, whorled nodules that are distinct from the surrounding myometrium. They are not friable or invasive in this manner.

Endometriosis (Option C): This condition involves the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. While it can cause bleeding, it does not present as a large, intracavitary uterine mass. It typically manifests as cysts or implants on the ovaries, peritoneum, or other pelvic organs.

Adenomyosis (Option D): This is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. It causes a diffuse, symmetric enlargement of the uterus with a thickened myometrium and does not form a discrete, friable mass within the endometrial cavity.

question_text: A 45-year-old female patient was diagnosed with cervical carcinoma and radiotherapy has been planned. The radiation oncologist is reviewing the treatment plan focusing on Point A, which is a key reference point for radiation delivery. What is the dose of radiation in point A radiotherapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Point A is anatomically defined as 2 cm superior to the external cervical os and 2 cm lateral to the uterine canal, corresponding to the paracervical tissue where the uterine artery crosses the ureter.
  • Prescribing 7000 centigray to Point A ensures effective tumor control while minimizing damage to surrounding organs such as the bladder and rectum.
  • The standard range delivered at Point A in high-dose brachytherapy is 7000-8000 RADs (or centigray).
  • Point B, located 3 cm lateral to Point A, represents the obturator lymph nodes at the pelvic sidewall and typically receives a lower dose (~6000 RADs).

Explanation of Other Options:

2500 centigray (Option A):

  • Subtherapeutic dose; insufficient for tumoricidal effect at Point A.
  • May lead to local recurrence if used as the prescribed dose.

5000 centigray (Option C):

  • Below standard curative dose; used only in palliative scenarios or dose-reduced protocols for specific high-risk patients.
  • Not standard for definitive brachytherapy in cervical carcinoma.

10,000 centigray (Option D):

Excessive dose; exceeds tissue tolerance limits of adjacent organs.

Would increase risk of severe complications such as bladder or rectal necrosis.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Brachytherapy dose prescription is critical for local control of cervical carcinoma.
  • Adhering to Point A dosing ensures high cure rates while reducing morbidity.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802172/

question_text: On radiological evaluation of a pregnant woman, the pelvic inlet appears oval-shaped with the largest diameter in the anteroposterior direction. According to Caldwell and Moloy's classification, what type of pelvis does this most likely represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

The anthropoid pelvis is characterized by:

  • Oval-shaped pelvic inlet.
  • Greatest anteroposterior diameter (pubic symphysis to sacral promontory) exceeds transverse diameter.
  • Accounts for ~23.5% of female pelves.
  • Narrow anterior segment, often associated with occiput posterior fetal position.
  • Radiological appearance aligns with the oval shape described.

Caldwell-Moloy Classification:

  • Pelvic types are classified based on inlet shape, transverse diameter, and anterior/posterior segment ratios.
  • Types: Gynecoid, Anthropoid, Android, Platypelloid.

Explanation of Other Options:

Android pelvis (Option A): Heart-shaped inlet; greatest transverse diameter is posterior. More common in males; ~32.5% of female pelves. Not consistent with the oval AP-dominant inlet.

Gynecoid pelvis (Option C): Round to slightly oval; transverse diameter slightly larger than AP. Most common (~41.4%). Opposite of AP-dominant oval inlet.

Platypelloid pelvis (Option D): Wide, flat inlet; transverse diameter much greater than AP. Rare (~2.6%). Opposite of anthropoid shape.

Key Take Away Points:

question_text: A woman, who is 5 days postpartum, presents with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's onset of symptoms within 4–5 days postpartum, including tearfulness, mood swings, and mild insomnia, is most consistent with Postpartum Blues, which is a transient, self-limiting condition.

Explanation of Other Options:

Postpartum anxiety (Option D): Characterized by excessive worry or tension after childbirth, often with somatic symptoms. Unlike postpartum blues, it is not transient and does not primarily involve tearfulness or mood swings. Treatment includes supportive counseling and sometimes SSRIs, generally safe with breastfeeding.

question_text: A woman develops atonic postpartum hemorrhage that does not respond to initial measures and medical management. What is the next best step in management that can be done in the labour room?
explanation:
Explanation:

When atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is refractory to uterine massage and pharmacological agents, the next step in the management algorithm is typically a mechanical or procedural intervention.

Intrauterine balloon tamponade (e.g., using a Bakri balloon) is the most appropriate next step that can be performed quickly and effectively in the labor room.

Stepwise Management of Atonic PPH:

  1. Initial Measures (Labour Room):
    • Bimanual uterine massage + Tranexamic acid + Oxytocin (WHO first-line)
    • If unresponsive → add:
      • Methyl ergometrine
      • Carboprost
      • Misoprostol (add-on drug)
  2. If unresponsive >30 mins → Mechanical Compression (Still in Labour Room):
    • Intrauterine balloon tamponade (principle: pressure on venous sinuses by warm saline filled device → Controls bleeding)
      • Bakri balloon catheter (max 500 mL)
      • Sengstaken-Blakemore (S.B.) esophageal catheter
      • Ellavi Balloon / Uterine Tamponade System
      • Condom catheter (Foley's condom catheter) → low-cost, labour-room option
    • Can add vaginal balloon if persistent vaginal ooze.
  3. If Bleeding Persists → Surgical/Advanced Measures (OT):
    • If vitals stable: External aortic compression (temporary, check femoral pulse)
    • If vitals unstable: Uterine artery ligation (Option B ruled out)
    • Still bleeds: Compression sutures like B-Lynch (m/c), Hayman, Cho square, Pereira, Gurshella (Option D ruled out)
    • If facilities available → uterine artery embolization (stable vitals).
  4. If Still Bleeding:
    • Stepwise devascularization (bilateral uterine → ovarian → internal iliac artery ligation). (Option C ruled out)
    • Subtotal hysterectomy (if life-threatening, uterus not preserved).
    • Pelvic pressure packs (umbrella/parachute pack) as last resort if still bleeding continues.

question_text: Immediately following a vaginal delivery, a patient develops massive postpartum hemorrhage. The uterus is found to be soft and boggy. Despite administration of oxytocin and prostaglandins, the bleeding continues. Which of the following statements is true regarding the procedure shown?
option_a: It is primarily used to remove retained placental tissue.
option_b: It must always be performed under general anesthesia.
option_c: It is a second-line measure when uterotonics fail to contract the uterus.
option_d: All of the above are true.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts bimanual uterine compression, a critical temporizing maneuver in the management of Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) caused by uterine atony. This procedure is employed when first-line medical management with uterotonic agents (like oxytocin, misoprostol, carboprost) has failed to achieve adequate uterine contraction and control the bleeding.

  • Mechanism: One hand is placed as a fist in the anterior vaginal fornix to compress the anterior uterine wall, while the other hand compresses the posterior wall through the abdomen. This direct compression of the uterine vessels at the placental site helps to stanch the bleeding while further resuscitative measures are undertaken.

Explanation of Other Options:

Used for retained placental tissue (Option A): While retained placenta is a cause of PPH, bimanual compression is not the treatment for it. The definitive management for retained tissue is manual removal or curettage.

Should be done under GA (Option B): Bimanual compression is an emergency, life-saving procedure that is often initiated immediately at the bedside without anesthesia. While analgesia is beneficial, waiting for general anesthesia would cause a critical delay.

All of the above (Option D): This is incorrect because options A and B are false.

Key Takeaways: Management of PPH due to Uterine Atony

question_text: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman, who has never been pregnant (nulliparous) and is currently on hormone replacement therapy (HRT), presents with abdominal pain. On examination, a non-tender palpable mass is felt in the right adnexal region. During laparotomy, both ovaries appear as shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ovarian carcinoma is a common cause of adnexal masses in postmenopausal women, especially in those with risk factors such as nulliparity and hormone replacement therapy.

Key Diagnostic Features:

  • Age: Postmenopausal women (over 50) are at higher risk.
  • Nulliparity: Increases lifetime risk due to uninterrupted ovulation cycles.
  • HRT use: Can stimulate ovarian epithelium and promote tumor growth.
  • Non-tender adnexal mass: Suggests a neoplastic (not inflammatory) lesion.
  • Laparotomy findings: Typically show irregular, solid or cystic, enlarged ovaries with surface excrescences.

Explanation for other options:

Hydrosalpinx (option A):

  • A medical condition where one or both fallopian tubes become blocked and fill with fluid, preventing eggs from travelling to the uterus and increasing the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
  • This is often caused by infections that lead to inflammation and scarring, such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or certain sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
  • Causes
  • Infections: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and some sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are common causes due to the inflammation and scarring they create.
  • Other medical conditions: Endometriosis can also lead to hydrosalpinx.

Chocolate cyst of the ovary (option B):

  • Also known as endometrioma, it is a cystic lesion filled with old, dark brown blood ("chocolate-like" fluid).
  • Typically occurs in premenopausal women with endometriosis.
  • Symptoms often include dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility- none of which are seen in this postmenopausal woman.
  • Endometriosis and chocolate cysts rarely occur after menopause unless reactivated by exogenous estrogen, which is still much less likely than carcinoma in this age group.

Ovarian fibroid (option C):

  • Fibroids (leiomyomas)arise from the uterine smooth muscle, not from ovarian tissue.
  • The term "ovarian fibroid" is incorrect, though fibromas(benign ovarian stromal tumours) can occur.
  • However, ovarian fibromas are typically benign, solid, and firm but do not correlate strongly with HRT use or postmenopausal age-related risk of carcinoma.
  • Given her age, HRT, and presentation, malignancy (ovarian carcinoma) is far more likely.

Key takeaway:

question_text: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 2 with two miscarriages, presents with foul-smelling vaginal bleeding. She has been diagnosed with FIGO Stage IIIB cervical cancer. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
option_d: Radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymph node dissection
explanation:
Explanation:

For FIGO Stage IIIB cervical cancer, where the tumor involves the pelvic wall and/or causes hydronephrosis, concurrent chemoradiation is the treatment of choice. This approach:

  • Combines external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) with cisplatin-based chemotherapy
  • Controls local tumor growth
  • Improves survival compared to radiation alone
  • Preserves patient suitability for potential palliative procedures if needed later

Explanation of Other Options:

Radical hysterectomy (Option B): Reserved for early-stage cervical cancer (up to Stage IIA) but not feasible in Stage IIIB due to pelvic wall involvement.

Pelvic exenteration (Option C): A salvage procedure for recurrent or extensively invasive disease involving adjacent organs (bladder, rectum) but not indicated as initial therapy.

Radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymph node dissection (Option D): Appropriate for early-stage tumors (up to Stage IIA) with no pelvic wall extension but unsuitable for Stage IIIB.

Key Take Away Points:

  • Stage IIIB is inoperable, and chemoradiation is standard of care.
  • Surgery is reserved for early stages or post-radiation recurrences.

question_text: Post coital test detects all of the following except:
explanation:
Post coital test (Sims or Huhner’s test) is a test for evaluation of the potential role of Cervical factor in infertility. It is designed to assess:

  • The quality of cervical mucus.
  • Presence and number of motile sperms in the female reproductive tract. after coitus.
  • Interaction between cervical mucus and sperms.
  • It gives an approximate idea of sperm count: (normally 10 – 50 motile sperms are seen per high power field in cervical mucus, if count is < 10 sperms / HPF it indicates the need for complete semen analysis).
  • Post coital test gives a very rough idea about sperm count, motility and morphology.
  • As far as fallopian tube block is concerned postcoital test has no relation whatsoever with it and we have to select

Single best answer, therefore Option “a” Fallopian tube block is the answer of choice.

Time of test:

  • It should be performed 1 or 2 days before the anticipated time of ovulation, when maximum estrogen secretion is present.
  • For patients with irregular cycles, a patient's urinary LH surge may be helpful in scheduling the test.

Prerequisites for the test: Abstinence of 2 days.

  • Intercourse is to be performed 2–12 hours before the test.
  • No use of lubricant.

question_text: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents for routine evaluation. Which of the following conditions is least likely to be responsible for postmenopausal vaginal bleeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Ovarian follicular cysts are functional ovarian cysts that are common in reproductive-aged women but are rarely active in postmenopausal women. They are usually asymptomatic and do not secrete estrogen to cause endometrial proliferation, making them least likely to cause bleeding after menopause.

Explanation of Other Options:

Endometrial carcinoma (Option A):

  • Most common malignant cause of postmenopausal bleeding (~10% of cases)
  • Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants evaluation to rule out endometrial cancer
  • Early symptom: spotting or bleeding is often the first sign

Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary (Option B):

  • Estrogen-producing ovarian tumor
  • Can induce endometrial hyperplasia and subsequent bleeding
  • Rare but significant cause of postmenopausal bleeding due to unopposed estrogen effect

Genital tract trauma (Option C):

  • Trauma (e.g., accidental, iatrogenic, or post-coital) can cause bleeding at any age
  • Less common than malignancy or estrogenic tumors, but still plausible in postmenopausal women

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Functional ovarian cysts are uncommon post-menopause and rarely lead to bleeding.

question_text: What is the preferred diagnostic investigation for a 55-year-old woman presenting with postmenopausal bleeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The woman in this case is postmenopausal and presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. For such patients, the investigation of choice is an endometrial biopsy.

During the postmenopausal period, it's essential to perform an endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial carcinoma. It is a safe, minimally invasive outpatient procedure that allows for histological evaluation of the endometrial tissue. This can help detect malignancies or other abnormalities.

Dilatation and curettage is another method for obtaining endometrial tissue, but it's more commonly used when biopsy samples are inadequate or further assessment is required.

Explanation for other options:

Ultrasound (Option A): Typically the initial test used to assess endometrial thickness. If results are concerning (e.g. thickened lining), a biopsy is indicated.

Fractional Curettage (Option C): A more invasive procedure usually done under general anesthesia. It's reserved for cases where endometrial biopsy is inconclusive, or not feasible (e.g. cervical stenosis), or when cancer is strongly suspected.

CA-125 (Option D): A tumor marker mainly used to monitor ovarian epithelial tumors. Though it can be elevated in endometrial cancer and other gynecological conditions, it lacks sensitivity and specificity and is not suitable for routine screening.

question_text: All are true about serous cystadenoma of the ovary except:
explanation:
Serous cystadenoma:

  • Most common of cystic neoplasms.
  • It accounts for 50% of all ovarian tumors, of these 60% are benign, 15% are borderline, 25% of malignant.
  • Occur in the 3rd, 4th and 5th decade of life.
  • Half cases are bilateral. It is a unilocular cyst.
  • Delicate papillary excrescences may be seen on the surface and within the loculi of a benign cyst.
  • Histologically – the benign variety shows cystic spaces and the lining of the tumor consists of tall columnar ciliated epithelium resembling the endosalpinx.
  • The loculi contain a thin serous straw coloured fluid, which may be blood stained when malignant transformation occurs. Rate of malignant transformation-40%
  • Option "d" :Mucinous cystadenoma have glistening surface and cut surface shows loculi filled with mucinous material. The content is thick, viscid, and mucin. The cyst is frequently multiloculated.

question_text: Which of the following ovarian tumors is most prone to undergo torsion during pregnancy?
explanation:
Dermoid Cyst (Mature cystic teratoma)

  • Dermoid cyst is a benign teratoma.
  • Teratomas are the most common germ cell neoplasm.

On the basis of maturity teratoma can be divided into:

Mature (Benign) teratoma = dermoid cyst

  • Most common benign tumor of ovary in reproductive age group.
  • Most common benign neoplasm diagnosed during pregnancy.
  • Most common Germ cell tumor.
  • It is the commonest tumor to undergo torsion.
  • It frequently arise in association with mucinous cystadenoma:
  • Age for a combined tumor is 20–30 years.
  • Age for a simple dermoid cyst is 40–50 years.
  • Bilateral in 10% to 15% of cases.
  • Lining epithelium is stratified squamous epithelium (if dermoid cyst undergoes malignant change - Squamous cell Ca is seen).
  • Dermoid cyst usually contain derivatives of ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm. Most common tissue element in the dermoid cyst is ectodermal.
  • On cross section – they typically show an area of localized growth from which hair projects, teeth and bone are seen. It is called the Rokitansky protuberance or dermoid process.
  • Malignant change in a dermoid cyst occurs in 0.5–2% cases in patients more than 40 years. Most common malignancy which develops is squamous cell carcinoma.

Immature (Malignant) teratoma

  • Rare, mostly solid, differ from benign teratomas in the component tissue which resembles that observed in the fetus or embryo rather than mature adult tissue.
  • Tumor occurs chiefly in prepubertal adolescents and young women.
  • Tumor grade is correlated with prognosis and extra-ovarian spread.

Monodermal or specialized teratomas = (Struma ovarii and carcinoid)

  • Patients usually present with hyperthyroidism.
  • Most of the tumors are innocent, but malignant thyroid tumor have been recorded.

Rare group of tumor, struma ovarii composed entirely of mature thyroid tissue which is hyperfunctional

Reference: Novak 14th/ed pg 1479-1480; 15th/ed pg 137

question_text: Features of dysgerminoma are:
explanation:
In contrast to slow growing epithelial ovarian tumors, germ cell malignancies grow rapidly and are characterised by subacute pelvic pain.

  • Most common germ cell Tumor – Mature teratoma or Dermoid cyst (Benign in nature).
  • Most common malignant GCT – Dysgerminoma.
  • Second most common malignant GCT – Endodermal sinus Tumor. (Yolk Sac tumor)
  • Most common benign Tumor of ovary – Dermoid cyst

Management of Dysgerminoma:

  • The treatment of early dysgerminoma.

Surgical – including resection of the primary lesion (unilateral oophorectomy) and proper surgical dissection.

  • Metastatic Disease – Chemotherapy or Radiation therapy.

Chemotherapy:

The most frequently used chemotherapy regimens for germ cell tumors are:

  • BEP – Bleomycin, Etoposide, Cisplatin
  • VBP – Vinblastine, Bleomycin, Cisplatin
  • VAC – Vincristine, Actinomycin, Cyclophosphamide

Results suggest that patients with advanced stage, incompletely resected dysgerminoma have an excellent prognosis when treated with cisplatin based combination chemotherapy.

The best regimen is 4 cycles of BEP.

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed pg 378
