question_text: Which of the following strategies has been recommended to reduce the heredity risk for ovarian cancer in women with BRCA - 1 and BRCA - 2 mutations?
explanation:
• BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 are tumour suppressor genes.
  • Individuals who inherit mutations of BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 are highly susceptible for the development of hereditary breast or ovarian cancer. The mutations are inherited as autosomal dominant.

Strategies for prevention of hereditary ovarian cancer

  • Genetic testing for susceptibility to ovarian cancer is rapidly becoming integrated into the clinical practice of oncology.

Strategies have been adopted to reduce the incidence of ovarian cancer in patients with BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 mutations.

A. Prophylactic oophorectomy:

"The only proven way to prevent ovarian cancer is surgical oophorectomy. Another possible site of disease among these high risk patients is fallopian tube therefore should be removed. IN BRCA 1 or BRCA-2 mutation carriers, prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BS0) may be performed on either completion of childbearing or at age

In these patients, the procedure is approximately 90% effective in preventing epithelial ovarian cancer. In women with HNPCC, the risk reduction approaches 100%." ... William Gynae 1st/ed pg 719

  • Additional benefit of prophylactic oophorectomy is that the risk of breast cancer is reduced by 50-80%.

B. Oral contraceptive pills:

  • Data received from a multicenter control of genetic screening centers indicates that the use of oral contraceptive pills is associated with 50% decreased risk for developing ovarian cancer in women who have a mutation in either BRCA - 1 or BRCA - 2. However there is a short term increased risk of developing breast cancer.

C. Role of screening with CA 125 and transvaginal ultrasound:

"In BRCA1- BRCA2 mutation carriers who don't wish to undergo prophylactic surgery a combination of through pelvic examination, transvaginal sonographic examination and CA125 blood testing should be done".

... Williams Gynae 1th/ed pg 719

  • Best method of prevention: Prophylactic hysterectomy and BSO at 35 years or as soon as the family is complete.
  • 2nd line: OCP’s + screening
  • Screening: TVS + Ca 125 started at 35 years and done every 6 or 12 months, breast screening by MRI and mammography at 30 years done annually.

Reference: Novak 14th/ed pg 1471; Wililams Gynae 1st/ed pg 718-719

question_text: Sample should be taken from which wall of vagina, for hormonal analysis;

  • Squamous epithelium is resistant to gonococcal infection hence theoretically gonococcal vaginitis can occur in new born females

question_text: Smt. Pushpa is a suspected case of ovarian tumors. On laparotomy bilaterally enlarged ovaries with smooth surface was seen:
explanation:
Krukenberg tumor:

  • Krukenberg tumor by definition represents carcinoma of stomach metastasis to ovary. But the eponym is commonly used to denote any gastric cancer metastatic to ovary
  • Tumor arises by retrograde lymphatic spread e. carcinoma cells pass from the stomach to the superior gastric lymph node which also receives lymphatics from the ovary.

Characteristics of Krukenberg Tumour:

  1. Always bilateral
  2. Have smooth surface
  3. No tendency to form adhesions
  4. Freely mobile
  5. No infiltration through the capsule.
  6. Histologically the tumour has signet ring cells in the background of myxomatous stroma.
  7. They retain the shape of a normal ovary.
  8. Have waxy consistency.

question_text: A lady with CA ovary in follow-up with raised CA 125 level, next step:
option_d: Clinical exam and serial follow up of CA 125
explanation:
In a case of treated ovarian cancer - Treatment assessment is done by:

  • Tumor marker CA 125 - It is a reliable indicator of disease response or progression.
    • If CA 125 levels decrease after treatment - It indicates response to treatment.
    • If CA 125 levels increase after treatment - It indicates relapse after treatment.
    • A review of the literature suggests that an elevated Ca 125 level predicts persistent disease at second look surgery in 97% of the cases but CA 125 is not sensitive enough to exclude subclinical disease in many patients.
    • Follow up in a patients ovarian cancer is done by physical and pelvic examination along with estimation of CA 125 levels. Patients are advised to visit every 3-4 months for the first 2 years and then 6 monthly for 5 years.
  • Clinical examination and CA 125 together can detect 90% of recurrences. Radiological procedures are not required in all cases.
  • But since here CA 125 is elevated and we have to choose one option - the best is PET as:
    • CT scan cannot distinguish between a relapsed tumour and fibrosis whereas PET scan will exactly demonstrate whether it is a relapsed tumour or a fibrosis. (In a patient treated with chemotherapy or radiotherapy fibrosis is common. It can present as a mass so it is essential to differentiate between relapsed tumour and fibrosis.)

Reference: Novak's Gynae 14th/ed pg 1496

question_text: An 18-year-old girl presents with rapid onset hirsutism and amenorrhea. Best investigation is:
explanation:
"A variety of ovarian neoplasms, both benign and malignant may produce testosterone and lead to virilization. Specifically, women with an abrupt onset, typically within several months, or sudden worsening of virilizing signs should prompt concern for a hormone producing ovarian or adrenal tumor. Symptoms may include deepening of voice, frontal balding, severe acne or hirsutism or both, increased muscle mass and clitoromegaly. Accordingly, serum testosterone levels may be used to exclude these tumors. Free testosterone levels are more sensitive than total testosterone levels as an indicator of hyperandrogenism. Although improving, current free testosterone assays lack a uniform laboratory standard. For this reason, total testosterone levels remain the best approach for excluding a tumor. Threshold values beyond 200 ng /dl of total testosterone warrant evaluation for an ovarian lesion."- Williams Gynae 1st/ed p 391

So now I do not need to explain that testosterone estimation is the best investigation in case of rapid onset hirsutism and amenorrhea.

Lines of Leon Speroff further support the answer:

"A serum testosterone concentration greater than 150 mg/dl identifies almost all women with a potential androgen producing tumor. However, a tumor still should be suspected and excluded in a woman with rapidly progressive hirsutism or signs and symptoms of virilization, even when the serum testosterone concentration is below the threshold value." _ Leon Speroff 8th/ed p 520

DHEA sulphate is produced exclusively by the adrenal gland. Therefore, serum DHEAS levels above 700 mcg/dl are highly sensitive for the presence of an adrenal neoplasm.

Adrenal imaging with abdominal CT or MRI is indicated for any patient with DHEAS levels that exceed this value.

Reference: Dutta Gynae 4th/ed p 524; Leon Speroff 7th/ed p 502-511, 515; Williams Gynae 1st/ed p 391.

question_text: Lactational amenorrhea is due to:
explanation:
• In breastfeeding females, prolactin levels are increased in response to the suckling stimulus of breastfeeding.
  • These observations suggest that high concentrations of prolactin can work at both central level (by inhibiting pulsatile secretion of GnRH) and peripheral level i.e. ovarian sites (by inhibiting synthesis of progesterone and by changing testosterone/dihydrotestosterone ratio i.e. increasing local antiestrogen concentrations) to produce lactational amenorrhea and anovulation.
  • The principle of GnRH suppression by prolactin is reinforced by the demonstration that treatment of amenorrheic, lactating women with pulsatile GnRH, fully restores pituitary secretion and normal ovarian cyclic activity.

question_text: Which of the following is endodermal in origin
explanation:
After the 5th week of fertilization, two GONADAL RIDGES appear in the dorsal aspect of the embryo.

These are formed by proliferation of coelomic epithelium and underlying mesodermal cells. (mesodermal origin)

COELOMIC CELLS → germinal epithelium and ovarian cortex (granulosa cells)

BASAL MESODERM → ovarian stroma

The primordial germ cells (oogonia) are formed from cells of the dorsal part of the hindgut (originally yolk sac) , ENDODERMAL origin.

Oogonia migrates to ovaries and with the surrounding layer of follicular cells forms primordial follicles.

question_text: True about endodermal sinus tumors except:
option_d: It is seen in young individuals
explanation:
Endodermal sinus tumor/Yolk sac tumor:

  • Endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumour is third most common malignant germ cell tumour of ovary affecting mostly children or young women. (Age group 14–20 years)
  • Tumor is highly malignant and is the most rapidly growing tumors of the whole body.
  • Histologically the pathognomonic finding is Schiller - Duval bodies which is a single papilla lined by tumour cells with a central blood vessel.
  • Due to the high rate of growth, the tumour usually presents with an acute abdomen.
  • Unilateral in 100% cases therefore biopsy of the opposite ovary is contraindicated.
  • Almost all cases are associated with raised AFP and Alpha 1 antitrypsin.
  • It is the most deadly malignant ovarian germ cell tumor.
  • Treatment: Chemotherapy.
  • It has a high propensity for rapid growth, peritoneal spread and distant hematogenous dissemination to the lungs.

question_text: Meigs syndrome is associated with:
explanation:
Meigs syndrome:

  • Ascites and right sided hydrothorax is association with fibroma of ovary is called as Meig’s syndrome.
  • It can also be seen in Brenner’s tumour and Granulosa cell tumour where it is called as Pseudo Meigs syndrome.
  • True meig’s syndrome is rare, occurring in < 5 percent of fibromas.
  • Hydrothorax can be bilateral also.
  • Ascites is caused by transudation of fluid from the ovarian fibroma. Hydrothorax develops secondary to flow of ascitic fluid into the pleural space via lymphatics of the diaphragm.
  • Ascites occur (in 50% cases) when tumour size is > 6 cms.
  • Tumours producing Meig’s syndrome manifest in the late childbearing period i.e., 30–40 years.
  • Both ascites and hydrothorax resolve spontaneously after removal of the tumour.

Criteria for diagnosis of Meig’s syndrome:

  • Tumour must be ovarian, solid and benign.
  • Both hydrothorax and ascites must be present.
  • Removal of the tumour must result in their spontaneous and permanent cure.

PseudoMeig’s syndrome:

  • Can be seen in association with either benign or malignant tumour.
  • Hydrothorax could be a manifestation of pulmonary metastasis.
  • Syndrome can result from overstimulation of the ovaries with gonadotropins but, in such cases, the peritoneal exudate is more likely to be caused by an electrolyte imbalance rather than by ovarian tumour.

Reference: Jeffcoate 7th/ed pg 543

question_text: Following are a few steps involved in management of stage III ovarian cancer except:
explanation:
Management of Advanced stage disease (stages III and IV) in ovarian cancer:

  • Advanced stage disease: Exploratory Laparotomy → Cytoreductive or debulking surgery. This includes: Total abdominal hysterectomy bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, complete omentectomy, retroperitoneal lymph node sampling and resection of any metastatic tumor. Optimum cytoreductive surgery is aimed to reduce the residual tumor load < 1–2 cm in diameter. Lesser the residual tumor volume (< 1 cm), better is the survival.
  • Chemotherapy: Chemotherapy is used widely following surgery to improve the result in terms of survival. Drugs are given for five or six cycles at 3–4 weekly intervals.
  • Combination chemotherapy: Paclitaxel (175 mg/m2) and carboplatin (400 mg/m2) are commonly used.
  • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and interval cytoreductive surgery: Few cycles of chemotherapy followed by interval primary cytoreductive surgery may be done. Indications are:
  1. Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer,
  2. High risk for surgery,
  3. Associated comorbid conditions (pleural effusion),
  4. Predicted to be suboptimally resected. Patient should have histological diagnosis of the tumor (biopsy). Benefits of neoadjuvant chemotherapy are:
    1. Rapid clinical improvement.
    2. Subsequent surgery is easier and morbidity is reduced,
    3. Optimum cytoreduction with minimal residual disease may be possible.
  • Radiotherapy: There is very little scope of radiotherapy as an adjunct to surgery because of the advent of chemotherapy.

Reference: Shaw 15th/ed pg 428; Dutta Gynae 6th/ed pg 378-9

question_text: Tests for ovarian reserve are all except:
explanation:
Ovarian reserve tests are to assess the quantity as well as the quality of primordial follicles present in the women’s ovary. These tests are done to determine how the ovaries will respond to therapy (ovulation induction) in other words it is the assessment of the reproductive potential of the woman.

The Tests Done Are:

  1. Estimation of basal level of serum FSH on D3 and again on D10 following clomiphene citrate challenge test (CCCT): 100 mg orally each day from D5–D9: values >10 IU/L (more than 2SD) indicates poor ovarian reserve.
  2. Basal (D3) serum estradiol level > 70–80 pg/mL, poor ovarian reserve.
  3. Serum inhibin B (D5): Reduced inhibin B levels (less than 40 pg/mL) are

observed in women with advanced age.

Serum antimüllerian Hormone (AMH): Levels of serum AMH is a good predictor of ovarian stimulation response. Its level also comes with the direct proportion of antral follicle count. Levels of AMH (1ng/mL) declines with age and with poor ovarian reserve. Levels of AMH can be measured any time in the menstrual cycle.

question_text: In low ovarian reserve, anti mullerian hormone level will be:
explanation:
Serum antimüllerian Hormone (AMH): Levels of serum AMH is a good predictor of ovarian stimulation response. Its level also comes with the direct proportion of antral follicle count. Levels of AMH(1ng/mL) declines with age and with poor ovarian reserve. Levels of AMH can be measured any time in the menstrual cycle.

AMH: AMH is produced by the granulosa cells of the preantral small follicles. Serum levels of estradiol and inhibin B depend on pituitary FSH feedback mechanism. Level of AMH is not dependent on feedback mechanism. This is one of the reasons for which AMH is being considered as a better predictor of ovarian reserve compared to estradiol and inhibin B. Levels of AMH can be measured at anytime in the menstrual cycle. It therefore understood that AMH is qualitative whereas Antral Follicle Count(AFC) is a quantitative marker of ovarian reserve.

question_text: A 20-year-old female presents with an ovarian solid-cystic mass on ultrasound. Which combination of tumor markers is most appropriate for further evaluation of the likely ovarian tumor?
explanation:
Explanation:

These markers collectively help evaluate the most common ovarian tumors in young females, particularly germ cell tumors like yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and dysgerminoma.

  • In young women (especially under 30), the most common ovarian tumors are germ cell tumors rather than epithelial ovarian cancers.
  • The appropriate tumor markers help in diagnosing and monitoring specific subtypes:
    • AFP (Alpha-fetoprotein): Elevated in yolk sac tumors (endodermal sinus tumors).
    • β-hCG (Human chorionic gonadotropin): Elevated in choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma.
    • LDH (Lactate dehydrogenase): Elevated in dysgerminoma, the most common malignant germ cell tumor in this age group.
    • CA-125: Typically elevated in epithelial ovarian cancer, but still assessed to rule out rare epithelial malignancy or in case of mixed pathology.
  • This combination is routinely ordered when evaluating ovarian masses in adolescents and young women to cover all common germ cell tumors.

Ovarian tumor classification:

Ovarian Tumor Markers:

Explanation of other options:

question_text: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) have been shown to provide protective effects against several cancers. Which of the following cancers is not protected against by the use of combined OCPs?
explanation:
Explanation:

Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) have several protective effects against cancers, particularly ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers. The hormonal suppression of ovulation and regulation of endometrial proliferation play a crucial role in this benefit.

  • However, unlike these protective effects, current COC users have an increased relative risk of cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer.
  • This risk declines after discontinuation and usually returns to baseline after about 10 years of stopping use.
  • Thus, while COCs are beneficial in reducing the risk of some cancers, they do not protect against cervical cancer.

Explanation for other Options:

Ovarian carcinoma (Option A): COCs offer strong protection against ovarian cancer. This protective effect is long-lasting and increases with duration of use.

Endometrial carcinoma (Option B): COCs reduce the risk by suppressing endometrial proliferation through the progestin component.

Colorectal carcinoma (Option C): Studies show that ever-users of COCs have reduced rates of colorectal cancer compared with never-users.

Chancre is the primary lesion of primary syphilis.

  • It is most commonly found on the labium majus, labium minus, fourchette, clitoris, urethral orifice, or cervix, but can be found anywhere on the lower genital tract.

question_text: A 45-year-old asymptomatic woman comes for her annual wellness checkup. She has no personal or family history of cancer. Considering evidence-based preventive screening, which test should be prioritized to detect the most prevalent malignancy in women?
explanation:
Explanation:

Breast cancer is the most common malignancy affecting women worldwide, making early detection via screening critical.

Mammography:

  • Gold standard for breast cancer screening
  • Can detect tumors before clinical palpation
  • Recommended age:
    • Most guidelines: 40-50 years onwards
    • High-risk women: may start earlier
  • Frequency: Every 1-2 years depending on risk and guidelines

Remember:

  • Early detection reduces mortality
  • Screening is indicated for asymptomatic, average-risk women
  • Mammogram can detect microcalcifications and small masses

Explanation of Other Options:

Pap Smear (Option B):

  • Screens for cervical cancer
  • Cervical cancer is less common than breast cancer in most populations
  • Recommended every 3 years for women 21-65 (with or without HPV testing)
  • Important but not the priority for age 45 in general population screening

Transvaginal Ultrasound (Option C):

  • Evaluates uterus, endometrium, and ovaries
  • Typically investigative, not screening, used for symptoms (e.g., abnormal bleeding, pelvic mass)
  • Not a routine cancer screening tool for asymptomatic women

Colonoscopy (Option D):

  • Screens for colorectal cancer
  • Recommended starting at age 45-50 in average-risk individuals
  • Less common in women compared to breast cancer, so not prioritized in routine female cancer screening

Key Takeaway Points:

  1. Most common female malignancy: Breast cancer → screen with mammogram
  2. Cervical cancer: Screen with Pap smear → high-yield but lower incidence than breast cancer
  3. Ovarian cancer: No routine screening recommended in asymptomatic women; TVS only if symptomatic or high-risk
  4. Colorectal cancer: Screen starting 45-50 years, lower incidence in women compared to breast cancer

References:

NCBI Bookshelf: Preventive Gynecology,

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559310/

American Cancer Society Guidelines, 2023

Genital Warts:

  • Genital warts are lesions created from productive infection with HPV (most common type 6 and 11).
  • They display various morphologies and appearances ranging from flat papules to the classic verrucous, polyphytic lesions, termed "condyloma acuminata".
  • Sites: External genital warts may develop at sites in the lower reproductive tract, urethra, anus, or mouth.
  • Diagnosis : They are typically diagnosed by clinical infection, and biopsy is not required unless co-existing neoplasia is suspected. HPV serotyping is not required for routine diagnosis.

  • Effect of treatment on future viral transmission is unclear. In addition, very large, bulky lesions may be managed with cavitational ultrasonic surgical aspiration.

Medical Management of Genital Warts:

Note: Intralesional injection of interferon has high cost, is painful and is inconvenient to administer, So this therapy is not recommended as a primary modality and is best reserved for recalcitrant cases.

question_text: All of the following are risk factors of vulval ca except

explanation:
Explanation:

LBC with HPV testing and cervical biopsy offers the most comprehensive evaluation for cervical dysplasia and malignancy.

  • In a woman presenting with abnormal vaginal discharge, intermenstrual spotting, and visible cervical erosion, the clinical concern includes cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or early cervical carcinoma, particularly in the context of persistent infection by high-risk HPV types.
  • Hence, a triple assessment is warranted:
    • LBC (Liquid-Based Cytology): Modern alternative to conventional Pap smear, with better cell preservation and less debris.Useful for identifying cytological abnormalities like koilocytes, dyskaryosis, and CIN.
    • HPV antigen testing: Essential for detecting high-risk HPV strains (especially 16, 18), which are implicated in >95% of cervical cancers.
    • Cervical biopsy: Provides a histopathological diagnosis to confirm dysplasia or malignancy, especially when there are suspicious cervical lesions or persistent symptoms.
  • This combination maximizes diagnostic sensitivity and guides further management (colposcopy, LEEP, etc.).

Koilocytes

Explanation of other options:

Pap smear, HSV testing, Cervical biopsy (Option B): HSV testing is not warranted here as there's no vesicular lesion or ulcerative complaint suggestive of herpes. Pap smear is acceptable, but LBC is superior.

Pap smear, HBV DNA, Cervical biopsy (Option C): HBV DNA is unrelated to cervical complaints; it is relevant in liver disease, not gynecological evaluation.

LBC, HSV testing only (Option D): Missing HPV testing and biopsy-two essential components in evaluating pre-malignant/malignant cervical lesions.

explanation:
Vulval cancer:

  • 2–4% of all malignancies of the female genital tract.
  • Age: occurs in 6th or 7th decade.
  • Most common histologic type is epidermoid cancer (squamous cell CA) seen in 90% cases.
  • Nulliparous, women of low parity are predisposed to vulval CA.
  • The etiology is same as of carcinoma in situ cervix (that is viral predisposition by viruses - HIV, HPV, HSV-II).
  • Most common site – Labia majora (Anterior 2/3rd) followed by clitorus and labia minora.
  • Associated with cervical cancer in 20% cases.
  • Presents with pruritus and visible lesion. All though pain, bleeding and ulceration also may be the initial complaints.
  • Spread of tumor – mainly by direct spread and lymphatics.
  • First superficial inguinal nodes are involved and then it spreads to deep nodes and via glands of Cloquet to external iliac nodes, obturator and common iliac nodes in late stages.

Staging : Mainly clinical:

  • Both FIGO staging and TNM staging are done in case of vulval cancer.
  • Recommended is FIGO staging

Note: Vulval cancer is the only genital malignancy which can be staged using TNM staging.

Treatment:

  • Early stages : Radical/Partial Vulvectomy with inguinal nodes dissection.
  • Late stages : chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Prognosis:

  • Overall survival rates of women with vulval cancer are excellent.
  • Lymph Node involvement is the single most important prognostic factor.
  • Presence of inguinal lymph node metastasis reduces the overall survival rate by 50%.

Note:

  • “Skinning vulvectomy” refers to removal of only the skin and superficial subcutaneous tissue. This surgery plays no role in the treatment of invasive vulvar cancer but may be used in noninvasive disease such as cases with widespread multifocal VIN 3.
  • Sentinel node biopsy – At present, the Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) is conducting a multicenter trial to evaluate the benefit of sentinel node biopsy for vulvar cancer.

question_text: Karyotyping of fetus can be done through all of the following invasive methods except:
explanation:
Currently there are 3 techniques available for obtaining fetal tissue for fetal karyotyping:

Chorionic villi sampling:

  • Performed at 10-13 weeks. A catheter is passed through the cervix or through the abdominal wall into the uterus under ultrasound guidance, and a sample of chorionic villi surrounding the sac is obtained.
  • The chorionic villi are formed by trophoblast and hence study material is trophoblast.
  • In a morula the outer layer is trophoblast and inside is inner cell mass, So whatever chromosomal abnormalities are seen in fetus can be detected by CVS.

Amniocentesis:

  • It is an invasive procedure performed between 15 to 20 weeks for detecting fetal karyotype.
  • It is done under ultrasound guidance using a 22 gauge spinal needle. The spinal needle is passed through the mothers lower abdomen into the amniotic cavity inside the uterus and 10-20 ml of amniotic fluid is collected. Amniotic fluid has cells from amnion, fetal skin and lungs which are collected and cultured for fetal karyotyping, biochemical and metabolic analysis.

Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS/Cordocentesis):

  • The most frequent indication for cordocentesis is rapid karyotyping of the fetus (with PUBS-high quality karyotype can be obtained in 48-72 hours rather than in 10-14 days that is needed for amniotic cell culture).

Reference: Williams 23/e, p 299-301

question_text: Which of the following is not an indication for cesarean section?
explanation:
Explanation:

A prior history of delivering a macrosomic baby is not, by itself, an indication for cesarean section. Many women with a history of macrosomia may still deliver vaginally without complications in subsequent pregnancies. Therefore, this option is not considered a standard indication for cesarean delivery.

Indications for Cesarean Section:

Absolute indications include:

  • Absolute cephalopelvic disproportion (Option A ruled out)
  • Central placenta previa (Option C ruled out)
  • Advanced carcinoma cervix (Option D ruled out)
  • Maternal pelvic deformity
  • Uterine rupture
  • Abnormal lie and presentation (e.g., transverse lie, brow presentation)
  • Umbilical cord prolapse
  • Eclampsia and HELLP syndrome (uncontrolled)
  • Chorioamnionitis with fetal compromise
  • Fetal asphyxia or acidosis

Relative indications include:

  • Failure to progress in labor (prolonged labor, secondary arrest)
  • Pathological CTG findings suggesting acute hypoxia or fetal asphyxia (if not correctable)
  • Previous cesarean section (depends on scar type and maternal-fetal condition)

Reference: Indications for and Risks of Elective Cesarean Section - PMC

question_text: What is the preferred treatment option for a 55-year-old patient diagnosed with simple endometrial hyperplasia with atypia?
explanation:
Explanation:

The recommended treatment for simple endometrial hyperplasia with atypia is a simple hysterectomy, as this condition has a significant risk of progressing to carcinoma.

Endometrial hyperplasia is classified into three types: simple, glandular, and atypical. About 80% of cases of simple hyperplasia without atypia respond well to progestogen therapy. However, only around 50% of cases with atypia respond to progestogens, and these cases still carry a high risk of developing endometrial cancer. Therefore, atypical endometrial hyperplasia is best managed by hysterectomy.

Explanation for other options:

Medroxyprogesterone acetate (option B) is recommended for treatment of Hyperplasia without atypia

Levonorgestrel (Option C) is recommended for young premenopausal women diagnosed with cystic or adenomatous hyperplasia without atypia. The treatment duration is typically 6 to 9 months, with endometrial sampling performed every six months to monitor progress.

Radiotherapy (Option D) is generally not the first-choice treatment for endometrial hyperplasia. However, it may be considered for patients who are unsuitable for surgery, have significant surgical risks, or decline surgical intervention.

question_text: A 54-year-old woman is diagnosed with advanced carcinoma of the cervix. She has a 14-year-old daughter who is currently asymptomatic and has no history of any illness. What is the most appropriate preventive advice you would give for the daughter?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

HPV vaccine is the most effective primary preventive strategy against cervical cancer and should be advised for the daughter of a cervical cancer patient.

  • Cervical cancer is strongly linked to infection by high-risk types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV), especially types 16 and 18, which together cause over 95% of cervical cancer cases.
  • The HPV vaccine targets the L1 capsid protein of the virus and is most effective when administered before the onset of sexual activity, ideally between 9 to 14 years of age.
  • Since the patient's daughter is 14 years old, HPV vaccination is the most appropriate and timely preventive measure to reduce her future risk of developing cervical cancer.
  • HPV Virology Summary:
    • HPV is a double-stranded DNA virus.
    • It infects squamous epithelial or metaplastic cells.
    • E1 and E2 proteins are involved in viral replication.
    • Low-risk HPV (types 6, 11): Genital warts, rarely oncogenic.
    • High-risk HPV (types 16, 18): Strongly associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cervical carcinoma.

Explanation of other options:

Screen for BRCA mutation (Option A): BRCA mutations are associated with breast and ovarian cancers, not cervical cancer. There is no role for BRCA testing in the daughter of a cervical cancer patient.

Screen for PTEN mutation (Option C): PTEN mutations are associated with Cowden syndrome, which increases the risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers, not cervical cancer.

Perform cervical biopsy (Option D): A cervical biopsy is a diagnostic tool, not a screening method. It is not warranted in an asymptomatic 14-year-old girl with no risk factors or abnormal findings. Preventive vaccination is the priority.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the cervix?
option_a: Ectocervix is rich in nerve endings making it very sensitive to touch, hence manipulation with an instrument can sometimes lead to vasovagal shock
option_b: In parous women due to stretching and tearing of skeletal muscles surrounding internal os, external os looks like a slit
option_c: Endocervix is lined by high columnar ciliated epithelium , direction of the cilia is towards the external os
option_d: Cervix contains only 10% of muscle fibers out of which 30% are in lower 1/3 of cervix
explanation:
The cervix is insensitive to touch, heat and also when it is grasped by any instrument. The uterus, too, is insensitive to handling and even to incision over its wall. The stroma of the endocervix unlike the ectocervix is rich in nerve endings; hence, manipulation of the cervical canal can cause an unexpected vasovagal attack and severe bradycardia or even cardiac arrest.

In nulliparous, the vaginal part of the cervix is conical with the external os looking circular, whereas in parous, it is cylindrical with the external os having bilateral slits. The slit is due to invariable tear of the circular muscles surrounding the external os and gives rise to anterior and posterior lips of the cervix.

The endocervix is lined by a single layer of high columnar ciliated epithelium with spindle shaped nuclei lying adjacent to the basement membrane with abundant cytoplasm and mucin. The direction of the cilia is downwards towards the external os

Cervix contains mainly collagen and only 10% of muscle fibers. Light microscopic examination reveals 29% muscle fibers in its upper one-third, 18% in the middle one-third and only 6% in the lower one-third, whereas the body of the uterus contains 70% muscle fibers.

Reference: Shaw’s textbook of gynecology, 16th edition, chapter 1

question_text: Uterine artery is a branch of:

    • As a terminal branch of anterior division of the internal iliac artery, the uterine artery runs downwards and medially to cross the ureter near the cervix (2 cm lateral to cervix). It then ascends along the lateral border of the uterus in a tortuous course giving branches to both uterine surfaces.

Branches of uterine artery to uterus:

U = Uterine artery

A = Arcuate artery—supplies outer 1/3rd of myometrium

R = Radial artery—supplies inner 2/3rd of myometrium

B = Basal artery—supplies basal endometrium

S = Spiral artery—supplies superficial endometrium

question_text: Which of the following methods for cervical ripening is classified as a hygroscopic dilator?
option_c: Foley catheter at the internal of the cervix
explanation:
Explanation:

Cervical ripening involves the softening and dilation of the cervix in preparation for labour or gynaecological procedures. Methods for cervical ripening can be pharmacological, mechanical, or hygroscopic.

Hygroscopic dilators work by absorbing moisture from surrounding cervical tissues, causing gradual expansion and gentle dilation.

  • Intracervical laminaria tent:
    • Derived from dried seaweed stems.
    • Absorbs moisture from cervical tissues.
    • Expands slowly to dilate the cervix in a controlled manner.
    • Often preferred for gradual and gentle ripening, especially before procedures like D&C or induction of labour.

Explanation of Other Options:

Intracervical dinoprostone gel (Option A): A pharmacological agent (prostaglandin E2) that softens and thins the cervix. It does not work through hygroscopic properties.

Foley catheter at the internal of the cervix (Option C): A mechanical method. The balloon is inflated in the cervix to apply pressure and induce dilation. No hygroscopic mechanism is involved.

Misoprostol in posterior fornix (Option D): A pharmacological method. Misoprostol (prostaglandin E1 analogue) induces cervical ripening by chemical action, not by absorbing moisture.

Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2660035/

question_text: Which filter is used in a colposcope?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In colposcopy, a green (red-free) light filter is used to enhance contrast, making it easier to visualize vascular patterns.
  • Colposcopy is a diagnostic procedure that uses a lighted magnifying instrument called a colposcope to closely examine the cervix, vagina, and vulva.
  • It is typically performed in patients with an abnormal Pap smear, those testing positive for high-risk HPV DNA, or when the cervix appears suspicious on clinical examination, even if cytology is normal.
  • Additionally, colposcopy may be used for post-treatment surveillance following therapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or invasive cervical cancer.

Explanation of other options:

Black (Option A): The black filter is not used in colposcopy because it reduces light transmission, making it difficult to visualize the cervical tissue.

Red (Option B): Red filters are rarely used as they can distort the natural color of the cervical tissue, affecting accurate assessment.

Yellow (Option D): While yellow filters may enhance some tissue features, they are not commonly preferred for routine colposcopic examinations.

question_text: A 30-year woman who is P2L2 underwent a screening PAP smear. The cytology report came out to be carcinoma in situ. What is the next step in management?

question_text: A 60-year-old woman presents with chronic vulval itching and pain. Examination reveals a lesion suspicious for vulval carcinoma. Which lymph node group should be examined during a sentinel lymph node biopsy to assess possible metastasis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In vulval carcinoma, the first site of lymphatic drainage is the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Therefore, these are the sentinel lymph nodes-the first nodes likely to harbour metastasis.

A sentinel node biopsy targets these nodes to detect early regional spread, helping avoid unnecessary extensive lymph node dissection and related complications.

Key Facts about Vulval Cancer:

Lymphatic Spread and Nodes Involved:

Investigations and Management:

  • Biopsy:
    • Excisional biopsy (<1 cm lesion)
    • Incisional or punch biopsy (≥1 cm lesion)
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy: To detect early nodal metastasis (superficial inguinal nodes).
  • Surgery: Partial or total vulvectomy ± lymph node dissection based on stage.

Prognosis: Worsens significantly with lymph node involvement.

Explanation for other options:

Pelvic lymph nodes (Option A): Involved only in advanced disease; not sentinel nodes.

Cloquet node (Option B): A deep inguinal node near the femoral canal; may be affected later in the disease.

Deep inguinal nodes (Option D): Receive lymph from superficial nodes; involvement suggests disease progression, not early spread.

question_text: A 52-year-old woman diagnosed with stage 2B cervical cancer has been recommended radiotherapy. Which of the following statements about radiotherapy is incorrect?
option_a: Point B is 3 cm lateral to point A
option_b: Point A is 2 cm above the external os and 5 cm lateral to the interna uterine canal
option_c: Point A receives a dose of 7000 cGy
option_d: Point B received a dose of 6000 cGy
explanation:
Explanation:

Point A is located 2 cm superior and 2 cm lateral to the external cervical os, not 5 cm lateral.

Radiotherapy in Carcinoma Cervix (Stage IIB and beyond):

1. External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT / Teletherapy)

  • Delivers high-energy radiation to the pelvis.
  • Targets both the primary cervical tumor and regional lymph nodes.
  • Commonly used in combination with brachytherapy for optimal tumor control.

2. Brachytherapy

  • Involves internal radiation delivered via an intracavitary applicator or implant placed close to the tumor.
  • Administered after EBRT to provide a high dose ("boost") directly to the tumor site.
  • Minimizes exposure to surrounding healthy tissues.

3. Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT)

  • An advanced form of EBRT.
  • Allows precise targeting of the tumor while sparing adjacent normal tissues (e.g., bladder, rectum).
  • Reduces radiation-related side effects.

Radiation Dosimetry Points:

  • Point A
    • 2 cm superior and 2 cm lateral to the external cervical os.
    • Maximum radiation delivered is up to 7000 to 8000 rads. (Option C)
  • Point B
    • It is located 3 cm lateral to Point A (Option A) and corresponds to the obturator lymph nodes
    • Maximum radiation delivered is up to 6000 rads. (Option D)

question_text: Which type of hysterectomy is done in a case of carcinoma cervix stage I B?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The standard treatment for stage IB cervical cancer is Radical Hysterectomy (Type III hysterectomy) with pelvic lymphadenectomy.
  • Stage IB definition:
    • Tumor confined to cervix, invasion >5 mm.
    • IB1: <2 cm
    • IB2: 2–4 cm
    • IB3: ≥4 cm

Type III hysterectomy removes:

  • Uterus + cervix
  • Upper one-third of vagina
  • Parametrial tissues extensively

This ensures adequate clearance of microscopic disease and prevents local recurrence.

Stage-wise Management:

LVSI (Lymphovascular Space Invasion):

  • Indicates higher recurrence risk.
  • Requires more radical surgery (Type II or III) + lymphadenectomy.

Radical Trachelectomy (Fertility-Sparing):

  • Removes cervix, upper vagina, and parametrium.
  • Places permanent cerclage to support pregnancy.
  • Performed with PLND (± SNLB) in young women desiring fertility.

Lymph Nodes Removed in Radical Procedures:

  • Paracervical
  • Parametrial
  • Obturator
  • Internal iliac
  • External iliac
  • (Paraaortic nodes not routinely removed unless suspicious for metastasis)

Ovarian Preservation:

  • In young women, ovaries are often preserved to prevent premature menopause.
  • Prevents long-term complications such as osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline.

Explanation of Other Options:

Type I hysterectomy (Simple / Total hysterectomy) (Option A):

  • Removes uterus and cervix only.
  • Adequate for Stage IA1 disease without lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI).
  • Inadequate for Stage IB, as it does not address parametrial spread.

Type II hysterectomy (Modified Radical hysterectomy) (Option B):

  • Removes uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and partial parametrium.
  • Suitable for IA1 with LVSI, or early IA2.
  • Insufficient for Stage IB disease, where complete parametrial clearance is needed.

Type IV hysterectomy (Pelvic Exenteration) (Option D):

  • Removes uterus, cervix, parametrium, upper vagina, and adjacent pelvic organs (bladder/rectum).
  • Reserved for recurrent or advanced cervical cancers not amenable to standard surgery.
  • Not used in primary treatment of Stage IB.

References: Conization

question_text: An 80-year-old female who has never taken estrogen, develops pink vaginal discharge. An endometrial biopsy shows an adenocarcinoma of the endometrium. Papanicolaou smear is negative. Of the following, what is the most important indicator of prognosis?
explanation:
Prognostic factors in endometrial adenocarcinoma

  • Most important prognostic factor is lymph node metastasis
  • Age at diagnosis (older the patient poorer the prognosis).
  • Stage of the disease.
  • Histologic type (endometrioid adenocarcinoma have good prognosis, clear cell carcinoma have poor prognosis).
  • Histologic grade.
  • Myometrial penetration (Increasing depth of invasion is associated with increasing likelihood of extrauterine spread and recurrence).
  • Extension to cervixes Involvement of cervix, isthmus or both is associated with increased risk of extrauterine disease and LN metastasis.
  • Tumor size (> 2 cm–more lymph node metastasis).
  • Hormone receptor status (receptor positive–better prognosis).
  • Ploidy status: Aneuploid have got better prognosis compared to diploid tumors.
  • Oncogene expression: HER: 2/neu, k-ras poor prognosis.

Role of Peritoneal cytology on prognosis is controversial.

Reference: Novak 15th/ed pg 1266–8

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding the evaluation of endometrial hyperplasia?
option_a: Endometrial thickness <5 mm always rules out hyperplasia
option_b: Endometrial aspiration is the gold standard for diagnosis
option_c: Gold standard is hysteroscopy followed by biopsy
option_d: Endometrial hyperplasia never progresses to carcinoma
explanation:
Explanation:

The evaluation of endometrial hyperplasia ultimately requires histological confirmation, since imaging alone cannot reliably differentiate between benign thickening, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.

The gold standard method is hysteroscopy followed by endometrial biopsy (or curettage).

  • Hysteroscopy allows direct visualization of the uterine cavity and any focal lesions such as polyps or localized areas of abnormal endometrium.
  • Tissue can then be obtained under direct guidance, ensuring more accurate sampling compared with blind methods.
  • This approach not only increases diagnostic accuracy for endometrial hyperplasia, but also helps detect coexisting carcinoma, which may be missed by less targeted methods.

Explanation for other Options:

Endometrial thickness <5 mm always rules out hyperplasia (Option A): Ultrasound cannot definitively exclude hyperplasia; thickness varies with the menstrual cycle in premenopausal women, and ≤4 mm in postmenopausal women rules out cancer with high NPV but not hyperplasia in all cases.

Endometrial aspiration is the gold standard for diagnosis (Option B): While Pipelle biopsy is simple, safe, and sensitive, it can miss focal lesions due to blind sampling, so it is not considered the gold standard.

Endometrial hyperplasia never progresses to carcinoma (Option D): Hyperplasia with atypia (EIN) has a significant risk of progression to or coexistence with carcinoma.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560693/

explanation:
Tamoxifen causes a two- to threefold higher risk of developing endometrial cancer by its modest "unopposed" estrogenic effect on the endometrium.

The increased risk of endometrial cancer affects postmenopausal women almost exclusively, and cancer rates increase linearly with the duration and cumulative dose of tamoxifen therapy.

Accordingly, women taking tamoxifen are counseled regarding this endometrial risk and should report vaginal spotting, bleeding, or discharge. That said, unless a tamoxifen-treated patient has such symptoms or is identified to be at otherwise high risk for endometrial cancer, routine endometrial surveillance does not increase early detection rates.

Risk Factor

Endometrial cancer occurs as a result of unopposed estrogen exposure in body.

Premalignant Lesions of Endometrium are:

Complex hyperplasia: Endometrium is thicker. The glands are crowded and arranged back to back with reduced stroma. Most glands have irregular outlines. There are papillary processes and intraluminal bridges within the glands. Epithelial pseudostratification is present.

Atypical hyperplasia: The endometrial glands have cytologic atypia. The gland outlines are of complex hyperplasia in type. The nuclei of the glands show enlargement, irregular size and shape, hyperchromasia and coarse chromatin.

Carcinoma-in-situ: Commonly describes a lesion with severe cytologic as well as architectural abnormalities of the glands.

question_text: Which of the following investigations should be conducted in a 7-month-old child who has a hemoglobin level of 6.3, a history of recurrent blood transfusions, an MCV of 70 fl, normal MCH, normal MCHC, and a peripheral smear indicating a hypochromic microcytic image?
explanation:
Explanation:

In an infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia requiring transfusions, the most likely diagnosis is beta-thalassemia major. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the definitive test, which would show a significant increase in Hemoglobin F (HbF) and possibly Hemoglobin A2 (HbA2), with absent or reduced Hemoglobin A (HbA).

Explanation of other options:

Serum iron (Option A): Would be normal or elevated in thalassemia (due to transfusions), but low in iron deficiency. It is not the definitive test.

Direct coomb's test (Option B): Used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Osmotic fragility test (Option C): Used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, which causes a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, not microcytic.

Key Takeaways:

  • Thalassemia major presents in infancy with severe transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia.
  • Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the key diagnostic test.

question_text: The risk of endometrial cancer is highest with which of the following histological patterns of endometrial hyperplasia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Endometrial hyperplasia is a condition involving the proliferation of endometrial glands, leading to a greater gland-to-stroma ratio than is found in the normal endometrium. The presence of nuclear atypia is the most significant predictor of progression to endometrial carcinoma. Complex hyperplasia with atypia (also known as endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia) involves both architectural complexity (crowded, branching glands) and significant cytological atypia, and it carries the highest risk of malignant transformation.

Explanation of Other Options:

(A) Simple hyperplasia without atypia: This has the lowest risk of progression to cancer, estimated at around 1%.

(B) Simple hyperplasia with atypia: The presence of atypia increases the risk, but the simple glandular structure makes it less likely to progress than complex atypical hyperplasia. The risk is estimated to be around 8%.

(C) Complex hyperplasia without atypia: While there is glandular complexity, the absence of cellular atypia means a lower risk of progression compared to atypical forms. The risk is estimated to be around 3%.


Key Takeaway:

The classification of endometrial hyperplasia is critical for assessing the risk of progression to endometrial cancer. The presence of cytological atypia is the most important prognostic factor. Complex atypical hyperplasia has the highest malignant potential, with a progression risk reported to be as high as 29-30%.

A rare, inherited metabolic disease in which a glycolipid, ceramide trihexoside, accumulates in blood vessels, as well as in numerous tissues and organs. question_text: Which of the following is present in labia minora
explanation:
Structurally, the labia minora are composed of connective tissue with many small vessels, elastin fibers, but very little smooth muscle. Nerve fibers are numerous.

The epithelia of the labia minora differ by location. Thinly keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the outer surface of each labium. question_text: A patient is having discharge per vagina, evaluated and on endocervical biopsy Chlamydia was found. Appropriate treatment would be:
explanation:
Management of Chlamydia

Uncomplicated chlamydia can be treated with Tetracycline (500 mg 4 times daily), Doxycycline (1000 mg twice daily), Erythromycin (500 mg 4 times daily), Fluoroquinolone -ofloxacin 300 mg twice daily, or Azithromycin -single dose - 1 g

Advantages of Azithromycin are

  • Single dose regimen – 1 g stat dose (It is as effective as 7 days of doxycycline treatment).
  • Better patient compliance.
  • Fewer gastrointestinal side effects.

Contact tracing:

  • Patients with asymptomatic infection and their sex partners form a major burden of chlamydial infection so, contact tracing should always be done (wherever possible).

Reference: William's Gynae 1st/ed p 66;

question_text: According to Ferriman Gallwey scoring system-hirsutism is diagnosed when score is more than:
explanation:
Ferriman-Gallwey scoring is a scoring method for detecting hirsutism. In the original system—hair growth at 11 sites was noted-

  1. Upper lip
  2. Chin
  3. Chest
  4. Upper back
  5. Lower back
  6. Upper abdomen
  7. Lower abdomen
  8. Upper arms
  9. Forearms
  10. Thighs
  11. Legs

In the modified method—2 sites were deleted-forearms and legs. Thus in the modified scoring system–hair growth is seen at 9 sites. In each of the nine locations-a score between 0-4 is given depending on growth of terminal hair Maximum score= 36

In causasian women a score of 8 or higher is regarded as indicative of androgen excess.

question_text: Bonney's test demonstrates:
explanation:
Bonney’s test is performed in the clinical evaluation of SUI. In the Bonney’s test, two fingers are placed in the vagina at the UV junction on either side of the urethra and the bladder neck is elevated.

On straining or coughing, leakage of urine indicates a positive test.

A positive test indicates that the SUI is due to bladder neck descent and urethral hypermobility and can be corrected by bladder neck suspension surgeries.

A negative test i.e. leakage of urine-means SUI is due to intrinsic urethral sphincteric deficiency and results of performing bladder neck suspension surgery will not be good.

What is the underlying reason for the lack of fructose in seminal fluid?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fructose, which provides a vital energy source for sperm, is produced by the seminal vesicles and is present in the semen. Therefore, any obstruction of the ejaculatory duct or absence of seminal vesicles results in a decreased concentration of fructose in the semen.

Lack of fructose can be seen in:

  • Congenital absence of seminal vesicle
  • Inflammation or Obstruction of ejaculatory duct, vas deferens or seminal vesicle
  • Congenital absence of the vas deferens

The Pap stain is a polychromatic stain developed by George Papanicolaou that leverages the use of five different basic and acidic dyes (hematoxylin, orange green 6, eosin Y, light green SF, and Bismarck brown Y) to differentially stain various cell components
